pointillism.c: Pointillism Neoimpressionism Ne`o*im*pres"sion*ism (nē`o*ĭm*prĕsh"ŭn*ĭz'm), n. (Painting) A theory or practice which is a further development, on more rigorously scientific lines, of the theory and practice of Impressionism, originated by George Seurat (1859-91), and carried on by Paul Signac (1863- -) and others. Its method is marked by the laying of pure primary colors in minute dots upon a white ground, any given line being produced by a variation in the proportionate quantity of the primary colors employed. This method is also known as Pointillism (stippling).

p.c: P P (pē), the sixteenth letter of the English alphabet, is a nonvocal consonant whose form and value come from the Latin, into which language the letter was brought, through the ancient Greek, from the Phœnician, its probable origin being Egyptian. Etymologically P is most closely related to b, f, and v; as hobble, hopple; father, paternal; recipient, receive. See B, F, and M.

pa.c: Pa Pa (pä), n. A shortened form of Papa.

paage.c: Paage Pa"age (pā"aj; 48), n. [OF. paage, paiage, F. péage, fr. (assumed) LL. pedaticum, fr. L. pes, pedis, foot. See Pedage, Pedal.] (O. Eng. Law) A toll for passage over another person's grounds. [Written also peage and pedage.] Burke.

paard.c: Paard ‖Paard (pärd), n. [D., a horse.] The zebra. [S. Africa]

paas.c: Paas Paas (päs), n. [D. paash. See Pasch.] The Easter festival. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

pabular.c: pabular pab"u*lar (?), a. [L. pabularis.] Of, pertaining to, or fit for, pabulum or food; affording food.

pabulation.c: Pabulation Pab`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. pabulatio, fr. pabulari to feed, fr. pabulum food. See Pabulum.]

pabulous.c: Pabulous Pab"u*lous (?), a. [L. pabulosus.] Affording pabulum, or food; alimental. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

pabulum.c: pabulum pab"u*lum (?), n. [L., akin to pascere to pasture. See Pastor.] 1. The means of nutriment to animals or plants; food; nourishment. [wns=1]

pac.c: Pac Pac (păk), n. A kind of moccasin, having the edges of the sole turned up and sewed to the upper. Knight.

paca.c: paca pa"ca (Pg. pä"kȧ; E. pā"kȧ), n. [Pg., from the native name.] 1. (Zool.) A large burrowing South American rodent (Agouti paca syn. Cuniculus paca, formerly Cœlogenys paca), having blackish brown fur, with four parallel rows of white spots along its sides; the spotted cavy. It is closely allied to the agouti and the Guinea pig and is highly esteemed as food.

pacable.c: Pacable Pa"ca*ble (?), a. [L. pacare to pacify.] Placable. [R.] Coleridge.

pacane.c: Pacane Pa*cane" (?), n. (Bot.) A species of hickory. See Pecan.

pacate.c: pacate pa"cate (pā"kat), a. [L. pacatus, p. p. of pacare to pacify, fr. pax, pacis, peace. See Pay to requite, Peace.] Appeased; pacified; placated; tranquil. [R.]

pacation.c: Pacation Pa*ca"tion (?), n. [L. pacatio.] The act of pacifying; a peacemaking. Coleridge.

pace.c: pace pace (pās), n. [OE. pas, F. pas, from L. passus a step, pace, orig., a stretching out of the feet in walking; cf. pandere, passum, to spread, stretch; perh. akin to E. patent. Cf. Pas, Pass.] 1. A single movement from one foot to the other in walking; a step.

Pace Pace (pās), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Paced (pāst); p. pr. & vb. n. Pacing (pā"sĭng).] 1. To go; to walk; specifically, to move with regular or measured steps. “I paced on slowly.” Pope. “With speed so pace.” Shak.
Pace Pace, v. t. 1. To walk over with measured tread; to move slowly over or upon; as, the guard paces his round. “Pacing light the velvet plain.” T. Warton.

paced.c: Paced Paced (?), a. Having, or trained in, [such] a pace or gait; trained; -- used in composition; as, slow-paced; a thorough-paced villain.

pacer.c: pacer pa"cer (?), n. One who, or that which, paces.

pacha.c: Pacha Pa*cha" (?), n. [F.] A civil or military authority in Turkey or Egypt; same as Pasha.

pachacamac.c: Pachacamac ‖Pa`cha*ca*mac" (?), prop. n. A divinity worshiped by the ancient Peruvians as the creator of the universe.

pachak.c: Pachak ‖Pa*chak" (?), n. (Bot.) The fragrant roots of the Saussurea Costus, exported from India to China, and used for burning as incense. It is supposed to be the costus of the ancients. [Written also putchuck.]

parchisi.c: Parchisi Parchesi Pachisi ‖Pa*chi"si (?), Par*che"si, Par*chi"si (?), n. [Hind., fr. pachis twenty-five, the highest throw in the game.] 1. A game, somewhat resembling backgammon, originating in India.

pachometer.c: pachometer pa*chom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. pa`chos thickness + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring thickness, as of the glass of a mirror, or of paper; a pachymeter.

pachonta.c: pachonta ‖pa*chon"ta (?), n. (Bot.) A substance resembling gutta-percha, and used to adulterate it, obtained from the East Indian tree Isonandra acuminata.

pachuca.c: pachuca tank pa*chu"ca tank (?). (Metallurgy) A high and narrow tank, with a central cylinder for the introduction of compressed air, used in the agitation and settling of pulp (pulverized ore and water) during treatment by the cyanide process; -- so named because, though originally devised in New Zealand, it was first practically introduced in Pachuca, Mexico.

pachy.c: Pachy- Pach"y- (?). [Gr. pachy`s thick.] A combining form meaning thick; as, pachyderm, pachydactyl.

pachycarpous.c: Pachycarpous Pach`y*car"pous (?), a. [Pachy- + Gr. karpo`s fruit.] (Bot.) Having the pericarp thick.

pachydactyl.c: Pachydactyl Pach`y*dac"tyl (?), n. [Pachy- + dactyl.] (Zool.) A bird or other animal having thick toes.

pachyderm.c: pachyderm pach"y*derm (păk"ĭ*dẽrm), n. [Cf. F. pachyderme.] (Zool.) Any of various nonruminant hoofed mammals having very thick skin, including the elephant, rhinoceros, and hippopotamus, one of the Pachydermata.

pachydermal.c: pachydermal pach`y*der"mal (păk"ĭ*dẽr"mail), a. (Zool.) Of or relating to the pachyderms; as, pachydermal dentition.

pachydermata.c: Pachydermata ‖Pach`y*der"ma*ta (păk`ĭ*dẽr"mȧ*tȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. pachy`dermos thick-skinned; pachy`s thick + de`rma skin.] (Zool.) A group of hoofed mammals distinguished for the thickness of their skins, including the elephant, hippopotamus, rhinoceros, tapir, horse, and hog; the pachyderms. It is now considered an artificial group.

pachydermatous.c: Pachydermatous Pach`y*der"ma*tous (?), a. 1. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the pachyderms.

pachydermoid.c: Pachydermoid Pach`y*der"moid (?), a. [Pachyderm + -oid.] (Zool.) Related to the pachyderms.

pachyglossal.c: Pachyglossal Pach`y*glos"sal (păk`ĭ*glŏs"sail), a. [Pachy- + Gr. glw^ssa tongue.] (Zool.) Having a thick tongue; -- applied to a group of lizards (Pachyglossæ), including the iguanas and agamas.

pachymeningitis.c: Pachymeningitis Pach`y*men`in*gi"tis (?), n. [Pachy- + meningitis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the dura mater or outer membrane of the brain.

pachyote.c: Pachyote Pach"y*ote (?), n. [Pachy- + Gr. o'y^s, 'wto`s, ear.] (Zool.) One of a family of bats, including those which have thick external ears.

pacifiable.c: pacifiable pac"i*fi`a*ble (?), a. Capable of being pacified or appeased; placable.

pacific.c: pacific pa*cif"ic (?), a. [L. pacificus: cf. F. pacifique. See Pacify.] Of or pertaining to peace; of a peaceful character; not warlike; not quarrelsome; as, a pacific nature or condition. [wns=3]

pacifical.c: pacifical pa*cif"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to peace; pacific. [R.] Sir H. Wotton. -- Pa*cif"ic*al*ly, adv. [R.]

pacification.c: Pacification Pa*cif`i*ca"tion (?), n. [L. pacificatio: cf. F. pacification. See Pacify.] The act or process of pacifying, or of making peace between parties at variance; reconciliation. “An embassy of pacification.” Bacon.

pacificator.c: Pacificator Pa*cif"i*ca`tor (?), n. [L.] One who, or that which, pacifies; a peacemaker. Bacon.

pacificatory.c: Pacificatory Pa*cif"i*ca*to*ry (?), a. [L. pacificatorius.] Tending to make peace; conciliatory. Barrow.

pacifico.c: Pacifico ‖Pa*ci"fi*co (?), n. [Sp. See Pacific.] A peaceful person; -- applied specif. by the Spaniards to the natives in Cuba and the Philippine Islands who did not oppose the Spanish arms.

pacifier.c: Pacifier Pac"i*fi`er (?), n. 1. One who or that which pacifies.

pacify.c: Pacify Pac"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pacified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pacifying (?).] [F. pacifier, L. pacificare; pax, pacis, peace + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Peace, and -fy.] To make to be at peace; to appease; to calm; to still; to quiet; to allay the agitation, excitement, or resentment of; to tranquillize; as, to pacify a man when angry; to pacify pride, appetite, or importunity. “Pray ye, pacify yourself.” Shak.

pacinian.c: Pacinian Pa*cin"i*an (?), a. (Anat.) Of, pertaining to, or discovered by, Filippo Pacini (1812-1883), an Italian physician of the 19th century.

pack.c: Pack Pack (păk), n. [Cf. Pact.] A pact. [Obs.] Daniel.
Pack Pack, n. [Akin to D. pak, G. pack, Dan. pakke, Sw. packa, Icel. pakki, Gael. & Ir. pac, Arm. pak. Cf. Packet.]

Pack Pack (păk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Packed (păkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Packing.] [Akin to D. pakken, G. packen, Dan. pakke, Sw. packa, Icel. pakka. See Pack, n.] 1. To make a pack of; to arrange closely and securely in a pack; hence, to place and arrange compactly as in a pack; to press into close order or narrow compass; as, to pack goods in a box; to pack fish.
Pack Pack, v. i. 1. To make up packs, bales, or bundles; to stow articles securely for transportation.
Pack horse Pack horse. See under 2d Pack.
Pack thread Pack saddle { Pack saddle, Pack thread. } See under 2d Pack.

package.c: Package Pack"age (păk"aj; 48), n. 1. Act or process of packing.

packer.c: packer pack"er (păk"ẽr), n. 1. A person whose business is to pack things; especially, one who packs food for preservation or for the market; as, a pork packer.

packet.c: packet pack"et (păk"ĕt), n. [F. paquet, dim. fr. LL. paccus, from the same source as E. pack. See Pack.]
Packet Pack"et, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Packeted; p. pr. & vb. n. Packeting.] 1. To make up into a packet or bundle.
Packet Pack"et, v. i. To ply with a packet or dispatch boat.

packfong.c: Packfong Pack"fong` (păk"fŏng`), n. [Chin. peh tung.] (Metal.) A Chinese alloy of nickel, zinc, and copper, resembling German silver.

packhouse.c: Packhouse Pack"house` (păk"hous`), n. Warehouse for storing goods.

packing.c: Packing Pack"ing, n. 1. The act or process of one who packs.

packman.c: Packman Pack"man (?), n.; pl. Packmen (?). One who bears a pack; a peddler.

packway.c: Packway Pack"way` (păk"wā`), n. A path, as over mountains, followed by pack animals.

pacos.c: Pacos Paco { Pa"co (?), Pa"cos (?), } n. [Sp. paco, fr. Peruv. paco. Cf. Alpaca.] 1. (Zool.) Same as Alpaca.

pact.c: pact pact (păkt), n. [L. pactum, fr. paciscere to make a bargain or contract, fr. pacere to settle, or agree upon; cf. pangere to fasten, Gr. phgny`nai, Skr. pāça bond, and E. fang: cf. F. pacte. Cf. Peace, Fadge, v.] An agreement; a league; a compact; a covenant. Bacon.

paction.c: Paction Pac"tion (?), n. [L. pactio: cf. F. paction. See Pact.] An agreement; a compact; a bargain. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

pactional.c: Pactional Pac"tion*al (?), a. Of the nature of, or by means of, a paction. Bp. Sanderson.

pactitious.c: Pactitious Pac*ti"tious (?), a. [L. pactitius, pacticius.] Setted by a pact, or agreement. [R.] Johnson.

pactolian.c: Pactolian Pac*to"li*an (?), a. Pertaining to the Pactolus, a river in ancient Lydia famous for its golden sands.

pacu.c: Pacu Pa"cu (?), n. (Zool.) A South American fresh-water fish (Myletes pacu), of the family Characinidæ. It is highly esteemed as food.

pad.c: pad pad (păd), n. [D. pad. √21. See Path.] 1. A footpath; a road. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
Pad Pad, v. t. To travel upon foot; to tread. [Obs.]
Pad Pad, v. i. 1. To travel heavily or slowly. Bunyan.
Pad Pad, n. [Perh. akin to pod.] 1. A soft, or small, cushion; a mass of anything soft; stuffing.
Pad Pad, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Padded; p. pr. & vb. n. Padding.] 1. To stuff; to furnish with a pad or padding.
Pad elephant Pad elephant. An elephant that is furnished with a pad for carrying burdens instead of with a howdah for carrying passengers.

padar.c: Padar Pad"ar (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] Groats; coarse flour or meal. [Obs.] Sir. H. Wotton.

padder.c: Padder Pad"der (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, pads.

padding.c: Padding Pad"ding, n. 1. The act or process of making a pad or of inserting stuffing.

paddle.c: Paddle Pad"dle (?), v. i. [Prob. for pattle, and a dim. of pat, v.; cf. also E. pad to tread, Prov. G. paddeln, padden, to walk with short steps, to paddle, G. patschen to splash, dash, dabble, F. patouiller to dabble, splash, fr. patte a paw. √21.] 1. To use the hands or fingers in toying; to make caressing strokes. [Obs.] Shak.
Paddle Pad"dle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Paddled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Paddling (?)] 1. To pat or stroke amorously, or gently. [Obsolescent]
Paddle Pad"dle, n. [See Paddle, v. i.] 1. An implement with a broad blade, which is used without a fixed fulcrum in propelling and steering canoes and boats.
paddle box paddlebox paddlebox, paddle box n. 1. a wooden covering for the upper part of the paddle wheel of a steam vessel.

paddlefish.c: Paddlefish Pad"dle*fish` (?), n. (Zool) A large ganoid fish (Polyodon spathula) found in the rivers of the Mississippi Valley. It has a long spatula-shaped snout. Called also duck-billed cat, and spoonbill sturgeon.

paddler.c: Paddler Pad"dler (?), n. One who, or that which, paddles.

paddlewood.c: Paddlewood Pad"dle*wood` (?), n. (Bot.) The light elastic wood of the Aspidosperma excelsum, a tree of Guiana having a fluted trunk readily split into planks.

paddock.c: Paddock Pad"dock (?), n. [OE. padde toad, frog + -ock; akin to D. pad, padde, toad, Icel. & Sw. padda, Dan. padde.] (Zool.) A toad or frog. Wyclif. “Loathed paddocks.” Spenser
Paddock Pad"dock, n. [Corrupted fr. parrock. See Parrock.]

paddy.c: Paddy Pad"dy (?), a. [Prov. E. paddy worm-eaten.] Low; mean; boorish; vagabond. “Such pady persons.” Digges (1585). “The paddy persons.” Motley.
Paddy Pad"dy, n.; pl. Paddies (#). [Corrupted fr. St. Patrick, the tutelar saint of Ireland.] A jocose or contemptuous name for an Irishman; -- usually considered offensive. [Obsolescent]
Paddy Pad"dy, n. [Either fr. Canarese bhatta or Malay pādī.] (Bot.) Unhusked rice; -- commonly so called in the East Indies.

padelion.c: Padelion Pad`e*li"on (?), n. [F. pas de lion lion's foot.] (Bot.) A plant with pedately lobed leaves; the lady's mantle.

padella.c: Padella ‖Pa*del"la (?), n. [It., prop., a pan, a friing pan, fr. L. patella a pan.] A large cup or deep saucer, containing fatty matter in which a wick is placed, -- used for public illuminations, as at St. Peter's, in Rome. Called also padelle.

pademelon.c: pademelon pad`e*mel"on n. (Zool.) Any of several small reddish-brown wallabies of scrubby areas of Australia and New Guinea, especially those belonging to the genus Thylogale; a paddymelon. See Wallaby

padge.c: Padge Padge, n. (Zool.) The barn owl; -- called also pudge, and pudge owl. [Prov. Eng.]

padishah.c: Padishah ‖Pa`di*shah" (?), n. [Per. pādishāh. Cf. Pasha.] Chief ruler; monarch; sovereign; -- a title of the Sultan of Turkey, and of the Shah of Persia.

padlock.c: Padlock Pad"lock` (?), n. [Perh. orig., a lock for a pad gate, or a gate opening to a path, or perh., a lock for a basket or pannier, and from Prov. E. pad a pannier. Cf. Pad a path, Paddler.] 1. A portable lock with a bow which is usually jointed or pivoted at one end so that it can be opened, the other end being fastened by the bolt, -- used for fastening by passing the bow through a staple over a hasp or through the links of a chain, etc.
Padlock Pad"lock`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Padlocked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Padlocking.] To fasten with, or as with, a padlock; to stop; to shut; to confine as by a padlock. Milton. Tennyson.

padnag.c: Padnag Pad"nag` (?), n. [1st pad + nag.] An ambling nag. “An easy padnag.” Macaulay.

padow.c: Padow Pad"ow (?), n. (Zool.) A paddock, or toad.

padre.c: Padre ‖Pa"dre (pä"drā), n.; pl. Sp. & Pg. Padres (pä"drās); It. Padri (pä"drē). [Sp., Pg., & It., fr. L. pater father. See Father.] 1. A Christian priest or monk; used as a term of address for priests in some churches (especially Roman or Orthodox Catholic in Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Spanish America); -- also used in the American military.

padrone.c: Padrone ‖Pa*dro"ne (?), n.; pl. It. Padroni (#), E. Padrones. [It. See Patron.] 1. A patron; a protector.

paduasoy.c: Paduasoy Pad`u*a*soy" (?), n. [From Padua, in Italy + F. soie silk; or cf. F. pou-de-soie.] A rich and heavy silk stuff. [Written also padesoy.]

paducahs.c: Paducahs Pa*du"cahs (pȧ*dū"kȧz), n. pl.; sing. Paducah (-kȧ). (Ethnol.) See Comanches.

paean.c: Paean Pæ"an (pē`ain), n. [L. paean, Gr. paia`n, fr. Paia`n the physician of the gods, later, Apollo. Cf. Pæon, Peony.] [Written also pean.] 1. An ancient Greek hymn in honor of Apollo as a healing deity, and, later, a song addressed to other deities.

paedogenesis.c: paedogenesis pæ`do*gen"esis (pē`do*jĕn"e*sĭs), n. [Gr. pai^s, paido`s, child + E. genesis.] (Zool.) Reproduction by young or larval animals.

paedogenetic.c: paedogenetic pæ`do*ge*net"ic (pē`do*je*nĕt"ĭk), a. (Zool.) Producing young while in the immature or larval state; -- said of certain insects, etc.

paeon.c: paeon pæ"on (pē"ŏn), n. [L. paeon, Gr. paiw`n a solemn song, also, a pæon, equiv. to paia`n. See Pæan.] (Anc. Poet.) A foot of four syllables, one long and three short, admitting of four combinations, according to the place of the long syllable. [Written also, less correctly, pæan.]

paeonine.c: paeonine pæ"o*nine (pē"o*nĭn), n. (Chem.) An artifical red nitrogenous dyestuff, called also red coralline.

paeony.c: Paeony paeony pae"o*ny, Pæ"o*ny (pē"o*ny̆), n. (Bot.) Any of numerous plants widely cultivated for their showy single or double red or pink or white flowers; the Peony.

pagan.c: Pagan Pa"gan (pā"gain), n. [L. paganus a countryman, peasant, villager, a pagan, fr. paganus of or pertaining to the country, rustic, also, pagan, fr. pagus a district, canton, the country, perh. orig., a district with fixed boundaries: cf. pangere to fasten. Cf. Painim, Peasant, and Pact, also Heathen.] One who worships false gods; an idolater; a heathen; one who is neither a Christian, a Mohammedan, nor a Jew.

Pagan Pa"gan, a. [L. paganus of or pertaining to the country, pagan. See Pagan, n.] Of or pertaining to pagans; relating to the worship or the worshipers of false goods; heathen; idolatrous, as, pagan tribes or superstitions.

pagandom.c: Pagandom Pa"gan*dom (-dŭm), n. The pagan lands; pagans, collectively; paganism. [R.]

paganical.c: Paganical Paganic { Pa*gan"ic (pȧ*găn"ĭk), Pa*gan"ic*al (-ĭ*kail), } a. Of or pertaining to pagans or paganism; heathenish; paganish. [R.] “The paganic fables of the goods.” Cudworth. -- Pa*gan"ic*al*ly, adv. [R.]

paganish.c: Paganish Pa"gan*ish (pā"gain*ĭsh), a. Of or pertaining to pagans; heathenish. “The old paganish idolatry.” Sharp

paganism.c: Paganism Pa"gan*ism (-ĭz'm), n. [L. paganismus: cf. F. paganisme. See Pagan, and cf. Painim.] The state of being pagan; pagan characteristics; esp., the worship of idols or false gods, or the system of religious opinions and worship maintained by pagans; heathenism.

paganity.c: Paganity Pa*gan"i*ty (pȧ*găn"ĭ*ty̆), n. [L. Paganitas.] The state of being a pagan; paganism. [R.] Cudworth.

paganize.c: Paganize Pa"gan*ize (pā"gain*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Paganized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Paganizing (?).] To render pagan or heathenish; to convert to paganism. Hallywell.
Paganize Pa"gan*ize, v. i. To behave like pagans. Milton.

paganly.c: Paganly Pa"gan*ly, adv. In a pagan manner. Dr. H. More.

page.c: Page Page (pāj), n. [F., fr. It. paggio, LL. pagius, fr. Gr. paidi`on, dim. of pai^s, paido`s, a boy, servant; perh. akin to L. puer. Cf. Pedagogue, Puerile.] 1. A serving boy; formerly, a youth attending a person of high degree, especially at courts, as a position of honor and education; now commonly, in England, a youth employed for doing errands, waiting on the door, and similar service in households; in the United States, a boy or girl employed to wait upon the members of a legislative body. Prior to 1960 only boys served as pages in the United States Congress
page page, v. t. 1. To attend (one) as a page. [Obs.] Shak.
Page Page, n. [F., fr. L. pagina; prob. akin to pagere, pangere, to fasten, fix, make, the pages or leaves being fastened together. Cf. Pact, Pageant, Pagination.]
Page Page, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Paged (pājd); p. pr. & vb. n. Paging (pā"jĭng).] To mark or number the pages of, as a book or manuscript; to furnish with folios.

pageant.c: Pageant Pag"eant (păj"eint or pā"jeint; 277), n. [OE. pagent, pagen, originally, a movable scaffold or stage, hence, what was exhibited on it, fr. LL. pagina, akin to pangere to fasten; cf. L. pagina page, leaf, slab, compaginare to join together, compages a joining together, structure. See Pact, Page of a book.]
Pageant Pag"eant, a. Of the nature of a pageant; spectacular. “Pageant pomp.” Dryden.
Pageant Pag"eant, v. t. To exhibit in show; to represent; to mimic. [R.] “He pageants us.” Shak.

pageantry.c: Pageantry Pag"eant*ry (-ry̆), n. Scenic shows or spectacles, taken collectively; spectacular quality; splendor.

pagehood.c: Pagehood Page"hood (?), n. The state of being a page.

pagina.c: Pagina ‖Pag"i*na (?), n.; pl. Paginæ (#). [L.] (Bot.) The surface of a leaf or of a flattened thallus.

paginal.c: Paginal Pag"i*nal (?), a. [L. paginalis.] Consisting of pages. “Paginal books.” Sir T. Browne.

pagination.c: Pagination Pag`i*na"tion (păj`ĭ*nā"shŭn), n. The act or process of paging a book; also, the characters used in numbering the pages; page number. Lowndes.

paging.c: Paging Pa"ging (?), n. The marking or numbering of the pages of a book.

pagod.c: Pagod Pa"god (?), n. [Cf. F. pagode. See Pagoda.] 1. A pagoda. [R.] “Or some queer pagod.” Pope.

pagoda.c: Pagoda Pa*go"da (?), n. [Pg. pagoda, pagode, fr. Hind. & Per. but-kadah a house of idols, or abode of God; Per. but an idol + kadah a house, a temple.] 1. A term by which Europeans designate religious temples and tower-like buildings of the Hindoos and Buddhists of India, Farther India, China, and Japan, -- usually but not always, devoted to idol worship.
Pagoda sleeve Pa*go"da sleeve. (Costume) A funnel-shaped sleeve arranged to show the sleeve lining and an inner sleeve.

pagodite.c: Pagodite Pa*go"dite (?), n. (Min.) Agalmatolite; -- so called because sometimes carved by the Chinese into the form of pagodas. See Agalmatolite.

paguma.c: Paguma ‖Pa*gu"ma (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of several species of East Indian viverrine mammals of the genus Paguma. They resemble a weasel in form.

pagurian.c: Pagurian Pa*gu"ri*an (?), n. [L. pagurus a kind of crab, Gr. pa`goyros.] (Zool.) Any one of a tribe of anomuran crustaceans, of which Pagurus is a type; the hermit crab. See Hermit crab, under Hermit.

pah.c: Pah Pah (?), interj. An exclamation expressing disgust or contempt. See Bah.
Pah ‖Pah (?), n. [From native name.] A kind of stockaded intrenchment. [New Zealand.] Farrow.

pahi.c: Pahi Pa"hi (?), n. (Naut.) A large war canoe of the Society Islands.

pahlevi.c: Pahlevi Pahlavi Pah"la*vi, Pah"le*vi (?), n. 1. The language of Sassanian Persia. See Pehlevi.

pahoehoe.c: Pahoehoe ‖Pa*ho"e*ho`e (?), n. (Min.) A name given in Hawaii (formerly the Sandwich Islands) to lava having a relatively smooth or billowing surface, in distinction from the rough-surfaced lava, called aa.

paid.c: Paid Paid (?), imp., p. p., & a. from Pay. 1. Receiving pay; compensated; hired; as, a paid attorney.

paideutics.c: paideutics pai*deu"tics (pa*dū"tĭks), n. [Gr. paideytikh`, fr. paidey`ein to teach, fr. pai^s, paido`s, a boy.] The science or art of teaching.

paigle.c: Paigle Pai"gle (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Bot.) A species of Primula, either the cowslip or the primrose. [Written also pagle, pagil, peagle, and pygil.]

pail.c: Pail Pail (pāl), n. [OE. paile, AS. pægel a wine vessel, a pail, akin to D. & G. pegel a watermark, a gauge rod, a measure of wine, Dan. pægel half a pint.] A vessel of wood or tin, etc., usually cylindrical and having a bail, -- used esp. for carrying liquids, as water or milk, etc.; a bucket. It may, or may not, have a cover. Shak.

pailful.c: Pailful Pail"ful (?), n.; pl. Pailfuls (?). The quantity that a pail will hold. “By pailfuls.” Shak.

paillasse.c: Paillasse Pail*lasse" (?; F.?), n. [F., fr. paille straw. See Pallet a bed.] An under bed or mattress of straw. [Written also palliasse.]

paillon.c: Paillon ‖Pail`lon" (?), n.; pl. -lions (#). [F., fr. paille straw.] A thin leaf of metal, as for use in gilding or enameling, or to show through a translucent medium.

pain.c: pain pain (pān), n. [OE. peine, F. peine, fr. L. poena, penalty, punishment, torment, pain; akin to Gr. poinh` penalty. Cf. Penal, Pine to languish, Punish.] 1. Punishment suffered or denounced; suffering or evil inflicted as a punishment for crime, or connected with the commission of a crime; penalty. Chaucer.

Pain Pain, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pained (pānd); p. pr. & vb. n. Paining.] [OE. peinen, OF. pener, F. peiner to fatigue. See Pain, n.] 1. To inflict suffering upon as a penalty; to punish. [Obs.] Wyclif (Acts xxii. 5).

painable.c: Painable Pain"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. pénible.] Causing pain; painful. [Obs.]

painful.c: Painful Pain"ful (?), a. 1. Full of pain; causing uneasiness or distress, either physical or mental; afflictive; disquieting; distressing. Addison.

painim.c: Painim Pai"nim (?), n. [OE. painime pagans, paganism, fr. OF. paienisme paganism, LL. paganismus. See Paganism, Pagan.] A pagan; an infidel; -- used also adjectively. [Written also panim and paynim.] Peacham.

painless.c: Painless Pain"less (?), a. Free from pain; without pain. -- Pain"less*ly, adv. -- Pain"less*ness, n.

pains.c: Pains Pains (pānz), n. Labor; toilsome effort; care or trouble taken; -- plural in form, but used with a singular or plural verb, commonly the former.

painstaker.c: Painstaker Pains"tak`er (pānz"tāk`ẽr), n. One who takes pains; one careful and faithful in all work. Gay.

painstaking.c: Painstaking Pains"tak`ing (pānz"tāk`ĭng), a. Careful in doing; diligent; faithful; attentive. “Painstaking men.” Harris.
Painstaking Pains"tak`ing, n. The act of taking pains; carefulness and fidelity in performance. Beau. & Fl.

painsworthy.c: Painsworthy Pains"wor`thy (pānz"wûr`thy̆), a. Worth the pains or care bestowed.

paint.c: Paint Paint (pānt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Painted; p. pr. & vb. n. Painting.] [OE. peinten, fr. F. peint, p. p. of peindre to paint, fr. L. pingere, pictum; cf. Gr. poiki`los many-colored, Skr. piç to adorn. Cf. Depict, Picture, Pigment, Pint.] 1. To cover with coloring matter; to apply paint to; as, to paint a house, a signboard, etc.
Paint Paint, v. t. 1. To practice the art of painting; as, the artist paints well.
Paint Paint, n. 1. (a) A pigment or coloring substance. (b) The same prepared with a vehicle, as oil, water with gum, or the like, for application to a surface.

painted.c: Painted Paint"ed, a. 1. Covered or adorned with paint; portrayed in colors.

painter.c: Painter Paint"er (pānt"ẽr), n. [OE, pantere a noose, snare, F. pantière, LL. panthera, L. panther a hunting net, fr. Gr. panqh`ra; pa^s all + qh`r beast; cf. Ir. painteir a net, gin, snare, Gael. painntear.] (Naut.) A rope at the bow of a boat, used to fasten it to anything. Totten.
Painter Paint"er, n. [Corrupt. of panther.] (Zool.) The panther, or puma. [A form representing an illiterate pronunciation, U. S.] J. F. Cooper.

Painter Paint"er, n. [See 1st Paint.] One whose occupation is to paint; esp.: (a) One who covers buildings, ships, ironwork, and the like, with paint. (b) An artist who represents objects or scenes in color on a flat surface, as canvas, plaster, or the like.

painterly.c: Painterly Paint"er*ly (pānt"ẽr*ly̆), a. Like a painter's work. [Obs.] “A painterly glose of a visage.” Sir P. Sidney.

paintership.c: Paintership Paint"er*ship, n. The state or position of being a painter. [R.] Bp. Gardiner.

painting.c: Painting Paint"ing, n. 1. The act or employment of laying on, or adorning with, paints or colors.

paintless.c: Paintless Paint"less, a. Not capable of being painted or described. “In paintless patience.” Savage.

painture.c: Painture Pain"ture (pān"tur; 135), n. [F. peinture. See Paint, v. t., and cf. Picture.] The art of painting. [Obs.] Chaucer. Dryden.

painty.c: Painty Paint"y (pānt"y̆), a. Unskillfully painted, so that the painter's method of work is too obvious; also, having too much pigment applied to the surface. [Cant]

pair.c: Pair Pair (pâr), n. [F. paire, LL. paria, L. paria, pl. of par pair, fr. par, adj., equal. Cf. Apparel, Par equality, Peer an equal.]
Pair Pair, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Paired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pairing.] 1. To be joined in pairs; to couple; to mate, as for breeding.
Pair Pair, v. t. 1. To unite in couples; to form a pair of; to bring together, as things which belong together, or which complement, or are adapted to one another.
Pair Pair, v. t. [See Impair.] To impair. [Obs.] Spenser.

pairer.c: Pairer Pair"er (pâr"ẽr), n. One who impairs. [Obs.] Wyclif.

pairing.c: Pairing Pair"ing, n. [See Pair, v. i.] 1. The act or process of uniting or arranging in pairs or couples.

pais.c: Pais ‖Pa`is (pȧ`e"), n. [OF. puïs, F. pays, country.] (O. E. Law) The country; the people of the neighborhood.

paisano.c: Paisano ‖Pa`i*sa"no (pä`e*sä"no), n. [Sp., of the country, native.] 1. (Zool.) The chaparral cock; the roadrunner.

pajamas.c: Pajamas Pa*ja"mas (?), n. pl. [Hind. pā-jāma, pāejāma, lit., leg closing.] Originally, in India, loose drawers or trousers, such as those worn, tied about the waist, by Mohammedan men and women; by extension, a similar garment adopted among Europeans, Americans, etc., for wear in the dressing room and during sleep; also, a suit consisting of drawers and a loose upper garment for such wear. [Also spelled pyjamas.]

Pajamas Pyjamas Py*ja"mas (?), or, chiefly U. S., Pa*ja"mas (?), n. pl. A garment, similar to the Oriental pyjama (which see), adopted among Europeans, Americans, and other Occidentals, for wear in the dressing room and during sleep; also, a suit of drawers and blouse for such wear.

pal.c: Pal Pal (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A mate; a partner; esp., an accomplice or confederate. [Slang]

palace.c: Palace Pal"ace (păl"as; 48), n. [OE. palais, F. palais, fr. L. palatium, fr. Palatium, one of the seven hills of Rome, on which Augustus had his residence. Cf. Paladin.]

paladin.c: Paladin Pal"a*din (?), n. [F., fr.It. paladino, fr. L. palatinus an officer of the palace. See Palatine.] A knight-errant; a distinguished champion; as, the paladins of Charlemagne. Sir W. Scott.

palaeotype.c: Palaeotype Pa"læ*o*type (?), n. [Palæo- + -type.] (Phon.) A system of representing all spoken sounds by means of the printing types in common use. Ellis. -- Pa`læ*o*typ"ic*al (#), a. -- Pa`læ*o*typ"ic*al*ly, adv.

palaetiologist.c: Palaetiologist Pa*læ`ti*ol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in palætiology.

palaetiology.c: Palaetiology palaetiology palaetiology, Pa*læ`ti*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Palæo- + ætiology.] The science which explains, by the law of causation, the past condition and changes of the earth; the explanation of past events in terms of scientific causes, such as geological causes. -- Pa*læ`ti*o*log"ic*al (#), a.

palama.c: Palama ‖Pal"a*ma (păl"ȧ*mȧ), n.; pl. Palamæ (păl"ȧ*mē). [NL., fr. Gr. pala`mh the palm.] (Zool.) A membrane extending between the toes of a bird, and uniting them more or less closely together.

palamedeae.c: Palamedeae ‖Pal`a*me"de*æ (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) An order, or suborder, including the kamichi, and allied South American birds; -- called also screamers. In many anatomical characters they are allied to the Anseres, but they externally resemble the wading birds.

palanka.c: Palanka ‖Pa*lan"ka (pȧ*lȧṉ"kȧ), n. [Cf. It., Pg., & Sp. palanca, fr. L. palanga, phalanga a pole, Gr. fa`lagx.] (Mil.) A camp permanently intrenched, attached to Turkish frontier fortresses.

palanquin.c: Palanquin Pal`an*quin" (?), n. [F. palanquin, Pg. palanquim, Javan. palangki, OJavan. palangkan, through Prakrit fr. Skr. paryaṅka, palyaṅka, bed, couch; pari around (akin to E. pref. peri-) + aṅka a hook, flank, probably akin to E. angle fishing tackle. Cf. Palkee.] An inclosed carriage or litter, commonly about eight feet long, four feet wide, and four feet high, borne on the shoulders of men by means of two projecting poles, -- used in India, China, etc., for the conveyance of a single person from place to place. [Written also palankeen.]

palapteryx.c: Palapteryx Pa*lap"te*ryx (?), n. [Paleo- + apteryx.] (Paleon.) A large extinct ostrichlike bird of New Zealand.

palatable.c: Palatable Pal"a*ta*ble (?), a. [From Palate.] Agreeable to the palate or taste; savory; hence, acceptable; pleasing; as, palatable food; palatable advice. Opposite of unpalatable.

palatableness.c: Palatableness Pal"a*ta*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being agreeable to the taste; relish; acceptableness.

palatably.c: Palatably Pal"a*ta*bly, adv. In a palatable manner.

palatal.c: Palatal Pal"a*tal (?), a. [Cf. F. palatal.] 1. Of or pertaining to the palate; palatine; as, the palatal bones.
Palatal Pal"a*tal, n. (Phon.) A sound uttered, or a letter pronounced, by the aid of the palate, as the letters k and y.

palatalize.c: Palatalize Pal"a*tal*ize (?), v. t. (Phon.) To modify, as the tones of the voice, by means of the palate; especially: to pronounce a consonant with the tongue against the palate; as, to palatalize a letter or sound; to palatize. See palatalized.

palate.c: Palate Pal"ate (?), n. [L. palatum: cf. F. palais, Of. also palat.] 1. (Anat.) The roof of the mouth.
Palate Pal"ate, v. t. To perceive by the taste. [Obs.] Shak.

palatial.c: Palatial Pa*la"tial (?), a. [L. palatium palace. See Palace.] Of or pertaining to a palace; suitable for a palace; resembling a palace; royal; magnificent; as, palatial structures. “Palatial style.” A. Drummond.
Palatial Pa*la"tial, a. [From Palate.] (Anat.) Palatal; palatine. [Obs.] Barrow.
Palatial Pa*la"tial, n. A palatal letter. [Obs.] Sir W. Jones.

palatinate.c: palatinate pa*lat"i*nate (?), n. [F. palatinat. See Palatine.] The province or seigniory of a palatine; the dignity of a palatine. Howell.
Palatinate Pa*lat"i*nate (?), v. t. To make a palatinate of. [Obs.] Fuller.

palatine.c: palatine pal"a*tine (?), a. [F. palatin, L. palatinus, fr. palatium. See Palace, and cf. Paladin.] 1. Of or pertaining to a palace, or to a high officer of a palace; hence, possessing royal privileges.
Palatine Pal"a*tine (?), n. 1. One invested with royal privileges and rights within his domains; a count palatine. See Count palatine, under 4th Count.
palatine pal"a*tine, a. [From Palate.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the palate; palatal.

palative.c: Palative Pal"a*tive (?), a. Pleasing to the taste; palatable. [Obs.] “Palative delights.” Sir T. Browne.

palatize.c: Palatize Pal"a*tize (?), v. t. To modify, as the tones of the voice, by means of the palate; to palatalize; as, to palatize a letter or sound. -- Pal`a*ti*za"tion (#), n. J. Peile.

palato.c: Palato- Pal"a*to- (?). [From Palate.] A combining form used in anatomy to indicate relation to the palate, or connection with the palate; as in palatolingual.

palatonares.c: Palatonares ‖Pal`a*to*na"res (?), n. pl. [NL. See Palato-, and Nares.] (Anat.) The posterior nares. See Nares.

palatopterygoid.c: Palatopterygoid Pal`a*top*ter"y*goid (?), a. [Palato- + pterygoid.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the palatine and pterygoid region of the skull; as, the palatopterygoid cartilage, or rod, from which the palatine and pterygoid bones are developed.

palaver.c: Palaver Pa*la"ver (?), n. [Sp. palabra, or Pg. palavra, fr. L. parabola a comparison, a parable, LL., a word. See Parable.]

Palaver Pa*la"ver, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Palavered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Palavering.] To make palaver with, or to; to used palaver; to talk idly or deceitfully; to employ flattery; to cajole; as, to palaver artfully.

palaverer.c: Palaverer Pa*la"ver*er (?), n. One who palavers; a flatterer.

pale.c: Pale Pale (pāl), a. [Compar. Paler (pāl"ẽr); superl. Palest.] [F. pâle, fr. pâlir to turn pale, L. pallere to be or look pale. Cf. Appall, Fallow, pall, v. i., Pallid.]
Pale Pale, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Paled (pāld); p. pr. & vb. n. Paling.] To turn pale; to lose color or luster. Whittier.
Pale Pale, v. t. To make pale; to diminish the brightness of.

Pale Pale, n. [F. pal, fr. L. palus: cf. D. paal. See Pole a stake, and 1st Pallet.] 1. A pointed stake or slat, either driven into the ground, or fastened to a rail at the top and bottom, for fencing or inclosing; a picket.
Pale Pale, v. t. To inclose with pales, or as with pales; to encircle; to encompass; to fence off.

paleaceous.c: Paleaceous Pa`le*a"ceous (?), a. [L. palea chaff.] (Bot.) Chaffy; resembling or consisting of paleæ, or chaff; furnished with chaff; as, a paleaceous receptacle.

palearctic.c: Palearctic Pa`le*arc"tic (?), a. [Paleo- + arctic.] Belonging to a region of the earth's surface which includes all Europe to the Azores, Iceland, and all temperate Asia.

paled.c: Paled Paled (?), a. [See 5th Pale.] 1. Striped. [Obs.] “[Buskins]... paled part per part.” Spenser.

paleechinoidea.c: Paleechinoidea ‖Pa`le*ëch`i*noi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Paleo-, and Echinoidea.] (Zool.) An extinct order of sea urchins found in the Paleozoic rocks. They had more than twenty vertical rows of plates. Called also Palaeechini. [Written also Palaeechinoidea.]

paleface.c: Paleface Pale"face` (pāl"fās`), n. A white person; -- an appellation supposed to have been applied to the whites by the American Indians. J. F. Cooper.

paleichthyes.c: Paleichthyes ‖Pa`le*ich"thy*es (?), n. pl. [NL. See Paleo-, and Ichthyology.] (Zool.) A comprehensive division of fishes which includes the elasmobranchs and ganoids. [Written also Palæichthyes.]

palely.c: Palely Pale"ly (?), adv. [From Pale, a.] In a pale manner; dimly; wanly; not freshly or ruddily. Thackeray.

palempore.c: Palempore Pal`em*pore" (păl`ĕm*pōr"), n. A superior kind of dimity made in India, -- used for bed coverings. [Written also palampore, palampoor, etc.] De Colange.

paleness.c: Paleness Pale"ness (?), n. The quality or condition of being pale; want of freshness or ruddiness; a sickly whiteness; lack of color or luster; wanness.

palenque.c: Palenque Pa*len"que (?), n. pl. (Ethnol.) A collective name for the Indians of Nicaragua and Honduras.

paleo.c: Paleo- Pa"le*o- (?). [Gr. palaio`s, adj.] A combining form meaning old, ancient; as, palearctic, paleontology, paleothere, paleography. [Written also palæo-.]

paleobotanist.c: Paleobotanist Pa`le*o*bot"a*nist (?), n. One versed in paleobotany.

paleobotany.c: Paleobotany Pa`le*o*bot"a*ny (?), n. [Paleo- + botany.] That branch of paleontology which treats of fossil plants.

paleocarida.c: Paleocarida ‖Pa`le*o*car"ida (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. palaio`s ancient + kari`s, -i`dos, a kind of crustacean.] (Zool.) Same as Merostomata. [Written also Palæocarida.]

paleocrinoidea.c: Paleocrinoidea ‖Pa`le*o*cri*noi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Paleo-, and Crinoidea.] (Zool.) A suborder of Crinoidea found chiefly in the Paleozoic rocks.

paleocrystic.c: Paleocrystic Pa`le*o*crys"tic (?), a. [Paleo- + Gr. kry`stallos ice.] Of, pertaining to, or derived from, a former glacial formation.

paleogaean.c: Paleogaean Pa`le*o*gæ"an (?), a. [Paleo- + Gr. gai^a the earth.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Eastern hemisphere. [Written also palæogæan.]

paleographer.c: Paleographer Pa`le*og"ra*pher (?), n. One skilled in paleography; a paleographist.

paleographical.c: Paleographical Paleographic { Pa`le*o*graph"ic (?), Pa`le*o*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. paléographique.] Of or pertaining to paleography.

paleographist.c: Paleographist Pa`le*og"ra*phist (pā`le*ŏg"rȧ*fĭst), n. One versed in paleography; a paleographer.

paleography.c: Paleography Pa`le*og"ra*phy (pā`le*ŏg"rȧ*fy̆), n. [Paleo- + -graphy: cf. F. paléographie.] 1. An ancient manner of writing; ancient writings, collectively; as, Punic paleography.

paleola.c: Paleola ‖Pa*le"o*la (?), n.; pl. Paleolæ (#). [NL., dim. of L. palea.] (Bot.) A diminutive or secondary palea; a lodicule.

paleolith.c: Paleolith Pa"le*o*lith (pā"le*o*lĭth), n. [Paleo- + -lith.] (Geol.) A relic of the Paleolithic era.

paleolithic.c: Paleolithic Pa`le*o*lith"ic (pā`le*o*lĭth"ĭk), a. (Geol.) Of or pertaining to an era marked by early stone implements. The Paleolithic era (as proposed by Lubbock) includes the earlier half of the “Stone Age;” the remains belonging to it are for the most part of extinct animals, with relics of human beings.

paleologist.c: Paleologist Pa`le*ol"ogist (?), n. One versed in paleology; a student of antiquity.

paleology.c: Paleology Pa`le*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Paleo- + -logy.] The study or knowledge of antiquities, esp. of prehistoric antiquities; a discourse or treatise on antiquities; archæology.

paleontographical.c: Paleontographical Pa`le*on`to*graph"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to the description of fossil remains.

paleontography.c: Paleontography Pa`le*on*tog"ra*phy (pā`le*ŏn*tŏg"rȧ*fy̆), n. [Paleo- + Gr. 'o`nta existing things + -graphy.] The description of fossil remains.

paleontological.c: Paleontological Pa`le*on`to*log"ic*al (pā`le*ŏn`to*lŏj"ĭ*kail), a. Of or pertaining to paleontology. -- Pa`le*on`to*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

paleontologist.c: Paleontologist Pa`le*on*tol"o*gist (pā`le*ŏn*tŏl"o*jĭst), n. [Cf. F. paléontologiste.] One versed in paleontology.

paleontology.c: Paleontology Pa`le*on*tol"o*gy (pā`le*ŏn*tŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Paleo- + Gr. 'o`nta existing things + -logy. Cf. Ontology.] The science which treats of the ancient life of the earth, or of fossils which are the remains of such life.

paleornithology.c: Paleornithology Pa`le*or`ni*thol"o*gy (pā`le*ôr`nĭ*thŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Paleo- + ornithology.] The branch of paleontology which treats of fossil birds.

paleosaurus.c: Paleosaurus Pa`le*o*sau"rus (pā`le*o*sä"rŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. palaio`s ancient + say^ros a lizard.] (Paleon.) A genus of fossil saurians found in the Permian formation.

paleotechnic.c: Paleotechnic Pa`le*o*tech"nic (pā`le*o*tĕk"nĭk), a. [Paleo- + technic.] Belonging to, or connected with, ancient art. “The paleotechnic men of central France.” D. Wilson.

paleothere.c: Paleothere Pa"le*o*there (pā"le*o*thēr), n. [F. paléothère.] (Paleon.) Any species of Paleotherium.

paleotherian.c: Paleotherian Pa`le*o*the"ri*an (pā`le*o*thē"rĭ*ain), a. [F. paléothérien.] (Paleon.) Of or pertaining to Paleotherium.

paleotherium.c: Paleotherium ‖Pa`le*o*the"ri*um (pā`le*o*thē"rĭ*ŭm), n. [NL., fr. Gr. palaio`s ancient + qhri`on beast.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of herbivorous Tertiary mammals, once supposed to have resembled the tapir in form, but now known to have had a more slender form, with a long neck like that of a llama. [Written also Palæotherium.]

paleotheroid.c: Paleotheroid Pa`le*o*the"roid (pā`le*o*thē"roid), [Paleothere + -oid.] (Paleon.) Resembling Paleotherium. -- n. An animal resembling, or allied to, the paleothere.

paleous.c: Paleous Pa"le*ous (pā`le*ŭs), a. [L. palea chaff.] Chaffy; like chaff; paleaceous. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

paleozoic.c: Paleozoic Pa`le*o*zo"ic (pā`le*o*zō"ĭk), a. [Paleo- + Gr. zwh` life, fr. zh^n to live.] (Geol.) Of or pertaining to, or designating, the older division of geological time during which life is known to have existed, including the Silurian, Devonian, and Carboniferous ages, and also to the life or rocks of those ages. See Chart of Geology.
Paleozoic Pa`le*o*zo"ic (pā`le*o*zō"ĭk), n. (Geol.) The Paleozoic time or strata.

paleozoology.c: Paleozoology Pa`le*o*zo*öl"o*gy (pā`le*o*zo*ŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Paleo- + Zoology.] The science of extinct animals, a branch of paleontology.

palesy.c: Palesy Palesie { Pale"sie (päl"ze), Pale"sy }, n. Palsy. [Obs.] Wyclif.

palestinean.c: Palestinean Palestinian { Pal`es*tin"i*an (?), Pal`es*tin"e*an (?), } a. Of or pertaining to Palestine.

palestra.c: Palestra Pa*les"tra (?), n.; pl. L. Palestræ (#), E. Palestras (#). [NL., fr. L. palaestra, Gr.?, fr.? to wrestle.] [Written also palæstra.] (Antiq.) (a) A wrestling school; hence, a gymnasium, or place for athletic exercise in general. (b) A wrestling; the exercise of wrestling.

palestrical.c: Palestrical Palestric Palestrian { Pa*les"tri*an (?), Pa*les"tric (?), Pa*les"tric*al (?), } a. [L. palaestricus, Gr.?.] Of or pertaining to the palestra, or to wrestling.

palet.c: Palet Pal"et (?), n. [See Palea.] (Bot.) Same as Palea.

paletot.c: Paletot ‖Pal"e*tot (?), n. [F. paletot, OF. palletoc, prob. fr. L. palla (see Palla) + F. toque cap, and so lit., a frock with a cap or hood; cf. Sp. paletoque.] (a) An overcoat. Dickens. (b) A lady's outer garment, -- of varying fashion.

palette.c: Palette Pal"ette (?), n. [See Pallet a thin board.]

palewise.c: Palewise Pale"wise` (?), adv. (Her.) In the manner of a pale or pales; by perpendicular lines or divisions; as, to divide an escutcheon palewise.

palfrey.c: Palfrey Pal"frey (?), n. [OE. palefrai, OF. palefrei, F. palefroi, LL. palafredus, parafredus, from L. paraveredus a horse for extraordinary occasions, an extra post horse; Gr. para` along, beside + L. veredus a post horse.]

palfreyed.c: Palfreyed Pal"freyed (?), a. Mounted on a palfrey. Tickell.

pali.c: Pali Pa"li (?), n. [Ceylonese, fr. Skr. pāli row, line, series, applied to the series of Buddhist sacred texts.] A dialect descended from Sanskrit, and like that, a dead language, except when used as the sacred language of the Buddhist religion in Farther India, etc.

palification.c: Palification Pal`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. palus a stake + -ficare (in comp.) to make: cf. F. palification. See -fy.] The act or practice of driving piles or posts into the ground to make it firm. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.

paliform.c: Paliform Pa"li*form (?), a. (Zool.) Resembling a palus; as, the paliform lobes of the septa in corals.

palilogy.c: Palilogy Pa*lil"o*gy (?), n. [L. palilogia, Gr. palillogi`a; pa`lin again + le`gein to speak.] (Rhet.) The repetition of a word, or part of a sentence, for the sake of greater emphasis; as, “The living, the living, he shall praise thee.” Is. xxxviii. 19.

palimpsest.c: palimpsest pal"imp*sest (păl"ĭmp*sĕst), n. [L. palimpsestus, Gr. pali`mpshstos scratched or scraped again, pali`mpshston a palimpsest; pa`lin again + psh^n to rub, rub away: cf. F. palimpseste.] A parchment which has been written upon twice, the first writing having been erased to make place for the second. The erasures of ancient writings were usually carried on in monasteries, to allow the production of ecclesiastical texts, such as copies of church services and lives of the saints. The difficulty of recovering the original text varied with the process used to prepare the parchment for a fresh writing; the original texts on parchments which had been washed with lime-water and dried were easily recovered by a chemical process, but those erased by scraping the parchment and bleaching are difficult to interpret. Most of the manuscripts underlying the palimpsests that have been revived are fragmentary, but some are of great historical value. One Syriac version of the Four Gospels was discovered in 1895 in St. Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai by Mrs. Agnes Smith Lewis. See also the notes below. Longfellow.

palindrome.c: Palindrome Pal"in*drome (?), n. [Gr. pali`ndromos running back again; pa`lin again + dramei^n to run: cf. F. palindrome.] A word, verse, or sentence, that is the same when read backward or forward; as, madam; Hannah; or Lewd did I live, & evil I did dwel.

palindromical.c: Palindromical Palindromic { Pal`in*drom"ic (?), Pal`in*drom"ic*al (?), } a. Of, pertaining to, or like, a palindrome.

palindromist.c: Palindromist Pa*lin"dro*mist (?), n. A writer of palindromes.

paling.c: Paling Pal"ing (?), n. 1. Pales, in general; a fence formed with pales or pickets; a limit; an inclosure.

palingenesy.c: Palingenesy Palingenesis { Pal`in*gen"e*sis (?), Pal`in*gen"e*sy (?), } n. [Gr.?; pa`lin again +? birth: cf. F. palingénésie. See Genesis.]

palingenetic.c: Palingenetic Pal`in*ge*net"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to palingenesis: as, a palingenetic process. -- Pal`in*ge*net"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

palinode.c: Palinode Pal"i*node (?), n. [L. palinodia, from Gr.?; pa`lin again +? a song. See Ode.] 1. An ode recanting, or retracting, a former one; also, a repetition of an ode.

palinodial.c: Palinodial Pal`i*no"di*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a palinode, or retraction. J. Q. Adams.

palinurus.c: Palinurus Pal`inu"rus (?), n. [So called from L. Palinurus, the pilot of Aeneas.] (Naut.) An instrument for obtaining directly, without calculation, the true bearing of the sun, and thence the variation of the compass.

palisade.c: Palisade Pal`i*sade" (?), n. [F. palissade, cf. Sp. palizada, It. palizzata, palizzo, LL. palissata; all fr. L. palus a stake, pale. See Pale a stake.] 1. (Fort.) A strong, long stake, one end of which is set firmly in the ground, and the other is sharpened; also, a fence formed of such stakes set in the ground as a means of defense.
Palisade Pal`i*sade", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Palisaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Palisading.] [Cf. F. palissader.] To surround, inclose, or fortify, with palisades.

palisading.c: Palisading Pal`i*sad"ing (?), n. (Fort.) A row of palisades set in the ground.

palisado.c: Palisado Pal`i*sa*"do (?), n.; pl. Palisadoes (?). A palisade{1}. [Obs.] Shak.
Palisado Pal`i*sa"do, v. t. To palisade. [Obs.] Sterne.

palish.c: Palish Pal"ish (?), a. Somewhat pale or wan.

palissander.c: Palissander Pal`is*san"der (?), n. [F. palissandre.] (Bot.) (a) Violet wood. (b) Rosewood.

palissy.c: Palissy Pal"is*sy (?), a. Designating, or of the nature of, a kind of pottery made by Bernard Palissy, in France, in the 16th centry.

palkee.c: Palkee ‖Pal"kee (?), n. [Hind. pālkī; of the same origin as E. palanquin.] A palanquin. Malcom.

pall.c: Pall Pall, n. [OE. pal, AS. pæl, from L. pallium cover, cloak, mantle, pall; cf. L. palla robe, mantle.] 1. An outer garment; a cloak mantle.
Pall Pall, v. t. To cloak. [R.] Shak

Pall Pall, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Palled (päld); p. pr. & vb. n. Palling.] [Either shortened fr. appall, or fr. F. pâlir to grow pale. Cf. Appall, Pale, a.] To become vapid, tasteless, dull, or insipid; to lose strength, life, spirit, or taste; as, the liquor palls.
Pall Pall, v. t. 1. To make vapid or insipid; to make lifeless or spiritless; to dull; to weaken. Chaucer.

palla.c: Palla ‖Pal"la (?), n. [L. See Pall a cloak.] (Rom. Antiq.) An oblong rectangular piece of cloth, worn by Roman ladies, and fastened with brooches.

palladian.c: Palladian Pal*la"di*an (păl*lā"dĭ*ain), prop. a. (Arch.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, a variety of the revived classic style of architecture, founded on the works of Andrea Palladio, an Italian architect of the 16th century; as, a Palladian window.

palladic.c: Palladic Pal*la"dic (păl*lā"dĭk or păl*lăd"ĭk), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or derived from, palladium; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which the element has a higher valence as contrasted with palladious compounds.

palladious.c: Palladious Pal*la"di*ous (păl*lā"dĭ*ŭs), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or containing, palladium; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which palladium has a lower valence as compared with palladic compounds.

palladium.c: Palladium Pal*la"di*um (păl*lā"dĭ*ŭm), n. [L., fr. Gr. Palla`dion, fr. Palla`s, Palla`dos, Pallas.]

Palladium Pal*la"di*um, n. [NL.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element of the light platinum group, found native, and also alloyed with platinum and gold. It is a silver-white metal resembling platinum, and like it permanent and untarnished in the air, but is more easily fusible, with a melting point of 1555° C. It can also be prepared as a finely divided black powder. It is unique in its power of absorbing hydrogen, which it does to the extent of nearly a thousand volumes, forming the alloy Pd2H. It is used for graduated circles and verniers, for plating certain silver goods, and somewhat in dentistry. It was so named in 1804 by Wollaston from the asteroid Pallas, which was discovered in 1802. Symbol Pd. Atomic number, 46. Atomic weight, 106.42. Density 12.0.

palladiumize.c: palladiumize pal*la"di*um*ize (păl"lā"dĭ*ŭm*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Palladiumized (păl"lā"dĭ*ŭm*īzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Palladiumizing (păl"lā"dĭ*ŭm*ī`zĭng).] To cover or coat with palladium. [R.]

pallah.c: pallah pal"lah (păl"lȧ), n. (Zool.) A large South African antelope (Aepyceros melampus). The male has long lyrate and annulated horns. The general color is bay, with a black crescent on the croup. Called also roodebok.

pallas.c: Pallas Pal"las (păl"lais), prop. n. [L., fr. Gr. Palla`s, Palla`dos.] (Gr. Myth.) Pallas Athena, the Grecian goddess of wisdom, called also Athena, Pallas Athene or Athene, and identified, at a later period, with the Roman Minerva.

pallbearer.c: pallbearer pall"bear*er (päl"bâr*ẽr), n. One of those who attend the coffin at a funeral; -- so called from the pall being formerly carried by them.

pallet.c: pallet pal"let (păl"lĕt), n. [OE. paillet, F. paillet a heap of straw, fr. paille straw, fr. L. palea chaff; cf. Gr.? fine meal, dust, Skr. pala straw, palāva chaff. Cf. Paillasse.] A small and mean bed; a bed of straw. Milton.
Pallet Pal"let, n. [Dim. of pale. See Pale a stake.] (Her.) A perpendicular band upon an escutcheon, one half the breadth of the pale.
Pallet Pal"let, n. [F. palette: af. It. paletta; prop. and orig., a fire shovel, dim. of L. pala a shovel, spade. See Peel a shovel.] 1. (Paint.) Same as Palette.

pallial.c: Pallial Pal"li*al (?), a. [L. pallium a mantle. See Pall.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to a mantle, especially to the mantle of mollusks; produced by the mantle; as, the pallial line, or impression, which marks the attachment of the mantle on the inner surface of a bivalve shell. See Illust. of Bivalve.

palliament.c: Palliament Pal"li*a*ment (?), n. [LL. palliare to clothe, fr. L. pallium a mantle. See Pall the garment.] A dress; a robe. [Obs.] Shak.

palliard.c: Palliard Pal"liard (?), n. [F. paillard, orig., one addicted to the couch, fr. paille straw. See Pallet a small bed.]

palliate.c: Palliate Pal"li*ate (?), a. [L. palliatus, fr. pallium a cloak. See Pall the garment.] 1. Covered with a mantle; cloaked; hidden; disguised. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Palliate Pal"li*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Palliated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Palliating (?).] 1. To cover with a mantle or cloak; to cover up; to hide. [Obs.]

palliation.c: Palliation Pal`li*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. palliation.] 1. The act of palliating, or state of being palliated; extenuation; excuse; as, the palliation of faults, offenses, vices.

palliative.c: Palliative Pal"li*a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. palliatif.] Serving to palliate; serving to extenuate, mitigate, or alleviate.
Palliative Pal"li*a*tive (?), n. That which palliates; a palliative agent. Sir W. Scott.

pallid.c: Pallid Pal"lid (?), a. [L. pallidus, fr. pallere to be or look pale. See pale, a.] Deficient in color; pale; wan; as, a pallid countenance; pallid blue. Spenser.

pallidly.c: Pallidly Pal"lid*ly (?), adv. In a pallid manner.

pallidness.c: Pallidness Pal"lid*ness, n. The quality or state of being pallid; paleness; pallor; wanness.

palliobranchiate.c: Palliobranchiate Pal`li*o*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [See Pallium, and Branchia.] (Zool.) Having the pallium, or mantle, acting as a gill, as in brachiopods.

pallium.c: Pallium ‖Pal"li*um (?), n.; pl. L. Pallia (?), E. Palliums (#). [L. See Pall the garment.] 1. (Anc. Costume) A large, square, woolen cloak which enveloped the whole person, worn by the Greeks and by certain Romans. It is the Roman name of a Greek garment.

pallmall.c: Pall-mall Pall`-mall" (?), n. [OF. palemail, It. pallamagio; palla a ball (of German origin, akin to E. ball) + magio hammer, fr. L. malleus. See 1st Ball, and Mall a beetle.] A game formerly common in England, in which a wooden ball was driven with a mallet through an elevated hoop or ring of iron. The name was also given to the mallet used, to the place where the game was played, and to the street, in London, still called Pall Mall. [Written also pail-mail and pell-mell.] Sir K. Digby. Evelyn.

pallone.c: Pallone Pal*lo"ne (?), n. [It., a large ball, fr. palla ball. See Balloon.] An Italian game, played with a large leather ball.

pallor.c: pallor pal"lor (?), n. [L., fr. pallere to be or look pale. See Pale, a.] Paleness; want of color; pallidity; as, pallor of the complexion. Jer. Taylor.

palm.c: palm palm (päm), n. [OE. paume, F. paume, L. palma, Gr. pala`mh, akin to Skr. pāṇi hand, and E. fumble. See Fumble, Feel, and cf. 2d Palm.] 1. (Anat.) The inner and somewhat concave part of the hand between the bases of the fingers and the wrist.
Palm Palm, n. [AS. palm, L. palma; -- so named fr. the leaf resembling a hand. See 1st Palm, and cf. Pam.]
Palm Palm (päm), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Palmed (pämd); p. pr. & vb. n. Palming.] 1. To handle. [Obs.] Prior.

Palm Sunday Palm" Sun`day (?). (Eccl.) The Sunday next before Easter; -- so called in commemoration of the triumphal entry of Jesus Christ into Jerusalem, when the multitude strewed palm branches in the way. The event is commemorated in Christian churches by distribution of blessed palm leaves.

palmaceous.c: Palmaceous Pal*ma"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to palms; of the nature of, or resembling, palms.

palma.c: Palma Christi ‖Pal"ma Chris"ti (?). [L., palm of Christ.] (Bot.) A plant (Ricinus communis) with ornamental peltate and palmately cleft foliage, growing as a woody perennial in the tropics, and cultivated as an herbaceous annual in temperate regions; -- called also castor-oil plant. [Sometimes corrupted into palmcrist.]

palmar.c: Palmar Pal"mar (?), a. [L. palmaris, fr. palma the palm of the hand: cf. F. palmaire.] 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or corresponding with, the palm of the hand.

palmarium.c: Palmarium ‖Pal*ma"ri*um (?), n.; pl. Palmaria (#). [NL. See Palmar.] (Zool.) One of the bifurcations of the brachial plates of a crinoid.

palmary.c: Palmary Pal"ma*ry, a. [L. palmarius, palmaris, belonging to palms, deserving the palm or prize, fr. palma a palm.] Worthy of the palm; palmy; preëminent; superior; principal; chief; as, palmary work. Br. Horne.

palmate.c: Palmate Pal"mate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of palmic acid; a ricinoleate. [Obsoles.]

palmated.c: Palmated Palmate { Pal"mate (?), Pal"ma*ted (?), } a. [L. palmatus marked with the palm of a hand, from palma the palm of the hand.]

palmately.c: Palmately Pal"mate*ly (?), adv. In a palmate manner.

palmatifid.c: Palmatifid Pal*mat"i*fid (?), a. [L. palmatus palmate + root of findere to split.] (Bot.) Palmate, with the divisions separated but little more than halfway to the common center.

palmatilobed.c: Palmatilobed Pal*mat"i*lobed (?), a. [L. palmatus palmate + E. lobed.] (Bot.) Palmate, with the divisions separated less than halfway to the common center.

palmatisected.c: Palmatisected Palmatisect { Pal*mat"i*sect (?), Pal*mat`i*sect"ed (?), } a. [L. palmatus palmate + secare to cut.] (Bot.) Divided, as a palmate leaf, down to the midrib, so that the parenchyma is interrupted.

palmcrist.c: Palmcrist Palm"crist (?), n. The palma Christi. (Jonah iv. 6, margin, and Douay version, note.)

palmed.c: Palmed Palmed (?), a. Having or bearing a palm or palms.

palmer.c: Palmer Palm"er (?), n. [From Palm, v. t.] One who palms or cheats, as at cards or dice.
Palmer Palm"er, n. [From Palm the tree.] A wandering religious votary; especially, one who bore a branch of palm as a token that he had visited the Holy Land and its sacred places. Chaucer.

palmerworm.c: Palmerworm Palm"er*worm` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) Any hairy caterpillar which appears in great numbers, devouring herbage, and wandering about like a palmer. The name is applied also to other voracious insects. Joel. i. 4. (b) In America, the larva of any one of several moths, which destroys the foliage of fruit and forest trees, esp. the larva of Ypsolophus pometellus, which sometimes appears in vast numbers.

palmette.c: Palmette Pal*mette" (?), n. [F., dim. of palme a palm.] A floral ornament, common in Greek and other ancient architecture; -- often called the honeysuckle ornament.

palmetto.c: Palmetto Pal*met"to (?), n. [Dim. of palm the tree: cf. Sp. palmito.] (Bot.) A name given to palms of several genera and species growing in the West Indies and the Southern United States. In the United States, the name is applied especially to the Chamærops Palmetto, or Sabal Palmetto, the cabbage tree of Florida and the Carolinas. See Cabbage tree, under Cabbage.

Palmetto flag Pal*met"to flag. Any of several flags adopted by South Carolina after its secession. That adopted in November, 1860, had a green cabbage palmetto in the center of a white field; the final one, January, 1861, had a white palmetto in the center of a blue field and a white crescent in the upper left-hand corner.
Palmetto State Palmetto State. prop. n. South Carolina; -- a nickname alluding to the State Arms, which contain a representation of a palmetto tree.

palmic.c: Palmic Pal"mic (?), a. [Cf. F. palmique.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or derived from, the castor-oil plant (Ricinus communis, or Palma Christi) and other species of the family Euphorbiaceae; -- formerly used to designate an acid now called ricinoleic acid (d-12-hydroxyoleic acid, C18H34O3). [Obsoles.]

palmidactyles.c: Palmidactyles ‖Pal`mi*dac"ty*les (?), n. pl. [NL. See Palm, and Dactyl.] (Zool.) A group of wading birds having the toes webbed, as the avocet.

palmiferous.c: Palmiferous Pal*mif"er*ous (?), a. [L. palmifer; palma a palm + ferre to bear: cf. F. palmifère.] Bearing palms.

palmigrade.c: Palmigrade Pal"mi*grade (?), a. [L. palma palm of the hand + gradi to walk.] (Zool.) Putting the whole foot upon the ground in walking, as some mammals.

palmin.c: Palmin Pal"min (?), n. [From palma Christi: cf. F. palmine.] (Chem.) (a) A white waxy or fatty substance obtained from castor oil. (b) Ricinolein. [Obs.]

palmiped.c: Palmiped Pal"mi*ped (?), a. [L. palmipes, -edis, broad-footed; palma the palm of the hand + pes a foot; cf. F. palmipède.] (Zool.) Web-footed, as a water fowl. -- n. A swimming bird; a bird having webbed feet.

palmister.c: Palmister Pal"mis*ter (?), n. [From Palm of the hand.] One who practices palmistry. Bp. Hall.

palmistry.c: Palmistry Pal`mis*try (?), n. [See Palmister.] 1. The art or practice of divining or telling fortunes, or of judging of character, by the lines and marks in the palm of the hand; chiromancy. Ascham. Cowper.

palmitate.c: Palmitate Pal"mi*tate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of palmitic acid.

palmite.c: Palmite Pal"mite (?), n. [From Palm.] (Bot.) A South African plant (Prionium Palmita) of the Rush family, having long serrated leaves. The stems have been used for making brushes.

palmitic.c: Palmitic Pal*mit"ic (?), a. (Physiol. Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, palmitin or palm oil; as, palmitic acid (C16H32O2), a white crystalline substance belonging to the fatty acid series. It is readily soluble in hot alcohol, and melts to a liquid oil at 62° C.

palmitin.c: Palmitin Pal"mi*tin (?), n. [So called because abundant in palm oil.] (Physiol. Chem.) A solid crystallizable fat, found abundantly in animals and in vegetables. It occurs mixed with stearin and olein in the fat of animal tissues, with olein and butyrin in butter, with olein in olive oil, etc. Chemically, it is a glyceride of palmitic acid, three molecules of palmitic acid being united to one molecule of glyceryl, and hence it is technically called tripalmitin, or glyceryl tripalmitate.

palmitolic.c: Palmitolic Pal`mi*tol"ic (?), a. [Palmitic + -oleic + ic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an artificial acid of the oleic acid series, isomeric with linoleic acid.

palmitone.c: Palmitone Pal"mi*tone (?), n. (Chem.) The ketone of palmitic acid.

palmy.c: Palmy Palm"y (?), a. 1. Bearing palms; abounding in palms; derived from palms; as, a palmy shore. Pope.

palmyra.c: Palmyra Pal*my"ra (?), n. (Bot.) A species of palm (Borassus flabelliformis) having a straight, black, upright trunk, with palmate leaves. It is found native along the entire northern shores of the Indian Ocean, from the mouth of the Tigris to New Guinea. More than eight hundred uses to which it is put are enumerated by native writers. Its wood is largely used for building purposes; its fruit and roots serve for food, its sap for making toddy, and its leaves for thatching huts.

palo.c: Palo ‖Pa"lo (?), n. [Sp. See Pale a stake.] A pole or timber of any kind; -- in the names of trees. [Sp. Amer.]

Palo blanco ‖Pa"lo blan"co (?). [Sp. blanco white.] (a) A western American hackberry (Celtis reticulata), having light-colored bark. (b) A Mexican mimosaceous tree (Lysiloma candida), the bark of which is used in tanning.

palolo.c: Palolo worm Palolo { Pa*lo"lo (?), n., or Palolo worm }. [From native name.] (Zool.) A polystome worm (Palolo viridis) that burrows in the coral reefs of certain of the Pacific Islands. A little before the last quarter of the moon in October and November, they swarm in vast numbers at the surface of the sea for breeding, and are gathered and highly esteemed as food by the natives. An allied species inhabits the tropical Atlantic and swarms in June or July.

palometa.c: Palometa ‖Pa`lo*me"ta (?), n. (Zool.) A type of pompano (Palometa simillima) that is smaller than the Florida pompano; it is common in West Indies. Called also the California pompano.

palp.c: Palp Palp (pălp), n. [Cf. F. palpe. See Palpable.] (Zool.) Same as Palpus.
Palp Palp, v. t. [L. palpare: cf. F. palper.] To have a distinct touch or feeling of; to feel. [Obs.]

palpability.c: Palpability Pal`pa*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being palpable, or perceptible by the touch. Arbuthnot.

palpable.c: Palpable Pal"pa*ble (?), a. [F. palpable, L. palpabilis, fr. palpare to feel, stroke; cf. palpus the soft palm of the hand.] 1. Capable of being touched and felt; perceptible by the touch; as, a palpable form. Shak.

palpation.c: Palpation Pal*pa"tion (?), n. [L. palpatio, fr. palpare. See Palpable.] 1. Act of touching or feeling.

palpator.c: Palpator ‖Pal*pa"tor (?), n. [L., a stroker.] (Zool.) One of a family of clavicorn beetles, including those which have very long maxillary palpi.

palpebral.c: Palpebral Pal"pe*bral (?), a. [L. palpebralis, fr. palpebra: cf. F. palpébral.] Of or pertaining to the eyelids.

palpi.c: Palpi ‖Pal"pi (păl"pī), n., pl. of Palpus. (Zool.) See Palpus.

palpicorn.c: Palpicorn Pal"pi*corn (?), n. [See Palpus, and Cornu.] (Zool.) One of a group of aquatic beetles (Palpicornia) having short club-shaped antennæ, and long maxillary palpi.

palpifer.c: Palpifer Pal"pi*fer (?), n. [Palpus + L. ferre to bear.] (Zool.) Same as Palpiger.

palpiform.c: Palpiform Pal"pi*form (?), a. [Palpus + -form: cf. F. palpiforme.] (Zool.) Having the form of a palpus.

palpiger.c: Palpiger Pal"pi*ger (?), n. [See Palpigerous.] (Zool.) That portion of the labium which bears the palpi in insects.

palpigerous.c: Palpigerous Pal*pig"er*ous (?), a. [Palpus + -gerous.] (Zool.) Bearing a palpus. Kirby.

palpitant.c: Palpitant Pal"pi*tant (?), a. [L. palpitans, p. pr.] Palpitating; throbbing; trembling. Carlyle.

palpitate.c: Palpitate Pal"pi*tate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Palpitated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Palpitating (?).] [L. palpitare, palpitatum, v. intens. fr. pappare. See Palpable.] To beat rapidly and more strongly than usual; to throb; to bound with emotion or exertion; to pulsate violently; to flutter; -- said specifically of the heart when its action is abnormal, as from excitement.

palpitation.c: Palpitation Pal`pi*ta"tion (?), n. [L. palpitatio: cf. F. palpitation.] A rapid pulsation; a throbbing; esp., an abnormal, rapid beating of the heart as when excited by violent exertion, strong emotion, or by disease.

palpocil.c: Palpocil Pal"po*cil (?), n. [See Palpus, and Cilium.] (Zool.) A minute soft filamentary process springing from the surface of certain hydroids and sponges.

palpus.c: Palpus ‖Pal"pus (?), n.; pl. Palpi (#). [NL. See Palp.] (Zool.) A feeler; especially, one of the jointed sense organs attached to the mouth organs of insects, arachnids, crustaceans, and annelids; as, the mandibular palpi, maxillary palpi, and labial palpi. The palpi of male spiders serve as sexual organs. Called also palp. See Illust. of Arthrogastra and Orthoptera.

palsgrave.c: Palsgrave Pals"grave` (?), n. [D. paltsgraaf; palts palace (l. palatium) + graaf count; cf. G. pfalzgraf. See Palace, and Landgrave.] (Ger. Hist.) A count or earl who presided in the domestic court, and had the superintendence, of a royal household in Germany.

palsgravine.c: Palsgravine Pals"gra*vine` (?), n. [D. paltsgravin: cf. G. pfalzgrafin.] The consort or widow of a palsgrave.

palsical.c: Palsical Pal"si*cal (?), a. [From Palsy.] Affected with palsy; palsied; paralytic. [R.] Johnson.

palsied.c: Palsied Pal"sied (?), a. Affected with palsy; paralyzed.

palstave.c: Palstave Pal"stave` (?), n. [Dan. paalstav.] A peculiar bronze adz, used in prehistoric Europe about the middle of the bronze age. Dawkins.

palster.c: Palster Pal"ster (?), n. [D. palsterstaf.] A pilgrim's staff. [Obs.] Halliwell.

palsy.c: Palsy Pal"sy (?), n.; pl. Palsies (#). [OE. palesie, parlesy, OF. paralesie, F. paralysie, L. paralysis. See Paralysis.] (Med.) Paralysis, complete or partial. See Paralysis. “One sick of the palsy.” Mark ii. 3.
Palsy Pal"sy, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Palsied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Palsying.] To affect with palsy, or as with palsy; to deprive of action or energy; to paralyze.

palsywort.c: Palsywort Pal"sy*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) The cowslip (Primula veris); -- so called from its supposed remedial powers. Dr. Prior.

palter.c: Palter Pal"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Paltered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Paltering.] [See Paltry.] 1. To haggle. [Obs.] Cotgrave.
Palter Pal"ter, v. t. To trifle with; to waste; to squander in paltry ways or on worthless things. [Obs.] “Palter out your time in the penal statutes.” Beau. & Fl.

palterer.c: Palterer Pal"ter*er (?), n. One who palters. Johnson.

palterly.c: Palterly Pal"ter*ly, a. & adv. Paltry; shabby; shabbily; paltrily. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] “In palterly clothes.” Pepys.

paltock.c: Paltock Pal"tock (?), n. [See Paletot.] A kind of doublet; a jacket. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

paltrily.c: paltrily pal"tri*ly (päl"trĭ*ly̆), adv. In a paltry manner.

paltriness.c: paltriness pal"tri*ness, n. The state or quality of being paltry.

paltry.c: paltry pal"try (päl"try̆), a. [Compar. Paltrier (päl"trĭ*ẽr); superl. Paltriest.] [Cf. Prov. E. paltry refuse, rubbish, LG. palterig ragged, palte, palter, a rag, a tatter, Dan. pialt, Sw. palta, pl. paltor.] Mean; vile; worthless; despicable; contemptible; pitiful; trifling; as, a paltry excuse; paltry gold. Cowper.

paludal.c: Paludal Pa*lu"dal (?), a. [L. palus, -udis, a marsh.] Of or pertaining to marshes or fens; marshy. [R.]

paludamentum.c: Paludamentum ‖Pa*lu`da*men*tum (?), n.; pl. Paladumenta (?). (Rom. Antiq.) A military cloak worn by a general and his principal officers.

paludicolae.c: Paludicolae ‖Pal`u*dic"o*læ (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. palus, -udis, a marsh + colere to inhabit.] (Zool.) A division of birds, including the cranes, rails, etc.

paludicole.c: Paludicole Pa*lu"di*cole (?), a. [Cf. F. paludicole.] (Zool.) Marsh-inhabiting; belonging to the Paludicolæ

paludina.c: Paludina ‖Pal`u*di"na (?), n.; pl. L. Paludinæ (#), E. Paludinas (#). [NL., fr. L. palus, -udis, a marsh, pool.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of freshwater pectinibranchiate mollusks, belonging to Paludina, Melantho, and allied genera. They have an operculated shell which is usually green, often with brown bands. See Illust. of Pond snail, under Pond.

paludinal.c: Paludinal Pal`u*di"nal (?), a. Inhabiting ponds or swamps.

paludine.c: Paludine Pal"u*dine (?), a. [L. palus, -udis, a marsh.] Of or pertaining to a marsh. Buckland.

paludinous.c: Paludinous Pa*lu"di*nous (?), a. 1. (Zool.) (a) Paludinal. (b) Like or pertaining to the genus Paludina.

paludism.c: Paludism Pa*lu"dism (?), n. (Med.) The morbid phenomena produced by dwelling among marshes; malarial disease or disposition.

paludose.c: Paludose Pal"u*dose` (?), a. [L. paludosus marshy.] Growing or living in marshy places; marshy.

palule.c: Palule Pal"ule (?), n. (Zool.) See Palulus or Palus.

palulus.c: Palulus ‖Pal"u*lus (?), n.; pl. Paluli (#). [NL., dim. of L. palus a stake.] (Zool.) Same as Palus.

palus.c: Palus ‖Pa"lus (?), n.; pl. Pali (#). [L., a stake.] (Zool.) One of several upright slender calcareous processes which surround the central part of the calicle of certain corals.

palustral.c: Palustral Pa*lus"tral (?), a. [L. paluster, -ustris.] Of or pertaining to a bog or marsh; boggy. [R.]

palustrine.c: Palustrine Pa*lus"trine (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or living in, a marsh or swamp; marshy.

paly.c: Paly Pal"y (?), a. [From Pale, a.] Pale; wanting color; dim. [Poetic] Shak. Whittier.
Paly Pal"y, a. [Cf. F. palé. See Pale a stake.] (Her.) Divided into four or more equal parts by perpendicular lines, and of two different tinctures disposed alternately.

pam.c: pam pam (?), n. [From Palm victory; cf. trump, fr. triumph, and perh. fr. F. pamphile from Pamphile, a man's name.] 1. The knave of clubs. [Obs.] Pope.

pampas.c: Pampas Pam"pas (?), n. pl. [Sp., fr. Peruv. pampa a field, plain.] Vast grass-covered plains in the central and southern part of the Argentine Republic in South America. The term is sometimes used in a wider sense for the plains east of the Andes extending from Bolivia to Southern Patagonia.

pamper.c: Pamper Pam"per (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pampered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pampering.] [Cf. LG. pampen, slampampen, to live luxuriously, pampe thick pap, and E. pap.]

pampered.c: Pampered Pam"pered (?), a. Fed luxuriously; indulged to the full; hence, luxuriant; as, pampered children. “Pampered boughs.” Milton. “Pampered insolence.” Pope. -- Pam"pered*ness, n. Bp. Hall.

pamperer.c: Pamperer Pam"per*er (?), n. One who, or that which, pampers. Cowper.

pamperize.c: Pamperize Pam"per*ize (?), v. t. To pamper. [R.] Sydney Smith.

pampero.c: Pampero ‖Pam*pe"ro (?), n. [Sp., fr. pampa a plain.] A violent wind from the west or southwest, which sweeps over the pampas of South America and the adjacent seas, often doing great damage. Sir W. Parish.

pamperos.c: Pamperos Pam*pe"ros (?), n. pl.; sing. Pampero (?). [Sp. American.] (Ethnol.) A tribe of Indians inhabiting the pampas of South America.

pamphlet.c: Pamphlet Pam"phlet (păm"flĕt), n. [OE. pamflet, pamfilet, paunflet, possibly fr. OF. palme the palm of the hand, F. paume (see Palm) + OF. fueillet a leaf, dim. of fueil, m., F. feuille, f., fr. L. folium, pl. folia, thus meaning, a leaf to be held in the hand; or perh. through old French, fr. L. Pamphila, a female historian of the first century who wrote many epitomes; prob., however, fr. OF. Pamflette, the Old French name given to Pamphilus, a poem in Latin verse of the 12th century, pamphlets being named from the popularity of this poem.] 1. A writing; a book. Testament of love.
Pamphlet Pam"phlet (păm"flĕt), v. i. To write a pamphlet or pamphlets. [R.] Howell.

pamphleteer.c: Pamphleteer Pam`phlet*eer" (păm`flĕt*ēr"), n. A writer of pamphlets; a scribbler. Dryden. Macaulay.
Pamphleteer Pam`phlet*eer", v. i. To write or publish pamphlets.

pampiniform.c: Pampiniform Pam*pin"i*form (?), a. [L. pampinus a tendril + -form.] (Anat.) In the form of tendrils; -- applied especially to the spermatic and ovarian veins.

pampre.c: Pampre Pam"pre (păm"pẽr), n. [F. pampre a vine branch, L. pampinus.] (Sculp.) An ornament, composed of vine leaves and bunches of grapes, used for decorating spiral columns.

pamprodactylous.c: Pamprodactylous Pam`pro*dac"tyl*ous (?), a. [Pan- + Gr. pro` forward + da`ktylos finger.] (Zool.) Having all the toes turned forward, as the colies.

panto.c: Panto- Panta- Pan- { Pan- (?), Pan"ta- (?), Pan"to- (?) }. [Gr.?, m.,?, neut., gen.?, all.] Combining forms signifying all, every; as, panorama, pantheism, pantagraph, pantograph. Pan- becomes pam- before b or p, as pamprodactylous.

pan.c: Pan Pan, n. [OE. See 2d Pane.] 1. A part; a portion.
Pan Pan, v. t. & i. [Cf. F. pan skirt, lappet, L. pannus a cloth, rag, W. panu to fur, to full.] To join or fit together; to unite. [Obs.] Halliwell.
Pan Pan (?), n. [Hind. pān, Skr. parna leaf.] The betel leaf; also, the masticatory made of the betel leaf, etc. See Betel.

Pan Pan (?), prop. n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] (Gr. Myth.) The god of shepherds, guardian of bees, and patron of fishing and hunting. He is usually represented as having the head and trunk of a man, with the legs, horns, and tail of a goat, and as playing on the shepherd's pipe (also called the pipes of Pan), which he is said to have invented.

Pan Pan, n. [OE. panne, AS. panne; cf. D. pan, G. pfanne, OHG. pfanna, Icel., Sw., LL., & Ir. panna, of uncertain origin; cf. L. patina, E. paten.] 1. A shallow, open dish or vessel, usually of metal, employed for many domestic uses, as for setting milk for cream, for frying or baking food, etc.; also employed for various uses in manufacturing. “A bowl or a pan.” Chaucer.
Pan Pan, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Panned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Panning.] 1. (Mining) To separate, as gold, from dirt or sand, by washing in a kind of pan. [U. S.]
Pan Pan, v. i. 1. (Mining) To yield gold in, or as in, the process of panning; -- usually with out; as, the gravel panned out richly.

panabase.c: Panabase Pan"a*base (?), n. [Pan- + base. So called in allusion to the number of metals contained in it.] (Min.) Same as Tetrahedrite.

panacea.c: Panacea Pan`a*ce"a (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. pana`keia fr. panakh`s all-healing; pa^s pa^n, all + 'akei^sqai to heal.]

panacean.c: Panacean Pan`a*ce"an (?), a. Having the properties of a panacea. [R.] “Panacean dews.” Whitehead.

panache.c: Panache Pa*nache" (?), n. [F., fr. L. penna a feather. See Pen a feather.] 1. A plume or bunch of feathers, esp. such a bunch worn on the helmet; any military plume, or ornamental group of feathers.

panade.c: Panade Panada { Pa*na"da (?), Pa*nade" (?), } n. [Sp. panada, fr. L. panis bread: cf. F. panade. See Pantry.] Bread boiled in water to the consistence of pulp, and sweetened or flavored. [Written also panado.]

panama.c: Panama hat Pan`a*ma" hat` (?). A fine plaited hat, made in Central America of the young leaves of a plant (Carludovica palmata).

panamanian.c: Panamanian Pan`a*ma"ni*an (?), a. Of or pert. to Panama. -- n. A native or citizen of Panama.

panamerican.c: Pan-American Pan`-A*mer"i*can (?), a. [See Pan-.] Of or pertaining to both North and South America.

Pan-American Congress Pan-American Congress. Any of several meetings of delegates from various American states; esp.: (a) One held in 1889-90 in the United States, at which all the independent states except Santo Domingo were represented and of which the practical result was the establishment of the Bureau of American Republics for the promotion of trade relations. (b) One held in Mexico in 1901-1902. (c) One held at Rio de Janeiro in 1906.

panamericanism.c: Pan-Americanism Pan-A*mer"i*can*ism, n. The principle or advocacy of a political alliance or union of all the states of America.
