peregrine.c: Peregrine Per"e*grine (pĕr"e*grĭn; 277), a. [L. peregrinus. See Pilgrim.] Foreign; not native; extrinsic or from without; exotic. [Spelt also pelegrine.] “Peregrine and preternatural heat.” Bacon.

peregrinity.c: Peregrinity Per`e*grin"i*ty (pĕr`e*grĭn"ĭty̆), n. [L. peregrinitas: cf. F. pérégrinité.] 1. Foreignness; strangeness. [Obs.] “Somewhat of a peregrinity in their dialect.” Johnson.

perempt.c: Perempt Per*empt" (?), v. t. [L. peremptus, p. p. of perimere to take away entirely, to destroy; per (see Per-) + OL. emere to take. See Redeem.] (Law) To destroy; to defeat. [R.] Ayliffe.

peremption.c: Peremption Per*emp"tion (?), n. [L. peremptio: cf. F. péremption.] (Law) A quashing; a defeating. [Obs.]

peremptorily.c: Peremptorily Per"emp*to*ri*ly (?), adv. In a peremptory manner; absolutely; positively. Bacon.

peremptoriness.c: Peremptoriness Per"emp*to*ri*ness, n. The quality of being peremptory; positiveness.

peremptory.c: Peremptory Per"emp*to*ry (?), a. [L. peremptorius destructive, deadly, decisive, final: cf. F. péremptorie. See Perempt.] 1. Precluding debate or expostulation; not admitting of question or appeal; positive; absolute; decisive; conclusive; final.

perennial.c: Perennial Per*en"ni*al (pĕr*ĕn"nĭ*ail), a. [L. perennis that lasts the whole year through; per through + annus year. See Per-, and Annual.] 1. Lasting or continuing through the year; as, perennial fountains.
Perennial Per*en"ni*al, n. (Bot.) A perennial plant; a plant which lives or continues more than two years, whether it retains its leaves in winter or not.

perennially.c: Perennially Per*en"ni*al*ly, adv. In a perennial manner.

perennibranchiata.c: Perennibranchiata ‖Per*en`ni*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Perennial, and Branchia.] (Zool.) Those Batrachia which retain their gills through life, as the menobranchus.

perennibranchiate.c: Perennibranchiate Per*en`ni*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [See Perennial, and Branchiate.] 1. (Anat.) Having branchæ, or gills, through life; -- said especially of certain Amphibia, like the menobranchus. Opposed to caducibranchiate.

perennity.c: Perennity Per*en"ni*ty (pĕr*ĕn"nĭ*yy̆), n. [L. perennitas.] The quality of being perennial. [R.] Derham.

pererration.c: Pererration Per`er*ra"tion (?), n. [L. pererrare, pererratum, to wander through.] A wandering, or rambling, through various places. [R.] Howell.

perfect.c: Perfect Per"fect (pẽr"fĕkt), a. [OE. parfit, OF. parfit, parfet, parfait, F. parfait, L. perfectus, p. p. of perficere to carry to the end, to perform, finish, perfect; per (see Per-) + facere to make, do. See Fact.] 1. Brought to consummation or completeness; completed; not defective nor redundant; having all the properties or qualities requisite to its nature and kind; without flaw, fault, or blemish; without error; mature; whole; pure; sound; right; correct.
Perfect Per"fect (pẽr"fĕkt), n. The perfect tense, or a form in that tense.

Perfect Per"fect (pẽr*fĕkt" or pẽr"fĕkt; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perfected; p. pr. & vb. n. Perfecting.] [L. perfectus, p. p. of perficere. See Perfect, a.] To make perfect; to finish or complete, so as to leave nothing wanting; to give to anything all that is requisite to its nature and kind.

perfecter.c: Perfecter Per"fect*er (?), n. One who, or that which, makes perfect. “The... perfecter of our faith.” Barrow.

perfectibilian.c: Perfectibilian Per*fect`i*bil"i*an (?), n. A perfectionist. [R.] Ed. Rev.

perfectibilist.c: Perfectibilist Per`fec*tib"i*list (?), n. A perfectionist. See also Illuminati, 2. [R.]

perfectibility.c: Perfectibility Per*fect`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. perfectibilité.] The quality or state of being perfectible.

perfectible.c: Perfectible Per*fect"i*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. perfectible.] Capable of becoming, or being made, perfect.

perfection.c: Perfection Per*fec"tion (?), n. [F. perfection, L. perfectio.] 1. The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; entire development; consummate culture, skill, or moral excellence; the highest attainable state or degree of excellence; maturity; as, perfection in an art, in a science, or in a system; perfection in form or degree; fruits in perfection.
Perfection Per*fec"tion, v. t. To perfect. [Obs.] Foote.

perfectional.c: Perfectional Per*fec"tion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to perfection; characterized by perfection. [R.] Bp. Pearson.

perfectionate.c: Perfectionate Per*fec"tion*ate (?), v. t. To perfect. Dryden.

perfectionism.c: Perfectionism Per*fec"tion*ism (?), n. 1. The doctrine of the Perfectionists.

perfectionist.c: Perfectionist Per*fec"tion*ist, n. 1. One pretending to perfection; esp., one pretending to moral perfection; one who believes that persons may and do attain to moral perfection and sinlessness in this life. South.

perfectionment.c: Perfectionment Per*fec"tion*ment (?), n. [Cf. F. perfectionnement.] The act of bringing to perfection, or the state of having attained to perfection. [R.] I. Taylor.

perfective.c: Perfective Per*fect"ive (pẽr*fĕk"tĭv), a. 1. Tending or conducing to make perfect, or to bring to perfection; -- usually followed by of. “A perfective alteration.” Fuller.

perfectively.c: Perfectively Per*fec"tive*ly, adv. In a perfective manner.

perfectly.c: Perfectly Per"fect*ly (?), adv. In a perfect manner or degree; in or to perfection; completely; wholly; thoroughly; faultlessly. “Perfectly divine.” Milton.

perfectness.c: Perfectness Per"fect*ness, n. The quality or state of being perfect; perfection. “Charity, which is the bond of perfectness.” Col. iii. 14.

perfervid.c: Perfervid Per*fer"vid (?), a. [Pref. per- + fervid.] Very fervid; too fervid; glowing; ardent.

perficient.c: Perficient Per*fi"cient (?), a. [L. perficiens, p. pr. of perficere to perform. See Perfect.] Making or doing thoroughly; efficient; effectual. [R.] Blackstone.
Perficient Per*fi"cient, n. One who performs or perfects a work; especially, one who endows a charity. [R.]

perfidious.c: Perfidious Per*fid"i*ous (pẽr*fĭd"ĭ*ŭs; 277), a. [L. perfidious.] 1. Guilty of perfidy; violating good faith or vows; false to trust or confidence reposed; treacherous; faithless; as, a perfidious friend. Shak.

perfidiously.c: Perfidiously Per*fid"i*ous*ly, adv. In a perfidious manner.

perfidiousness.c: Perfidiousness Per*fid"i*ous*ness, n. The quality of being perfidious; perfidy. Clarendon.

perfidy.c: Perfidy Per"fi*dy (pẽr"fĭ*dy̆), n.; pl. Perfidies (pẽr"fĭ*dĭz). [L. perfidia, fr. L. perfidus faithless; per (cf. Skr. parā away) + fides faith: cf. F. perfidie. See Faith.] The act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of a promise or vow, or of trust reposed; faithlessness; treachery.

perfix.c: Perfix Per*fix" (pẽr"fĭks), v. t. [Pref. per- + fix.] To fix surely; to appoint. [Obs.]

perflable.c: Perflable Per"fla*ble (?), a. [L. perflabilis. See Perflate.] Capable of being blown through. [Obs.]

perflate.c: Perflate Per*flate" (?), v. t. [L. perflatus, p. p. of perflare to blow through.] To blow through. [Obs.] Harvey.

perflation.c: Perflation Per*fla"tion (?), n. [L. perflatio.] The act of perflating. [Obs.] Woodward.

perfoliate.c: Perfoliate Per*fo"li*ate (?), a. [Pref. per- + L. folium leaf.] 1. (Bot.) Having the basal part produced around the stem; -- said of leaves which the stem apparently passes directory through.

perforata.c: Perforata Per`fo*ra"ta (pẽr`fo*rā"tȧ), n. pl. [NL. See Perforate.] (Zool.) (a) A division of corals including those that have a porous texture, as Porites and Madrepora; -- opposed to Aporosa. (b) A division of Foraminifera, including those having perforated shells.

perforate.c: Perforate Per"fo*rate (pẽr"fo*rāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perforated (pẽr"fo*rā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Perforating.] [L. perforatus, p. p. of perforare to perforate; per through + forare to bore. See Bore, v.] To bore through; to pierce through with a pointed instrument; to make a hole or holes through by boring or piercing; to pierce or penetrate the surface of. Bacon.

perforated.c: Perforated Perforate { Per"fo*rate (pẽr"fo*rat), Per"fo*ra`ted (pẽr"fo*rā"tĕd), } a. Pierced with a hole or holes, or with pores; having transparent dots resembling holes.

perforation.c: Perforation Per`fo*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. perforation.] 1. The act of perforating, or of boring or piercing through. Bacon.

perforative.c: Perforative Per"fo*ra*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. perforatif.] Having power to perforate or pierce.

perforator.c: Perforator Per"fo*ra`tor (?), n. [Cf. F. perforateur.] One who, or that which, perforates; esp., a cephalotome.

perforce.c: Perforce Per*force" (?), adv. [F. par (L. per) + force.] By force; of necessity; at any rate. Shak.
Perforce Per*force", v. t. To force; to compel. [Obs.]

perform.c: Perform Per*form" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Performed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Performing.] [OE. performen, parfourmen, parfournen, OF. parfornir, parfournir, to finish, complete; OF. & F. par (see Par) + fournir to finish, complete. The word has been influenced by form; cf. L. performare to form thoroughly. See Furnish.] 1. To carry through; to bring to completion; to achieve; to accomplish; to execute; to do.

Perform Per*form", v. i. To do, execute, or accomplish something; to acquit one's self in any business; esp., to represent sometimes by action; to act a part; to play on a musical instrument; as, the players perform poorly; the musician performs on the organ.

performable.c: Performable Per*form"a*ble (?), a. Admitting of being performed, done, or executed; practicable.

performance.c: Performance Per*form"ance (?), n. The act of performing; the carrying into execution or action; execution; achievement; accomplishment; representation by action; as, the performance of an undertaking of a duty.

performer.c: Performer Per*form"er (?), n. One who performs, accomplishes, or fulfills; as, a good promiser, but a bad performer; especially, one who shows skill and training in any art; as, a performer of the drama; a performer on the harp.

perfricate.c: Perfricate Per"fri*cate (?), v. t. [L. perfricatus, p. p. of perfricare.] To rub over. Bailey.

perfumatory.c: Perfumatory Per*fu"ma*to*ry (?), a. Emitting perfume; perfuming. [R.] Sir E. Leigh.

perfume.c: Perfume Per*fume" (pẽr*fūm"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perfumed (pẽr*fūmd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Perfuming.] [F. parfumer (cf. Sp. perfumar); par (see Par) + fumer to smoke, L. fumare, fr. fumus smoke. See Fume.] To fill or impregnate with a perfume; to scent.

Perfume Per"fume (pẽr"fūm or pẽr*fūm"; 277), n. [F. parfum; cf. Sp. perfume. See Perfume, v.] 1. The scent, odor, or odoriferous particles emitted from a sweet-smelling substance; a pleasant odor; fragrance; aroma.

perfumer.c: Perfumer Per*fum"er (pẽr*fūm"ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, perfumes.

perfunctorily.c: Perfunctorily Per*func"to*ri*ly (pẽr*fŭṉk"to*rĭ*ly̆), adv. In a perfunctory manner; formally; carelessly. Boyle.

perfunctoriness.c: Perfunctoriness Per*func"to*ri*ness, n. The quality or state of being perfunctory.

perfunctory.c: Perfunctory Per*func"to*ry (pẽr*fŭṉk"to*ry̆), a. [L. perfunctorius, fr. perfunctus dispatched, p. p. of perfungi to discharge, dispatch; per (see Per) + fungi to perform. See Function.] 1. Done merely to get rid of a duty; performed mechanically and as a thing of rote; done in a careless and superficial manner; characterized by indifference; as, perfunctory admonitions; a perfunctory greeting. Macaulay.

perfuncturate.c: Perfuncturate Per*func"tu*rate (?), v. t. To perform in a perfunctory manner; to do negligently. [R.]

perfuse.c: Perfuse Per*fuse" (pẽr*fūz"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perfused (pẽr*fūzd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Perfusing.] [L. perfusus, p. p. of perfundere to pour over; per + fundere to pour.] 1. To suffuse; to fill full or to excess. Harvey.

perfusion.c: Perfusion Per*fu"sion (?), n. [L. perfusio.] The act of perfusing.

perfusive.c: Perfusive Per*fu"sive (?), a. Of a nature to flow over, or to spread through.

pergamentaceous.c: Pergamentaceous Pergamenous { Per`ga*me"no*us (?), Per`ga*men*ta"ceous (?), } a. [L. pergamena parchment. See Parchment.] Like parchment.

pergola.c: Pergola Per"go*la (?), n. [It., fr. L. pergula shed, shop, vine arbor.] Lit., an arbor or bower; specif.: (Italian art) An arbor or trellis treated architecturally, as with stone columns or similar massive structure.

pergolo.c: Pergolo ‖Per"go*lo (?), n. [It.] A continuous colonnade or arcade; -- applied to the decorative groups of windows, as in Venetian palazzi.

perhaps.c: Perhaps Per*haps" (pẽr*hăps"), adv. [Per + hap chance.] Posibly; by chance; peradventure; perchance; it may be.

peri.c: Peri- Per"i- (pĕr"ĭ-). [Gr. peri`, prep.] A prefix used to signify around, by, near, over, beyond, or to give an intensive sense; as, perimeter, the measure around; perigee, point near the earth; periergy, work beyond what is needed; perispherical, quite spherical.

Peri Pe"ri (pē"rĭ), n.; pl. Peris (pē"rĭz). [Per. perī a female genus, a fairy.] (Persian Myth.) An imaginary being, male or female, like an elf or fairy, represented as a descendant of fallen angels, excluded from paradise till penance is accomplished. Moore.

perianth.c: Perianth Per"i*anth (pĕr"ĭ*ănth), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr. 'anqos flower: cf. F. périanthe.] (Bot.) (a) The leaves of a flower generally, especially when the calyx and corolla are not readily distinguished. (b) A saclike involucre which incloses the young fruit in most hepatic mosses. See Illust. of Hepatica.

periapt.c: Periapt Per"i*apt (pĕr"ĭ*ăpt), n. [Gr. peri`apton, fr. peri`aptos hung about, peria`ptein to hang about; peri` about + 'a`ptein to tie: cf. F. périapte.] A charm worn as a protection against disease or mischief; an amulet. Coleridge.

periastral.c: Periastral Per`i*as"tral (?), a. Among or around the stars. “Comets in periastral passage.” R. A. Proctor.

periastron.c: Periastron Per`i*as"tron (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about + 'a`stron a star.] (Astron.) That point, in the real or apparent orbit of one star revolving around another, at which the former is nearest to the latter.

periauger.c: Periauger Per"i*au"ger (?), n. See Pirogue. W. Irving.

periblast.c: Periblast Per"i*blast (?), a. [Gr. periblasta`nein to grow around. See Peri-, and -blast.] (Biol.) The protoplasmic matter which surrounds the entoblast, or cell nucleus, and undergoes segmentation. -- Per`i*blas"tic, a.

periblem.c: Periblem Per"i*blem (?), n. [Pref. peri- + root of Gr.? to sprout.] (Bot.) Nascent cortex, or immature cellular bark.

peribolos.c: Peribolos ‖Pe*rib"o*los (?), n. [Nl., fr. Gr. peri`bolos, fr. peri`bolos, adj., going round, fr. periba`llein to throw round; cf. L. peribolus.] In ancient architecture, an inclosed court, esp., one surrounding a temple.

peribranchial.c: Peribranchial Per`i*bran"chi*al (?), a. (Anat.) Surrounding the branchiæ; as, a peribranchial cavity.

peribronchial.c: Peribronchial Per`i*bron"chi*al (?), a. (Anat.) Around the bronchi or bronchial tubes; as, the peribronchial lymphatics.

pericambium.c: Pericambium ‖Per`i*cam"bi*um (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Cambium.] (Biol.) A layer of thin-walled young cells in a growing stem, in which layer certain new vessels originate.

pericardial.c: Pericardial Pericardiac { Per`i*car"di*ac (?), Per`i*car"di*al (?), } a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to pericardium; situated around the heart.

pericarditus.c: Pericarditus ‖Per`i*car*di"tus (?), n. [NL. See Pericardium, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the pericardium. Dunglison.

pericardium.c: Pericardium Per`i*car"di*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. perika`rdion, fr. perika`rdios about or near the heart; peri` about + kardi`a heart.] (Anat.) The double baglike fold of serous membrane which incloses the heart.

pericarp.c: Pericarp Per"i*carp (?), n. [Gr. perika`rpion; peri` around + karpo`s fruit: cf. F. péricarpe.] (Bot.) The ripened ovary; the walls of the fruit. See Illusts. of Capsule, Drupe, and Legume.

pericarpic.c: Pericarpic Pericarpial { Per`i*car"pi*al (?), Per`i*car"pic (?) }, a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to a pericarp.

pericellular.c: Pericellular Per`i*cel"lu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Surrounding a cell; as, the pericellular lymph spaces surrounding ganglion cells.

perichaeth.c: Perichaeth Per"i*chaeth (?), n. [See Perichaetium.] (Bot.) The leafy involucre surrounding the fruit stalk of mosses; perichaetium; perichete.

perichaetial.c: Perichaetial Per`i*chae"ti*al (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to the perichæth.

perichaetium.c: Perichaetium ‖Per`i*chae"ti*um (?), n.; pl. Perichaetia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. about +? flowing hair, foliage.] (Bot.) Same as Perichæth.

perichaetous.c: Perichaetous Per`i*chæ"tous (?), a. [See Perichætium.] (Zool.) Surrounded by setæ; -- said of certain earthworms (genus Perichætus).

perichondrial.c: Perichondrial Per`i*chon"dri*al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the perichondrium; situated around cartilage.

perichondritis.c: Perichondritis ‖Per`i*chon*dri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Perichondrium, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the perichondrium.

perichondrium.c: Perichondrium ‖Per`i*chon"dri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` around + cho`ndros cartilage.] (Anat.) The membrane of fibrous connective tissue which closely invests cartilage, except where covering articular surfaces.

perichordal.c: Perichordal Per`i*chor"dal (?), a. Around the notochord; as, a perichordal column. See Epichordal.

periclasite.c: Periclasite Periclase { Per"i*clase (?), Per`i*cla"site (?), } n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? to break.] (Min.) A grayish or dark green mineral, consisting essentially of magnesia (magnesium oxide), occurring in granular forms or in isometric crystals.

periclinium.c: Periclinium ‖Per`i*clin"i*um (?), n.; pl. Periclinia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. peri` around +? a bed.] (Bot.) The involucre which surrounds the common receptacle in composite flowers.

periclitate.c: Periclitate Pe*ric"li*tate (?), v. t. [L. periclitatus, p. p. of periclitari, fr. periculum.] To endanger. [Obs.]

periclitation.c: Periclitation Pe*ric`li*ta"tion (?), n. [L. periclitatio: cf. F. périclitation.] 1. Trial; experiment. [Obs.]

pericope.c: Pericope ‖Pe*ric"o*pe (?), n. [L., section of a book, Gr.?; peri` around +? to cut.] A selection or extract from a book; especially (Theol.), a selection from the Bible, appointed to be read in the churches or used as a text for a sermon.

pericranial.c: Pericranial Per`i*cra"ni*al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the pericranium.

pericranium.c: Pericranium Per`i*cra"ni*um (?), n. [NL.] (Anat.) The periosteum which covers the cranium externally; the region around the cranium.

periculous.c: Periculous Pe*ric"u*lous (?), a. [L. periculosus. See Perilous.] Dangerous; full of peril. [Obs.]

periculum.c: Periculum ‖Pe*ric"u*lum (?), n.; pl. Pericula (#). [L.] (Rom. & O.Eng. Law) 1. Danger; risk.

pericystitis.c: Pericystitis Per`i*cys*ti"tis (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Cystitis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the tissues surrounding the bladder.

periderm.c: Periderm Per"i*derm (?), n. 1. (Bot.) The outer layer of bark.

peridiastole.c: Peridiastole ‖Per`i*di*as"to*le (?), n. (Physiol.) The almost inappreciable time which elapses between the systole and the diastole of the heart.

peridium.c: Peridium ‖Pe*rid"i*um (?), n.; pl. Peridia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about +?, a dim. ending.] (Bot.) The envelope or coat of certain fungi, such as the puffballs and earthstars.

peridotite.c: Peridotite Per"i*do*tite (?), n. [Cf. F. péridotite.] (Min.) An eruptive rock characterized by the presence of chrysolite (peridot). It also usually contains pyroxene, enstatite, chromite, etc. It is often altered to serpentine.

peridrome.c: Peridrome Per"i*drome (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? running around, fr.? to run round; peri` round +? to run: cf. F. péridrome.] (Archæol.) The space between the columns and the wall of the cella, in a Greek or a Roman temple.

perienteron.c: Perienteron ‖Per`i*en"te*ron (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Enteron.] (Anat.) The primitive perivisceral cavity.

periergy.c: Periergy Per"i*er`gy (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? overcareful; peri` about, beyond +? work.] 1. Excessive care or diligence. [Obs.]

periganglionic.c: Periganglionic Per`i*gan`gli*on"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Surrounding a ganglion; as, the periganglionic glands of the frog.

perigastric.c: Perigastric Per`i*gas"tric (?), a. (Zool.) Surrounding the stomach; -- applied to the body cavity of Bryozoa and various other Invertebrata.

perigean.c: Perigean Per`i*ge"an (?), a. Pertaining to the perigee.

perigeum.c: Perigeum Perigee { Per"i*gee (?), Per`i*ge"um (?), } n. [NL. perigeum, fr. Gr. peri` about, near + gh^ the earth: cf. F. périgée.] (Astron.) That point, in the orbit of the moon or other body orbiting the earth, which is nearest to the earth; -- opposed to apogee. It is sometimes, but rarely, used of the nearest points of bodies not orbiting the earth, such as of a comet, a planet, etc. Called also epigee, epigeum.

perigenesis.c: Perigenesis Per`i*gen"e*sis (?), n. (Biol.) A theory which explains inheritance by the transmission of the type of growth force possessed by one generation to another.

perigenetic.c: Perigenetic Per`i*gen"e*tic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to perigenesis.

perigone.c: Perigone Per"i*gone (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? productive organs.] 1. (Bot.) (a) Any organ inclosing the essential organs of a flower; a perianth. (b) In mosses, the involucral bracts of a male flower.

perigonium.c: Perigonium ‖Per`i*go"ni*um (?), n.; pl. Perigonia (#). [NL.] Same as Perigone.

perigord.c: Perigord pie Per"i*gord pie` (?). [From Périgord, a former province of France.] A pie made of truffles, much esteemed by epicures.

perigraph.c: Perigraph Per"i*graph (?), n. [Gr.? outline;? round, about +? to write.] A careless or inaccurate delineation of anything. [R.]

perigynium.c: Perigynium ‖Per`i*gyn"i*um (?), n.; pl. Perigynia (#). [NL. See Perigynous.] (Bot.) Some unusual appendage about the pistil, as the bottle-shaped body in the sedges, and the bristles or scales in some other genera of the Sedge family, or Cyperaceæ.

perigynous.c: Perigynous Pe*rig"y*nous (?), a. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? woman.] (Bot.) Having the ovary free, but the petals and stamens borne on the calyx; -- said of a flower such as that of the cherry or peach.

perihelium.c: Perihelium Perihelion { Per`i*hel"ion (?), Per`i*he"li*um (?), } n.; pl. Perihelia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about, near + "h`lios the sun.] (Astron.) That point of the orbit of a planet or comet which is nearest to the sun; -- opposed to aphelion.

peril.c: Peril Per"il (?), n. [F. péril, fr. L. periculum, periclum, akin to peritus experienced, skilled, and E. fare. See Fare, and cf. Experience.] Danger; risk; hazard; jeopardy; exposure of person or property to injury, loss, or destruction.
Peril Per"il, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Periled (?) or Perilled; p. pr. & vb. n. Periling or Perilling.] To expose to danger; to hazard; to risk; as, to peril one's life.
Peril Per"il (?), v. i. To be in danger. [Obs.] Milton.

perilla.c: Perilla ‖Pe*ril"la (?), prop. n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Bot.) A genus of labiate herbs, of which one species (Perilla ocimoides, or Perilla Nankinensis) is often cultivated for its purple or variegated foliage.

perilous.c: Perilous Per"il*ous (?), a. [OF. perillous, perilleus, F. périlleux, L. periculosus. See Peril.] [Written also perillous.] 1. Full of, attended with, or involving, peril; dangerous; hazardous; as, a perilous undertaking.

perilymph.c: Perilymph Per"i*lymph (?), n. (Anat.) The fluid which surrounds the membranous labyrinth of the internal ear, and separates it from the walls of the chambers in which the labyrinth lies.

perilymphangial.c: Perilymphangial Per`i*lym*phan"gi*al (?), a. (Anat.) Around, or at the side of, a lymphatic vessel.

perilymphatic.c: Perilymphatic Per`i*lym*phat"ic (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Pertaining to, or containing, perilymph. (b) Perilymphangial.

perimeter.c: Perimeter Per*im"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.?; peri` around +? measure: cf. F. périmètre.] 1. (Geom.) The outer boundary of a body or figure, or the sum of all the sides.

perimetrical.c: Perimetrical Perimetric { Per`i*met"ric (?), Per`i*met"ric*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to the perimeter, or to perimetry; as, a perimetric chart of the eye.

perimetry.c: Perimetry Per*im"e*try (?), n. The art of using the perimeter; measurement of the field of vision.

perimorph.c: Perimorph Per"i*morph (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr. morfh` form.] (Min.) A crystal of one species inclosing one of another species. See Endomorph.

perimysial.c: Perimysial Per`i*my"sial (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Surrounding a muscle or muscles. (b) Of or pertaining to the perimysium.

perimysium.c: Perimysium ‖Per`i*my"si*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about + my^s muscle.] (Anat.) The connective tissue sheath which surrounds a muscle, and sends partitions inwards between the bundles of muscular fibers.

perineal.c: Perineal Per`i*ne"al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the perineum.

perineoplasty.c: Perineoplasty Per`i*ne"o*plas`ty (?), n. [Perineum + -plasty.] (Med.) The act or process of restoring an injured perineum.

perineorrhaphy.c: Perineorrhaphy Per`i*ne*or"rha*phy (?), n. [Perineum + Gr.? to sew.] (Med.) The operation of sewing up a ruptured perineum.

perinephritis.c: Perinephritis ‖Per`i*ne*phri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Nephritis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the cellular tissue around the kidney. -- Per`i*ne*phrit"ic, a.

perineum.c: Perineum ‖Per`i*ne"um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri`naion about + peri`neos.] (Anat.) The region which is included within the outlet of the pelvis, and is traversed by the urinogenital canal and the rectum.

perineurial.c: Perineurial Per`i*neu"ri*al (?), a. (Anat.) Surrounding nerves or nerve fibers; of or pertaining to the perineurium.

perineurium.c: Perineurium ‖Per`i*neu"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about + ney^ron a nerve.] (Anat.) The connective tissue sheath which surrounds a bundle of nerve fibers. See Epineurium, and Neurilemma.

perinuclear.c: Perinuclear Per`i*nu"cle*ar (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to a nucleus; situated around a nucleus; as, the perinuclear protoplasm.

period.c: Period Pe"ri*od (?), n. [L. periodus, Gr. peri`odos a going round, a way round, a circumference, a period of time; peri` round, about + "odo`s a way: cf. F. période.] 1. A portion of time as limited and determined by some recurring or cyclic phenomenon, as by the completion of a revolution of one of the heavenly bodies; a division of time, as a series of years, months, or days, in which something is completed, and ready to recommence and go on in the same order; as, the period of the sun, or the earth, or a comet; the period of an electromagnetic wave is the time interval between maxima.
Period Pe"ri*od (pē"rĭ*ŭd), v. t. To put an end to. [Obs.] Shak.
Period Pe"ri*od, v. i. To come to a period; to conclude. [Obs.] “You may period upon this, that,” etc. Felthman.

periodate.c: Periodate Per*i"o*date (pẽr*ī"o*dāt), n. (Chem.) A salt of periodic acid.

periodic.c: Periodic Per`i*od"ic (pẽr`i*ŏd"ĭk), a. [Pref. per- + iodic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, the highest oxygen acid (HIO4) of iodine.

periodical.c: Periodical Periodic { Pe`ri*od"ic (pē`rĭ*ŏd"ĭk), Pe`ri*od"ic*al (pē`rĭ*ŏd"ĭ*kail), } a. [L. periodicus, Gr. periodiko`s: cf. F. périodique.] 1. Of or pertaining to a period or periods, or to division by periods.
Periodical Pe`ri*od"ic*al, n. A magazine or other publication which appears at stated or regular intervals.

periodicalist.c: Periodicalist Pe`ri*od"ic*al*ist, n. One who publishes, or writes for, a periodical.

periodically.c: Periodically Pe`ri*od"ic*al*ly, adv. In a periodical{4} manner; as, flooding occurs periodically in the valley.

periodicity.c: Periodicity Pe`ri*o*dic"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Periodicities (#). [Cf. F. périodicité.] The quality or state of being periodical, or regularly recurrent; as, the periodicity in the vital phenomena of plants. Henfrey.

periodide.c: Periodide Per*i"o*dide (?), n. [Pref. per- + iodide.] An iodide containing a higher proportion of iodine than any other iodide of the same substance or series.

periodontal.c: Periodontal Per`i*o*don"tal (pĕr*ĭ*o*dŏn"tail), a. [Pref. peri- + Gr. 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, tooth.] (Anat.) Surrounding the teeth.

periodoscope.c: Periodoscope Pe`ri*od"o*scope (?), n. [Period + -scope.] (Med.) A table or other means for calculating the periodical functions of women. Dunglison.

perioecians.c: Perioecians Perioeci { ‖Per`i*œ"ci, Per`i*œ"cians, } n. pl. [NL. perioeci, fr. Gr.?; peri` around +? house, dwelling.] Those who live on the same parallel of latitude but on opposite meridians, so that it is noon in one place when it is midnight in the other. Compare Antœci.

periople.c: Periople Per"i*o*ple (?), n. [F. périople, from Gr. peri` about +? the hoof of a horse.] (Anat.) The external smooth horny layer of the hoof of the horse and allied animals.

perioplic.c: Perioplic Per`i*op"lic (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the periople; connected with the periople.

periosteal.c: Periosteal Per`i*os"te*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated around bone; of or pertaining to the periosteum.

periosteum.c: Periosteum ‖Per`i*os"te*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. perio`steos round the bones; peri` around + 'oste`on a bone: cf. L. periosteon.] (Anat.) The membrane of fibrous connective tissue which closely invests all bones except at the articular surfaces.

periostitis.c: Periostitis ‖Per`i*os*ti"tis (?), n. [NL. See Periosteum, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the periosteum.

periostracum.c: Periostracum ‖Per`i*os"tra*cum (?), n.; pl. Periostraca (#). [NL., fr. Gr. peri` around +? shell of a testacean.] (Zool.) A chitinous membrane covering the exterior of many shells; -- called also epidermis.

periotic.c: Periotic Per`i*o"tic (?), a. [Pref. peri- + Gr.?,?, the ear.] (Anat.) Surrounding, or pertaining to the region surrounding, the internal ear; as, the periotic capsule. -- n. A periotic bone.

peripatetic.c: Peripatetic Per`i*pa*tet"ic (?), a. [L. peripateticus, Gr.?, fr.? to walk about; peri` about +? to walk: cf. F. péripatétique.] 1. Walking about; itinerant.
Peripatetic Per`i*pa*tet"ic, n. 1. One who walks about; a pedestrian; an itinerant. Tatler.

peripateticism.c: Peripateticism Per`i*pa*tet"i*cism (?), n. [Cf. F. péripatétisme.] The doctrines or philosophical system of the peripatetics. See Peripatetic, n., 2. Lond. Sat. Rev.

peripatus.c: Peripatus Peripatopsis Pe`ri*pa*top"sis, Pe*rip"a*tus prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri`patos a walking about.] (Zool.) The type genus of Peripatopsidae, consisting of onychophorans (lowly organized invertebrates related evolutionarily to the arthropods, also called “walking worms” AND “velvet worms”) found chiefly in Asiatic and African tropical regions, in South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and tropical America.

peripetalous.c: Peripetalous Per`i*pet"al*ous (?), a. (Bot.) Surrounding, or situated about, the petals.

peripheral.c: Peripheral Pe*riph"er*al (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a periphery; constituting a periphery; peripheric.

peripherical.c: Peripherical Peripheric { Per`i*pher"ic (?), Per`i*pher"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. périphérique. See Periphery.] See Peripheral.

periphery.c: Periphery Pe*riph"er*y (?), n.; pl. Peripheries (#). [L. peripheria, Gr. perife`reia; peri` around + fe`rein to bear, carry: cf. F. périphérie.] 1. The outside or superficial portions of a body; the surface.

periphrase.c: Periphrase Per"i*phrase (?), n. [L. periphrasis, Gr.?, fr.? to think about, to be expressed periphrastically;? +? to speak: cf. F. périphrase. See Phrase.] (Rhet.) The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocution. “To describe by enigmatic periphrases.” De Quincey.
Periphrase Per"i*phrase, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Periphrased (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Periphrasing.] [Cf. F. périphraser.] To express by periphrase or circumlocution.
Periphrase Per"i*phrase, v. i. To use circumlocution.

periphrastical.c: Periphrastical Periphrastic { Per`i*phras"tic (?), Per`i*phras"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?: cf. F. périphrastique.] Expressing, or expressed, in more words than are necessary; characterized by periphrase; circumlocutory.

periplast.c: Periplast Per"i*plast (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? to mold, form.] (Biol.) Same as Periblast. -- Per`i*plas"tic (#), a. Huxley.

peripneumony.c: Peripneumony Peripneumonia { ‖Per`ip*neu*mo"ni*a (?), Per`ip*neu"mo*ny (?), } n. [L. peripneumonia, Gr.?: cf. F. péripneumonie. See Peri-, Pneumonia.] (Med.) Pneumonia. [Obsoles.]

peripneumonic.c: Peripneumonic Per`ip*neu*mon"ic (?), a. [L. peripneumonicus, Gr.?: cf. F. péripneumonique.] (Med.) Of or pertaining to peripneumonia.

periproct.c: Periproct Per"i*proct (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? the anus.] (Zool.) The region surrounding the anus, particularly of echinoderms.

periproctitis.c: Periproctitis ‖Per`i*proc*ti"tis (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Proctitus.] (Med.) Inflammation of the tissues about the rectum.

peripteral.c: Peripteral Pe*rip"ter*al (?), a. [Gr., fr.? +? feather, wing, row of columns.] (Arch.) Having columns on all sides; -- said of an edifice. See Apteral.

periptery.c: Periptery Pe*rip"ter*y (?), n. [Gr.? flying round about.] The region surrounding a moving body, such as the wing of a bird or a gliding aëroplane, within which cyclic or vortical motion of the air occur.

perique.c: Perique Pe*rique" (?), n. [Louisiana F.] A kind of tobacco with medium-sized leaf, small stem, tough and gummy fiber, raised in Louisiana, and cured in its own juices, so as to be very dark colored, usually black. It is marketed in tightly wrapped rolls called carottes.

perisarc.c: Perisarc Per"i*sarc (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.?,?, flesh.] (Zool.) The outer, hardened integument which covers most hydroids.

periscian.c: Periscian Pe*ris"cian (?), a. [Gr.?; peri` around +? shadow: cf. F. périscien.] Having the shadow moving all around.

periscii.c: Periscii Periscians { Pe*ris"cians (?), ‖Pe*ris"ci*i (?), } n. pl. [NL. See Periscian.] Those who live within a polar circle, whose shadows, during some summer days, will move entirely round, falling toward every point of the compass.

periscope.c: Periscope Per"i*scope (?), n. [Pref. peri- + -scope.] A general or comprehensive view. [archaic]

periscopic.c: Periscopic Per`i*scop"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. périscopique.] Viewing all around, or on all sides.

perish.c: Perish Per"ish (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Perished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perishing.] [OE. perissen, perisshen, F. périr, p. pr. périssant, L. perire to go or run through, come to nothing, perish; per through + ire to go. Cf. Issue, and see -ish.] To be destroyed; to pass away; to become nothing; to be lost; to die; hence, to wither; to waste away.
Perish Per"ish, v. t. To cause perish. [Obs.] Bacon.

perishable.c: Perishable Per"ish*a*ble (?), a. [F. périssable.] Liable to perish; subject to decay, destruction, or death; as, perishable goods; our perishable bodies.

perishableness.c: Perishableness Per"ish*a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being perishable; liability to decay or destruction. Locke.

perishably.c: Perishably Per"ish*a*bly, adv. In a perishable degree or manner.

perishment.c: Perishment Per"ish*ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. perissement.] The act of perishing. [R.] Udall.

perisoma.c: Perisoma ‖Per`i*so"ma (?), n.; pl. Perisomata (#). [NL.] (Zool.) Same as Perisome.

perisome.c: Perisome Per"i*some (?), n. [Pref. peri- + -some body.] (Zool.) The entire covering of an invertebrate animal, as echinoderm or cœlenterate; the integument.

perisperm.c: Perisperm Per"i*sperm (?), n. [F. périsperme. See Peri-, and Sperm.] (Bot.) The albumen of a seed, especially that portion which is formed outside of the embryo sac. -- Per`i*sper"mic (#), a.

perispherical.c: Perispherical Perispheric { Per`i*spher"ic (?), Per`i*spher"ic*al (?), } a. Exactly spherical; globular.

perispomenon.c: Perispomenon ‖Per`i*spom"e*non (?), n.; pl. Perispomena (#). [NL., from Gr.?, pr. pass. p. of? to draw around, to circumflex; peri` around +? to draw.] (Gr. Gram.) A word which has the circumflex accent on the last syllable. Goodwin.

perispore.c: Perispore Per"i*spore (?), n. (Bot.) The outer covering of a spore.

perissad.c: Perissad Per"is*sad (?), a. [Gr.? odd, from? over.] (Chem.) Odd; not even; -- said of elementary substances and of radicals whose valence is not divisible by two without a remainder. Contrasted with artiad. [Archaic]

perisse.c: Perisse Per"isse (?), v. i. To perish. [Obs.] Chaucer.

perissodactyl.c: Perissodactyl Per`is*so*dac"tyl (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Perissodactyla.

perissodactyla.c: Perissodactyla ‖Per`is*so*dac"ty*la (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? odd (fr.? over) +? finger.] (Zool.) A division of ungulate mammals, including those that have an odd number of toes, as the horse, tapir, and rhinoceros; -- opposed to Artiodactyla.

perissological.c: Perissological Per`is*so*log"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. périssologique.] Redundant or excessive in words. [R.]

perissology.c: Perissology Per`is*sol"o*gy (?), n. [L. perissologia, Gr.?;? odd, superfluous +? discourse.] Superfluity of words. [R.] G. Campbell.

peristalsis.c: Peristalsis ‖Per`i*stal"sis (?), n. [NL. See Peristaltic.] (Physiol.) Peristaltic contraction or action.

peristaltic.c: Peristaltic Per`i*stal"tic (?), a. [Gr.? clasping and compressing, fr.? to surround, wrap up;? round +? to place, arrange: cf. F. péristaltique.] (Physiol.) Pertaining to a wormlike wave motion of the intestines, and by analogy, of other flexible tubular structures. In the body it is produced by a progressive contraction of the muscular fibers of their walls, forcing their contents onwards in the direction of the wave; as, peristaltic movement. -- Per`i*stal"tic*al*ly (#), adv.

peristeria.c: Peristeria ‖Per`is*te"ri*a (?), prop. n. [NL. See Peristerion.] (Bot.) A genus of orchidaceous plants. See Dove plant.

peristerion.c: Peristerion ‖Per`is*te"ri*on (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a dovecote, a kind of verbena, fr. peristera` a dove, pigeon; cf. L. peristereon.] (Bot.) The herb vervain (Verbena officinalis).

peristerite.c: Peristerite Pe*ris"ter*ite (?), n. [Gr. peristera` a pigeon.] (Min.) A variety of albite, whitish and slightly iridescent like a pigeon's neck.

peristeromorphous.c: Peristeromorphous Pe*ris`ter*o*mor"phous (?), a. [Gr. peristera` a pigeon + -morphous.] (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the pigeons or Columbæ.

peristeropodous.c: Peristeropodous Pe*ris`ter*op"o*dous (?), a. [Gr. peristera` a pigeon + poy`s, podo`s, foot.] (Zool.) Having pigeonlike feet; -- said of those gallinaceous birds that rest on all four toes, as the curassows and megapods.

peristole.c: Peristole Pe*ris"to*le (pe*rĭs"to*le), n. [NL.: cf. F. péristole. See Peristaltic.] (Physiol.) Peristaltic action, especially of the intestines.

peristoma.c: Peristoma ‖Pe*ris"to*ma (pe*rĭs"to*mȧ), n.; pl. Peristomata (pĕr`ĭ*stŏm"ȧ*tȧ). [NL.] Same as Peristome.

peristome.c: Peristome Per"i*stome (per"ĭ*stōm), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr. sto`ma, sto`matos, mouth.] 1. (Bot.) The fringe of teeth around the orifice of the capsule of mosses. It consists of 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 teeth, and may be either single or double.

peristomial.c: Peristomial Per`i*sto"mi*al (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to a peristome.

peristrephic.c: Peristrephic Per`i*streph"ic (?), a. [Gr.? to turn round.] Turning around; rotatory; revolving; as, a peristrephic painting (of a panorama).

peristyle.c: Peristyle Per"i*style (?), n. [L. peristylum, Gr. peri`stylon, peri`stylos; peri` about + sty^los a column: cf. F. péristyle.] (Arch.) A range of columns with their entablature, etc.; specifically, a complete system of columns, whether on all sides of a court, or surrounding a building, such as the cella of a temple. Used in the former sense, it gives name to the larger and inner court of a Roman dwelling, the peristyle. See Colonnade.

perisystole.c: Perisystole Per`i*sys"to*le (?), n. [Pref. peri- + systole: cf. F. périsystole.] (Physiol.) The interval between the diastole and systole of the heart. It is perceptible only in the dying.

perithecium.c: Perithecium ‖Per`i*the"ci*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` around +? box.] (Bot.) An organ in certain fungi and lichens, surrounding and enveloping the masses of fructification. Henslow.

peritomous.c: Peritomous Pe*rit"o*mous (?), a. [Gr.? cut off all around. See Peri-, and Tome.] (Min.) Cleaving in more directions than one, parallel to the axis.

peritoneal.c: Peritoneal Per`i*to*ne"al (?), a. [Cf. F. péritonéal.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the peritoneum.

peritoneum.c: Peritoneum Per`i*to*ne"um (?), n. [L. peritoneum, peritonaeum, Gr.?,?, fr.? to stretch all around or over; peri` around +? to stretch.] (Anat.) The smooth serous membrane which lines the cavity of the abdomen, or the whole body cavity when there is no diaphragm, and, turning back, surrounds the viscera, forming a closed, or nearly closed, sac. [Written also peritonæum.]

peritonitis.c: Peritonitis ‖Per`i*to*ni"tis (?), n. [NL. See Peritoneum, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the peritoneum.

peritreme.c: Peritreme Per"i*treme (?), n. [Pref. peri- + Gr.? a hole.] (Zool.) (a) That part of the integument of an insect which surrounds the spiracles. (b) The edge of the aperture of a univalve shell.

peritricha.c: Peritricha ‖Pe*rit"ri*cha (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. peri` about +?,?, hair.] (Zool.) A division of ciliated Infusoria having a circle of cilia around the oral disk and sometimes another around the body. It includes the vorticellas. See Vorticella.

peritrochium.c: Peritrochium ‖Per`i*tro"chi*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?; peri` around +? a wheel.] (Mech.) The wheel which, together with the axle, forms the axis in peritrochio, which see under Axis.

peritropal.c: Peritropal Per*it"ro*pal (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to turn around; peri` around +? to turn: cf. F. péritrope.] 1. Rotatory; circuitous. [R.]

perityphlitis.c: Perityphlitis ‖Per`i*typh*li"tis (?), n. [NL. See Peri-, and Typhlitis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the connective tissue about the cæcum.

perivascular.c: Perivascular Per`i*vas"cu*lar (?), a. Around the blood vessels; as, perivascular lymphatics.

perivisceral.c: Perivisceral Per`i*vis"cer*al (?), a. (Anat.) Around the viscera; as, the perivisceral cavity.

perivitelline.c: Perivitelline Per`i*vi*tel"line (?), a. [Pref. peri- + vitelline.] (Biol.) Situated around the vitellus, or between the vitellus and zona pellucida of an ovum.

periwig.c: Periwig Per"i*wig (pĕr"ĭ*wĭg), n. [OE. perrwige, perwicke, corrupt. fr. F. perruque; cf. OD. peruyk, from French. See Peruke, and cf. Wig.] A headdress of false hair, usually covering the whole head, and representing the natural hair; a wig. Shak.
Periwig Per"i*wig, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perwigged (pĕr"ĭ*wĭgd); p. pr. & vb. n. Perwigging (pĕr"ĭ*wĭg*gĭng).] To dress with a periwig, or with false hair. Swift.

periwinkle.c: Periwinkle Per"i*win`kle (?), n. [From AS. pinewincla a shellfish, in which pine- is fr. L. pina, pinna, a kind of mussel, akin to Gr.?. Cf. Winkle.] (Zool.) Any small marine gastropod shell of the genus Littorina. The common European species (Littorina littorea), in Europe extensively used as food, has recently become naturalized abundantly on the American coast. See Littorina.
Periwinkle Per"i*win`kle, n. [OE. pervenke, AS. pervince, fr. L. pervinca.] (Bot.) A trailing herb of the genus Vinca.

perjenet.c: Perjenet Per"jen*et (?), n. [Cf. Pear, and Jenneting.] A kind of pear. [Obs.] Chaucer.

perjure.c: Perjure Per"jure (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perjured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perjuring.] [F. parjurer, L. perjurare, perjerare; per through, over + jurare to swear. See Jury.] 1. To cause to violate an oath or a vow; to cause to make oath knowingly to what is untrue; to make guilty of perjury; to forswear; to corrupt; -- often used reflexively; as, he perjured himself.
Perjure Per"jure, n. [L. perjurus: cf. OF. parjur, F. parjure.] A perjured person. [Obs.] Shak.

perjured.c: Perjured Per"jured (?), a. Guilty of perjury; having sworn falsely; forsworn. Shak. “Perjured persons.” 1 Tim. i. 10. “Their perjured oath.” Spenser.

perjurer.c: Perjurer Per"jur*er (?), n. One who is guilty of perjury; one who perjures or forswears, in any sense.

perjurous.c: Perjurous Perjurious { Per*ju"ri*ous (?), Per"ju*rous (?), } a. [L. perjuriosus, perjurus.] Guilty of perjury; containing perjury. [Obs.] Quarles. B. Johnson.

perjury.c: Perjury Per"ju*ry (?), n.; pl. Perjuries (#). [L. perjurium. See Perjure, v.] 1. False swearing.

perk.c: Perk Perk (pẽrk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perked (pẽrkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Perking.] [Cf. W. percu to trim, to make smart.] To make trim or smart; to straighten up; to erect; to make a jaunty or saucy display of; as, to perk the ears; to perk up one's head. Cowper. Sherburne.
Perk Perk, v. i. 1. To exalt one's self; to bear one's self loftily. “To perk over them.” Barrow.
Perk Perk, a. Smart; trim; spruce; jaunty; vain. “Perk as a peacock.” Spenser.
Perk Perk, v. i. To peer; to look inquisitively. Dickens.

perkin.c: Perkin Per"kin (pẽr"kĭn), n. A kind of weak perry.

perkinism.c: Perkinism Per"kin*ism (pẽr"kĭn*ĭz'm), n. (Med.) A remedial treatment, by drawing the pointed extremities of two rods, each of a different metal, over the affected part; tractoration, -- first employed by Dr. Elisha Perkins of Norwich, Conn. See Metallotherapy. [archaic]

perky.c: Perky Perk"y (?), a. Perk; pert; jaunty; trim.

perlaceous.c: Perlaceous Per*la"ceous (?), a. [See Pearl.] Pearly; resembling pearl.

perlid.c: Perlid Per"lid (?), n. (Zool.) Any insect of the genus Perla, or family Perlidæ. See Stone fly, under Stone.

perlitic.c: Perlitic Per*lit"ic (?), a. (Min.) Relating to or resembling perlite, or pearlstone; as, the perlitic structure of certain rocks. See Pearlite.

perlustration.c: Perlustration Per`lus*tra"tion (?), n. [L. perlustrare to wander all through, to survey. See 3d Luster.] The act of viewing all over. [Archaic] Howell.

permanency.c: Permanency Permanence { Per"ma*nence (?), Per"ma*nen*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. permanence.] The quality or state of being permanent; continuance in the same state or place; duration; fixedness; as, the permanence of institutions; the permanence of nature.

permanent.c: Permanent Per"ma*nent (?), a. [L. permanens, -entis, p. pr. of permanere to stay or remain to the end, to last; per + manere to remain: cf. F. permanent. See Per-, and Mansion.] Continuing in the same state, or without any change that destroys form or character; remaining unaltered or unremoved; abiding; durable; fixed; stable; lasting; as, a permanent impression.

permanently.c: Permanently Per"ma*nent*ly, adv. In a permanent manner.

permanganate.c: Permanganate Per*man"ga*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of permanganic acid.

permanganic.c: Permanganic Per`man*gan"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, one of the higher acids of manganese, HMnO4, which forms salts called permanganates.

permansion.c: Permansion Per*man"sion (?), n. [L. permansio. See Permanent.] Continuance. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

permeability.c: Permeability Per`me*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. perméabilité.] The quality or state of being permeable.

permeable.c: Permeable Per"me*a*ble (?), a. [L. permeabilis: cf. F. perméable. See Permeate.] Capable of being permeated, or passed through; yielding passage; passable; penetrable; -- used especially of substances which allow the passage of fluids; as, wood is permeable to oil; glass is permeable to light. I. Taylor.

permeably.c: Permeably Per"me*a*bly, adv. In a permeable manner.

permeance.c: Permeance Per"me*ance (?), n. [See Permeant.] Permeation; specif. (Magnetism), the reciprocal of reluctance.

permeant.c: Permeant Per"me*ant (?), a. [L. permeans, p. pr.] Passing through; permeating. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

permeate.c: Permeate Per"me*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Permeated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Permeating.] [L. permeatus, p. p. of permeare to permeate; per + meare to go, pass.] 1. To pass through the pores or interstices of; to penetrate and pass through without causing rupture or displacement; -- applied especially to fluids which pass through substances of loose texture; as, water permeates sand. Woodward.

permeation.c: Permeation Per`me*a"tion (?), n. The act of permeating, passing through, or spreading throughout, the pores or interstices of any substance.

permian.c: Permian Per"mi*an (?), prop. a. [From the ancient kingdom of Permia, where the Permian formation exists.] (Geol.) Belonging or relating to the period, and also to the formation, next following the Carboniferous, and regarded as closing the Carboniferous age and Paleozoic era. -- n. The Permian period. See Chart of Geology.

permians.c: Permians Per"mi*ans (?), n. pl.; sing. Permian (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe belonging to the Finnic race, and inhabiting a portion of Russia.

permiscible.c: Permiscible Per*mis"ci*ble (?), a. [L. permiscere to mingle; per + miscere to mix.] Capable of being mixed.

permiss.c: Permiss Per*miss" (?), n. [See Permit.] A permitted choice; a rhetorical figure in which a thing is committed to the decision of one's opponent. [Obs.] Milton.

permissibility.c: Permissibility Per*mis`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being permissible; permissibleness; allowableness.

permissible.c: Permissible Per*mis"si*ble (?), a. That may be permitted; allowable; admissible. -- Per*mis"si*ble*ness, n. -- Per*mis"si*bly, adv.

permission.c: Permission Per*mis"sion (pẽr*mĭsh"ŭn), n. [L. permissio: cf. F. permission. See Permit.] The act of permitting or allowing; formal consent; authorization; leave; license or liberty granted.

permissive.c: Permissive Per*mis"sive (pẽr*mĭs"sĭv), a. 1. Permitting; granting leave or liberty. “By his permissive will.” Milton.

permissively.c: Permissively Per*mis"sive*ly, adv. In a permissive manner.

permistion.c: Permistion Per*mis"tion (pẽr*mĭs"chŭn), n. [L. permistio, permixtio, fr. permiscere, permistum, and permixtum. See Permiscible.] The act of mixing; the state of being mingled; mixture. [Written also permixtion.]

permit.c: Permit Per*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Permitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Permitting.] [L. permittere, permissum, to let through, to allow, permit; per + mittere to let go, send. See Per-, and Mission.] 1. To consent to; to allow or suffer to be done; to tolerate; to put up with.
Permit Per*mit", v. i. To grant permission; to allow.
Permit Per"mit (?), n. Warrant; license; leave; permission; specifically, a written license or permission given to a person or persons having authority; as, a permit to land goods subject to duty.

Permit Per*mit" (?), n. [Cf. Sp. palamida a kind of scombroid fish.] (a) A large pompano (Trachinotus goodei) of the West Indies, Florida, etc. It becomes about three feet long. (b) The round pompano. (Trachinotus falcatus). [Local, U. S.]

permittance.c: Permittance Per*mit"tance (?), n. The act of permitting; allowance; permission; leave. Milton.

permittee.c: Permittee Per`mit*tee" (?), n. One to whom a permission or permit is given.

permix.c: Permix Per*mix" (?), v. t. To mix; to mingle. [Obs.]

permulator.c: Permulator Per"mu*la`tor (?), n. (Elec.) A special form of rotary converter with stationary commutator and rotating brushes, in which the exciting field is induced by the alternating current in a short-circuited magnetic core instead of being produced by an external magnet.

permutable.c: Permutable Per*mut"a*ble (pẽr*mū"tȧ*b'l), a. [Cf. F. permutable.] Capable of being permuted; exchangeable. -- Per*mut"a*ble*ness, n. -- Per*mut"a*bly, adv.

permutation.c: Permutation Per`mu*ta"tion (pẽr`mu"tā"snŭn), n. [L. permutatio: cf. F. permutation. See Permute.] 1. The act of permuting; exchange of the thing for another; mutual transference; interchange.

permute.c: Permute Per*mute" (pẽr*mūt"), v. t. [L. permutare, permutatum; per + mutare to change: cf. F. permuter.] 1. To interchange; to transfer reciprocally.

pern.c: Pern Pern (pẽrn), v. t. [See Pernancy.] To take profit of; to make profitable. [Obs.] Sylvester.

pernancy.c: Pernancy Per"nan*cy (pẽr"nain*sy̆), n. [OF. prenance, fr. prendre, prenre, penre, to take, L. prendere, prehendere.] (Law) A taking or reception, as the receiving of rents or tithes in kind, the receiving of profits. Blackstone.

pernicion.c: Pernicion Per*ni"cion (?), n. [See 2d Pernicious.] Destruction; perdition. [Obs.] hudibras.

pernicious.c: Pernicious Per*ni"cious (?), a. [L. pernix, -icis.] Quick; swift (to burn). [R.] Milton.

Pernicious Per*ni"cious, a. [L. perniciosus, from pernicies destruction, from pernecare to kill or slay outright; per + necare to kill, slay: cf. F. pernicieux. Cf. Nuisance, Necromancy.] Having the quality of injuring or killing; destructive; very mischievous; baleful; malicious; wicked.

pernicity.c: Pernicity Per*nic"i*ty (?), n. [L. pernicitas. See 1st Pernicious.] Swiftness; celerity. [R.] Ray.

pernicketty.c: Pernicketty Pernickety { Per*nick"et*y, Per*nick"et*ty } (?), a. Finical or fussy; full of petty details. [Colloq.]

pernoctalian.c: Pernoctalian Per`noc*ta"li*an (?), n. One who watches or keeps awake all night.

pernoctation.c: Pernoctation Per`noc*ta"tion (?), n. [L. pernoctatio, fr. pernoctare to stay all night; per + nox, noctis, night.] The act or state of passing the whole night; a remaining all night. “Pernoctation in prayer.” Jer. Taylor.

pernor.c: Pernor Per"nor (?), n. [See Pern, v.] (Law) One who receives the profits, as of an estate.

pernot.c: Pernot furnace Per"not fur"nace (?). [So called from Charles Pernot, its inventor.] A reverberatory furnace with a circular revolving hearth, -- used in making steel.

pernyi.c: Pernyi moth Per"ny*i moth" (?). (Zool.) A silk-producing moth (Attacus Pernyi) which feeds upon the oak. It has been introduced into Europe and America from China.

perofskite.c: Perofskite Per*of"skite (?), n. [From von Perovski, of St.Petersburg.] (Min.) Same as Perovskite.

peronate.c: Peronate Per"o*nate (?), a. [L. peronatus rough-booted, fr. pero, -onis, a kind of rough boot.] (Bot.) A term applied to the stipes or stalks of certain fungi which are covered with a woolly substance which at length becomes powdery. Henslow.

peroneal.c: Peroneal Per`o*ne"al (?), a. [Gr.? the fibula.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the fibula; in the region of the fibula.

perorate.c: Perorate Per"o*rate (?), v. i. [See Peroration.] To make a peroration; to harangue. [Colloq.]

peroration.c: Peroration Per`o*ra"tion (?), n. [L. peroratio, fr. perorate, peroratum, to speak from beginning to end; per + orate to speak. See Per-, and Oration.] (Rhet.) The concluding part of an oration; especially, a final summing up and enforcement of an argument. Burke.

perovskite.c: Perovskite Per*ov"skite (?), n. [From von Perovski, of St. Petersburg.] (Min.) A titanate of lime occurring in octahedral or cubic crystals. [Written also Perofskite.]

peroxidation.c: Peroxidation Per*ox`i*da"tion (?), n. Act, process, or result of peroxidizing; oxidation to a peroxide.

peroxide.c: Peroxide Per*ox"ide (?), n. (Chem.) An oxide containing more oxygen than some other oxide of the same element. Formerly peroxides were regarded as the highest oxides. Cf. Per-, 2.

peroxidize.c: Peroxidize Per*ox"i*dize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Peroxidized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Peroxidizing.] (Chem.) To oxidize to the utmost degree, so as to form a peroxide.

perpend.c: Perpend Per*pend" (?), v. t. [L. perpendere, perpensum; per + pendere to weight.] To weight carefully in the mind. [R.] “Perpend my words.” Shak.
Perpend Per*pend", v. i. To attend; to be attentive. [R.] Shak.

perpender.c: Perpender Per*pend"er (?), n. [F. parpaing, pierre parpaigne; of uncertain origin.] (Masonry) A large stone reaching through a wall so as to appear on both sides of it, and acting as a binder; -- called also perbend, perpend stone, and perpent stone.

perpendicle.c: Perpendicle Per*pen"di*cle (?), n. [L. perpendiculum; per + pendere to hang: cf. F. perpendicule.] Something hanging straight down; a plumb line. [Obs.]

perpendicular.c: Perpendicular Per`pen*dic"u*lar (?), a. [L. perpendicularis, perpendicularius: cf. F. perpendiculaire. See Perpendicle, Pension.] 1. Exactly upright or vertical; pointing to the zenith; at right angles to the plane of the horizon; extending in a right line from any point toward the center of the earth.
Perpendicular Per`pen*dic"u*lar (?), n. 1. A line at right angles to the plane of the horizon; a vertical line or direction.

perpendicularity.c: Perpendicularity Per`pen*dic`u*lar"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. perpendicularité.] The quality or state of being perpendicular.

perpendicularly.c: Perpendicularly Per`pen*dic"u*lar*ly (?), adv. In a perpendicular manner; vertically.

perpension.c: Perpension Per*pen"sion (?), n. [See Perpend.] Careful consideration; pondering. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

perpession.c: Perpession Per*pes"sion (?), n. [L. perpessio, fr. perpeti, perpessus, to bear steadfastly; per + pati to bear.] Suffering; endurance. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

perpetrable.c: Perpetrable Per"pe*tra"ble (?), a. Capable of being perpetrated. R. North.

perpetrate.c: Perpetrate Per"pe*trate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perpetrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perpetrating.] [L. perpetratus, p. p. of perpetrare to effect, perpetrare; per + patrare to perform.] To do or perform; to carry through; to execute, commonly in a bad sense; to commit (as a crime, an offense); to be guilty of; as, to perpetrate a foul deed.

perpetration.c: Perpetration Per`pe*tra"tion (?), n. [L. perpetratio: cf. F. perpétration.] 1. The act of perpetrating; a doing; -- commonly used of doing something wrong, as a crime.

perpetrator.c: Perpetrator Per"pe*tra`tor (?), n. [L.] One who perpetrates; esp., one who commits an offense or crime.

perpetuable.c: Perpetuable Per*pet"u*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being perpetuated or continued.

perpetual.c: Perpetual Per*pet"u*al (?), a. [OE. perpetuel, F. perpétuel, fr. L. perpetualis, fr. perpetuus continuing throughout, continuous, fr. perpes, -etis, lasting throughout.] Neverceasing; continuing forever or for an unlimited time; unfailing; everlasting; continuous.

Perpetual calendar Per*pet"u*al cal"en*dar. A calendar that can be used perpetually or over a wide range of years. That of Capt. Herschel covers, as given below, dates from 1750 to 1961 only, but is capable of indefinite extension.

perpetually.c: Perpetually Per*pet"u*al*ly, adv. In a perpetual manner; constantly; continually.

perpetualty.c: Perpetualty Per*pet"u*al*ty (?), n. The state or condition of being perpetual. [Obs.] Testament of Love.

perpetuate.c: Perpetuate Per*pet"u*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perpetuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perpetuating.] [L. perpetuatus, p. p. of perpetuare to perpetuate. See Perpetual.] To make perpetual; to cause to endure, or to be continued, indefinitely; to preserve from extinction or oblivion; to eternize. Addison. Burke.
Perpetuate Per*pet"u*ate (?), a. [L. perpetuatus, p. p.] Made perpetual; perpetuated. [R.] Southey.

perpetuation.c: Perpetuation Per*pet`u*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. perpétuation.] The act of making perpetual, or of preserving from extinction through an endless existence, or for an indefinite period of time; continuance. Sir T. Browne.

perpetuity.c: Perpetuity Per`pe*tu"i*ty (?), n. [L. perpetuitas: cf. F. perpétuité.] 1. The quality or state of being perpetual; as, the perpetuity of laws. Bacon.

perplex.c: Perplex Per*plex" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perplexed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perplexing.] [L. perplexari. See Perplex, a.] 1. To involve; to entangle; to make intricate or complicated, and difficult to be unraveled or understood; as, to perplex one with doubts.
Perplex Per*plex", a. [L. perplexus entangled, intricate; per + plectere, plexum, to plait, braid: cf. F. perplexe. See Per-, and Plait.] Intricate; difficult. [Obs.] Glanvill.

perplexed.c: Perplexed Per*plexed" (?), a. Entangled, involved, or confused; hence, embarrassd; puzzled; doubtful; anxious. -- Per*plex"ed*ly (#), adv. -- Per*plex"ed*ness, n.

perplexing.c: Perplexing Per*plex"ing (?), a. Embarrassing; puzzling; troublesome. “Perplexing thoughts.” Milton.

perplexity.c: Perplexity Per*plex"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Perplexities (#). [L. perplexitas: cf. F. perplexité.] The quality or state of being perplexed or puzzled; complication; intricacy; entanglement; distraction of mind through doubt or difficulty; embarrassment; bewilderment; doubt.

perplexiveness.c: Perplexiveness Per*plex"ive*ness (?), n. The quality of being perplexing; tendency to perplex. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

perpotation.c: Perpotation Per`po*ta"tion (?), n. [L. perpotatio, fr. perpotate. See Per-, and Potation.] The act of drinking excessively; a drinking bout. [Obs.]

perquisite.c: Perquisite Per"qui*site (?), n. [L. perquisitum, fr. perquisitus, p. p. of perquirere to ask for diligently; per + quaerere to seek. See Per-, and Quest.] 1. Something gained from a place or employment over and above the ordinary salary or fixed wages for services rendered; -- examples are, a fee allowed by law to an officer for a specific service; the use of a company automobile or other company property.

perquisited.c: Perquisited Per"qui*sit*ed, a. Supplied with perquisites. [Obs.] “Perquisited varlets frequent stand.” Savage.

perquisition.c: Perquisition Per`qui*si"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. perquisition.] A thorough inquiry of search. [R.] Berkeley.

perradial.c: Perradial Per*ra"di*al (?), a. (Zool.) Situated around the radii, or radial tubes, of a radiate.

perrie.c: Perrie Per"rie (?), n. [F. pierreries, pl., fr. pierre stone, L. petra.] Precious stones; jewels. [Obs.] [Written also perre, perrye, etc.] Chaucer.

perrier.c: Perrier Per"ri*er (?), n. [OF. perriere, perrier, F. perrier. Cf. Pederero.] (Mil.) A short mortar used formerly for throwing stone shot. Hakluyt.

perron.c: Perron Per"ron (?), n. [F.] (Arch.) An out-of-door flight of steps, as in a garden, leading to a terrace or to an upper story; -- usually applied to mediævel or later structures of some architectural pretensions.

perruquier.c: Perruquier Per*ru"qui*er (?), n. [F.] A maker of perukes or wigs.

perry.c: Perry Per"ry (?), n. [OF. peré, F. poiré, fr. poire a pear, L. pirum. See Pear the fruit.] A fermented liquor made from pears; pear cider. Mortimer.
Perry Per"ry, n. A sudden squall. See Pirry. [Obs.]

pers.c: Pers Pers (?), a. [F. pers.] Light blue; grayish blue; -- a term applied to different shades at different periods. -- n. A cloth of sky-blue color. [Obs.] “A long surcoat of pers.” Chaucer.

persalt.c: Persalt Per"salt` (?), n. (Chem.) A term formerly given to the salts supposed to be formed respectively by neutralizing acids with certain peroxides. [Obsoles.]

persant.c: Persant Per"sant (?), a. [F. perçant, p. pr. of percer to pierce.] Piercing. [Obs.] Spenser.

perscrutation.c: Perscrutation Per`scru*ta"tion (?), n. [L. perscrutatio, fr. perscrutari to search through.] A thorough searching; a minute inquiry or scrutiny. Carlyle

persecute.c: Persecute Per"se*cute (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Persecuted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Persecuting.] [F. persécueter, L. persequi, persecutus, to pursue, prosecute; per + sequi to follow, pursue. See Per-, and Second.] 1. To pursue in a manner to injure, grieve, or afflict; to beset with cruelty or malignity; to harass; especially, to afflict, harass, punish, or put to death, for adherence to a particular religious creed or mode of worship.

persecution.c: Persecution Per`se*cu"tion (?), n. [F. persécution, L. persecutio.] 1. The act or practice of persecuting; especially, the infliction of loss, pain, or death for adherence to a particular creed or mode of worship.

persecutor.c: Persecutor Per"se*cu`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. persécuteur.] One who persecutes, or harasses. Shak.

persecutrix.c: Persecutrix Per"se*cu`trix (?), n. [L.] A woman who persecutes.

perseid.c: Perseid Per"se*id (?), n. [From Perseus.] (Astron.) One of a group of shooting stars which appear yearly about the 10th of August, and cross the heavens in paths apparently radiating from the constellation Perseus. They are probably fragments of Swift's comet of 1862 (III).

perseus.c: Perseus Per"se*us (?), prop. n. [L., from Gr. Persey`s.] 1. (Class. Myth.) A Grecian legendary hero, son of Jupiter and Danaë, who slew the Gorgon Medusa.

perseverance.c: Perseverance Per`se*ver"ance (pẽr`se*vēr"ains), n. [F. persévérance, L. perseverantia.] 1. The act of persevering; persistence in anything undertaken; continued pursuit or prosecution of any business, or enterprise begun. “The king-becoming graces... perseverance, mercy, lowliness.” Shak.

perseverant.c: Perseverant Per`se*ver"ant (pẽr`se*vēr"aint), a. [L. perseverans, -antis, p. pr.: cf. F. persévérant.] Persevering. [R.] “Perseverant faith.” Whitby. -- Per`se*ver"ant*ly, adv. [R.]

persevere.c: Persevere Per`se*vere" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Persevered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Persevering.] [F. persévérer, L. perseverare, fr. perseverus very strict; per + severus strict, severe. See Per-, and Severe.] To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken; to pursue steadily any project or course begun; to maintain a purpose in spite of counter influences, opposition, or discouragement; not to give or abandon what is undertaken.

persevering.c: Persevering Per`se*ver"ing (?), a. Characterized by perseverance; persistent. -- Per`se*ver"ing*ly, adv.

persian.c: Persian Per"sian (?), a. [From Persia: cf. It. Persiano. Cf. Parsee, Peach, Persic.] Of or pertaining to Persia, to the Persians, or to their language.
Persian Per"sian, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of Persia.

persic.c: Persic Per"sic (?), a. [L. Persicus. Cf. Persian.] Of or relating to Persia. -- n. The Persian language.

persicaria.c: Persicaria ‖Per`si*ca"ri*a (?), n. [NL., from LL. persicarius a peach tree. See Peach.] (Bot.) See Lady's thumb.

persicot.c: Persicot Per"si*cot (?), n. [F. See Peach.] A cordial made of the kernels of apricots, nectarines, etc., with refined spirit.

persienne.c: Persienne Per`si*enne" (pẽr`sĭ*ĕn"; pẽr`shĭ*ĕn"; F. pẽr`syĕn"), n. [F., fem. of presien Persian.] Properly, printed calico, whether Oriental or of fanciful design with flowers, etc., in Western work. Hence, as extended in English, material of a similar character.

persiennes.c: Persiennes Per`si*ennes" (pẽr`sĭ*ĕnz"; F. pẽr`syĕn"), n. pl. [F.] Window blinds having movable slats, similar to Venetian blinds.

persiflage.c: Persiflage ‖Per`si`flage" (?), n. [F., fr. persifler to quiz, fr. L. per + siffler to whistle, hiss, L. sibilare, sifilare.] Frivolous or bantering talk; a frivolous manner of treating any subject, whether serious or otherwise; light raillery. Hannah More.

persifleur.c: Persifleur ‖Per`si`fleur (?), n. [F.] One who indulges in persiflage; a banterer; a quiz. Carlyle.

persimmon.c: Persimmon Per*sim"mon (?), n. [Virginia Indian.] (Bot.) An American tree (Diospyros Virginiana) and its fruit, found from New York southward. The fruit is like a plum in appearance, but is very harsh and astringent until it has been exposed to frost, when it becomes palatable and nutritious.

persis.c: Persis Per"sis (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A kind of coloring matter obtained from lichens.

persism.c: Persism Per"sism (?), n. An ancient Persian religion, esp. as represented by the Magi; a form of Zoroastrianism.

persist.c: Persist Per*sist" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Persisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Persisting.] [L. persistere; per + sistere to stand or be fixed, fr. stare to stand: cf. F. persister. See Per-, and Stand.] To stand firm; to be fixed and unmoved; to stay; to continue steadfastly; especially, to continue fixed in a course of conduct against opposing motives; to persevere; -- sometimes conveying an unfavorable notion, as of doggedness or obstinacy.

persistency.c: Persistency Persistence { Per*sist"ence (?), Per*sist"en*cy (?), } n. [See Persistent.] 1. The quality or state of being persistent; staying or continuing quality; hence, in an unfavorable sense, doggedness; obstinacy.

persistent.c: Persistent Per*sist"ent (?), a. [L. persistens, -entis, p. pr. of persistere. See Persist.] 1. Inclined to persist; having staying qualities; tenacious of position or purpose.

persistently.c: Persistently Per*sist"ent*ly, adv. In a persistent manner.

persisting.c: Persisting Per*sist"ing, a. Inclined to persist; tenacious of purpose; persistent. -- Per*sist"ing*ly, adv.

persnickety.c: Persnickety Per*snick"et*y (?), a. 1. Finicky or fussy; demanding excessive attention to petty details or niceties; unduly particular; fastidious; -- of people. [Colloq.]

persolve.c: Persolve Per*solve" (?), v. t. [L. persolvere.] To pay wholly, or fully. [Obs.] E. Hall.

person.c: Person Per"son (pẽr"s'n; 277), n. [OE. persone, persoun, person, parson, OF. persone, F. personne, L. persona a mask (used by actors), a personage, part, a person, fr. personare to sound through; per + sonare to sound. See Per-, and cf. Parson.] 1. A character or part, as in a play; a specific kind or manifestation of individual character, whether in real life, or in literary or dramatic representation; an assumed character. [Archaic]
Person Per"son (?), v. t. To represent as a person; to personify; to impersonate. [Obs.] Milton.

persona.c: Persona ‖Per*so"na (?), n.; pl. Personæ (#). [L.] (Biol.) Same as Person, n., 8.

personable.c: Personable Per"son*a*ble (pẽr"sŭn*ȧ*b'l), a. 1. Having a well-formed body, or person; graceful; comely; of good appearance; presentable; as, a personable man or woman.

personage.c: Personage Per"son*age (pẽr"sŭn*aj: 48), n. [F. personnage.] 1. Form, appearance, or belongings of a person; the external appearance, stature, figure, air, and the like, of a person. “In personage stately.” Hayward.

personal.c: Personal Per"son*al (pẽr"sŭn*ail), a. [L. personalis: cf. F. personnel.] 1. Pertaining to human beings as distinct from things.
Personal Per"son*al, n. (Law) A movable; a chattel.

personalism.c: Personalism Per"son*al*ism (?), n. The quality or state of being personal; personality. [R.]

personality.c: Personality Per`son*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Personalities (#). [Cf. F. personnalité. Cf. Personality.] 1. That which constitutes distinction of person; the externally evident aspects of the character or behavior of a person; individuality.

personalize.c: Personalize Per"son*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Personalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Personalizing (?).] To make personal. “They personalize death.” H. Spencer.

personally.c: Personally Per"son*al*ly, adv. 1. In a personal manner; by bodily presence; in person; not by representative or substitute; as, to deliver a letter personally.

personalty.c: Personalty Per"son*al*ty (?), n. 1. The state of being a person; personality. [R.]

personate.c: Personate Per"son*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Personated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Personating (?).] [L. personare to cry out, LL., to extol. See Person.] To celebrate loudly; to extol; to praise. [Obs.]

Personate Per"son*ate, v. t. [L. personatus masked, assumed, fictitious, fr. persona a mask. See Person.] 1. To assume the character of; to represent by a fictitious appearance; to act the part of; to impersonate{3}; hence, to counterfeit; to feign; as, he tried to personate his brother; a personated devotion. Hammond.
Personate Per"son*ate, v. i. To play or assume a character.

Personate Per"son*ate (?), a. [L. personatus masked.] (Bot.) Having the throat of a bilabiate corolla nearly closed by a projection of the base of the lower lip; masked, as in the flower of the snapdragon.

personation.c: Personation Per`son*a"tion (?), n. The act of personating, or conterfeiting the person or character of another; impersonation.

personator.c: Personator Per"son*a`tor (?), n. One who personates. “The personators of these actions.” B. Jonson.

personification.c: Personification Per*son`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. personnification.] 1. The act of personifying; impersonation; embodiment. C. Knight.

personify.c: Personify Per*son"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Personified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Personifying (?).] [Person + -fy: cf. F. personnifier.] 1. To regard, treat, or represent as a person; to represent as a rational being.

personnel.c: Personnel ‖Per`son`nel" (?), n. [F. See Personal.] The body of persons employed in some public service, as the army, navy, etc.; -- distinguished from materiel.

perspective.c: Perspective Per*spec"tive (pẽr*spĕk"tĭv), a. [L. perspicere, perspectum, to look through; per + spicere, specere, to look: cf. F. perspectif; or from E. perspective, n. See Spy, n.] 1. Of or pertaining to the science of vision; optical. [Obs.] Bacon.

Perspective Per*spec"tive, n. [F. perspective, fr. perspectif: cf. It. perspettiva. See Perspective, a.] 1. A glass through which objects are viewed. [Obs.] “Not a perspective, but a mirror.” Sir T. Browne.

perspectively.c: Perspectively Per*spec"tive*ly (pẽr*spĕk"tĭv*ly̆), adv. 1. Optically; as through a glass. [R.]

perspectograph.c: Perspectograph Per*spec"to*graph (pẽr*spĕk"to*grȧf), n. [L. perspectus (p. p. of perspicere to look through) + -graph.] An instrument for obtaining, and transferring to a picture, the points and outlines of objects, so as to represent them in their proper geometrical relations as viewed from some one point.

perspectography.c: Perspectography Per`spec*tog"ra*phy (pẽr`spĕk*tŏg"rȧ*fy̆), n. The science or art of delineating objects according to the laws of perspective; the theory of perspective.

perspicable.c: Perspicable Per"spi*ca*ble (pẽr"spĭ*kȧ*b'l), a. [L. perspicabilis, fr. perspicere.] Discernible. [Obs.] Herbert.

perspicacious.c: Perspicacious Per`spi*ca"cious (pẽr`spĭ*kā"shŭs), a. [L. perspicax, -acis, fr. perspicere to look through: cf. F. perspicace. See Perspective.] 1. Having the power of seeing clearly; quick-sighted; sharp of sight.

perspicacity.c: Perspicacity Per`spi*cac"i*ty (pẽr`spĭ*kăs"ĭ*ty̆), n. [L. perspicacitas: cf. F. perspicacité. See Perspicacious.] The state of being perspicacious; acuteness of sight or of intelligence; acute discernment. Sir T. Browne.

perspicience.c: Perspicience Per*spi"cience (pẽr*spĭsh"eins), n. [L. perspicientia, fr. perspiciens, p. p. of perspicere. See Perspective.] The act of looking sharply. [Obs.] Bailey.

perspicil.c: Perspicil Per"spi*cil (pẽr"spĭ*sĭl), n. [LL. perspicilla, fr. L. perspicere to look through.] An optical glass; a telescope. [Obs.] Crashaw.

perspicuity.c: Perspicuity Per`spi*cu"i*ty (pẽr`spĭ*kū"ĭ*ty̆), n. [L. perspicuitas: cf. F. perspicuité.] 1. The quality or state of being transparent or translucent. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

perspicuous.c: Perspicuous Per*spic"u*ous (?), a. [L. perspicuus, from perspicere to look through. See Perspective.] 1. Capable of being through; transparent; translucent; not opaque. [Obs.] Peacham.

perspirability.c: Perspirability Per*spir`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being perspirable.

perspirable.c: Perspirable Per*spir"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. perspirable.] 1. Capable of being perspired. Sir T. Browne.

perspiration.c: Perspiration Per`spi*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. perspiration.] 1. The act or process of perspiring.

perspirative.c: Perspirative Per*spir"a*tive (?), a. Performing the act of perspiration; perspiratory.

perspiratory.c: Perspiratory Per*spir"a*to*ry (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or producing, perspiration; as, the perspiratory ducts.

perspire.c: Perspire Per*spire" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Perspired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perspiring.] [L. perspirare to breathe through; per + spirare. See Per-, and Spirit.] 1. (Physiol.) To excrete matter through the skin; esp., to excrete fluids through the pores of the skin; to sweat.
Perspire Per*spire", v. t. To emit or evacuate through the pores of the skin; to sweat; to excrete through pores.

perstreperous.c: Perstreperous Per*strep"er*ous (?), a. [L. perstrepere to make a great noise.] Noisy; obstreperous. [Obs.] Ford.

perstringe.c: Perstringe Per*stringe" (?), v. t. [L. perstringere; per + stringere to bind up, to touch upon.] 1. To touch; to graze; to glance on. [Obs.]

persuadable.c: Persuadable Per*suad"a*ble (?), a. That may be persuaded. -- Per*suad"a*ble*ness, n. -- Per*suad"a*bly, adv.

persuade.c: Persuade Per*suade" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Persuaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Persuading.] [L. persuadere, persuasum; per + suadere to advise, persuade: cf. F. persuader. See Per-, and Suasion.] 1. To influence or gain over by argument, advice, entreaty, expostulation, etc.; to draw or incline to a determination by presenting sufficient motives.
Persuade Per*suade" (?), v. i. To use persuasion; to plead; to prevail by persuasion. Shak.

persuaded.c: Persuaded Per*suad"ed, p. p. & a. Prevailed upon; influenced by argument or entreaty; convinced. -- Per*suad"ed*ly, adv. -- Per*suad"ed*ness, n.

persuader.c: Persuader Per*suad"er (?), n. One who, or that which, persuades or influences. “Powerful persuaders.” Milton.

persuasibility.c: Persuasibility Per*sua`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capability of being persuaded. Hawthorne.

persuasible.c: Persuasible Per*sua"si*ble (?), a. [Cf. L. persuasibilis persuasive, F. persuasible persuasible.] 1. Capable of being persuaded; persuadable.

persuasion.c: Persuasion Per*sua"sion (?), n. [L. persuasio; Cf. F. persuasion.] 1. The act of persuading; the act of influencing the mind by arguments or reasons offered, or by anything that moves the mind or passions, or inclines the will to a determination.

persuasive.c: Persuasive Per*sua"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. persuasif.] Tending to persuade; having the power of persuading; as, persuasive eloquence. “Persuasive words.” Milton.
Persuasive Per*sua"sive, n. That which persuades; an inducement; an incitement; an exhortation. -- Per*sua"sive*ly, adv. -- Per*sua"sive*ness, n.

persuasory.c: Persuasory Per*sua"so*ry (?), a. Persuasive. Sir T. Browne.

persulphate.c: Persulphate Per*sul"phate (?), n. (Chem.) A sulphate of the peroxide of any base. [R.]

persulphide.c: Persulphide Per*sul"phide (?), n. (Chem.) A sulphide containing more sulphur than some other compound of the same elements; as, iron pyrites is a persulphide; -- formerly called persulphuret.

persulphocyanate.c: Persulphocyanate Per*sul`pho*cy"a*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of persulphocyanic acid. [R.]

persulphocyanic.c: Persulphocyanic Per*sul`pho*cy*an"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline substance (called also perthiocyanic acid), analogous to sulphocyanic acid, but containing more sulphur.

persulphocyanogen.c: Persulphocyanogen Per*sul`pho*cy*an"o*gen (?), n. (Chem.) An orange-yellow substance, produced by the action of chlorine or boiling dilute nitric acid and sulphocyanate of potassium; -- called also pseudosulphocyanogen, perthiocyanogen, and formerly sulphocyanogen.

pert.c: Pert Pert (?), a. [An aphetic form of OE. & OF. apert open, known, true, free, or impudent. See Apert.] 1. Open; evident; apert. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.
Pert Pert, v. i. To behave with pertness. [Obs.] Gauden.

pertain.c: Pertain Per*tain" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Pertained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pertaining.] [OE. partenen, OF. partenir, fr. L. pertinere to stretch out, reach, pertain; per + tenere to hold, keep. See Per-, and Tenable, and cf. Appertain, Pertinent.] 1. To belong; to have connection with, or dependence on, something, as an appurtenance, attribute, etc.; to appertain; as, saltness pertains to the ocean; flowers pertain to plant life.

perterebration.c: Perterebration Per*ter`e*bra"tion (?), n. [L. perterebratus, p. p. of perterebrare to bore through.] The act of boring through. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

perthite.c: Perthite Perth"ite (?), n. [So called from Perth, in canada.] (Min.) A kind of feldspar consisting of a laminated intertexture of albite and orthoclase, usually of different colors. -- Per*thit"ic (#), a.
