pertinacious.c: Pertinacious Per`ti*na"cious (?), a. [L. pertinax, -acis; per + tenax tenacious. See Per-, and Tenacious.] 1. Holding or adhering to any opinion, purpose, or design, with obstinacy; perversely persistent; obstinate; as, pertinacious plotters; a pertinacious beggar.

pertinacity.c: Pertinacity Per`ti*nac"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. pertinacité.] The quality or state of being pertinacious; obstinacy; perseverance; persistency. Macaulay.

pertinacy.c: Pertinacy Per"ti*na*cy (?), n. [L. pertinere to pertain. See Pertinence.] The quality or state of being pertinent; pertinence. [Obs.]
Pertinacy Per"ti*na*cy, n. [L. pertinacia, fr. pertinax. See Pertinacious.] Pertinacity. [Obs.] Chaucer.

pertinency.c: Pertinency Pertinence { Per"ti*nence (?), Per"ti*nen*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. pertinence. See Pertinent.] The quality or state of being pertinent; justness of relation to the subject or matter in hand; fitness; appositeness; relevancy; suitableness.

pertinent.c: Pertinent Per"ti*nent (?), a. [L. pertinens, -entis, p. pr. of pertinere: cf. F. pertinent. See Pertain.] 1. Belonging or related to the subject or matter in hand; fit or appropriate in any way; adapted to the end proposed; apposite; material; relevant; as, pertinent illustrations or arguments; pertinent evidence.

pertly.c: Pertly Pert"ly (?), adv. In a pert manner.

pertness.c: Pertness Pert"ness, n. The quality or state of being pert.

pertransient.c: Pertransient Per*tran"sient (?), a. [L. pertransiens, p. pr. of pertransire.] Passing through or over. [R.]

perturb.c: Perturb Per*turb" (?), v. t. [L. perturbare, perturbatum; per + turbare to disturb, fr. turba a disorder: cf. OF. perturber. See Per-, and Turbid.] 1. To disturb; to agitate; to vex; to trouble; to disquiet.

perturbability.c: Perturbability Per*turb`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being perturbable.

perturbable.c: Perturbable Per*turb"a*ble (?), a. Liable to be perturbed or agitated; liable to be disturbed or disquieted.

perturbance.c: Perturbance Per*turb"ance (?), n. Disturbance; perturbation. [R.] “Perturbance of the mind.” Sharp.

perturbate.c: Perturbate Per"tur*bate (?), v. t. [From L. perturbatus, p. p.] To perturb. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

perturbation.c: Perturbation Per`tur*ba"tion (?), n. [L. perturbatio: cf. F. perturbation.] 1. The act of perturbing, or the state of being perturbed; esp., agitation of mind.

perturbational.c: Perturbational Per`tur*ba"tion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to perturbation, esp. to the perturbations of the planets. “The perturbational theory.” Sir J. Herschel.

perturbative.c: Perturbative Per"tur*ba*tive (?), a. Tending to cause perturbation; disturbing. Sir J. Herschel.

perturbed.c: Perturbed Per*turbed" (?), a. Agitated; disturbed; troubled. Shak. -- Per*turb"ed*ly, adv.

perturber.c: Perturber Per*turb"er (?), n. One who, or that which, perturbs, or cause perturbation.

pertusate.c: Pertusate Per*tus"ate (?), a. [See Pertuse.] (Bot.) Pierced at the apex.

pertused.c: Pertused Pertuse { Per*tuse" (?), Per*tused" (?) }, a. [L. pertusus, p. p. of pertundere to beat or thrust through, to bore through; per + tundere to beat: cf. F. pertus. Cf. Pierce.] Punched; pierced with, or having, holes.

pertusion.c: Pertusion Per*tu"sion (?), n. [L. pertusio.] The act of punching or piercing with a pointed instrument; as, pertusion of a vein. [R.] Arbuthnot.

pertussis.c: Pertussis ‖Per*tus"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. L. per through, very + tussis cough.] (Med.) The whooping cough.

peruke.c: Peruke Per"uke (?), n. [F. perruque, It. perrucca, parrucca, fr. L. pilus hair. Cf. Periwig, Wig, Peel to strip off, Plush, Pile a hair.] A wig; a periwig.
Peruke Per"uke, v. t. To dress with a peruke. [R.]

perula.c: Perula ‖Per"u*la (?), n.; pl. Perulæ (#). [L., dim. of pera wallet, Gr.?: cf. F. pérule.] 1. (Bot.) One of the scales of a leaf bud.

perusal.c: Perusal Pe*rus"al (?), n. [From Peruse.] 1. The act of carefully viewing or examining. [R.] Tatler.

peruse.c: Peruse Pe*ruse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Perusing.] [Pref. per- + use.] 1. To observe; to examine with care. [R.]

peruvian.c: Peruvian Pe*ru"vi*an (?), a. [Cf. F. péruvien, Sp. peruviano.] Of or pertaining to Peru, in South America. -- n. A native or an inhabitant of Peru.

pervade.c: Pervade Per*vade" (pẽr*vād"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pervaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Pervading.] [L. pervadere, pervasum; per + vadere to go, to walk. See Per-, and Wade.] 1. To pass or flow through, as an aperture, pore, or interstice; to permeate.

pervasion.c: Pervasion Per*va"sion (pẽr*vā"zhŭn), n. [L. pervasio. See Pervade.] The act of pervading, passing, or spreading through the whole extent of a thing. Boyle.

pervasive.c: Pervasive Per*va"sive (pẽr*vā"sĭv), a. Tending to pervade, or having power to spread throughout; of a pervading quality. “Civilization pervasive and general.” M. Arnold.

perverse.c: Perverse Per*verse" (pẽr*vẽrs"), a. [L. perversus turned the wrong way, not right, p. p. of pervertereto turn around, to overturn: cf. F. pervers. See Pervert.] 1. Turned aside; hence, specifically, turned away from the right; willfully erring; wicked; perverted.

perversely.c: Perversely Per*verse"ly, adv. In a perverse manner.

perverseness.c: Perverseness Per*verse"ness, n. The quality or state of being perverse. “Virtue hath some perverseness.” Donne.

perversion.c: Perversion Per*ver"sion (?), n. [L. perversio: cf. F. perversion. See Pervert.] The act of perverting, or the state of being perverted; a turning from truth or right; a diverting from the true intent or object; a change to something worse; a turning or applying to a wrong end or use. “Violations and perversions of the laws.” Bacon.

perversity.c: Perversity Per*ver"si*ty (?), n. [L. perversitas: cf. F. perversité.] The quality or state of being perverse; perverseness.

pervert.c: Pervert Per*vert" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Perverted; p. pr. & vb. n. Perverting.] [F. pervertir, L. pervertere, perversum; per + vertere to turn. See Per-, and Verse.] 1. To turn another way; to divert. [Obs.]
Pervert Per*vert", v. i. To become perverted; to take the wrong course. [R.] Testament of Love.
Pervert Per"vert (?), n. One who has been perverted; one who has turned to error, especially in religion; -- opposed to convert. See the Synonym of Convert.

perverter.c: Perverter Per*vert"er (?), n. One who perverts (a person or thing). “His own parents his perverters.” South. “A perverter of his law.” Bp. Stillingfleet.

pervertible.c: Pervertible Per*vert"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being perverted.

pervestigate.c: Pervestigate Per*ves"ti*gate (?), v. t. [L. pervestigatus, p. p. of pervestigare.] To investigate thoroughly. [Obs.]

pervestigation.c: Pervestigation Per*ves`ti*ga"tion (?), n. [L. pervestigatio.] Thorough investigation. [Obs.] Chillingworth.

pervial.c: Pervial Per"vi*al (?), a. [See Pervious.] Pervious. [Obs.] -- Per"vi*al*ly, adv. [Obs.] Chapman.

pervicacious.c: Pervicacious Per`vi*ca"cious (?), a. [L. pervicax, -acis.] Obstinate; willful; refractory. [Obs.] -- Per`vi*ca"cious*ly, adv. -- Per`vi*ca"cious*ness, n. [Obs.]

pervigilation.c: Pervigilation Per*vig`i*la"tion (?), n. [L. pervigilatio, fr. pervigilare.] Careful watching. [Obs.]

pervious.c: Pervious Per"vi*ous (?), a. [L. pervis; per + via a way. See Per-, and Voyage.] 1. Admitting passage; capable of being penetrated by another body or substance; permeable; as, a pervious soil.

perviousness.c: Perviousness Per"vi*ous*ness, n. The quality or state of being pervious; as, the perviousness of glass. Boyle.

pery.c: Pery Per"y (?), n. A pear tree. See Pirie. [Obs.]

pes.c: Pes ‖Pes (pēz), n.; pl. Pedes. [L., the foot.] (Anat.) The distal segment of the hind limb of vertebrates, including the tarsus and foot.

pesade.c: Pesade Pe*sade" (pe*sād"; F. pei*zȧd"), n. [F.] (Man.) The motion of a horse when, raising his fore quarters, he keeps his hind feet on the ground without advancing; rearing.

pesage.c: Pesage Pes"age (?), n. [F., fr. peser to weigh.] A fee, or toll, paid for the weighing of merchandise.

pesanted.c: Pesanted Pes"ant*ed (?), a. [F. pesant heavy.] Made heavy or dull; debased. [Obs.] “Pesanted to each lewd thought's control.” Marston.

pese.c: Pese Pese (?), n. [See Pea.] A pea. [Obs.] Chaucer.

peseta.c: Peseta ‖Pe*se"ta (?), n. [Sp.] A Spanish silver coin, and money of account, equal to about nineteen cents (ca. 1900), and divided into 100 centesimos. Now replaced by the euro.

peshitto.c: Peshitto Peshito { Pe*shit"o (?), Pe*shit"to (?), } n. [Syriac peshîtâ simple.] The earliest Syriac version of the Old Testament, translated from Hebrew; also, the incomplete Syriac version of the New Testament. [Written also peschito.]

pesky.c: Pesky Pes"ky (?), a. [Etymol. uncertain.] Pestering; vexatious; troublesome. Used also as an intensive. [Colloq. & Low, U.S.] Judd.

peso.c: Peso ‖Pe"so (?), n. [Sp.] A Spanish dollar; also, an Argentine, Chilian, Colombian, etc., coin, equal to from 75 cents to a dollar; also, a pound weight.

pessary.c: Pessary Pes"sa*ry (pĕs"sȧ*ry̆), n.; pl. Pessaries (#). [L. pessarium, pessum, pessus, Gr. pesso`s: cf. F. pessaire.] (Med.) (a) An instrument or device to be introduced into and worn in the vagina, to support the uterus, or remedy a malposition. (b) A medicinal substance in the form of a bolus or mass, designed for introduction into the vagina; a vaginal suppository.

pessimism.c: Pessimism Pes"si*mism (?), n. [L. pessimus worst, superl. of pejor worse: cf. F. pessimisme. Cf. Impair.] 1. (Metaph.) The opinion or doctrine that everything in nature is ordered for or tends to the worst, or that the world is wholly evil; -- opposed to optimism.

pessimist.c: Pessimist Pes"si*mist (?), n. [L. pessimus worst: cf. F. pessimiste.] 1. (Metaph.) One who advocates the doctrine of pessimism; -- opposed to optimist.

pessimistic.c: Pessimistic Pessimist { Pes"si*mist (?), Pes`si*mis"tic (?), } a. (Metaph.) Of or pertaining to pessimism; characterized by pessimism; gloomy; foreboding. “Giving utterance to pessimistic doubt.” Encyc. Brit.

pessimize.c: Pessimize Pes"si*mize (?), v. i. To hold or advocate the doctrine of pessimism. London Sat. Rev.

pessulus.c: Pessulus ‖Pes"su*lus (?), n.; pl. Pessuli (#). [L., a bolt.] (Anat.) A delicate bar of cartilage connecting the dorsal and ventral extremities of the first pair of bronchial cartilages in the syrinx of birds.

pest.c: Pest Pest (?), n. [L. pestis: cf. F. peste.] 1. A fatal epidemic disease; a pestilence; specif., the plague.

pestalozzian.c: Pestalozzian Pes`ta*loz"zi*an (?), a. Belonging to, or characteristic of, a system of elementary education which combined manual training with other instruction, advocated and practiced by Jean Henri Pestalozzi (1746-1827), a Swiss teacher. -- n. An advocate or follower of the system of Pestalozzi.

pestalozzianism.c: Pestalozzianism Pes`ta*loz"zi*an*ism (?), n. The system of education introduced by Pestalozzi.

pester.c: Pester Pes"ter (pĕs"tẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pestered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pestering.] [Abbrev. fr. impester, fr. OF. empaistrier, empestrer, to entangle the feet or legs, to embarrass, F. empêtrer; pref. em-, en- (L. in in) + LL. pastorium, pastoria, a fetter by which horses are prevented from wandering in the pastures, fr. L. pastorius belonging to a herdsman or shepherd, pastor a herdsman. See In, and Pasture, Pastor.] 1. To trouble; to disturb; to annoy; to harass with petty vexations.

pesterer.c: Pesterer Pes"ter*er (?), n. One who pesters or harasses.

pesterment.c: Pesterment Pes"ter*ment (?), n. The act of pestering, or the state of being pestered; vexation; worry. “The trouble and pesterment of children.” B. Franklin.

pesterous.c: Pesterous Pes"ter*ous (?), a. Inclined to pester. Also, vexatious; encumbering; burdensome. [Obs.] Bacon.

pestful.c: Pestful Pest"ful (?), a. Pestiferous. “After long and pestful calms.” Coleridge.

pesthouse.c: Pesthouse Pest`house" (?), n. A house or hospital for persons who are infected with any pestilential disease.

pestiduct.c: Pestiduct Pes"ti*duct (?), n. [L. pestis pest + ductus a leading, fr. ducere to lead.] That which conveys contagion or infection. [Obs.] Donne.

pestiferous.c: Pestiferous Pes*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. pestiferus, pestifer; pestis pest + ferre to bear: cf. F. pestifère.] 1. Pest-bearing; pestilential; noxious to health; malignant; infectious; contagious; as, pestiferous bodies. “Poor, pestiferous creatures begging alms.” Evelyn. “Unwholesome and pestiferous occupations.” Burke.

pestiferously.c: Pestiferously Pes*tif"er*ous*ly, adv. In a pestiferous manner.

pestilence.c: Pestilence Pes"ti*lence (?), n. [F. pestilence, L. pestilentia. See Pestilent.] 1. Specifically, the disease known as the plague; hence, any contagious or infectious epidemic disease that is virulent and devastating.

pestilent.c: Pestilent Pes"ti*lent (?), a. [L. pestilens, -entis, fr. pestis pest: cf. F. pestilent.] Pestilential; noxious; pernicious; mischievous. “Corrupt and pestilent.” Milton. “What a pestilent knave is this same!” Shak.

pestilential.c: Pestilential Pes`ti*len"tial (?), a. [Cf. F. pestilentiel.] 1. Having the nature or qualities of a pestilence. “Sends the pestilential vapors.” Longfellow.

pestilently.c: Pestilently Pes"ti*lent*ly (?), adv. In a pestilent manner; mischievously; destructively. “Above all measure pestilently noisome.” Dr. H. More.

pestilentness.c: Pestilentness Pes"ti*lent*ness, n. The quality of being pestilent.

pestillation.c: pestillation pes`til*la"tion (?), n. [LL. pestillum, L. pistillum. See Pestle.] The act of pounding and bruising with a pestle in a mortar. Sir T. Browne.

pestle.c: pestle pes"tle (pĕs"t'l or pĕs"'l; 277), n. [OE. pestel, OF. pestel, LL. pestellum, L. pistillum, pistillus, a pounder, pestle, fr. pisere, pinsere, to pound, crush, akin to Gr. pti`ssein, Skr. pish. Cf. Pistil.] 1. An implement for pounding and breaking or braying substances in a mortar; as, to grind with a mortar and pestle.
pestle pes"tle (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Pestled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pestling (?).] To pound, pulverize, bray, or mix with a pestle, or as with a pestle; to use a pestle.

pet.c: pet pet (pĕt), n. [Formerly peat, perhaps from Ir. peat, akin to Gael. peata.] 1. A cade lamb; a lamb brought up by hand.
pet pet, a. Petted; indulged; favorite; admired; cherished; as, a pet child; a pet lamb; a pet theory; a pet animal.
Pet Pet, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Petted; p. pr. & vb. n. Petting.] To treat as a pet; to fondle; to indulge; as, she was petted and spoiled.
Pet Pet, v. i. To be a pet. Feltham.

petal.c: Petal Pet"al (pĕt"ail; 277), n. [Gr. pe`talon a leaf, a leaf or plate of metal, fr. pe`talos outspread, broad, flat: cf. F. pétale. See Fathom.] 1. (Bot.) One of the leaves of the corolla, or the colored leaves of a flower. See Corolla, and Illust. of Flower.

petaled.c: Petaled Pet"aled (pĕt"aild), a. (Bot.) Having petals; as, a petaled flower; -- opposed to apetalous, and much used in compounds; as, one-petaled, three-petaled, etc.

petaliform.c: Petaliform Pe*tal"i*form (?), a. (Bot.) Having the form of a petal; petaloid; petal-shaped.

petaline.c: Petaline Pet"al*ine (pĕt"ail*ĭn), a. [Cf. F. pétalin.] (Bot.) Pertaining to a petal; attached to, or resembling, a petal.

petalism.c: Petalism Pet"al*ism (pĕt"ail*ĭz'm), n. [Gr. petalismo`s, fr. pe`talon a leaf: cf. F. pétalisme.] (Gr. Antiq.) A form of sentence among the ancient Syracusans by which they banished for five years a citizen suspected of having dangerous influence or ambition. It was similar to the ostracism in Athens; but olive leaves were used instead of shells for ballots.

petalite.c: Petalite Pet"al*ite (?), n. [Cf. F. pétalite.] (Min.) A rare mineral, occurring crystallized and in cleavable masses, usually white, or nearly so, in color. It is a silicate of aluminum and lithium.

petalody.c: Petalody Pe*tal"o*dy (?), n. [Petal + Gr. e'i^dos form.] (Bot.) The metamorphosis of various floral organs, usually stamens, into petals.

petaloid.c: Petaloid Pet"al*oid (?), a. [Petal + -oid: cf. F. pétaloïde.] (Bot.) Petaline.

petaloideous.c: Petaloideous Pet`al*oid"e*ous (?), a. (Bot.) Having the whole or part of the perianth petaline.

petalosticha.c: Petalosticha ‖Pet`a*los"ti*cha (?), PROP. n. pl. [NL., from Gr. pe`talon a leaf + sti`chos a row.] (Zool.) An order of Echini, including the irregular sea urchins, as the spatangoids. See Spatangoid.

petalous.c: Petalous Pet"al*ous (?), a. Having petals; petaled; -- opposed to apetalous.

petar.c: Petar Pe*tar" (?), n. See Petard. [Obs.] “Hoist with his own petar.” Shak.

petard.c: Petard Pe*tard" (?), n. [F. pétard, fr. péter to break wind, to crack, to explode, L. pedere, peditum.] (Mil.) A case containing powder to be exploded, esp. a conical or cylindrical case of metal filled with powder and attached to a plank, to be exploded against and break down gates, barricades, drawbridges, etc. It has been superseded.

petardier.c: Petardier Petardeer { Pet`ar*deer", Pet`ar*dier" } (?), n. [F. pétardier.] (Mil.) One who managed a petard.

petasus.c: Petasus ‖Pet"a*sus (?), n. [L., from Gr. pe`tasos.] (Gr. & Rom. Antiq.) The winged cap of Mercury; also, a broad-brimmed, low-crowned hat worn by Greeks and Romans.

petaurist.c: Petaurist Pe*tau"rist (pe*tä"rĭst), n. [L. petaurista a ropedancer, Gr. petayristh`s, fr. petayri`zein to dance on a rope, fr. pe`tayron a pole, a stage for ropedancers: cf. F. pétauriste.] (Zool.) Any flying marsupial of the genera Petaurus, Phalangista, Acrobata, and allied genera. See Flying mouse, under Flying, and Phalangister.

petechiae.c: Petechiae ‖Pe*tech"i*æ (?), n. pl.; sing. Petechia (?). [NL., fr. LL. peteccia; cf. F. pétéchie, It. petecchia, Sp. petequia, Gr. pitta`kion a label, plaster.] (Med.) Small crimson, purple, or livid spots, like flea-bites, due to extravasation of blood, which appear on the skin in malignant fevers, etc.

petechial.c: Petechial Pe*tech"i*al (?), a. [Cf. F. pétéchial, LL. petecchialis.] (Med.) Characterized by, or pertaining to, petechiæ; spotted.

peter.c: Peter Pe"ter (pē"tẽr), prop. n. A common baptismal name for a man. The name of one of the twelve apostles of Christ.

Peter Pet"er (pē"tẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Petered (pē"tẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Petering.] [Etymol. uncertain.] To become depleted; to run out; to fail; -- used generally with out; as, that mine has petered out. [Slang, U.S.]

peterman.c: Peterman Pe"ter*man (pē"tẽr*măn), n.; pl. Petermen (pē"tẽr*mĕn). A fisherman; -- so called after the apostle Peter. [An obs. local term in Eng.] Chapman.

petersham.c: Petersham Pe"ter*sham (pē"tẽr*shăm), n. [Named after Lord Petersham.] A rough, knotted woolen cloth, used chiefly for men's overcoats; also, a coat of that material.

peterwort.c: Peterwort Pe"ter*wort` (pē"tẽr*wût`), n. (Bot.) See Saint Peter's-wort, under Saint.

petiolary.c: Petiolary Petiolar { Pet"i*o*lar (?), Pet"i*o*la*ry (?), } a. [Cf. F. pétiolarie.] (Bot.) Of or pertaining to petiole, or proceeding from it; as, a petiolar tendril; growing or supported upon a petiole; as, a petiolar gland; a petiolar bud.

petiolated.c: Petiolated Petiolate { Pet"i*o*late (?), Pet"i*o*la`ted (?), } a. (Bot. & Zool.) Having a stalk or petiole; as, a petioleate leaf; the petiolated abdomen of certain Hymenoptera.

petiole.c: Petiole Pet"i*ole (pĕt"ĭ*ōl), n. [F. pétiole, fr. L. petiolus a little foot, a fruit stalk; cf. pes, pedis, a foot.] 1. (Bot.) A leafstalk; the footstalk of a leaf, connecting the blade with the stem. See Illust. of Leaf.

petiolulate.c: Petiolulate Pet`i*ol"u*late (?), a. (Bot.) Supported by its own petiolule. Gray.

petiolule.c: Petiolule Pet"i*o*lule (?), n. [Cf. F. pétiolule.] (Bot.) A small petiole, or the petiole of a leaflet.

petit.c: Petit Pet"it (pĕt"y̆; F. pei*te"), a. [F. See Petty.] Small; little; insignificant; mean; -- Same as Petty. [Obs., except in legal language.]
Petit mal ‖Pe*tit" mal" (?). [F., lit., little sickness.] (Med.) The mildest form of epilepsy, with momentary faintness or unconsciousness, but without convulsions; -- opposed to grand mal.

petite.c: petite ‖pe*tite" (?), a. [F., fem. of petit.] Small, little; -- used especially of a woman or girl, of small size and trim figure; as, her petite figure.

petition.c: Petition Pe*ti"tion (?), n. [F. pétition, L. petitio, fr. petere, petitum, to beg, ask, seek; perh. akin to E. feather, or find.] 1. A prayer; a supplication; an imploration; an entreaty; especially, a request of a solemn or formal kind; a prayer to the Supreme Being, or to a person of superior power, rank, or authority; also, a single clause in such a prayer.

Petition Pe*ti"tion, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Petitioned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Petitioning.] To make a prayer or request to; to ask from; to solicit; to entreat; especially, to make a formal written supplication, or application to, as to any branch of the government; as, to petition the court; to petition the governor.
Petition Pe*ti"tion, v. i. To make a petition or solicitation.

petitionarily.c: Petitionarily Pe*ti"tion*a*ri*ly (?), adv. By way of begging the question; by an assumption. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

petitionary.c: Petitionary Pe*ti"tion*a*ry (?), a. 1. Supplicatory; making a petition.

petitionee.c: Petitionee Pe*ti`tion*ee" (?), n. A person cited to answer, or defend against, a petition.

petitioner.c: Petitioner Pe*ti"tion*er (?), n. One who presents a petition.

petitioning.c: Petitioning Pe*ti"tion*ing, n. The act of presenting apetition; a supplication.

petitor.c: Petitor Pet"i*tor (?), n. [L., fr. petere to seek.] One who seeks or asks; a seeker; an applicant. [R.] Fuller.

petitory.c: Petitory Pet"i*to*ry (?), a. [L. petitorius, fr. petere, petitum, to beg, ask: cf. F. pétitore.] Petitioning; soliciting; supplicating. Sir W. Hamilton.

petrary.c: Petrary Pet"ra*ry (?), n. [L. petra stone. Cf. Sp. petraria, and E. Pederero.] An ancient war engine for hurling stones.

petrean.c: Petrean Pe*tre"an (pe*trē"ain), a. [L. petraeus, Gr. petrai^os, fr. pe`tra a rock.] Of or pertaining to rock. G. S. Faber.

petrel.c: Petrel Pe"trel (?), n. [F. pétrel; a dim. of the name Peter, L. Petrus, Gr. pe`tros a stone (John i. 42); -- probably so called in allusion to St. Peter's walking on the sea. See Petrify.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of longwinged sea birds belonging to the family Procellaridæ. The small petrels, or Mother Carey's chickens, belong to Oceanites, Oceanodroma, Procellaria, and several allied genera.

petrescence.c: Petrescence Pe*tres"cence (?), n. The process of changing into stone; petrification.

petrescent.c: Petrescent Pe*tres"cent (?), a. [L. petra rock, stone, Gr. pe`tra.] Petrifying; converting into stone; as, petrescent water. Boyle.

petrifaction.c: Petrifaction Pet`ri*fac"tion (?), n. [See Petrify.] 1. The process of petrifying, or changing into stone; conversion of any organic matter (animal or vegetable) into stone, or a substance of stony hardness.

petrifactive.c: Petrifactive Pet`ri*fac"tive (?), a. 1. Having the quality of converting organic matter into stone; petrifying.

petrific.c: Petrific Pe*trif"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. pétrifique.] Petrifying; petrifactive.

petrification.c: Petrification Pet`ri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. pétrification. See Petrify.] 1. See Petrifaction.

petrify.c: Petrify Pet"ri*fy (pĕt"rĭ*fī), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Petrified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Petrifying (?).] [L. petra rock, Gr. pe`tra (akin to pe`tros a stone) + -fy: cf. F. pétrifier. Cf. Parrot, Petrel, Pier.] 1. To convert, as any animal or vegetable matter, into stone or stony substance; as, petrified wood.
Petrify Pet"ri*fy, v. i. 1. To become stone, or of a stony hardness, as organic matter by calcareous deposits.

petrine.c: Petrine Pe"trine (?), a. Of or pertaining to St. Peter; as, the Petrine Epistles.

petro.c: Petro- Pet"ro- (?). A combining form from Gr. pe`tra a rock, pe`tros a stone; as, petrology, petroglyphic.

petrogale.c: Petrogale Pe*trog"a*le (pe*trŏg"ȧ*lē), n. [NL., fr. Gr. pe`tra a rock + galh^ a weasel.] (Zool.) Any Australian kangaroo of the genus Petrogale, as the rock wallaby (Petrogale penicillata).

petroglyphic.c: Petroglyphic Pet`ro*glyph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to petroglyphs or petroglyphy.

petroglyphy.c: Petroglyphy Pe*trog"ly*phy (?), n. [Petro + Gr. gly`fein to carve.] The art or operation of carving figures or inscriptions on rock or stone.

petrographical.c: Petrographical Petrographic { Pet`ro*graph"ic (?), Pet`ro*graph"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to petrography.

petrography.c: Petrography Pe*trog"ra*phy (?), n. [Petro + -graphy.] 1. The art of writing on stone.

petrohyoid.c: petrohyoid pet`ro*hy"oid (pĕt`ro*hī"oid), a. [Petro + hyoid.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the petrous, or periotic, portion of the skull and the hyoid arch; as, the petrohyoid muscles of the frog.

petrolatum.c: Petrolatum Pet`ro*la"tum (?), n. (Chem. & Pharm.) A semisolid unctuous substance, neutral, and without taste or odor, derived from petroleum by distilling off the lighter portions and purifying the residue. It is a yellowish, fatlike mass, transparent in thin layers, and somewhat fluorescent. It is used as a bland protective dressing, and as a substitute for fatty materials in ointments. U. S. Pharm.

petroleum.c: Petroleum Pe*tro"le*um (pe*trō"le*ŭm), n. [NL., fr. L. petra a rock + oleum oil: cf. F. pétrole. Cf. Petrify, and Oil.] Rock oil, mineral oil, or natural oil, a dark brown or greenish inflammable liquid, which, at certain points, exists in the upper strata of the earth, from whence it is pumped, or forced by pressure of the gas attending it. It consists of a complex mixture of various hydrocarbons, largely of the methane series, but may vary much in appearance, composition, and properties. It is refined by distillation, and the products include kerosene, benzine, gasoline, paraffin, etc.

petroleuse.c: Petroleuse Petroleur { ‖Pé`tro`leur" (?), n. m. ‖Pé`tro`leuse" (?), n. f. } [F.] One who makes use of petroleum for incendiary purposes.

petroline.c: Petroline Pet"ro*line (?), n. (Chem.) A paraffin obtained from petroleum from Rangoon in India, and practically identical with ordinary paraffin.

petrological.c: Petrological Petrologic { Pet`ro*log"ic (?), Pet`ro*log"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to petrology.

petrologist.c: Petrologist Pe*trol"o*gist (?), n. One who is versed in petrology.

petrology.c: Petrology Pe*trol"o*gy (?), n. [Petro + -logy.] 1. The department of science which is concerned with the mineralogical and chemical composition of rocks, and with their classification: lithology.

petromastoid.c: Petromastoid Pet`ro*mas"toid (?), a. [Petro + mastoid.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the petrous and mastoid parts of the temporal bone; periotic.

petromyzont.c: Petromyzont Pet`ro*my"zont (?), n. [Petro + Gr. my`zein to suck in.] (Zool.) A lamprey.

petronel.c: Petronel Pet`ro*nel (?), n. [OF. petrinal, fr. peitrine, petrine, the breast, F. poitrine; so called because it was placed against the breast in order to fire. See Poitrel.] A sort of hand cannon, or portable firearm, used in France in the 15th century.

petrosal.c: Petrosal Pe*tro"sal (?), a. [See Petrous.] (Anat.) (a) Hard; stony; petrous; as, the petrosal bone; petrosal part of the temporal bone. (b) Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the petrous, or petrosal, bone, or the corresponding part of the temporal bone.
Petrosal Pe*tro"sal, n. (Anat.) (a) A petrosal bone. (b) The auditory capsule. Owen.

petrosilicious.c: Petrosilicious Pet`ro*si*li"cious (?), a. Containing, or consisting of, petrosilex.

petrostearine.c: Petrostearine Pet`ro*ste"a*rine (?), n. [Petro + stearine.] A solid unctuous material, of which candles are made.

petrous.c: Petrous Pe"trous (?), a. [L. petrosus, fr. petra a stone.] 1. Like stone; hard; stony; rocky; as, the petrous part of the temporal bone. Hooper.

petticoat.c: Petticoat Pet"ti*coat (?), n. (Zool.) [Petty + coat.] A loose under-garment worn by women, and covering the body below the waist.

pettifog.c: Pettifog Pet"ti*fog (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Pettifogged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pettifogging (?).] [Petty + fog to pettifog.] 1. To do a petty business as a lawyer; also, to do law business in a petty or tricky way. “He takes no money, but pettifogs gratis.” S. Butler.
Pettifog Pet"ti*fog, v. t. To advocate like a pettifogger; to argue trickily; as, to pettifog a claim. [Colloq.]

pettifogger.c: Pettifogger Pet"ti*fog`ger (?), n. A lawyer who deals in petty cases; an attorney whose methods are mean and tricky; an inferior lawyer.

pettifoggery.c: Pettifoggery Pet"ti*fog`ger*y (?), n.; pl. pettifoggeries (?). The practice or arts of a pettifogger; disreputable tricks; quibbles; chicanery.

pettifogulize.c: Pettifogulize Pet`ti*fog"u*lize (?), v. i. To act as a pettifogger; to use contemptible tricks. De Quincey.

pettily.c: Pettily Pet"ti*ly, adv. In a petty manner; frivolously.

pettiness.c: Pettiness Pet"ti*ness, n. The quality or state of being petty or paltry; littleness; meanness.

pettish.c: Pettish Pet"tish (?), a. [From Pet.] Fretful; peevish; moody; capricious; inclined to ill temper. “A pettish kind of humor.” Sterne. -- Pet"tish*ly, adv. -- Pet"tish*ness, n.

pettitoes.c: Pettitoes Pet"ti*toes (?), n. pl. [Petty + toes.] The toes or feet of a pig, -- often used as food; sometimes, in contempt, the human feet. Shak.

petto.c: Petto ‖Pet"to (pĕt"to), n. [It., fr. L. pectus.] The breast. [Obsolescent]

petty.c: Petty Pet"ty (pĕt"ty̆), a. [Compar. Pettier (pĕt"tĭ*ẽr); superl. Pettiest.] [OE. petit, F. petit; probably of Celtic origin, and akin to E. piece. Cf. Petit.] Little; trifling; inconsiderable; unimportant; also, inferior; subordinate; as, a petty fault; petty complaints; a petty prince. Denham.

pettychaps.c: Pettychaps Pet"ty*chaps (pĕt"ty̆*chŏps), n. (Zool.) Any one of several species of small European singing birds of the subfamily Sylviinæ, as the willow warbler, the chiff-chaff, and the golden warbler (Sylvia hortensis).

pettywhin.c: Pettywhin Pet"ty*whin (pĕt"ty̆*hwĭn), n. [Petty + whin.] (Bot.) The needle furze. See under Needle.

petulancy.c: Petulancy Petulance { Pet"u*lance (?), Pet"u*lan*cy (?), } n. [L. petulania: cf. F. pétulance. See Petulant.] The quality or state of being petulant; temporary peevishness; pettishness; capricious ill humor. “The petulancy of our words.” B. Jonson.

petulant.c: Petulant Pet"u*lant (?), a. [L. petulans, -antis, prop., making slight attacks upon, from a lost dim. of petere to fall upon, to attack: cf. F. pétulant. See Petition.] 1. Forward; pert; insolent; wanton. [Obs.] Burton.

petulantly.c: Petulantly Pet"u*lant*ly, adv. In a petulant manner.

petulcity.c: Petulcity Pe*tul"ci*ty (?), n. [See Petulcous.] Wantonness; friskiness. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

petulcous.c: Petulcous Pe*tul"cous (?), a. [L. petulcus. Cf. Petulant.] Wanton; frisky; lustful. [Obs.] J. V. Cane.

petune.c: Petune Pe*tune" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Petuned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Petuning.] [See Petunia.] (Agric.) To spray (tobacco) with a liquid intended to produce flavor or aroma.

petunia.c: Petunia Pe*tu"ni*a (pe*tū"nĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Braz. petun tobacco.] (Bot.) A genus of solanaceous herbs with funnel-form or salver-shaped corollas. Two species are common in cultivation, Petunia violacea, with reddish purple flowers, and Petunia nyctaginiflora, with white flowers. There are also many hybrid forms with variegated corollas.

petuntze.c: Petuntze Petuntse Petunse { Pe*tunse", Pe*tuntse", Pe*tuntze" } (pe*tŭns"), n. [From Chinese.] Powdered fledspar, kaolin, or quartz, used in the manufacture of porcelain.

petworth.c: Petworth marble Pet"worth mar"ble (?). A kind of shell marble occurring in the Wealden clay at Petworth, in Sussex, England; -- called also Sussex marble.

petzite.c: Petzite Petz"ite (?), n. [From Petz, who analyzed it.] (Min.) A telluride of silver and gold, related to hessite.

peucedanin.c: Peucedanin Peu*ced"a*nin (?), n. (Chem.) A tasteless white crystalline substance, extracted from the roots of the sulphurwort (Peucedanum), masterwort (Imperatoria), and other related plants; -- called also imperatorin.

peucil.c: Peucil Peu"cil (pū"sĭl), n. [Gr. pey`kh pine tree.] (Chem.) A liquid resembling camphene, obtained by treating turpentine hydrochloride with lime. [Written also peucyl.]

pew.c: Pew Pew (pū), n. [OE. pewe, OF. puie parapet, balustrade, balcony, fr. L. podium an elevated place, a jutty, balcony, a parapet or balcony in the circus, where the emperor and other distinguished persons sat, Gr. po`dion, dim. of poy`s, podo`s, foot; -- hence the Latin sense of a raised place (orig. as a rest or support for the foot). See Foot, and cf. Podium, Poy.] 1. One of the compartments in a church which are separated by low partitions, and have long seats upon which several persons may sit; -- sometimes called slip. Pews were originally made square, but are now usually long and narrow.
Pew Pew, v. t. To furnish with pews. [R.] Ash.

pewee.c: Pewee Pe"wee (?), n. [So called from its note.] 1. (Zool.) A common American tyrant flycatcher (Sayornis phœbe, or Sayornis fuscus). Called also pewit, and phœbe.

pewfellow.c: Pewfellow Pew"fel`low (?), n. 1. One who occupies the same pew with another.

pewit.c: Pewit Pe"wit (?), n. [Prob. of imitative origin; cf. OD. piewit, D. kievit, G. kibitz.] (Zool.) (a) The lapwing. (b) The European black-headed, or laughing, gull (Xema ridibundus). See under Laughing. (c) The pewee. [Written also peevit, peewit, pewet.]

pewter.c: Pewter Pew"ter (pū"tẽr), n. [OE. pewtyr, OF. peutre, peautre, piautre: cf. D. peauter, piauter, It. peltro, Sp. & Pg. peltre, LL. peutreum, pestrum. Cf. Spelter.] 1. A hard, tough, but easily fusible, alloy, originally consisting of tin with a little lead, but afterwards modified by the addition of copper, antimony, or bismuth.

pewterer.c: Pewterer Pew"ter*er (?), n. One whose occupation is to make utensils of pewter; a pewtersmith. Shak.

pewtery.c: Pewtery Pew"ter*y (?), a. Belonging to, or resembling, pewter; as, a pewtery taste.

pexity.c: Pexity Pex"i*ty (?), n. [L. pexitas, fr. pexus woolly, nappy, p. p. of pectere to comb.] Nap of cloth. [Obs.]

peyers.c: Peyer's glands Pey"er's glands` (?). [So called from J. K. Peyer, who described them in 1677.] (Anat.) Patches of lymphoid nodules, in the walls of the small intestiness; agminated glands; -- called also Peyer's patches. In typhoid fever they become the seat of ulcers which are regarded as the characteristic organic lesion of that disease.

peytrel.c: Peytrel Pey"trel (?), n. [OF. peitral. See Poitrel.] (Anc. Armor) The breastplate of a horse's armor or harness. [Spelt also peitrel.] See Poitrel. [Obs.] Chaucer.

peziza.c: Peziza ‖Pe*zi"za (?), prop. n. [NL., corrupt. from L. pezica a sessile mushroom, fr. Gr. pe`zis, fr. pe`za, poy`s, a foot.] (Bot.) A genus of fungi embracing a great number of species, some of which are remarkable for their regular cuplike form and deep colors.

pezizoid.c: Pezizoid Pez"i*zoid (?), a. [Peziza + -oid.] (Bot.) Resembling a fungus of the genus Peziza; having a cuplike form.

pfennig.c: Pfennig ‖Pfen"nig (?), n.; pl. Pfennigs (#), G. Pfennige (#). [G. See Penny.] A small copper coin of Germany. It is the hundredth part of a mark. In 2001 it was superseded by the euro.

phacellus.c: Phacellus ‖Pha*cel"lus (?), n.; pl. Phacelli (#). [NL., fr. Gr. fa`kelos a bundle of fagots.] (Zool.) One of the filaments on the inner surface of the gastric cavity of certain jellyfishes.

phacochere.c: Phacochere Phac"o*chere (?), n. [Gr. fako`s a lentil seed, a wart + choi^ros a pig.] (Zool.) The wart hog.

phacoid.c: Phacoid Pha"coid (?), a. [Gr. fako`s a lentil + -oid.] Resembling a lentil; lenticular.

phacolite.c: Phacolite Phac"o*lite (?), n. [Gr. fako`s lentil + -lite.] (Min.) A colorless variety of chabazite; the original was from Leipa, in Bohemia.

phacops.c: Phacops ‖Pha"cops (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. fako`s a lentil + 'w`ps, 'wpo`s, the eye.] (Paleon.) A genus of trilobites found in the Silurian and Devonian formations. Phacops bufo is one of the most common species.

phaeacian.c: Phaeacian Phæ*a"cian (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Phæacians, a fabulous seafaring people fond of the feast, the lyre, and the dance, mentioned by Homer.

phaenogam.c: Phaenogam Phæ"no*gam (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the class Phænogamia.

phaenogamia.c: Phaenogamia ‖Phæ`no*ga"mi*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. fai`nein to show + ga`mos marriage.] (Bot.) The class of flowering plants including all which have true flowers with distinct floral organs; phanerogamia.

phaenogamic.c: Phaenogamic Phaenogamian { Phæ`no*ga"mi*an (?), Phæ`no*gam"ic (?), } a. Same as Phænogamous.

phaenogamous.c: Phaenogamous Phæ*nog"a*mous (?), a. (Bot.) Having true flowers with distinct floral organs; flowering.

phaeospore.c: Phaeospore Phæ"o*spore (?), n. [Gr. faio`s dusky + E. spore.] (Bot.) A brownish zoospore, characteristic of an order (Phæosporeæ) of dark green or olive-colored algæ. -- Phæ`o*spor"ic (#), a.

phaethon.c: Phaethon Pha"ë*thon (fā"e*thŏn), prop. n. [L., Phaëthon (in sense 1), fr. Gr. Fae`qwn, fr. fae`qein, fa`ein, to shine. See Phantom.] 1. (Class. Myth.) The son of Helios (Phœbus), that is, the son of light, or of the sun. He is fabled to have obtained permission to drive the chariot of the sun, in doing which his want of skill would have set the world on fire, had he not been struck with a thunderbolt by Jupiter, and hurled headlong into the river Po.

phaeton.c: Phaeton Pha"ë*ton (fā"e*tŏn), n. [F. phaéton a kind of carriage, fr. Phaéthon Phaëthon, the son of Helios. See Phaëthon.] 1. A four-wheeled carriage (with or without a top), open, or having no side pieces, in front of the seat. It is drawn by one or two horses.

phagedena.c: Phagedena Phag`e*de"na (?), n. [L. phagedaena, Gr. fage`daina, fr. fagei^n to eat.] (Med.) (a) A canine appetite; bulimia. [Obs.] (b) Spreading, obstinate ulceration.

phagedenical.c: Phagedenical Phagedenic { Phag`e*den"ic (?), Phag`e*den"ic*al (?), } a. [L. phagedaenicus, Gr. fagedainiko`s: cf. F. phagédénique.] (Med.) Of, like, or pertaining to, phagedena; used in the treatment of phagedena; as, a phagedenic ulcer or medicine. -- n. A phagedenic medicine.

phagocyte.c: phagocyte phag"o*cyte (făg"o*sīt), n. [Gr. fagei^n to eat + ky`tos a hollow vessel.] (Physiol.) A leucocyte which plays a part in immunity and retrogressive processes by taking up (eating), in the form of fine granules, foreign objects such as bacteria or cellular parts to be removed. There are two principle subtypes, (1) microphages, polymorphonuclear lymphocytes which principally digest bacteria; and (2) macrophages, mononucleated cells which primarily scavenge dead tissue and degenerate cells. Stedman.

phainopepla.c: Phainopepla ‖Pha*i`no*pep"la (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. faeino`s shining + pe`plos robe.] (Zool.) A small crested passerine bird (Phaïnopepla nitens), native of Mexico and the Southern United States. The adult male is of a uniform glossy blue-black; the female is brownish. Called also black flycatcher.

phakoscope.c: Phakoscope Phak"o*scope (?), n. [Gr. fako`s a lentil, or lenticular body + -scope.] (Physiol.) An instrument for studying the mechanism of accommodation.

phalaena.c: Phalaena ‖Pha*læ"na (fȧ*lē"nȧ), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. fa`laina, fa`llaina, a kind of moth.] (Zool.) A linnæan genus which included the moths in general.

phalaenid.c: Phalaenid Pha*læ"nid (?), n. [Gr. fa`laina, fa`llaina, a kind of moth.] (Zool.) Any moth of the family Phalænidæ, of which the cankerworms are examples; a geometrid.

phalangal.c: Phalangal Phalangeal { Pha*lan"ge*al (?), Pha*lan"gal (?), } a. Of or pertaining to the phalanges. See Phalanx, 2.

phalanger.c: Phalanger Pha*lan"ger (?), n. [Cf. F. phalanger. See Phalanx.] (Zool.) Any marsupial belonging to Phalangista, Cuscus, Petaurus, and other genera of the family Phalangistidæ. They are arboreal, and the species of Petaurus are furnished with lateral parachutes. See Flying phalanger, under Flying.

phalangid.c: Phalangid Pha*lan"gid (?), n.; pl. Phalangides (?). (Zool.) One of the Phalangoidea.

phalangious.c: Phalangious Pha*lan"gi*ous (?), a. [L. phalangium a kind of venomous spider, Gr. fala`ggion, fr. fa`lagx a spider. Cf. Phalanx.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to Phalangoidea.

phalangist.c: Phalangist Pha*lan"gist (?), n. (Zool.) Any arboreal marsupial of the genus Phalangista. The vulpine phalangist (Phalangista vulpina) is the largest species, the full grown male being about two and a half feet long. It has a large bushy tail.

phalangistine.c: Phalangistine Phalangister { Phal`an*gis"ter (?), Phal`an*gis"tine (?), } n. (Zool.) Same as Phalangist.

phalangite.c: Phalangite Phal"an*gite (?), n. [Gr. falaggi`ths: cf. F. phalangite.] A soldier belonging to a phalanx. [Obs.]

phalangoidea.c: Phalangoidea ‖Phal`an*goi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL., from Phalangium the daddy longlegs (see Phalangious) + Gr. e'i^dos form.] (Zool.) A division of Arachnoidea, including the daddy longlegs or harvestman (Phalangium) and many similar kinds. They have long, slender, many-jointed legs; usually a rounded, segmented abdomen; and chelate jaws. They breathe by tracheæ. Called also Phalangides, Phalangidea, Phalangiida, and Opilionea.

phalansterian.c: Phalansterian Phal`an*ste"ri*an (?), a. [F. phalanstérien, a. & n.] Of or pertaining to phalansterianism.
Phalansterian Phal`an*ste"ri*an, n. One who favors the system of phalansteries proposed by Fourier.

phalansterianism.c: Phalansterianism Phalansterism { Pha*lan"ster*ism (?), Phal`an*ste"ri*an*ism (?), } n. A system of phalansteries proposed by Fourier; Fourierism.

phalanstery.c: Phalanstery Phal"an*ster*y (?), n.; pl. -ies (#). [F. phalanstère, fr. Gr. fa`lagx a phalanx + stereo`s firm, solid.] 1. An association or community organized on the plan of Fourier. See Fourierism.

phalanx.c: Phalanx Pha"lanx (?), n.; pl. Phalanxes (#), L. Phalanges (#). [L., from Gr. fa`lagx.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) A body of heavy-armed infantry formed in ranks and files close and deep. There were several different arrangements, the phalanx varying in depth from four to twenty-five or more ranks of men. “In cubic phalanx firm advanced.” Milton.

phalarope.c: Phalarope Phal"a*rope (?), n. [Gr. falaro`s having a patch of white + poy`s, podo`s, a foot: cf. F. phalarope.] (Zool.) Any species of Phalaropus and allied genera of small wading birds (Grallæ), having lobate toes. They are often seen far from land, swimming in large flocks. Called also sea goose.

phallic.c: Phallic Phal"lic (făl"lĭk), a. [Gr. falliko`s] Of or pertaining to the phallus, or to phallism.

phallism.c: Phallism Phal"lism (făl"lĭz'm), n. The worship of the generative principle in nature, symbolized by the phallus.

phallus.c: Phallus Phal"lus (făl"lŭs), n.; pl. Phalli (?). [L., a phallus (in sense 1), Gr. fallo`s.] 1. The emblem of the generative power in nature, carried in procession in the Bacchic orgies, or worshiped in various ways.

phanar.c: Phanar Phan"ar (făn"r), n. [Turk. fanar, fr. NGr. fana`ri lighthouse, Gr. fana`rion lantern; -- from a lighthouse on a point projecting into the Golden Horn.] A quarter of Constantinople which, after the Turkish conquest of the city, became the chief Greek quarter; hence, the Greek officials of Turkey, or phanariots, as a class.

phanariote.c: Phanariote Phanariot { Pha*nar"i*ot (fȧ*năr"ĭ*ŏt), n. Also Pha*nar"i*ote (fȧ*năr"ĭ*ōt)}. [NGr. Fanariw`ths, fr. Phanar. See Phanar.] One of the Greeks of Constantinople who after the Turkish conquest became powerful in clerical and other offices under Turkish patronage.

phanerite.c: Phanerite Phan"er*ite (făn"ẽr*īt), a. [Gr. fanero`s visible, from fai`nein to bring to light.] Evident; visible.

phanerocarpae.c: Phanerocarpae ‖Phan`er*o*car"pæ (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr. fanero`s evident + karpo`s fruit (but taken to mean, ovary).] (Zool.) Same as Acraspeda.

phanerocodonic.c: Phanerocodonic Phan`er*o*co*don"ic (?), a. [Gr. fanero`s evident + kw`dwn a bell.] (Zool.) Having an umbrella-shaped or bell-shaped body, with a wide, open cavity beneath; -- said of certain jellyfishes.

phanerocrystalline.c: Phanerocrystalline Phan`er*o*crys"tal*line (?), a. [Gr. fanero`s visible + E. crystalline.] (Geol.) Distinctly crystalline; -- used of rocks. Opposed to cryptocrystalline.

phanerodactyla.c: Phanerodactyla ‖Phan`er*o*dac"ty*la (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. fanero`s evident + da`ktylos finger.] (Zool.) Same as Saururæ.

phanerogamia.c: Phanerogamia ‖Phan`er*o*ga"mi*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. fanero`s visible (fr. fai`nein to bring to light) + ga`mos marriage.] (Bot.) That one of the two primary divisions of the vegetable kingdom which contains the phanerogamic, or flowering, plants.

phanerogamous.c: Phanerogamous Phanerogamic { Phan`er*o*gam"ic (?), Phan`er*og"a*mous (?), } a. Having visible flowers containing distinct stamens and pistils; -- said of plants.

phaneroglossal.c: Phaneroglossal Phan`er*o*glos"sal (?), a. [Gr. fanero`s evident + glw`ssa tongue.] (Zool.) Having a conspicious tongue; -- said of certain reptiles and insects.

phantascope.c: Phantascope Phan"ta*scope (făn"tȧ*skōp), n. [Gr. fa`ntasma image + -scope.] An optical instrument or toy, resembling the phenakistoscope, and illustrating the same principle; -- called also phantasmascope.

phantasm.c: Phantasm Phan"tasm (?), n. [L. phantasma. See Phantom, and cf. Fantasm.] [Spelt also fantasm.] 1. An image formed by the mind, and supposed to be real or material; a shadowy or airy appearance; sometimes, an optical illusion; a phantom; a dream.

phantasmagoria.c: Phantasmagoria Phan*tas`ma*go"ri*a (?), n. [NL., from Gr. fa`ntasma a phantasm + 'agora` an assembly, fr. 'agei`rein to gather: cf. F. phantasmagorie.] 1. An optical effect produced by a magic lantern. The figures are painted in transparent colors, and all the rest of the glass is opaque black. The screen is between the spectators and the instrument, and the figures are often made to appear as in motion, or to merge into one another.

phantasmagorial.c: Phantasmagorial Phan*tas`ma*go"ri*al (?), a. Of, relating to, or resembling phantasmagoria; phantasmagoric.

phantasmagoric.c: Phantasmagoric Phan*tas`ma*gor"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to phantasmagoria; phantasmagorial. Hawthorne.

phantasmal.c: Phantasmal Phan*tas"mal (?), a. Pertaining to, of the nature of, or resembling, a phantasm; spectral; illusive.

phantasmatical.c: Phantasmatical Phan`tas*mat"ic*al (?), a. [L. phantasmaticus.] Phantasmal. Dr. H. More.

phantasmatography.c: Phantasmatography Phan*tas`ma*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. fa`ntasma, fanta`smatos, phantasm + -graphy.] A description of celestial phenomena, as rainbows, etc.

phantastical.c: Phantastical Phantastic { Phan*tas"tic (?), Phan*tas"tic*al (?), } a. See Fantastic.

phantasy.c: Phantasy Phan"ta*sy (?), n. See Fantasy, and Fancy.

phantom.c: Phantom Phan"tom (?), n. [OE. fantome, fantosme, fantesme, OF. fantôme, fr. L. phantasma, Gr. fa`ntasma, fr. fai`nein to show. See Fancy, and cf. Phaëton, Phantasm, Phase.] That which has only an apparent existence; an apparition; a specter; a phantasm; a sprite; an airy spirit; an ideal image.
Phantom Phan"tom, a. Being, or of the nature of, a phantom.

Phantom circuit Phantom circuit. (Elec.) The equivalent of an additional circuit or wire, in reality not existing, obtained by certain arrangements of real circuits, as in some multiplex telegraph systems.

pharaoh.c: Pharaoh Pha"raoh (?), n. [Heb. parōh; of Egyptian origin: cf. L. pharao, Gr. faraw`. Cf. Faro.] 1. A title by which the sovereigns of ancient Egypt were designated.

pharaonic.c: Pharaonic Phar`a*on"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. pharaonique.] Of or pertaining to the Pharaohs, or kings of ancient Egypt.

phare.c: Phare Phare (?), n. [See Pharos.] 1. A beacon tower; a lighthouse. [Obs.]

pharisaical.c: Pharisaical Pharisaic { Phar`i*sa"ic (făr`ĭ*sā"ĭk), Phar`i*sa"ic*al (-ĭ*kail), } a. [L. Pharisaicus, Gr. Farisai:ko`s: cf. F. pharisaïque. See Pharisee.] 1. Of or pertaining to the Pharisees; resembling the Pharisees. “The Pharisaic sect among the Jews.” Cudworth.

pharisaism.c: Pharisaism Phar`i*sa"ism (?), n. [Cf. F. pharisaisme.] 1. The notions, doctrines, and conduct of the Pharisees, as a sect. Sharp.

pharisean.c: Pharisean Phar`i*se"an (?), a. [L. Pharisaeus, Gr. Farisai^os.] Following the practice of Pharisees; Pharisaic. [Obs.] “Pharisean disciples.” Milton.

pharisee.c: Pharisee Phar"i*see (făr"ĭ*sē), n. [L. Pharisaeus, Gr. Farisai^os, from Heb. pārash to separate.] One of a sect or party among the Jews, noted for a strict and formal observance of rites and ceremonies and of the traditions of the elders, and whose pretensions to superior sanctity led them to separate themselves from the other Jews.

pharmaceutical.c: Pharmaceutical Pharmaceutic { Phar`ma*ceu"tic (fär`mȧ*sū"tĭk), Phar`ma*ceu"tic*al (-tĭ*kail), } a. [L. pharmaceuticus, Gr. farmakeytiko`s, fr. farmakey`ein: cf. F. pharmaceutique. See Pharmacy.] Of or pertaining to the knowledge or art of pharmacy, or to the art of preparing medicines according to the rules or formulas of pharmacy; as, pharmaceutical preparations. -- Phar`ma*ceu"tic*al*ly, adv.

pharmaceutics.c: Pharmaceutics Phar`ma*ceu"tics (?), n. The science of preparing medicines.

pharmaceutist.c: Pharmaceutist Phar`ma*ceu"tist (?), n. One skilled in pharmacy; a pharmacist; a druggist. See the Note under Apothecary.

pharmacist.c: Pharmacist Phar"ma*cist (?), n. One skilled in pharmacy; a pharmaceutist; a druggist; an apothecary.

pharmacodymanics.c: Pharmacodymanics Phar`ma*co*dy*man"ics (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon medicine + E. dynamics.] That branch of pharmacology which treats of the action and the effects of medicines in the body, and also their distribution in various bodily tissues over time, and their breakdown and excretion.

pharmacognosis.c: Pharmacognosis Phar`ma*cog*no"sis (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon a drug + gnw^sis a knowing.] That branch of pharmacology which treats of unprepared medicines or simples; -- usually called pharmacognosy, and also pharmacography, and pharmacomathy.

pharmacography.c: Pharmacography Phar`ma*cog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon a drug + -graphy.] See Pharmacognosis.

pharmacolite.c: Pharmacolite Phar*mac"o*lite (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon drug, poisonous drug + -lite: cf. F. pharmacolithe.] (Min.) A hydrous arsenate of lime, usually occurring in silky fibers of a white or grayish color.

pharmacologist.c: Pharmacologist Phar`ma*col"o*gist (?), n. [Cf. F. pharmacologiste.] One skilled in pharmacology.

pharmacology.c: Pharmacology Phar`ma*col"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon drug + -logy: cf. F. pharmacologie.] 1. The science dealing with knowledge of the preparation, use, and effects of drugs or medicines; the art of preparing medicines.

pharmacomathy.c: Pharmacomathy Phar`ma*com"a*thy (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon a drug + manqa`nein to learn.] See Pharmacognosis.

pharmacon.c: Pharmacon Phar"ma*con (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. fa`rmakon.] A medicine or drug; also, a poison. Dunglison.

pharmacopoeia.c: Pharmacopoeia Phar`ma*co*pœ"ia (?), n. [NL., from Gr. farmakopoii:`a the preparation of medicines; fa`rmakon medicine + poiei^n to make.] 1. A book or treatise describing the drugs, preparations, etc., used in medicine; especially, one that is issued by official authority and considered as an authoritative standard.

pharmacopolist.c: Pharmacopolist Phar`ma*cop"o*list (?), n. [L. pharmacopola, Gr. farmakopw`lhs; fa`rmakon medicine + pwlei^n to sell.] One who sells medicines; an apothecary.

pharmacosiderite.c: Pharmacosiderite Phar`ma*co*sid"er*ite (?), n. [Gr. fa`rmakon drug, poison + E. siderite.] (Min.) A hydrous arsenate of iron occurring in green or yellowish green cubic crystals; cube ore.

pharmacy.c: Pharmacy Phar"ma*cy (?), n. [OE. fermacie, OF. farmacie, pharmacie, F. pharmacie, Gr. farmakei`a, fr. farmakey`ein to administer or use medicines, fr. fa`rmakon medicine.] 1. The art or practice of preparing and preserving drugs, and of compounding and dispensing medicines according to prescriptions of physicians; the occupation of an apothecary or a pharmaceutical chemist.

pharo.c: Pharo Pha"ro (?), n. 1. A pharos; a lighthouse. [Obs.]

pharology.c: Pharology Pha*rol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. fa`ros a lighthouse + -logy.] The art or science which treats of lighthouses and signal lights.

pharos.c: Pharos Pha"ros (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. fa`ros, fr. Fa`ros an island in the Bay of Alexandria, where king Ptolemy Philadelphus built a famous lighthouse, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.] A lighthouse or beacon for the guidance of seamen.

pharyngeal.c: Pharyngeal Phar`yn*ge"al (?), a. [See Pharynx.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the pharynx; in the region of the pharynx.

Pharyngeal Phar`yn*ge"al, n. (Anat.) A pharyngeal bone or cartilage; especially, one of the lower pharyngeals, which belong to the rudimentary fifth branchial arch in many fishes, or one of the upper pharyngeals, or pharyngobranchials, which are the dorsal elements in the complete branchial arches.

pharyngitis.c: Pharyngitis ‖Phar`yn*gi"tis (?), n. [NL. See Pharynx, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the pharynx.

pharyngobranchial.c: Pharyngobranchial Pha*ryn`go*bran"chi*al (?), a. [Pharynx + branchial.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the pharynx and the branchiæ; -- applied especially to the dorsal elements in the branchial arches of fishes. See Pharyngeal. -- n. A pharyngobranchial, or upper pharyngeal, bone or cartilage.

pharyngobranchii.c: Pharyngobranchii ‖Pha*ryn`go*bran"chi*i (?), n. pl. [NL. See Pharynx, and Branchia.] (Zool.) Same as Leptocardia.

pharyngognathi.c: Pharyngognathi ‖Phar`yn*gog"na*thi (?), n. pl. [NL. See Pharynx, and Gnathic.] (Zool.) A division of fishes in which the lower pharyngeal bones are united. It includes the scaroid, labroid, and embioticoid fishes.

pharyngolaryngeal.c: Pharyngolaryngeal Pha*ryn`go*lar`yn*ge"al (?), a. [Pharynx + laryngeal.] Of or pertaining both to pharynx and the larynx.

pharyngopneusta.c: Pharyngopneusta ‖Pha*ryn`gop*neus"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. fa`rygx the pharynx + pnei^n to breathe.] (Zool.) A group of invertebrates including the Tunicata and Enteropneusta. -- Pha*ryn`gop*neus"tal (#), a.

pharyngotome.c: Pharyngotome Pha*ryn"go*tome (?), n. (Surg.) An instrument for incising or scarifying the tonsils, etc.

pharyngotomy.c: Pharyngotomy Phar`yn*got"o*my (?), n. [Pharynx + Gr. te`mnein to cut: cf. F. pharyngotomie.] (Surg.) (a) The operation of making an incision into the pharynx, to remove a tumor or anything that obstructs the passage. (b) Scarification or incision of the tonsils.

pharynx.c: Pharynx Phar"ynx (?), n.; pl. pharynges (#). [NL., fr. Gr. fa`rygx, fa`ryggos: cf. F. pharynx.] (Anat.) The part of the alimentary canal between the cavity of the mouth and the esophagus. It has one or two external openings through the nose in the higher vertebrates, and lateral branchial openings in fishes and some amphibias.

phascolome.c: Phascolome Phas"co*lome (?), n. [Gr.? pouch +? mouse.] (Zool.) A marsupial of the genus Phascolomys; a wombat.

phase.c: Phase Phase (fāz), n.; pl. Phases (fāz"ĕz). [NL. phasis, Gr. fa`sis, fr. fai`nein to make to appear: cf. F. phase. See Phenomenon, Phantom, and Emphasis.] 1. That which is exhibited to the eye; the appearance which anything manifests, especially any one among different and varying appearances of the same object.
Phase Phase (fāz), v. t. [Cf. Feeze.] To disturb the composure of; to disconcert; to nonplus; -- an older spelling, now replaced by faze. [Colloq., Archaic]
Phase angle Phase angle. (Elec.) The angle expressing phase relation.
Phase converter Phase converter. (Elec.) A machine for converting an alternating current into an alternating current of a different number of phases and the same frequency.

Phase displacement Phase displacement. (Elec.) A charge of phase whereby an alternating current attains its maximum later or earlier. An inductance would cause a lag, a capacity would cause an advance, in phase.

Phase rule Phase rule. (Phys. Chem.) A generalization with regard to systems of chemical equilibrium, discovered by Prof. J. Willard Gibbs. It may be stated thus: The degree of variableness (number of degrees of freedom) of a system is equal to the number of components minus the number of phases, plus two. Thus, if the components be salt and water, and the phases salt, ice, saturated solution, and vapor, the system is invariant, that is, there is only one set of conditions under which these four phases can exist in equilibrium. If only three phases be considered, the system is univariant, that is, the fixing of one condition, as temperature, determines the others.
Phase splitter Phase splitter. (Elec.) A device by which a single-phase current is split into two or more currents differing in phase. It is used in starting single-phase induction motors.
Phase splitting Phase splitting. (Elec.) The dephasing of the two parts of a single alternating current in two dissimilar branches of a given circuit.

phasel.c: Phasel Pha"sel (?), n. [L. phaselus, phaseolus, Gr.?,?: cf. F. phaséole, faséole. Cf. Fesels.] The French bean, or kidney bean.

phaseless.c: Phaseless Phase"less (fāz"ls), a. Without a phase, or visible form. [R.] “A phaseless and increasing gloom.” Poe.

phasemeter.c: Phasemeter Phase meter { Phase meter, or Phase"me`ter }, n. (Elec.) A device for measuring the difference in phase of two alternating currents of electromotive forces.

phaseolus.c: Phaseolus ‖Pha*se"o*lus (?), prop. n. [L.] (Bot.) A genus of leguminous plants, including the Lima bean, the kidney bean, the scarlet runner, etc. See Bean.

phaseomannite.c: Phaseomannite Pha`se*o*man"nite (?), n. [So called because found in the unripe fruit of the bean (Phaseolus vulgaris).] (Chem.) Same as Inosite.

phasing.c: Phasing Phas"ing (?), a. (Elec.) Pertaining to phase or differences of phase.
Phasing current Phasing current. The momentary current between two alternating-current generators when juxtaposed in parallel and not agreeing exactly in phase or period.
Phasing transformer Phasing transformer. Any of several transformers (there must be at least two) for changing phase.

phasis.c: Phasis ‖Pha"sis (?), n.; pl. Phases (#). [NL.] See Phase. Creech.

phasma.c: Phasma Phasm { Phasm (?), Phas"ma (?), } n. [L. phasma, Gr. fa`sma. See Phase.] An apparition; a phantom; an appearance. [R.] Hammond. Sir T. Herbert.

phasmid.c: Phasmid Phas"mid (?), n. [See Phasm. Probably so called from its mimicking, or appearing like, inanimate objects.] (Zool.) Any orthopterous insect of the family Phasmidæ, as a leaf insect or a stick insect.

phassachate.c: Phassachate Phas"sa*chate (?), n. [Gr.? the wood pigeon +? the agate.] (Min.) The lead-colored agate; -- so called in reference to its color.

phatagin.c: Phatagin Phat"a*gin (?), n. [Cf. Gr.?; perhaps from native name.] (Zool.) The long-tailed pangolin (Manis tetradactyla); -- called also ipi.

pheasant.c: Pheasant Pheas"ant (fĕz"aint), n. [OE. fesant, fesaunt, OF. faisant, faisan, F. faisan, L. phasianus, Gr. fasiano`s (sc. 'o`rnis) the Phasian bird, pheasant, fr. Fa`sis a river in Colchis or Pontus.] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of large gallinaceous birds of the genus Phasianus, and many other genera of the family Phasianidæ, found chiefly in Asia.

pheasantry.c: Pheasantry Pheas"ant*ry (fĕz"aint*ry̆), n. [Cf. F. faisanderie.] A place for keeping and rearing pheasants. Gwilt.

pheese.c: Pheese Pheese (fēz), v. t. To comb; also, to beat; to worry. [Obs. or Local] See Feaze, v.
Pheese Pheese, n. Fretful excitement. [Obs. or Local] See Feaze, n.

phelloderm.c: Phelloderm Phel"lo*derm (?), n. [Gr. fello`s cork + -derm.] (Bot.) A layer of green parenchymatous cells formed on the inner side of the phellogen.

phellogen.c: Phellogen Phel"lo*gen (?), n. [Gr. fello`s cork + -gen.] (Bot.) The tissue of young cells which produces cork cells.

phelloplastics.c: Phelloplastics Phel`lo*plas"tics (?), n. [Gr. fello`s cork + pla`ssein to mold.] Art of modeling in cork.

phenacetine.c: Phenacetine Phenacetin { Phe*nac"e*tin, Phe*nac"e*tine } (?), n. [Phenyl + acetic + -in.] (Pharm.) A white, crystalline compound, C10H13O2N, once used in medicine principally as an antipyretic. It is now seldom used because of serious side effects.

phenacite.c: Phenacite Phen"a*cite (?), n. [Gr. fe`nax, fe`nakos, impostor, deceiver.] (Min.) A glassy colorless mineral occurring in rhombohedral crystals, sometimes used as a gem. It is a silicate of glucina, and receives its name from its deceptive similarity to quartz.

phenakistoscope.c: Phenakistoscope Phen`a*kis"to*scope (?), n. [Gr. fenakisth`s a deceiver + -scope.] A revolving disk on which figures drawn in different relative attitudes are seen successively, so as to produce the appearance of an object in actual motion, as an animal leaping, etc., in consequence of the persistence of the successive visual impressions of the retina. It is often arranged so that the figures may be projected upon a screen.

phenalgin.c: Phenalgin Phe*nal"gin (?), n. [Phenyl + analgetic + -in.] (Pharm.) An ammoniated compound of phenyl and acetamide, used as an analgesic and antipyretic. It resembles phenacetin in its therapeutic action.

phenanthrene.c: Phenanthrene Phe*nan"threne (?), n. [Phenyl + antracene.] (Chem.) A complex hydrocarbon, C14H10, found in coal tar, and obtained as a white crystalline substance with a bluish fluorescence.

phenanthridine.c: Phenanthridine Phe*nan"thri*dine (?), n. [Phenanthrene + pyridine.] (Chem.) A nitrogenous hydrocarbon base, C13H9N, analogous to phenanthrene and quinoline.

phenanthroline.c: Phenanthroline Phe*nan"thro*line (?), n. [Phenanthrene + quinoline.] (Chem.) Either of two metameric nitrogenous hydrocarbon bases, C12H8N2, analogous to phenanthridine, but more highly nitrogenized.

phenetol.c: Phenetol Phe"ne*tol (?), n. [Phenyl + ethyl + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) The ethyl ether of phenol, obtained as an aromatic liquid, C6H5.O.C2H5.

phenic.c: Phenic Phe"nic (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, phenyl or phenol.

phenicine.c: Phenicine Phen"i*cine (?), n. [Gr. foi^nix purple red: cf. F. phénicine.] (Chem.) (a) A purple powder precipitated when a sulphuric solution of indigo is diluted with water. (b) A coloring matter produced by the action of a mixture of strong nitric and sulphuric acids on phenylic alcohol. Watts.

phenicious.c: Phenicious Phe*ni"cious (?), a. [L. phoeniceus, Gr. foini`keos, from foi^nix purple red.] Of a red color with a slight mixture of gray. Dana.

phenicopter.c: Phenicopter Phen`i*cop"ter (?), n. [L. phoenicopterus, Gr. foiniko`pteros, i. e., red-feathered; foi^nix, foi`nikos, purple red + ptero`n feather: cf. F. phénicoptère.] (Zool.) A flamingo.

phenix.c: Phenix Phe"nix (?), n.; pl. Phenixes (#). [L. phoenix, Gr. foi^nix.] [Written also phœnix.] 1. (Gr. Myth.) A bird fabled to exist single, to be consumed by fire by its own act, and to rise again from its ashes. Hence, an emblem of immortality.

phenocryst.c: Phenocryst Phe"no*cryst (?), n. [Gr. fai`nesqai to appear + kry`stallos crystal.] (Geol.) One of the prominent embedded crystals of a porphyry.

phenogamous.c: Phenogamous Phenogamic Phenogamian { Phen`o*ga"mi*an (?), Phen`o*gam"ic (?), Phe*nog"a*mous (?) }, a. Same as Phænogamian, Phænogamic, etc.

phenol.c: Phenol Phe"nol (fē"nōl; 277), n. [Gr. fai`nein to show + -ol: cf. F. phénol.] (Chem.) 1. A white or pinkish crystalline substance, C6H5OH, produced by the destructive distillation of many organic bodies, as wood, coal, etc., and obtained from the heavy oil from coal tar.

Phenol phthalein Phenolphthalein Phe`nol*phthal"e*in (?), or Phenol phthalein., n. (Chem.) A white or yellowish white crystalline substance, C20H14O4, formed by condensation of the anhydride of phthalic acid and phenol. Its solution in alkalies is brilliant red, but is decolorized by acids. This reaction, being very delicate, is used as a pH indicator. It is sometimes used as a laxative in veterinary medicine.

phenolate.c: Phenolate Phe"no*late (?), n. [Phenol + -ate.] (Chem.) A compound of phenol analogous to a salt.

phenology.c: Phenology Phe*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Contracted from Phenomenology.] (Biol.) The science of the relations between climate and periodic biological phenomena, as the migrations and breeding of birds, the flowering and fruiting of plants, etc. -- Phe`no*log"ic*al (#), a. -- Phe`no*log"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Phe*nol"o*gist (#), n.

phenomenal.c: Phenomenal Phe*nom"e*nal (?), a. [Cf. F. phénoménal.] Relating to, or of the nature of, a phenomenon; hence, extraordinary; wonderful; as, a phenomenal memory. -- Phe*nom"e*nal*ly, adv.

phenomenalism.c: Phenomenalism Phe*nom"e*nal*ism (?), n. (Metaph.) That theory which limits positive or scientific knowledge to phenomena only, whether material or spiritual.

phenomenist.c: Phenomenist Phe*nom"e*nist (?), n. One who believes in the theory of phenomenalism.

phenomenology.c: Phenomenology Phe*nom`e*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Phenomenon + -logy: cf. F. phénoménologie.] A description, history, or explanation of phenomena. “The phenomenology of the mind.” Sir W. Hamilton.

phenomenon.c: Phenomenon Phe*nom"e*non (?), n.; pl. Phenomena (#). [L. phaenomenon, Gr. faino`menon, fr. fai`nesqai to appear, fai`nein to show. See Phantom.] 1. An appearance; anything visible; whatever, in matter or spirit, is apparent to, or is apprehended by, observation; as, the phenomena of heat, light, or electricity; phenomena of imagination or memory.

phenose.c: Phenose Phe"nose` (?), n. [Phenyl + dextrose.] (Chem.) A sweet amorphous deliquescent substance obtained indirectly from benzene, and isometric with, and resembling, dextrose.

phenyl.c: Phenyl Phe"nyl (?), n. [Gr. fai`nein to bring to light + -yl: cf. F. phényle. So called because it is a by-product of illuminating gas.] (Chem.) A hydrocarbon radical (C6H5) regarded as the essential residue of benzene, and the basis of an immense number of aromatic derivatives.

phenylamine.c: Phenylamine Phe`nyl*am"ine (?), n. [Phenyl + amine.] (Chem.) Any one of certain class of organic bases regarded as formed from ammonia by the substitution of phenyl for hydrogen.

phenylene.c: Phenylene Phe"nyl*ene (?), n. (Chem.) A hypothetic radical (C6H4) occurring in certain derivatives of benzene; as, phenylene diamine.

phenylic.c: Phenylic Phe*nyl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, phenyl.

pheon.c: Pheon Phe"on (?), n. [Prob. from Old French.] (Her.) A bearing representing the head of a dart or javelin, with long barbs which are engrailed on the inner edge.

phial.c: Phial Phi"al (fī"ail), n. [F. fiole, L. phiala a broad, flat, shallow cup or bowl, Gr. fia`lh. cf. Vial.] A glass vessel or bottle, especially a small bottle for medicines; a vial.
Phial Phi"al, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Phialed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Phialing.] To put or keep in, or as in, a phial.

philadelphian.c: Philadelphian Phil`a*del"phi*an (?), a. [Gr. filadelfia brotherly love, from fila`delfos brotherly; fi`los loved, loving, friendly + 'adelfo`s brother.] Of or pertaining to Ptolemy Philadelphus, or to one of the cities named Philadelphia, esp. the modern city in Pennsylvania.
Philadelphian Phil`a*del"phi*an, n. 1. A native or an inhabitant of Philadelphia.

philalethist.c: Philalethist Phil`a*le"thist (?), n. [Philo- + Gr. 'alh`qeia truth.] A lover of the truth. [Obs.] Brathwait.

philander.c: Philander Phi*lan"der (?), v. i. [Gr. fi`landros fond of men; fi`los loving + 'anh`r man.] To make love to women; to play the male flirt.
Philander Phi*lan"der, n. (Zool.) (a) A South American opossum (Didelphys philander). (b) An Australian bandicoot (Perameles lagotis).

philanderer.c: Philanderer Phi*lan"der*er (?), n. One who hangs about women; a male flirt. [R.] C. Kingsley.

philanthrope.c: Philanthrope Phil"an*thrope (?), n. [F.] A philanthropist. [Obs.] R. North.

philanthropical.c: Philanthropical Philanthropic { Phil`an*throp"ic (?), Phil`an*throp"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. philanthropique.] Of or pertaining to philanthropy; characterized by philanthropy; loving or helping mankind; as, a philanthropic enterprise. -- Phil`an*throp"ic*al*ly, adv.

philanthropinism.c: Philanthropinism Phil`an*throp"i*nism (?), n. A system of education on so-called natural principles, attempted in Germany in the last century by Basedow, of Dessau.

philanthropinist.c: Philanthropinist Phil`an*throp"i*nist (?), n. An advocate of, or believer in, philanthropinism.

philanthropist.c: Philanthropist Phi*lan"thro*pist (?), n. [Gr. fila`nqrwpos; fi`los loving + 'a`nqrwpos man: cf. F. philanthrope.] 1. One who practices philanthropy; one who loves mankind, and seeks to promote the good of others; especially, a wealthy individual who donates large amounts of money to charitable or philanthropic causes. Opposite of misanthrope.

philanthropistic.c: Philanthropistic Phi*lan`thro*pis"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or characteristic of, a philanthropist. [R.] Carlyle.

philanthropy.c: Philanthropy Phi*lan"thro*py (?), n. [L. philanthropia, Gr. filanqrwpi`a: cf. F. philanthropie.] Love to mankind; benevolence toward the whole human family; universal good will; desire and readiness to do good to all men; -- opposed to misanthropy. Jer. Taylor.

philatelic.c: Philatelic Phil`a*tel"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to philately.

philatelist.c: Philatelist Phi*lat"e*list (?), n. One versed in philately; one who collects postage stamps, as a hobby or for investment; a stamp collector.

philately.c: Philately Phi*lat"e*ly (?), n. [Philo- + Gr. 'ate`leia exemption from tax; cf. frank to send free.] The collection of postage stamps of various issues.

philathea.c: Philathea Phi*la"the*a (?), n. [Coined from Gr. fi`los loving + 'alh`qeia truth.] An international, interdenominational organization of Bible classes of young women.

philatory.c: Philatory Phil"a*to*ry (?), n. [OF. filatiere, philatiere. See Phylactery.] (Eccl.) A kind of transparent reliquary with an ornamental top.

philauty.c: Philauty Phil"au*ty (?), n. [Gr. filayti`a; fi`los loving + a'yto`s self.] Self-love; selfishness. [Obs.] Beaumont.

philharmonic.c: Philharmonic Phil`har*mon"ic (?), a. [Philo- + Gr. "armoni`a harmony: cf. F. philharmonique.] Loving harmony or music.
Philharmonic Phil`har*mon"ic, n. One who loves harmony or music; also (Colloq.), short for Philharmonic Society, Philharmonic concert, Philharmonic assemblage, or the like.

philhellene.c: Philhellene Phil*hel"lene (?), n. A friend of Greece, or of the Greeks; a philhellenist. Emerson.

philhellenic.c: Philhellenic Phil`hel*len"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to philhellenism.

philhellenist.c: Philhellenist Phil*hel"len*ist, n. [Philo- + Gr. "E`llhn a Greek: cf. F. philhellène.] A friend of Greece; one who supports the cause of the Greeks; particularly, one who supported them in their struggle for independence against the Turks; a philhellene.

philip.c: Philip Phil"ip (?), n. [So called from their notes.] (Zool.) (a) The European hedge sparrow. (b) The house sparrow. Called also phip. [Prov. Eng.]

philippian.c: Philippian Phi*lip"pi*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Philippi, a city of ancient Macedonia. -- n. A native or an inhabitant of Philippi.

philippic.c: Philippic Phi*lip"pic (?), n. [L. Philippiko`s belonging to Philip, Philippic, Gr. filippikos, fr. Fi`lippos Philip, fi`lippos fond of horses: cf. F. philippique.] 1. Any one of the series of famous orations of Demosthenes, the Grecian orator, denouncing Philip, king of Macedon.

philippium.c: Philippium Phi*lip"pi*um (?), n. [NL. So named from Philippe Plantamour, of Geneva, Switzerland.] (Chem.) A rare and doubtful metallic element said to have been discovered in the mineral samarskite.

philippize.c: Philippize Phil"ip*pize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Philippized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Philippizing.] [Gr.? to be on Philip's side.] 1. To support or advocate the cause of Philip of Macedon.

philister.c: Philister Phi*lis"ter (?), n. [G.] A Philistine; -- a cant name given to townsmen by students in German universities.

philistine.c: Philistine Phi*lis"tine (?), n. [L. Philistinus, Heb. Phlishthī, pl. Phlishthīm.] 1. A native or an inhabitant of ancient Philistia, a coast region of southern Palestine.
Philistine Phi*lis"tine, a. 1. Of or pertaining to the Philistines.

philistinism.c: Philistinism Phi*lis"tin*ism (?), n. The condition, character, aims, and habits of the class called Philistines. See Philistine, 3. [Recent] Carlyle.

phillipsite.c: Phillipsite Phil"lips*ite (?), n. [So named after John Phillips, an English mineralogist.] (Min.) A hydrous silicate of aluminia, lime, and soda, a zeolitic mineral commonly occurring in complex twin crystals, often cruciform in shape; -- called also christianite.

phillygenin.c: Phillygenin Phil*lyg"e*nin (?), n. [Phillyrin + -gen + -in.] (Chem.) A pearly crystalline substance obtained by the decomposition of phillyrin.

phillyrea.c: Phillyrea ‖Phil*lyr"e*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?.] (Bot.) A genus of evergreen plants growing along the shores of the Mediterranean, and bearing a fruit resembling that of the olive.

phillyrin.c: Phillyrin Phil"ly*rin (?), n. (Chem.) A glucoside extracted from Phillyrea as a bitter white crystalline substance. It is sometimes used as a febrifuge.

philo.c: Philo- Philo-. A combining form from Gr. fi`los loving, fond of, attached to; as, philosophy, philotechnic.

philogynist.c: Philogynist Phi*log"y*nist (?), n. [See Philogyny.] A lover or friend of women; one who esteems woman as the higher type of humanity; -- opposed to misogynist.

philogyny.c: Philogyny Phi*log"y*ny (?), n. [Gr. filogyni`a; fi`los loving + gynh` woman.] Fondness for women; uxoriousness; -- opposed to misogyny. [R.] Byron.

philologer.c: Philologer Phi*lol"o*ger (?), n. [Cf. L. philologus a man of letters, Gr. filo`logos, originally, fond of talking; hence, fond of learning and literature; fi`los loving + lo`gos speech, discourse.] A philologist. Burton.

philologic.c: Philologic Philological { Phil`o*log"ic*al (?), Phil`o*log"ic (?), } a. [Cf. F. philologique.] Of or pertaining to philology. -- Phil`o*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

philologist.c: Philologist Phi*lol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in philology.

philologize.c: Philologize Phi*lol"o*gize (?), v. i. To study, or make critical comments on, language. Evelyn.

philologue.c: Philologue Phil"o*logue (?), n. [Cf. F. philologue.] A philologist. [R.] Carlyle.

philology.c: Philology Phi*lol"o*gy (fĭ*lŏl"o*jy̆), n. [L. philologia love of learning, interpretation, philology, Gr. filologi`a: cf. F. philologie. See Philologer.] 1. Criticism; grammatical learning. [R.] Johnson.

philomath.c: Philomath Phil"o*math (fĭl"o*măth), n. [Gr. filomaqh`s; fi`los loving, a friend + ma`qh learning, fr. maqei^n, manqa`nein, to learn.] A lover of learning; a scholar. Chesterfield.

philomathic.c: Philomathic Phil`o*math"ic (fĭl`o*măth"ĭk), a. [Cf. F. philomathique.] 1. Of or pertaining to philomathy.

philomathy.c: Philomathy Phi*lom"a*thy (fĭ*lŏm"ȧ*thy̆), n. [Gr. filomaqi`a, filoma`qeia.] The love of learning or letters.

philomel.c: Philomel Phil"o*mel (?), n. Same as Philomela, the nightingale. [Poetic] Milton. Cowper.

philomela.c: Philomela Phil`o*me"la (?), n. [L. philomela, Gr. filomh`la, according to the legend, from Filomh`la Philomela (daughter of Pandion, king of Athens), who was changed into a nightingale.] 1. The nightingale; philomel. Shak.

philomot.c: Philomot Phil"o*mot (?), a. [See Filemot.] Of the color of a dead leaf. [Obs.] Addison.

philopena.c: Philopena Phil`o*pe"na (?), n. [Probably a corruption fr. G. vielliebchen, LG. vielliebken, or D. veelliebken, a philopena, literally, much loved; but influenced by Gr. fi`los a friend, and L. poena penalty, from an idea that the gift was a penalty of friendship or love.] A present or gift which is made as a forfeit in a social game that is played in various ways; also, the game itself. [Written also fillipeen and phillippine.]

philopolemical.c: Philopolemical Philopolemic { Phil`o*po*lem"ic (?), Phil`o*po*lem"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr. filopo`lemos fond of war, warlike; fi`los loving + po`lemos war.] Fond of polemics or controversy. [R.]

philoprogenitive.c: Philoprogenitive Phil`o*pro*gen"i*tive (?), a. Having the love of offspring; fond of children.

philoprogenitiveness.c: Philoprogenitiveness Phil`o*pro*gen"i*tive*ness, n. [Philo- + L. progenies offspring.] (Phren.) The love of offspring; fondness for children.

philosophaster.c: Philosophaster Phi*los"o*phas`ter (?), n. [L., a bad philosopher, fr. philosophus: cf. OF. philosophastre.] A pretender to philosophy. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

philosophate.c: Philosophate Phi*los"o*phate (?), v. i. [L. philosophatus, p. p. of philosophari to philosophize.] To play the philosopher; to moralize. [Obs.] Barrow.

philosophation.c: Philosophation Phi*los`o*pha"tion (?), n. Philosophical speculation and discussion. [Obs.] Sir W. Petty.

philosophe.c: Philosophe Phil"o*sophe (?), n. [F., a philosopher.] A philosophaster; a philosopher. [R.] Carlyle.

philosopheme.c: Philosopheme Phi*los"o*pheme (?), n. [Gr. filoso`fhma, from filosofei^n to love knowledge.] A philosophical proposition, doctrine, or principle of reasoning. [R.]

philosopher.c: Philosopher Phi*los"o*pher (?), n. [OE. philosophre, F. philosophe, L. philosophus, Gr. filo`sofos; fi`los loving + sofo`s wise. Cf. Philosophy.] 1. One who philosophizes; one versed in, or devoted to, philosophy.

philosophical.c: Philosophical Philosophic { Phil`o*soph"ic (?), Phil`o*soph"ic*al (?), } a. [L. philosophicus: cf. F. philosophique.] Of or pertaining to philosophy; versed in, or imbued with, the principles of philosophy; hence, characterizing a philosopher; rational; wise; temperate; calm; cool. -- Phil`o*soph"ic*al*ly, adv.

philosophism.c: Philosophism Phi*los"o*phism (fĭ*lŏs"o*fĭz'm), n. [Cf. F. philosophisme.] Spurious philosophy; the love or practice of sophistry. Carlyle.

philosophist.c: Philosophist Phi*los"o*phist (fĭ*lŏs"o*fĭst), n. [Cf. F. philosophiste.] A pretender in philosophy.

philosophistical.c: Philosophistical Philosophistic { Phi*los`o*phis"tic (?), Phi*los`o*phis"tic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to the love or practice of sophistry. [R.]

philosophize.c: philosophize phi*los"o*phize (fĭ*lŏs"o*fīz), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Philosophized (fĭ*lŏs"o*fīzd); p. pr. & vb. n. hilosophizing (fĭ*lŏs"o*fī`zĭng).] To reason like a philosopher; to search into the reason and nature of things; to investigate phenomena, and assign rational causes for their existence.

philosophy.c: Philosophy Phi*los"o*phy (fĭ*lŏs"o*fy̆), n.; pl. Philosophies (fĭ*lŏs"o*fĭz). [OE. philosophie, F. philosophie, L. philosophia, from Gr. filosofi`a. See Philosopher.] 1. Literally, the love of, inducing the search after, wisdom; in actual usage, the knowledge of phenomena as explained by, and resolved into, causes and reasons, powers and laws.

philostorgy.c: Philostorgy Phil`o*stor"gy (?), n. [Gr. filostorgi`a; fi`los loving + storgh` affection.] Natural affection, as of parents for their children. [R.]

philotechnical.c: Philotechnical Philotechnic { Phil`o*tech"nic (?), Phil`o*tech"nic*al (?), } a. [Philo- + Gr. te`chnh an art: cf. F. philotechnique.] Fond of the arts. [R.]

philter.c: Philter Phil"ter (?), n. [F. philtre, L. philtrum, Gr. fi`ltron, fr. filei^n to love, fi`los dear, loving.] A potion or charm intended to excite the passion of love. [Written also philtre.] Addison.
Philter Phil"ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Philtered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Philtering.] 1. To impregnate or mix with a love potion; as, to philter a draught.

phimosis.c: Phimosis ‖Phi*mo"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a muzzling, fr.? muzzle.] (Med.) A condition of the penis in which the prepuce can not be drawn back so as to uncover the glans penis.
