preexist.c: Preexist Pre`ëx*ist" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Preëxisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Preëxisting.] To exist previously; to exist before something else; to exist before the current activity commenced; as, preexisting illnesses are not covered by this insurance policy. [Also spelled pre-exist.]

preexistence.c: Preexistence Pre`ëx*ist"ence (?), n. 1. Existence in a former state, or previous to something else.

preexistent.c: Preexistent Pre`ëx*ist"ent (?), a. Existing previously; preceding existence; as, a preëxistent state. Pope.

preexistentism.c: Preexistentism Pre`ëx*ist"ent*ism (?), n. (Philos.) The theory of a preëxistence of souls before their association with human bodies. Emerson.

preexistimation.c: Preexistimation Pre`ëx*is`ti*ma"tion (?), n. Previous esteem or estimation. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

preface.c: Preface Pref"ace (?; 48), n. [F. préface; cf. Sp. prefacio, prefacion, It. prefazio, prefazione; all fr. L. praefatio, fr. praefari to speak or say beforehand; prae before + fari, fatus, to speak. See Fate.] 1. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book or essay; a proem; an introduction, or series of preliminary remarks.
Preface Pref"ace, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prefaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prefacing.] To introduce by a preface; to give a preface to; as, to preface a book discourse.
Preface Pref"ace, v. i. To make a preface. Jer. Taylor.

prefacer.c: Prefacer Pref"a*cer (?), n. The writer of a preface.

prefatorily.c: Prefatorily Pref"a*to*ri*ly (?), adv. In a prefatory manner; by way of preface.

prefatory.c: Prefatory Pref"a*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or of the nature of, a preface; introductory to a book, essay, or discourse; as, prefatory remarks.

prefect.c: Prefect Pre"fect (?), n. [L. praefectus, fr. praefectus, p. p. of praeficere to set over; prae before + facere to make: cf. F. préfet.] 1. A Roman officer who controlled or superintended a particular command, charge, department, etc.; as, the prefect of the aqueducts; the prefect of a camp, of a fleet, of the city guard, of provisions; the pretorian prefect, who was commander of the troops guarding the emperor's person.

prefectorial.c: Prefectorial Pre`fec*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a prefect.

prefectship.c: Prefectship Pre"fect*ship (?), n. The office or jurisdiction of a prefect.

prefecture.c: Prefecture Pre"fec*ture (?; 277), n. [L. praefectura: cf. F. préfecture.] The office, position, or jurisdiction of a prefect; also, his official residence.

prefecundation.c: Prefecundation Pre*fec`un*da"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) A term collectively applied to the changes or conditions preceding fecundation, especially to the changes which the ovum undergoes before fecundation.

prefecundatory.c: Prefecundatory Pre`fe*cun"da*to*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to prefecundation.

prefer.c: Prefer Pre*fer" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Preferred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preferring.] [F. préférer, L. praeferre; prae before + ferre to bear or carry. See 1st Bear.] 1. To carry or bring (something) forward, or before one; hence, to bring for consideration, acceptance, judgment, etc.; to offer; to present; to proffer; to address; -- said especially of a request, prayer, petition, claim, charge, etc.

preferability.c: Preferability Pref`er*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being preferable; preferableness. J. S. Mill.

preferable.c: Preferable Pref"er*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. préférable.] Worthy to be preferred or chosen before something else; more desirable; as, a preferable scheme. Addison.

preferableness.c: Preferableness Pref"er*a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being preferable.

preferably.c: Preferably Pref"er*a*bly, adv. In preference; by choice.

preference.c: Preference Pref"er*ence (?), n. [Cf. F. préférence.] 1. The act of Preferring, or the state of being preferred; the setting of one thing before another; precedence; higher estimation; predilection; choice; also, the power or opportunity of choosing; as, to give him his preference.

preferential.c: Preferential Pref`er*en"tial (?), a. Giving, indicating, or having a preference or precedence; as, a preferential claim; preferential shares.

Preferential voting Preferential voting. (Political Science) A system of voting, as at primaries, in which the voters are allowed to indicate on their ballots their preference (usually their first and second choices) between two or more candidates for an office, so that if no candidate receives a majority of first choices the one receiving the greatest number of first and second choices together in nominated or elected.

preferment.c: Preferment Pre*fer"ment (?), n. 1. The act of choosing, or the state of being chosen; preference. [R.]

prefidence.c: Prefidence Pref"i*dence (?), n. The quality or state of being prefident. [Obs.] Baxter.

prefident.c: Prefident Pref"i*dent (?), a. [Cf. L. praefidens overconfident. See Pre-, and Confident.] Trusting beforehand; hence, overconfident. [Obs.] Baxter.

prefigurate.c: Prefigurate Pre*fig"u*rate (?), v. t. [L. praefiguratus, p. p. See Prefigure.] To prefigure. [R.] Grafton.

prefiguration.c: Prefiguration Pre*fig`u*ra"tion (?), n. [L. praefiguratio.] The act of prefiguring, or the state of being prefigured.

prefigurative.c: Prefigurative Pre*fig"ur*a*tive (?), a. Showing by prefiguration. “The prefigurative atonement.” Bp. Horne.

prefigure.c: Prefigure Pre*fig"ure (?; 135), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prefigured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prefiguring.] [F. préfigurer, or L. praefigurare, praefiguratum; prae before + figurare to figure. See Figure, and cf. Prefigurate.] To show, suggest, or announce, by antecedent types and similitudes; to foreshadow. “Whom all the various types prefigured.” South.

prefigurement.c: Prefigurement Pre*fig"ure*ment (?), n. The act of prefiguring; prefiguration; also, that which is prefigured. Carlyle.

prefine.c: Prefine Pre*fine" (?), v. t. [L. praefinire; prae before + finire to limit, determine: cf. F. préfiner.] To limit beforehand. [Obs.] Knolles.

prefinite.c: Prefinite Pre*fi"nite (?), a. [L. praefinitus, p. p.] Prearranged. [Obs.] “ Set and prefinite time.” Holland.

prefinition.c: Prefinition Pref`i*ni"tion (?), n. [L. praefinitio.] Previous limitation. [Obs.] Fotherby.

prefix.c: Prefix Pre*fix" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prefixed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prefixing.] [L. praefixus, p. p. of praefigere to fix or fasten before; prae before + figere to fix: cf. F. préfix fixed beforehand, determined, préfixer to prefix. See Fix.]

Prefix Pre"fix (?), n. [Cf. F. préfixe.] That which is prefixed; esp., one or more letters or syllables combined or united with the beginning of a word to modify its signification; as, pre- in prefix, con- in conjure.

prefixion.c: Prefixion Pre*fix"ion (?), n. [Cf. OF. prefixion.] The act of prefixing. [R.] Bailey.

prefloration.c: Prefloration Pre`flo*ra"tion (?), n. [Pref. pre- + L. flos, floris, flower.] (Bot.) Aestivation.

prefoliation.c: Prefoliation Pre*fo`li*a"tion (?), n. [Pref. pre- + L. folium leaf.] (Bot.) Vernation.

preform.c: Preform Pre*form" (?), v. t. [L. praeformare. See Pre-, and Form.] To form beforehand, or for special ends. “Their natures and preformed faculties. ” Shak.

preformation.c: Preformation Pre`for*ma"tion (?), n. (Biol.) An old theory of the preëxistence of germs. Cf. Emboîtement.

preformative.c: Preformative Pre*form"a*tive (?), n. A formative letter at the beginning of a word. M. Stuart.

prefrontal.c: Prefrontal Pre*fron"tal (?), a. (Anat. & Zool.) Situated in front of the frontal bone, or the frontal region of the skull; ectethmoid, as a certain bone in the nasal capsule of many animals, and certain scales of reptiles and fishes. -- n. A prefrontal bone or scale.

prefulgency.c: Prefulgency Pre*ful"gen*cy (?), n. [L. praefulgens, p. pr. of praefulgere to shine forth. See Pre-, and Fulgent.] Superior brightness or effulgency. [R.] Barrow.

pregage.c: Pregage Pre*gage" (?), v. t. To preëngage. [Obs.] Fuller.

preglacial.c: Preglacial Pre*gla"cial (?), a. (Geol.) Prior to the glacial or drift period.

pregnable.c: Pregnable Preg"na*ble (?), a., [F. prenable. See Impregnable.] Capable of being entered, taken, or captured; expugnable; as, a pregnable fort. [R.] Cotgrave.

pregnancy.c: Pregnancy Preg"nan*cy (?), n. 1. The condition of being pregnant; the state of being with young.

pregnant.c: Pregnant Preg"nant (?), a. [L. praegnans, -antis; prae before + genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. prégnant. See Gender, 2d Kin.]
Pregnant Preg"nant, n. A pregnant woman. [R.] Dunglison.
Pregnant Preg"nant, a. [F. prenant taking. Cf. Pregnable.] Affording entrance; receptive; yielding; willing; open; prompt. [Obs.] “ Pregnant to good pity.” Shak.

pregnantly.c: Pregnantly Preg"nant*ly, adv. In a pregnant manner; fruitfully; significantly.
Pregnantly Preg"nant*ly, adv. Unresistingly; openly; hence, clearly; evidently. [Obs.] Shak.

pregravate.c: Pregravate Pre"gra*vate (?), v. t. [L. praegravatus, p. p. of praegravare to be heavy upon, fr. praegravis very heavy.] To bear down; to depress. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

pregravitate.c: Pregravitate Pre*grav"i*tate (?), v. i. To descend by gravity; to sink. [R.] Boyle.

pregustant.c: Pregustant Pre*gus"tant (?), a. [L. praegustans, p. pr. of praegustare to taste beforehand; prae before + gustare to taste.] Tasting beforehand; having a foretaste. [R.] Ed. Rev.

pregustation.c: Pregustation Pre`gus*ta"tion (?), n. The act of tasting beforehand; foretaste. [R.] Dr. Walker (1678).

prehallux.c: Prehallux ‖Pre*hal"lux (?), n. [NL. See Pre-, and Hallux.] (Anat.) An extra first toe, or rudiment of a toe, on the preaxial side of the hallux.

prehend.c: Prehend Pre*hend" (?), v. t. [L. prehendere. See Prehensile.] To lay hold of; to seize. [Obs.] Middleton.

prehensible.c: Prehensi-ble Pre*hen"si-ble (?), a. [Cf. F. préhensible.] Capable of being seized.

prehensile.c: Prehensile Pre*hen"sile (?), a. [L. prehensus, p. p. of prehendere to lay hold of, seize; pre- (equiv. to prae before) + hendere (in comp.), akin to E. get: cf. F. préhensile. See Get, and cf. Prison, Prize, n.] Adapted to seize or grasp; seizing; grasping; as, the prehensile tail of a monkey.

prehension.c: Prehension Pre*hen"sion (?), n. [L. prehensio; cf. F. préhension. See Prehensile.] The act of taking hold, seizing, or grasping, as with the hand or other member.

prehensory.c: Prehensory Pre*hen"so*ry (?), a. Adapted to seize or grasp; prehensile.

prehistoric.c: Prehistoric Pre`his*tor"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a period before written history begins; as, the prehistoric ages; prehistoric man.

prehnite.c: Prehnite Prehn"ite (?), n. [So called from the German Colonel Prehn, who first found it.] (Min.) A pale green mineral occurring in crystalline aggregates having a botryoidal or mammillary structure, and rarely in distinct crystals. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.

prehnitic.c: Prehnitic Prehn*it"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a tetrabasic acid of benzene obtained as a white crystalline substance; -- probably so called from the resemblance of the wartlike crystals to the mammillæ on the surface of prehnite.

preignition.c: Preignition Pre`ig*ni"tion (?), n. (Engin.) Ignition in an internal-combustion engine while the inlet valve is open or before compression is completed.

preindesignate.c: Preindesignate Pre`in*des"ig*nate (?), a. (Logic.) Having no sign expressive of quantity; indefinite. See Predesignate.

preindispose.c: Preindispose Pre*in`dis*pose" (?), v. t. To render indisposed beforehand. Milman.

preinstruct.c: Preinstruct Pre`in*struct" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Preinstructed; p. pr. & vb. n. Preinstructing.] To instruct previously or beforehand. Dr. H. More.

preintimation.c: Preintimation Pre*in`ti*ma"tion (?), n. Previous intimation; a suggestion beforehand. T. Scott.

prejudge.c: Prejudge Pre*judge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prejudged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prejudging.] [Pref. pre + judge: cf. F. préjuger. Cf. Prejudicate, Prejudice.] To judge before hearing, or before full and sufficient examination; to decide or sentence by anticipation; to condemn beforehand.

prejudgment.c: Prejudgment Pre*judg"ment (?), n. The act of prejudging; decision before sufficient examination.

prejudicacy.c: Prejudicacy Pre*ju"di*ca*cy (?), n. Prejudice; prepossession. [Obs.] Sir. H. Blount.

prejudical.c: Prejudical Pre*ju"di*cal (?), a. Of or pertaining to the determination of some matter not previously decided; as, a prejudical inquiry or action at law.

prejudicant.c: Prejudicant Pre*ju"di*cant (?), a. [L. praejudicans, p. pr.] Influenced by prejudice; biased. [R.] “ With not too hasty and prejudicant ears.” Milton.

prejudicate.c: Prejudicate Pre*ju"di*cate (?), a. [L. praejudicatus, p. p. of praejudicare to prejudge; prae before + judicare to judge. See Judge.] 1. Formed before due examination. “Ignorance and prejudicate opinions.” Jer. Taylor.
Prejudicate Pre*ju"di*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prejudicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prejudicating.] [Cf. Prejudge.] To determine beforehand, especially to disadvantage; to prejudge.
Prejudicate Pre*ju"di*cate, v. i. To prejudge. Sir P. Sidney.

prejudication.c: Prejudication Pre*ju`di*ca"tion (?), n. 1. The act of prejudicating, or of judging without due examination of facts and evidence; prejudgment.

prejudicative.c: Prejudicative Pre*ju"di*ca*tive (?), a. Forming a judgment without due examination; prejudging. Dr. H. More.

prejudice.c: Prejudice Prej"u*dice (?), n. [F. préjudice, L. praejudicium; prae before + judicium judgment. See Prejudicate, Judicial.] 1. Foresight. [Obs.]

Prejudice Prej"u*dice, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prejudiced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prejudicing (?).] [Cf. F. préjudicier. See Prejudice, n.] 1. To cause to have prejudice; to prepossess with opinions formed without due knowledge or examination; to bias the mind of, by hasty and incorrect notions; to give an unreasonable bent to, as to one side or the other of a cause; as, to prejudice a critic or a juryman.

prejudicial.c: Prejudicial Prej`u*di"cial (?), a. [L. praejudicialis belonging to a preceding judgment: cf. F. préjudiciel.]

prelacy.c: Prelacy Prel"a*cy (?), n.; pl. Prelacies (#). [LL. praelatia. See Prelate; cf. Prelaty.] 1. The office or dignity of a prelate; church government by prelates.

prelal.c: Prelal Pre"lal (?), a. [L. prelum a press.] Of or pertaining to printing; typographical. [Obs.] Fuller.

prelate.c: Prelate Prel"ate (?; 48), n. [F. prélat, LL. praelatus, fr. L. praelatus, used as p. p. of praeferre to prefer, but from a different root. See Elate.] A clergyman of a superior order, as an archbishop or a bishop, having authority over the lower clergy; a dignitary of the church.
Prelate Prel"ate (?), v. i. To act as a prelate. [Obs.]

prelateship.c: Prelateship Prel"ate*ship, n. The office of a prelate. Harmar.

prelatess.c: Prelatess Prel"a*tess (?), n. A woman who is a prelate; the wife of a prelate. Milton.

prelatical.c: Prelatical Prelatic { Pre*lat"ic (?), Pre*lat"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to prelates or prelacy; as, prelatical authority. Macaulay.

prelatically.c: Prelatically Pre*lat"ic*al*ly, adv. In a prelatical manner; with reference to prelates. Milton.

prelation.c: Prelation Pre*la"tion (?), n. [L. praelatio: cf. F. prélation. See Prelate, and cf. Prefer.] The setting of one above another; preference. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

prelatist.c: Prelatist Prel"a*tist (?), n. One who supports of advocates prelacy, or the government of the church by prelates; hence, a high-churchman. Hume.

prelatize.c: Prelatize Prel"a*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prelatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prelatizing (?).] To bring under the influence of prelacy. Palfrey.
Prelatize Prel"a*tize, v. i. To uphold or encourage prelacy; to exercise prelatical functions.

prelatureship.c: Prelatureship Prelature { Prel"a*ture (?; 135), Prel"a*ture*ship }, n. [F. prélature, or LL. praelatura.] The state or dignity of a prelate; prelacy. Milman.

prelect.c: Prelect Pre*lect" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prelected; p. pr. & vb. n. Prelecting.] [L. praelectus, p. p. of praelegere to read before. See Pre-, and Lection.] To read publicly, as a lecture or discourse.
Prelect Pre*lect", v. i. To discourse publicly; to lecture.

prelection.c: Prelection Pre*lec"tion (?), n. [L. praelectio.] A lecture or discourse read in public or to a select company. “The prelections of Faber.” Sir M. Hale.

prelector.c: Prelector Pre*lec"tor (?), n. [L. praelector.] A reader of lectures or discourses; a lecturer. Sheldon.

prelibation.c: Prelibation Pre`li*ba"tion (?), n. [L. praelibatio, fr. praelibare to taste beforehand: cf. F. prelibation.] 1. A tasting beforehand, or by anticipation; a foretaste; as, a prelibation of heavenly bliss.

preliminarily.c: Preliminarily Pre*lim"i*na*ri*ly (?), adv. In a preliminary manner.

preliminary.c: Preliminary Pre*lim"i*na*ry (?), a. [Pref. pre + L. liminaris belonging to a threshold, fr. limen, liminis, threshold, entrance: cf. F. préliminaire. Cf. Limit.] Introductory; previous; preceding the main discourse or business; prefatory; as, preliminary observations to a discourse or book; preliminary articles to a treaty; preliminary measures; preliminary examinations.

Preliminary Pre*lim"i*na*ry, n.; pl. Preliminaries (?). That which precedes the main discourse, work, design, or business; something introductory or preparatory; as, the preliminaries to a negotiation or duel; to take one's preliminaries the year before entering college.

prelimit.c: Prelimit Pre*lim"it (?), v. t. To limit previously. [R.]

prelook.c: Prelook Pre*look", v. i. To look forward. [Obs.] Surrey.

prelude.c: Prelude Pre"lude (?), n. [F. prélude (cf. It. preludio, LL. praeludium), fr. L. prae before + ludus play. See Prelude, v. t.] An introductory performance, preceding and preparing for the principal matter; a preliminary part, movement, strain, etc.; especially (Mus.), a strain introducing the theme or chief subject; a movement introductory to a fugue, yet independent; -- with recent composers often synonymous with overture.

Prelude Pre*lude" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Preluded; p. pr. & vb. n. Preluding.] [L. praeludere, praelusum; prae before + ludere to play: cf. F. préluder. See Ludicrous.] To play an introduction or prelude; to give a prefatory performance; to serve as prelude.
Prelude Pre*lude", v. t. 1. To introduce with a previous performance; to play or perform a prelude to; as, to prelude a concert with a lively air.

preluder.c: Preluder Pre*lud"er (?), n. One who, or that which, preludes; one who plays a prelude. Mason.

preludial.c: Preludial Pre*lud"i*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a prelude; of the nature of a prelude; introductory. [R.]

preludious.c: Preludious Pre*lud"i*ous (?), a. Preludial. [R.] Dr. H. More.

prelumbar.c: Prelumbar Pre*lum"bar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated immediately in front of the loins; -- applied to the dorsal part of the abdomen.

prelusive.c: Prelusive Pre*lu"sive (?), a. [See Prelude.] Of the nature of a prelude; introductory; indicating that something of a like kind is to follow. “Prelusive drops.” Thomson. --Pre*lu"sive*ly, adv.

prelusorily.c: Prelusorily Pre*lu"so*ri*ly (?), adv. In a prelusory way.

premature.c: Premature Pre`ma*ture" (?), a. [L. praematurus; prae before + maturus ripe. See Mature.] 1. Mature or ripe before the proper time; as, the premature fruits of a hotbed.

prematurity.c: Prematurity Pre`ma*tu"ri*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. prématurité.] The quality or state of being premature; early, or untimely, ripeness; as, the prematurity of genius.

premaxilla.c: Premaxilla ‖Pre"max*il"la (?), n.; pl. Premaxillæ (#). [NL. See Pre-, and Maxilla.] (Anat.) A bone on either side of the middle line between the nose and mouth, forming the anterior part of each half of the upper jawbone; the intermaxilla. In man the premaxillæ become united and form the incisor part of the maxillary bone.

premaxillary.c: Premaxillary Pre*max"il*la*ry (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the maxillary bones; pertaining to the premaxillæ; intermaxillary. -- n. A premaxilla.

premeditate.c: Premeditate Pre*med"i*tate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Premeditated (-tā`t?d); p. pr. & vb. n. Premeditating.] [L. praemeditatus, p. p. of praemeditari; prae before + meditari to meditate. See Meditate.] To think on, and revolve in the mind, beforehand; to contrive and design previously; as, to premeditate robbery.
Premeditate Pre*med"i*tate, v. i. To think, consider, deliberate, or revolve in the mind, beforehand.
Premeditate Pre*med"i*tate (?), a. [L. praemeditatus, p. p.] Premeditated; deliberate. [Archaic] Bp. Burnet.

premeditation.c: Premeditation Pre*med`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. praemeditatio: cf. F. préméditation.] The act of meditating or contriving beforehand; previous deliberation; forethought.

premerit.c: Premerit Pre*mer"it (?), v. t. To merit or deserve beforehand. [Obs.] Eikon Basi??ke.

premiant.c: Premiant Premial { Pre"mi*al (?), Pre"mi*ant (?), } a. [L. praemialis. See Premium.] Serving to reward; rewarding. [R.] Baxter.

premices.c: Premices Prem"i*ces (?), n. pl. [F. prémices, L. primitiae. See Primitia.] First fruits. [Obs.] Dryden.

premier.c: Premier Pre"mi*er (?), a. [F. premier, fr. L. primarius of the first rank, principal, fr. primus the first. See Primary, Prime, a.] 1. First; chief; principal; as, the premier place; premier minister. Camden. Swift.
Premier Pre"mi*er (?), n. The first minister of state; the prime minister.

premiere.c: Premiere ‖Pre*mière" (?), a. fem. [F., prop. fem. of premier first. See Premier, a.] First; chief; as, a première danseuse. -- n. fem.; pl. -mières (F. prei*myâr"). (a) The leading woman of a group, esp. in a theatrical cast. (b) A first performance, as of a play; a first night.

premiership.c: Premiership Pre"mi*er*ship, n. The office of the premier.

premillennial.c: Premillennial Pre`mil*len"ni*al (?), a. Previous to the millennium.

premious.c: Premious Pre"mi*ous (?), a. [L. praemiosus, fr. praemium a premium.] Rich in gifts. [R.] Clarke.

premise.c: Premise Prem"ise (?), n.; pl. Premises (?). [Written also, less properly, premiss.] [F. prémisse, fr. L. praemissus, p. p. of praemittere to send before; prae before + mittere to send. See Mission.] 1. A proposition antecedently supposed or proved; something previously stated or assumed as the basis of further argument; a condition; a supposition.

Premise Pre*mise" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Premised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Premising.] [From L. praemissus, p. p., or E. premise, n. See Premise, n.] 1. To send before the time, or beforehand; hence, to cause to be before something else; to employ previously. [Obs.]
Premise Pre*mise" (?), v. i. To make a premise; to set forth something as a premise. Swift.

premiss.c: Premiss Prem"iss (?), n. Premise. Whately. I. Watts

premit.c: Premit Pre*mit" (?), v. t. To premise. [Obs.] Donne.

premium.c: Premium Pre"mi*um (?), n.; pl. Premiums (#). [L. praemium, originally, what one has got before or better than others; prae before + emere to take, buy. See Redeem.] 1. A reward or recompense; a prize to be won by being before another, or others, in a competition; reward or prize to be adjudged; a bounty; as, a premium for good behavior or scholarship, for discoveries, etc.

premolar.c: Premolar Pre*mo"lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the molar teeth. --n. An anterior molar tooth which has replaced a deciduous molar. See Tooth.

premonish.c: Premonish Pre*mon"ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Premonished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Premonishing.] [Pref. pre- + monish: cf. L. praemonere.] To forewarn; to admonish beforehand. [R.] Herrick.

premonishment.c: Premonishment Pre*mon"ish*ment (?), n. Previous warning or admonition; forewarning. Sir H. Wotton.

premonition.c: Premonition Pre`mo*ni"tion (?), n. [L. praemonitio. See Premonish.] Previous warning, notice, or information; forewarning; as, a premonition of danger.

premonitor.c: Premonitor Pre*mon"i*tor (?), n. [L. praemonitor.] One who, or that which, gives premonition.

premonitory.c: Premonitory Pre*mon"i*to*ry (?), a. [L. praemonitorius.] Giving previous warning or notice; as, premonitory symptoms of disease. -- Pre*mon"i*to*ri*ly (#), adv.

premonstrate.c: Premonstrate Pre*mon"strate (?), v. t. [L. praemonstratus, p. p. of praemonstrare; prae before + monstrate to show.] To show beforehand; to foreshow. [R.] Herbert.

premonstratensian.c: Premonstratensian Pre*mon`stra*ten"sian (?), n. [F. prémontré, fr. Prémontré, fr. L. pratum monstratum.] (R. C. Ch.) One of a religious order of regular canons founded by St. Norbert at Prémontré, in France, in 1119. The members of the order are called also White Canons, Norbertines, and Premonstrants.

premonstration.c: Premonstration Pre`mon*stra"tion (?), n. [L. praemonstratio.] A showing beforehand; foreshowing.

premonstrator.c: Premonstrator Pre*mon"stra*tor (?), n. [L. praemonstrator.] One who, or that which, premonstrates. [R.]

premorse.c: Premorse Pre*morse" (?), a. [L. praemorsus, p. p. of praemordere to bite off; prae before + mordere to bite.] Terminated abruptly, or as it bitten off.

premosaic.c: Premosaic Pre`mo*sa"ic (?), a. Relating to the time before Moses; as, premosaic history.

premotion.c: Premotion Pre*mo"tion (?), n. [Pref. pre- + motion.] Previous motion or excitement to action.

premunite.c: Premunite Prem`u*nite" (?), v. t. [L. praemunitus, p. p. of praemunire to fortify in front; prae before + munire to fortify.] To fortify beforehand; to guard against objection. [Obs.] Fotherby.

premunition.c: Premunition Pre`mu*ni"tion (?), n. [L. praemunitio: cf. F. prémunition.] The act of fortifying or guarding against objections. [Obs.]

premunitory.c: Premunitory Pre*mu"ni*to*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to a premunire; as, a premunitory process.

prenasal.c: Prenasal Pre*na"sal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the nose, or in front of the nasal chambers.

prenatal.c: Prenatal Pre*na"tal (?), a. Being or happening before birth.

prender.c: Prender Pren"der (?), n. [F. prendre to take, fr. L. prehendere to take.] (Law) The power or right of taking a thing before it is offered. Burrill.

prenominal.c: Prenominal Pre*nom"i*nal (?), a. Serving as a prefix in a compound name. Sir T. Browne.

prenominate.c: Prenominate Pre*nom"i*nate (?), a. [L. praenominatus, p. p. of praenominare to give the prenomen to, to prenominate, fr. praenomen prenomen.] Forenamed; named beforehand. [R.] “Prenominate crimes.” Shak.
Prenominate Pre*nom"i*nate (?), v. t. To forename; to name beforehand; to tell by name beforehand. Shak.

prenomination.c: Prenomination Pre*nom`i*na*tion (?), n. The act of prenominating; privilege of being named first. Sir T. Browne.

prenostic.c: Prenostic Pre*nos"tic (?), n. [L. praenoscere to foreknow; prae before + noscere, notum, to know.] A prognostic; an omen. [Obs.] Gower.

prenote.c: Prenote Pre*note" (?), v. t. [L. praenotare; prae before + notare to note.] To note or designate beforehand. Foxe.

prenotion.c: Prenotion Pre*no"tion (?), n. [L. praenotio: cf. F. prénotion. See Prenostic.] A notice or notion which precedes something else in time; previous notion or thought; foreknowledge. Bacon.

prensation.c: Prensation Pren*sa"tion (?), n. [L. prensatio, from prensare, prehensare, v. freq. from prehendere to seize.] The act of seizing with violence. [Obs.] Barrow.

prentice.c: Prentice Pren"tice (?), n. [Aphetic form of apprentice.] An apprentice. [Obs. or Colloq.] Piers Plowman. “My accuser is my prentice.” Shak.

prenunciation.c: Prenunciation Pre*nun`ci*a"tion (?), n. [L. praenunciatio, fr. praenunciare to announce beforehand. See Pre-, and Announce.] The act of announcing or proclaiming beforehand. [Obs.]

prenuncious.c: Prenuncious Pre*nun"cious (?), a. [L. praenuncius.] Announcing beforehand; presaging. [Obs.] Blount.

preoblongata.c: Preoblongata ‖Pre*ob`lon*ga"ta (?), n. [NL. See Pre-, and Oblongata.] (Anat.) The anterior part of the medulla oblongata. B. G. Wilder.

preobtain.c: Preobtain Pre`ob*tain" (?), v. t. To obtain beforehand.

preoccupancy.c: Preoccupancy Pre*oc"cu*pan*cy (?), n. [See Preoccupate.] The act or right of taking possession before another; as, the preoccupancy of wild land.

preoccupate.c: Preoccupate Pre*oc"cu*pate (?), v. t. [L. praeoccupatus, p. p. of praeoccupare to preoccupy. See Preoccupy.]

preoccupation.c: Preoccupation Pre*oc`cu*pa"tion (?), n. [L. praeoccupatio: cf. F. préoccupation.] 1. The act of preoccupying, or taking possession of beforehand; the state of being preoccupied; prepossession.

preoccupy.c: Preoccupy Pre*oc"cu*py (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Preoccupied (-pīd); p. pr. & vb. n. Preoccupying (?).] [Cf. F. préoccuper. See Preoccupate, Occupy.] 1. To take possession of before another; as, to preoccupy a country not before held.

preocular.c: Preocular Pre*oc"u*lar (?), a. (Zool.) Placed just in front of the eyes, as the antennæ of certain insects. -- n. One of the scales just in front of the eye of a reptile or fish.

preominate.c: Preominate Pre*om"i*nate (?), v. t. To ominate beforehand; to portend. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

preopercular.c: Preopercular Pre`o*per"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the operculum; pertaining to the preoperculum. -- n. The preoperculum.

preoperculum.c: Preoperculum ‖Pre`o*per"cu*lum (?), n. [NL.] (Anat.) The anterior opercular bone in fishes.

preopinion.c: Preopinion Pre`o*pin"ion (?), n. Opinion previously formed; prepossession; prejudice. Sir T. Browne.

preoption.c: Preoption Pre*op"tion (?), n. Right of first choice.

preoral.c: Preoral Pre*o"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of, or anterior to, the mouth; as, preoral bands.

preorbital.c: Preorbital Pre*or"bit*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front or the orbit.

preordain.c: Preordain Pre`or*dain" (?), v. t. [Pref. pre + ordain: cf. L. praeordinare.] To ordain or appoint beforehand: to predetermine: to foreordain. Milton.

preorder.c: Preorder Pre*or"der (?), v. t. To order to arrange beforehand; to foreordain. Sir W. Hamilton.

preordinance.c: Preordinance Pre*or"di*nance (?), n. Antecedent decree or determination. Shak.

preordinate.c: Preordinate Pre*or"di*nate (?), a. [L. praeordinatus, p. p. See Preordain.] Preordained. [R.] Sir T. Elyot.

preordination.c: Preordination Pre*or`di*na"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. préordination.] The act of foreordaining: previous determination. “The preordination of God.” Bale.

preparable.c: Preparable Pre*par"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being prepared. “Medicine preparable by art.” Boyle.

preparation.c: Preparation Prep`a*ra"tion (?), n. [F. préparation, L. praeparatio. See Prepare.]

preparative.c: Preparative Pre*par"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. préparatif.] Tending to prepare or make ready; having the power of preparing, qualifying, or fitting; preparatory.

preparatively.c: Preparatively Pre*par"a*tive*ly, adv. By way of preparation.

preparator.c: Preparator Pre*par"a*tor (?), n. [L. praeparator.] One who prepares beforehand, as subjects for dissection, specimens for preservation in collections, etc. Agassiz.

preparatory.c: Preparatory Pre*par"a*to*ry (?), a. [L. praeparatorius: cf. F. préparatoire.] Preparing the way for anything by previous measures of adaptation; antecedent and adapted to what follows; introductory; preparative; as, a preparatory school; a preparatory condition.

prepare.c: Prepare Pre*pare" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prepared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preparing.] [F. préparer, L. praeparare; prae before + parare to make ready. See Pare.]
Prepare Pre*pare" (?), v. i. 1. To make all things ready; to put things in order; as, to prepare for a hostile invasion. “Bid them prepare for dinner.” Shak.

prepared.c: Prepared Pre*pared" (?), a. Made fit or suitable; adapted; ready; as, prepared food; prepared questions. -- Pre*par"ed*ly (#), adv. Shak. -- Pre*par"ed*ness, n.

preparer.c: Preparer Pre*par"er (?), n. One who, or that which, prepares, fits, or makes ready. Wood.

prepay.c: Prepay Pre*pay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prepaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prepaying.] To pay in advance, or beforehand; as, to prepay postage.

prepenial.c: Prepenial Pre*pe"ni*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of, or anterior to, the penis.

prepense.c: Prepense Pre*pense" (?), v. t. [Pref. pre + F. penser to think. See Pansy.] To weigh or consider beforehand; to premeditate. [Obs.] Spenser. Sir T. Elyot.
Prepense Pre*pense", v. i. To deliberate beforehand. [Obs.]

Prepense Pre*pense", a. [See Pansy, and cf. Prepense, v. t.] Devised, contrived, or planned beforehand; preconceived; premeditated; aforethought; -- usually placed after the word it qualifies; as, malice prepense.

prepensely.c: Prepensely Pre*pense"ly, adv. In a premeditated manner.

prepollency.c: Prepollency Prepollence { Pre*pol"lence (?), Pre*pol"len*cy (?), } n. [L. praepollentia.] The quality or state of being prepollent; superiority of power; predominance; prevalence. [R.] Coventry.

prepollent.c: Prepollent Pre*pol"lent (?), a. [L. praepollens, p. p. of praepollere to surpass in power; prae before + pollere to be powerful.] Having superior influence or power; prevailing; predominant. [R.] Boyle.
Prepollent ‖Pre*pol"lent (?), n.; pl. Prepollices (#). [NL. See Pre-, Pollex.] (Anat.) An extra first digit, or rudiment of a digit, on the preaxial side of the pollex.

preponderancy.c: Preponderancy Preponderance { Pre*pon"der*ance (?), Pre*pon"der*an*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. prépondérance.] 1. The quality or state of being preponderant; superiority or excess of weight, influence, or power, etc.; an outweighing.

preponderant.c: Preponderant Pre*pon"der*ant (?), a. [L. praeponderans, -antis: cf. F. prépondérant. See Preponderate.] Preponderating; outweighing; overbalancing; -- used literally and figuratively; as, a preponderant weight; of preponderant importance. -- Pre*pon"der*ant*ly, adv.

preponderate.c: Preponderate Pre*pon"der*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Preponderated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preponderating.] [L. praeponderatus, p. p. of praeponderare; prae before + ponderare to weigh, fr., pondus, ponderis, a weight. See Ponder.] 1. To outweigh; to overpower by weight; to exceed in weight; to overbalance.

Preponderate Pre*pon"der*ate, v. i. To exceed in weight; hence, to incline or descend, as the scale of a balance; figuratively, to exceed in influence, power, etc.; hence; to incline to one side; as, the affirmative side preponderated.

preponderatingly.c: Preponderatingly Pre*pon"der*a`ting*ly (?), adv. In a preponderating manner; preponderantly.

preponderation.c: Preponderation Pre*pon`der*a"tion (?), n. [L. praeponderatio.] The act or state of preponderating; preponderance; as, a preponderation of reasons. I. Watts.

prepose.c: Prepose Pre*pose" (?), v. t. [F. préposer; pref. pré- (L. prae before) + poser. See Pose.] To place or set before; to prefix. [Obs.] Fuller.

preposition.c: Preposition Prep`o*si"tion (?), n. [L. praepositio, fr. praeponere to place before; prae before + ponere to put, place: cf. F. préposition. See Position, and cf. Provost.]

prepositional.c: Prepositional Prep`o*si"tion*al (?), a. [Cf. F. prépositionnel.] Of or pertaining to a preposition; of the nature of a preposition. Early. -- Prep`o*si"tion*al*ly, adv.

prepositive.c: Prepositive Pre*pos"i*tive (?), a. [L. praepositivus: cf. F. prépositif.] (Gram.) Put before; prefixed; as, a prepositive particle. -- n. A prepositive word. Tooke.

prepositor.c: Prepositor ‖Pre*pos"i*tor (?), n. [NL.] A scholar appointed to inspect other scholars; a monitor. Todd.

prepositure.c: Prepositure Pre*pos"i*ture (?), n. [L. praepositura. See Preposition, and cf. Provost.] The office or dignity of a provost; a provostship. Lowth.

prepossess.c: Prepossess Pre`pos*sess" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prepossessed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prepossessing.]

prepossessing.c: Prepossessing Pre`pos*sess"ing (?), a. Tending to invite favor; attracting confidence, favor, esteem, or love; attractive; as, a prepossessing manner. -- Pre`pos*sess"ing*ly, adv.

prepossessor.c: Prepossessor Pre`*pos*sess"or (?), n. One who possesses, or occupies, previously. R. Brady.

preposterous.c: Preposterous Pre*pos"ter*ous (?), a. [L. praeposterus; prae before + posterus coming after, latter. See Posterior.]

prepotency.c: Prepotency Pre*po"ten*cy (?), n. [L. praepotentia: cf. F. prépotence.]

prepotent.c: Prepotent Pre*po"tent (?), a. [L. praepotens. See Pre-, and Potent.]

preprovide.c: Preprovide Pre`pro*vide" (?), v. t. To provide beforehand. “The materials preprovided.” Fuller.

prepubic.c: Prepubic Pre*pu"bic (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of, or anterior to, the pubis; pertaining to the prepubis.

prepubis.c: Prepubis ‖Pre*pu"bis (?), n. [NL. See Pre-, and Pubis.] (Anat.) A bone or cartilage, of some animals, situated in the middle line in front of the pubic bones.

prepuce.c: Prepuce Pre"puce (?), n. [F. prépuce, L. praeputium.] (Anat.) The foreskin.

preputial.c: Preputial Pre*pu"tial (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the prepuce.

preraphaelitism.c: Preraphaelitism Preraphaelism { Pre*raph"a*el*ism (?), Pre*raph"a*el*i`tism (?), } n. (Fine Arts) The doctrine or practice of a school of modern painters who profess to be followers of the painters before Raphael. Its adherents advocate careful study from nature, delicacy and minuteness of workmanship, and an exalted and delicate conception of the subject.

preraphaelite.c: Preraphaelite Pre*raph"a*el*ite (?), a. Of or pertaining to the style called preraphaelitism; as, a preraphaelite figure; a preraphaelite landscape. Ruskin.
Preraphaelite Pre*raph"a*el*ite, n. 1. One who favors or practices art as it was before Raphael; one who favors or advocates preraphaelitism.

preregnant.c: Preregnant Pre*reg"nant (?), n. One who reigns before another; a sovereign predecessor. [R.] Warner.

preremote.c: Preremote Pre`re*mote (?), a. More remote in previous time or prior order.

prerequire.c: Prerequire Pre`re*quire" (?), v. t. To require beforehand.

prerequisite.c: Prerequisite Pre*req"ui*site (?), a. Previously required; necessary as a preliminary to any proposed effect or end; as, prerequisite conditions of success.
Prerequisite Pre*req"ui*site, n. Something previously required, or necessary to an end or effect proposed.

preresolve.c: Preresolve Pre`re*solve" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Preresolved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preresolving.] To resolve beforehand; to predetermine. Sir E. Dering.

prerogative.c: Prerogative Pre*rog"a*tive (?), n. [F. prérogative, from L. praerogativa precedence in voting, preference, privilege, fr. praerogativus that is asked before others for his opinion, that votes before or first, fr. praerogare to ask before another; prae before + rogare to ask. See Rogation.]

prerogatived.c: Prerogatived Pre*rog"a*tived (?), a. Endowed with a prerogative, or exclusive privilege. [R.] Shak.

presage.c: Presage Pre"sage (?), n. [F. présage, L. praesagium, from praesagire. See Presage, v. t. ]
Presage Pre*sage" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Presaged (-sājd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Presaging. ] [F. présager, L. praesagire: prae before + sagire to perceive acutely or sharply. See Sagacious.]
Presage Pre*sage", v. i. To form or utter a prediction; -- sometimes used with of. Dryden.

presageful.c: Presageful Pre*sage"ful (?), a. Full of presages; ominous.

presager.c: Presager Pre*sa"ger (?), n. One who, or that which, presages; a foreteller; a foreboder. Shak.

presbyope.c: Presbyope Pres"by*ope (?), n. (Med.) One who has presbyopia; a farsighted person.

presbyopia.c: Presbyopia ‖Pres`by*o"pi*a (?) [NL., from Gr.? old, n., an old man +?,?, the eye.] (Med.) A defect of vision consequent upon advancing age. It is due to rigidity of the crystalline lens, which produces difficulty of accommodation and recession of the near point of vision, so that objects very near the eyes can not be seen distinctly without the use of convex glasses. Called also presbytia.

presbyopic.c: Presbyopic Pres`by*op"ic (?), a. Affected by presbyopia; also, remedying presbyopia; farsighted.

presbyopy.c: Presbyopy Pres"by*o`py (?), n. [Cf. F. presbyopie.] See Presbyopia.

presbyte.c: Presbyte Pres"byte (?), n. [Gr.? an old man.] Same as Presbyope.

presbyter.c: Presbyter Pres"by*ter (?), n. [L. an elder, fr. Gr.?. See Priest.]

presbyteral.c: Presbyteral Pres*byt"er*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a presbyter or presbytery; presbyterial.

presbyterate.c: Presbyterate Pres*byt"er*ate (?), n. [L. presbyteratus: cf. F. presbytérat.] A presbytery; also, presbytership. Heber.

presbyteress.c: Presbyteress Pres"by*ter*ess, n. A female presbyter. Bale.

presbyterial.c: Presbyterial Pres`by*te"ri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. presbytéral.] Presbyterian. “Presbyterial government.” Milton.

presbyterian.c: Presbyterian Pres`by*te"ri*an (?), a. [Cf. F. presbytérien.] Of or pertaining to a presbyter, or to ecclesiastical government by presbyters; relating to those who uphold church government by presbyters; also, to the doctrine, discipline, and worship of a communion so governed.
Presbyterian Pres`by*te"ri*an, n. [Cf. F. presbytérien.] One who maintains the validity of ordination and government by presbyters; a member of the Presbyterian church.

presbyterianism.c: Presbyterianism Pres`by*te"ri*an*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. presbytérianisme.] That form of church government which invests presbyters with all spiritual power, and admits no prelates over them; also, the faith and polity of the Presbyterian churches, taken collectively.

presbytership.c: Presbytership Pres"by*ter*ship (?), n. The office or station of a presbyter; presbyterate.

presbytery.c: Presbytery Pres"by*ter*y (?), n.; pl. Presbyteries (#). [L. presbyterium, Gr.?. See Presbyter, and cf. Presbyterium.]

prescapula.c: Prescapula ‖Pre*scap"u*la (?), n. [NL.] (Anat.) The part of the scapula in front of, or above, the spine, or mesoscapula.

prescapular.c: Prescapular Pre*scap"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the prescapula; supraspinous.

prescience.c: Prescience Pre"sci*ence (prē"shĭ*eins or prē"sheins; 277), n. [F. prescience, L. praescientia. See Prescient.] Knowledge of events before they take place; foresight.

prescient.c: Prescient Pre"sci*ent (prē"shĭ*eint or -sheint), a. [L. praesciens, -entis, p. pr. of praescire to foreknow; prae before + scire to know: cf. F. prescient. See Science.] Having knowledge of coming events; foreseeing; conscious beforehand. Pope.

presciently.c: Presciently Pre"sci*ent*ly, adv. With prescience or foresight.

prescind.c: Prescind Pre*scind" (pre*sĭnd"), v. t. [L. praescindere to cut off in front; prae before + scindere to cut asunder: cf. F. prescinder.]

prescindent.c: Prescindent Pre*scind"ent (?), a. [L. praescius; prae before + scius knowing, fr. scire to know.] Cutting off; abstracting. [R.] Cheyne.

prescious.c: Prescious Pre"scious (prē"shŭs), a. [L. praescius; prae before + scius knowing, fr. scire to know.] Foreknowing; having foreknowledge; as, prescious of ills. [R.] Dryden.

prescribe.c: Prescribe Pre*scribe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prescribed (?); p. pr & vb. n. Prescribing.] [L. praescribere, praescriptum; prae before + scriebe to write. See Scribe.]
Prescribe Pre*scribe", v. i. 1. To give directions; to dictate.

prescript.c: Prescript Pre"script (?), a. [L. praescriptus, p. p. of praescribere: cf. F. prescrit. See Prescribe.] Directed; prescribed. “ A prescript from of words.” Jer. Taylor.
Prescript Pre"script, n. [L. praescriptum: cf. OF. prescript.]

prescriptibility.c: Prescriptibility Pre*scrip`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being prescriptible. Story.

prescriptible.c: Prescriptible Pre*scrip"ti*ble (pre*skrĭp"tĭ*b'l), a. [Cf. F. prescriptible.] Depending on, or derived from, prescription; proper to be prescribed. Grafton.

prescription.c: Prescription Pre*scrip"tion (pre*skrĭp"shŭn), n. [F. prescription, L. praescriptio, an inscription, preface, precept, demurrer, prescription (in sense 3), fr. praescribere. See Prescribe.]

prescriptive.c: Prescriptive Pre*scrip"tive (?), a. [L. praescriptivus of a demurrer or legal exception.] 1. (Law) Consisting in, or acquired by, immemorial or long-continued use and enjoyment; as, a prescriptive right of title; pleading the continuance and authority of long custom.

prescutum.c: Prescutum ‖Pre*scu"tum (?), n.; pl. Prescuta (?). [NL. See Præ-, and Scutum.] (Zool.) The first of the four pieces composing the dorsal part, or tergum, of a thoracic segment of an insect. It is usually small and inconspicuous.

preseance.c: Preseance Pre"se*ance (?), n. [F. préséance. See Preside.] Priority of place in sitting.[Obs.] Carew.

preselect.c: Preselect Pre`se*lect" (?), v. t. To select beforehand.

presence.c: Presence Pres"ence (?), n. [F. présence, L. praesentia. See Present.] 1. The state of being present, or of being within sight or call, or at hand; -- opposed to absence.

presensation.c: Presensation Pre`sen*sa"tion (?), n. Previous sensation, notion, or idea. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

presension.c: Presension Pre*sen"sion (?), n. [L. praesensio, fr. praesentire to perceive beforehand. See Presentient.] Previous perception. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

present.c: Present Pres"ent (?), a. [F. présent, L. praesens,-entis, that is before one, in sight or at hand, p. p. of praeesse to be before; prae before + esse to be. See Essence.]
Present Pres"ent, n. [Cf. F. présent. See Present, a.] 1. Present time; the time being; time in progress now, or at the moment contemplated; as, at this present.

Present Pre*sent" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Presented; p. pr. & vb. n. Presenting.] [F. présenter, L. praesentare, fr. praesens, a. See Present, a.] 1. To bring or introduce into the presence of some one, especially of a superior; to introduce formally; to offer for acquaintance; as, to present an envoy to the king; (with the reciprocal pronoun) to come into the presence of a superior.
Present Pre*sent", v. i. (Med.) To appear at the mouth of the uterus so as to be perceptible to the finger in vaginal examination; -- said of a part of an infant during labor.
Present Pres"ent (?), n. [F. présent.] Anything presented or given; a gift; a donative; as, a Christmas present.
Present Pre*sent" (?), n. (Mil.) The position of a soldier in presenting arms; as, to stand at present.

Present worth Present value { Pres"ent value or Pres"ent worth } (of money payable at a future date). The principal which, drawing interest at a given rate, will amount to the given sum at the date on which this is to be paid; thus, interest being at 6%, the present value of $106 due one year hence is $100.

presentable.c: Presentable Pre*sent"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. présentable.] 1. Capable or admitting of being presented; suitable to be exhibited, represented, or offered; fit to be brought forward or set forth; hence, fitted to be introduced to another, or to go into society; as, ideas that are presentable in simple language; she is not presentable in such a gown.

presentaneous.c: Presentaneous Pres`en*ta"ne*ous (?), a. [L. praesentaneus. See Present, a.] Ready; quick; immediate in effect; as, presentaneous poison. [Obs.] Harvey.

presentation.c: Presentation Pres`en*ta"tion (?), n. [L. praesentatio a showing, representation: cf. F. présentation.] 1. The act of presenting, or the state of being presented; a setting forth; an offering; bestowal.

presentative.c: Presentative Pre*sent"a*tive (?), a. 1. (Eccl.) Having the right of presentation, or offering a clergyman to the bishop for institution; as, advowsons are presentative, collative, or donative. Blackstone.

presentee.c: Presentee Pres`en*tee" (?), n. [F. présenté, p. p. See Present, v. t. ] One to whom something is presented; also, one who is presented; specifically (Eccl.), one presented to benefice. Ayliffe.

presential.c: Presential Pre*sen"tial (?), a. [LL. praesentialis.] Implying actual presence; present, immediate. [Obs.]

presentiality.c: Presentiality Pre*sen`ti*al"i*ty (?), n. State of being actually present. [Obs.] South.

presentiate.c: Presentiate Pre*sen"ti*ate (?), v. t. To make present. [Obs.]

presentient.c: Presentient Pre*sen"tient (?), a. [L. praesentiens, p. pr. of praesentire to perceive beforehand; prae before + sentire to feel.] Feeling or perceiving beforehand.

presentific.c: Presentific Pres`en*tif"ic (?), a. [L. praesens, -entis, present + facere to make.] Making present. [Obs.]

presentiment.c: Presentiment Pre*sen"ti*ment (?), n. [Pref. pre- + sentiment: cf. F. pressentiment. See Presentient.] Previous sentiment, conception, or opinion; previous apprehension; especially, an antecedent impression or conviction of something unpleasant, distressing, or calamitous, about to happen; anticipation of evil; foreboding.

presentimental.c: Presentimental Pre*sen`ti*men"tal (?), a. Of nature of a presentiment; foreboding. [R.] Coleridge.

presentive.c: Presentive Pre*sent"ive (?), a. (Philol.) Bringing a conception or notion directly before the mind; presenting an object to the memory of imagination; -- distinguished from symbolic.

presently.c: Presently Pres"ent*ly (?), adv. 1. At present; at this time; now. [Obs.]

presentment.c: Presentment Pre*sent"ment (?), n. 1. The act of presenting, or the state of being presented; presentation. “ Upon the heels of my presentment.” Shak.

presentness.c: Presentness Pres"ent*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being present; presence. [Obs.] “Presentness of mind in danger.” Clarendon.

presentoir.c: Presentoir Pres`en*toir" (?), n. [Formed after analogy of French.] An ornamental tray, dish, or the like, used as a salver.

preservable.c: Preservable Pre*serv"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being preserved; admitting of preservation.

preservation.c: Preservation Pres`er*va"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. préservation.] The act or process of preserving, or keeping safe; the state of being preserved, or kept from injury, destruction, or decay; security; safety; as, preservation of life, fruit, game, etc.; a picture in good preservation.

preservative.c: Preservative Pre*serv"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. préservatif.] Having the power or quality of preserving; tending to preserve, or to keep from injury, decay, etc.
Preservative Pre*serv"a*tive, n. That which preserves, or has the power of preserving; a presevative agent.

preservatory.c: Preservatory Pre*serv"a*to*ry, n.; pl. Preservatories (?). 1. A preservative. [Obs.] Whitlock.

preserve.c: Preserve Pre*serve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Preserved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preserving.] [F. préserver, from L. prae before + servare to save, preserve; cf. L. praeservare to observe beforehand. See Serve.] 1. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to guard or defend from evil, harm, danger, etc.; to protect.
Preserve Pre*serve", v. i. 1. To make preserves. Shak.
Preserve Pre*serve", n. 1. That which is preserved; fruit, etc., seasoned and kept by suitable preparation; esp., fruit cooked with sugar; -- commonly in the plural.

preserver.c: Preserver Pre*serv"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, preserves, saves, or defends, from destruction, injury, or decay; esp., one who saves the life or character of another. Shak.

preside.c: Preside Pre*side" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Presided; p. pr. & vb. n. Presiding.] [L. praesidere; prae before + sedere to sit: cf. F. présider. See Sit.] 1. To be set, or to sit, in the place of authority; to occupy the place of president, chairman, moderator, director, etc.; to direct, control, and regulate, as chief officer; as, to preside at a public meeting; to preside over the senate.

presidency.c: Presidency Pres"i*den*cy (?), n.; pl. Presidencies (#). [Cf. F. présidence.] 1. The function or condition of one who presides; superintendence; control and care.

president.c: President Pres"i*dent, a. Occupying the first rank or chief place; having the highest authority; presiding. [R.]

President Pres"i*dent, n. [F. président, L. praesidens, -entis, p. pr. of praesidere. See Preside.] 1. One who is elected or appointed to preside; a presiding officer, as of a legislative body. Specifically: (a) The chief officer of a corporation, company, institution, society, or the like. (b) The chief executive officer of the government in certain republics; as, the president of the United States.

presidential.c: Presidential Pres`i*den"tial (?), a. 1. Presiding or watching over. “Presidential angels.” Glanvill.

presidentship.c: Presidentship Pres"i*dent*ship (?), n. The office and dignity of president; presidency. Hooker.

presidiary.c: Presidiary Presidial { Pre*sid"i*al (?), Pre*sid"i*a*ry (?), } a. [L. praesidialis and praesidiarius, fr. praesidium a presiding over, defense, guard. See Preside.] Of or pertaining to a garrison; having a garrison.
Presidiary Pre*sid"i*a*ry, n. [L. praesidiarium.] A guard. [Obs.] “Heavenly presidiaries.” Bp. Hall.

presidio.c: Presidio ‖Pre*si"di*o (?), n. [Sp.] A place of defense; a fortress; a garrison; a fortress; a garrison or guardhouse.

presignification.c: Presignification Pre*sig`ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [?. praesignificatio. See Presignify.] The act of signifying or showing beforehand.

presignify.c: Presignify Pre*sig"ni*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Presignified (?); imp. & p. p. Presignifying.] [L. praesignificare; prae before + significare to signify.] To intimate or signify beforehand; to presage.

presphenoid.c: Presphenoid Pre*sphe"noid (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the sphenoid bone; of or pertaining to the anterior part of the sphenoid bone (i. e., the presphenoid bone).

presphenoidal.c: Presphenoidal Pre`sphe*noid"al (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the presphenoid bone; presphenoid.

press.c: Press Press (?), n. (Zool.) An East Indian insectivore (Tupaia ferruginea). It is arboreal in its habits, and has a bushy tail. The fur is soft, and varies from rusty red to maroon and to brownish black.

Press Press, v. t. [Corrupt. fr. prest ready money advanced, a loan; hence, earnest money given soldiers on entering service. See Prest, n.] To force into service, particularly into naval service; to impress.
Press Press, n. [For prest, confused with press.] A commission to force men into public service, particularly into the navy.

Press Press, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pressed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pressing.] [F. presser, fr. L. pressare to press, fr. premere, pressum, to press. Cf. Print, v.] 1. To urge, or act upon, with force, as weight; to act upon by pushing or thrusting, in distinction from pulling; to crowd or compel by a gradual and continued exertion; to bear upon; to squeeze; to compress; as, we press the ground with the feet when we walk; we press the couch on which we repose; we press substances with the hands, fingers, or arms; we are pressed in a crowd.
Press Press, v. i. 1. To exert pressure; to bear heavily; to push, crowd, or urge with steady force.

Press Press, n. [F. presse. See 4th Press.] 1. An apparatus or machine by which any substance or body is pressed, squeezed, stamped, or shaped, or by which an impression of a body is taken; sometimes, the place or building containing a press or presses.

Press cake Press cake. A cake of compressed substance, as: in gunpowder manufacture, the cake resulting from compressing the meal powder; in the treatment of coal tar, the pressed product at various stages of the process; or, in beet-sugar manufacture, the vegetable residue after the sugar juice has been expressed.
Press proof Press proof. (Print.) (a) The last proof for correction before sending to press. (b) A proof taken on a press, esp. to show impression, margins, color, etc.
Press revise Press revise. (Print.) A proof for final revision.

pressboard.c: Pressboard Press"board` (?), n. A kind of highly sized rag paper or board, sometimes containing a small admixture of wood pulp; -- so called because used originally, as now, in presses for pressing and finishing knit underwear.

presser.c: Presser Press"er (?), n. One who, or that which, presses.

pressgang.c: Pressgang Press"gang` (?), n. See Press gang, under Press.

pressing.c: Pressing Press"ing, a. Urgent; exacting; importunate; as, a pressing necessity. -- Press"ing*ly, adv.

pression.c: Pression Pres"sion (?), n. [L. pressio: cf. F. pression. See 4th Press.] 1. The act of pressing; pressure. Sir I. Newton.

pressiroster.c: Pressiroster Pres`si*ros"ter (?), n. [L. presssus pressed (p. p. of premere) + rostrum beak: cf. F. pressirostre. See 4th Press.] (Zool.) One of a tribe of wading birds (Pressirostres) including those which have a compressed beak, as the plovers.

pressirostral.c: Pressirostral Pres`si*ros"tral (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the pressirosters.

pressitant.c: Pressitant Pres"si*tant (?), a. [See 4th Press.] Gravitating; heavy. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

pressive.c: Pressive Pres"sive (?), a. Pressing; urgent; also, oppressive; as, pressive taxation. [R.] Bp. Hall.

pressman.c: Pressman Press"man (?), n.; pl. Pressmen (?). 1. One who manages, or attends to, a press, esp. a printing press.
Pressman Press"man, n. [See 2d Press.] One of a press gang, who aids in forcing men into the naval service; also, one forced into the service.

pressor.c: Pressor Press"or (?), a. (Physiol.) Causing, or giving rise to, pressure or to an increase of pressure; as, pressor nerve fibers, stimulation of which excites the vasomotor center, thus causing a stronger contraction of the arteries and consequently an increase of the arterial blood pressure; -- opposed to depressor. Landois & Stirling.

presspack.c: Presspack Press"pack` (?), v. t. To pack, or prepare for packing, by means of a press.

pressure.c: Pressure Pres"sure (?; 138), n. [OF., fr. L. pressura, fr. premere. See 4th Press.] 1. The act of pressing, or the condition of being pressed; compression; a squeezing; a crushing; as, a pressure of the hand.
Pressure wires Pressure wires. (Elec.) Wires leading from various points of an electric system to a central station, where a voltmeter indicates the potential of the system at those points.

presswork.c: Presswork Press work Press"work` (prĕs"wûrk`), n. 1. The art of printing from the surface of type, plates, or engravings in relief, by means of a press; the work so done. MacKellar.
Presswork Press work Press"work` (prĕs"wûrk`), n. The work of a press agent. [Usually Press work] [Chiefly Theat. Cant]

prest.c: Prest Prest (prĕst), imp. & p. p. of Press.
Prest Prest, a. [OF. prest, F. prêt, fr. L. praestus ready. Cf. Presto.] 1. Ready; prompt; prepared. [Obs.]

Prest Prest, n. [OF. prest, F. prêt, fr. OF. prester to lend, F. prêter, fr. L. praestare to stand before, to become surety for, to fulfill, offer, supply; prae before + stare to stand. See Pre-, and Stand, and cf. Press to force into service.] 1. Ready money; a loan of money. [Obs.]
Prest Prest, v. t. To give as a loan; to lend. [Obs.]

prestation.c: Prestation Pres*ta"tion (?), n. [L. praestatio a performing, paying, fr. praestare: cf. F. prestation.] (O. Eng. Law) A payment of money; a toll or duty; also, the rendering of a service. Burrill.

prester.c: Prester Pres"ter (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, from? to kindle or burn, and? to blow up, swell out by blowing.] 1. A meteor or exhalation formerly supposed to be thrown from the clouds with such violence that by collision it is set on fire. [Obs.]
Prester Pres"ter, n. [OF. prestre. See Priest.] A priest or presbyter; as, Prester John. [Obs.]

presternum.c: Presternum Pre*ster"num (?), n. [NL.] (Anat.) The anterior segment of the sternum; the manubrium. -- Pre*ster"nal (#), a.

prestidigital.c: Prestidigital Pres`ti*dig"i*tal (?), a. Nimble-fingered; having fingers fit for prestidigitation, or juggling. [R.] “His prestidigital hand.” Charles Reade.

prestidigitation.c: Prestidigitation Pres`ti*dig`i*ta"tion (?), n. Legerdemain; sleight of hand; juggling.

prestidigitator.c: Prestidigitator Pres`ti*dig"i*ta`tor (?), n. [L. praesto ready + digitus finger: cf. F. prestidigitateur.] One skilled in legerdemain or sleight of hand; a juggler.

prestige.c: Prestige Pres"tige (?; 277), n. [F., fr. L. praestigum delusion, illusion, praestigae deceptions, jugglers' tricks, prob. fr. prae before + the root of stinguere to extinguish, originally, to prick. See Stick, v.] 1. Delusion; illusion; trick. [Obs.]

prestigiation.c: Prestigiation Pres*tig`i*a"tion (?), n. [L. praestigiare to deceive by juggling tricks, fr. praestigae. See Prestige.] Legerdemain; prestidigitation. [Obs.]

prestigiator.c: Prestigiator Pres*tig"i*a`tor (?), n. [L. praestigiator.] A juggler; prestidigitator. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

prestigiatory.c: Prestigiatory Pres*tig"i*a*to*ry (?), a. Consisting of impostures; juggling. [Obs.] Barrow.

prestigious.c: Prestigious Pres*tig"i*ous (?), a. [L. praestigiosus.] Practicing tricks; juggling. [Obs.] Cotton Mather.

prestimony.c: Prestimony Pres"ti*mo*ny (?), n. [LL. praestimonium, fr. L. praestare to furnish, supply: cf. F. prestimonie. See Prest, n.] (Canon Law) A fund for the support of a priest, without the title of a benefice. The patron in the collator.

prestissimo.c: Prestissimo ‖Pres*tis"si*mo (?), adv. [It., superl. of presto.] (Mus.) Very quickly; with great rapidity.

presto.c: Presto Pres"to (?), adv. [It. or Sp. presto quick, quickly. See Prest, a.] 1. Quickly; immediately; in haste; suddenly.

prestriction.c: Prestriction Pre*stric"tion (?), n. [L. praestrictio a binding fast, fr. praestringere. See Pre-, and Stringent.] Obstruction, dimness, or defect of sight. [Obs.] Milton.

presultor.c: Presultor Pre*sul"tor (?), n. [L. praesultor; prae before + salire to dance.] A leader in the dance. [R.]

presumable.c: Presumable Pre*sum"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. présumable.] Such as may be presumed or supposed to be true; that seems entitled to belief without direct evidence.

presumably.c: Presumably Pre*sum"a*bly, adv. In a presumable manner; by, or according to, presumption.

presume.c: Presume Pre*sume" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Presumed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Presuming.] [F. présumer, L. praesumere, praesumptum; prae before + sumere to take. See Assume, Redeem.] 1. To assume or take beforehand; esp., to do or undertake without leave or authority previously obtained.

Presume Pre*sume", v. i. 1. To suppose or assume something to be, or to be true, on grounds deemed valid, though not amounting to proof; to believe by anticipation; to infer; as, we may presume too far.

presumer.c: Presumer Pre*sum"er (?), n. One who presumes; also, an arrogant person. Sir H. Wotton.

presumption.c: Presumption Pre*sump"tion (?; 215), n. [L. praesumptio: cf. F. présomption, OF. also presumpcion. See Presume.] 1. The act of presuming, or believing upon probable evidence; the act of assuming or taking for granted; belief upon incomplete proof.

presumptive.c: Presumptive Pre*sump"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. présomptif.] 1. Based on presumption or probability; grounded on probable evidence; probable; as, presumptive proof.

presumptively.c: Presumptively Pre*sump"tive*ly, adv. By presumption, or supposition grounded or probability; presumably.

presumptuous.c: Presumptuous Pre*sump"tu*ous (?; 135), a. [L. praesumptuosus: cf. F. présomptueux, OF. also presumptuous. See Presumption.] 1. Full of presumption; presuming; overconfident or venturesome; audacious; rash; taking liberties unduly; arrogant; insolent; as, a presumptuous commander; presumptuous conduct.

presumptuously.c: Presumptuously Pre*sump"tu*ous*ly, adv. In a presumptuous manner; arrogantly.

presumptuousness.c: Presumptuousness Pre*sump"tu*ous*ness, n. The quality or state of being presumptuous.

presupposal.c: Presupposal Pre`sup*pos"al (?), n. Presupposition. [R.] “Presupposal of knowledge.” Hooker.

presuppose.c: Presuppose Pre`sup*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Presupposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Presupposing.] [Pref. pre- + suppose: cf. F. présupposer.] To suppose beforehand; to imply as antecedent; to take for granted; to assume; as, creation presupposes a creator.

presupposition.c: Presupposition Pre*sup`po*si"tion (?), n. [Pref. pre- + supposition: cf. F. présupposition.] 1. The act of presupposing; an antecedent implication; presumption.

presurmise.c: Presurmise Pre`sur*mise" (?), n. A surmise previously formed. Shak.

presystolic.c: Presystolic Pre`sys*tol"ic (?), a. (Physiol.) Preceding the systole or contraction of the heart; as, the presystolic friction sound.

pretemporal.c: Pretemporal Pre*tem"po*ral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the temporal bone.

pretenceless.c: Pretenceless Pretenceful Pretence Pre*tence" (?), n., Pre*tence"ful, a., Pre*tence"*less, a. See Pretense, Pretenseful, Pretenseless.

pretend.c: Pretend Pre*tend" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pretended; p. pr. & vb. n. Pretending.] [OE. pretenden to lay claim to, F. prétendre, L. praetendere, praetentum, to stretch forward, pretend, simulate, assert; prae before + tendere to stretch. See Tend, v. t. ] 1. To lay a claim to; to allege a title to; to claim.

Pretend Pre*tend", v. i. 1. To put in, or make, a claim, truly or falsely; to allege a title; to lay claim to, or strive after, something; -- usually with to. “Countries that pretend to freedom.” Swift.

pretendant.c: Pretendant Pre*tend"ant (?), n. A pretender; a claimant.

pretended.c: Pretended Pre*tend"ed, a. Making a false appearance; unreal; false; as, pretended friend. -- Pre*tend"ed*ly, adv.

pretendence.c: Pretendence Pre*tend"ence (?), n. The act of pretending; pretense. [Obs.] Daniel.

pretender.c: Pretender Pre*tend"er (?), n. 1. One who lays claim, or asserts a title (to something); a claimant. Specifically, The pretender (Eng. Hist.), the son or the grandson of James II., the heir of the royal family of Stuart, who laid claim to the throne of Great Britain, from which the house was excluded by law.

pretendership.c: Pretendership Pre*tend"er*ship, n. The character, right, or claim of a pretender. Swift.

pretendingly.c: Pretendingly Pre*tend"ing*ly, adv. As by right or title; arrogantly; presumptuously. Collier.

pretence.c: Pretence Pretense { Pre*tense", Pre*tence } (?), n. [LL. praetensus, for L. praetentus, p. p. of praetendere. See Pretend, and cf. Tension.] 1. The act of laying claim; the claim laid; assumption; pretension. Spenser.

pretensed.c: Pretensed Pre*tensed" (?), a. Pretended; feigned. [Obs.] -- Pre*tens"ed*ly (#), adv. [Obs.]

pretenseless.c: Pretenseless Pre*tense"less, a. Not having or making pretenses.

pretension.c: Pretension Pre*ten"sion (?), n. [Cf. F. prétention. See Pretend, Tension.] 1. The act of pretending, or laying claim; the act of asserting right or title.

pretentative.c: Pretentative Pre*ten"ta*tive (?), a. [Pref. pre- + tentative: cf. L. praetentare to try beforehand.] Fitted for trial beforehand; experimental. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.

pretentious.c: Pretentious Pre*ten"tious (?), a. [Cf. F. prétentieux. See Pretend.] Full of pretension; disposed to lay claim to more than is one's; presuming; assuming. -- Pre*ten"tious*ly, adv. -- Pre*ten"tious*ness, n.

preter.c: Preter- Pre"ter- (?). [L. praeter past, beyond, originally a compar. of prae before. See For, prep.] A prefix signifying past, by, beyond, more than; as, preter- mission, a permitting to go by; preternatural, beyond or more than is natural. [Written also præter.]

preterhuman.c: Preterhuman Pre`ter*hu"man (?), a. [Pref. preter- + human.] More than human.

preterient.c: Preterient Pre*te"ri*ent (?), a. [L. praeteriens, p. pr. See Preterit.] Passed through; antecedent; previous; as, preterient states. [R.]

preterimperfect.c: Preterimperfect Pre`ter*im*per"fect (?), a. & n. [Pref. preter- + imperfect.] (Gram.) Old name of the tense also called imperfect.

preterist.c: Preterist Pret"er*ist (?), n. [Pref. preter- + -ist.] 1. One whose chief interest is in the past; one who regards the past with most pleasure or favor.

preterit.c: Preterit Pret"er*it (?; 277), a. [L. praeteritus, p. p. of praeterire to go or pass by; praeter beyond, by + ire to go: cf. F. prétérit. See Issue.] [Written also preterite and præterite.] 1. (Gram.) Past; -- applied to a tense which expresses an action or state as past.
Preterit Pret"er*it, n. (Gram.) The preterit; also, a word in the preterit tense.

preterite.c: Preterite Pret"er*ite (?), a. & n. Same as Preterit.

preterition.c: Preterition Pre`ter*i"tion (?; 277), n. [L. praeteritio: cf. F. prétérition.] 1. The act of passing, or going past; the state of being past. Bp. Hall.

preteritive.c: Preteritive Pre*ter"i*tive (?), a. (Gram.) Used only or chiefly in the preterit or past tenses, as certain verbs.

preteritness.c: Preteritness Pret"er*it*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being past. Bentley. Lowell.

preterlapsed.c: Preterlapsed Pre`ter*lapsed" (?), a. [L. praeterlapsus, p. p. of praeterlabi to glide by. See Preter-, Lapse.] Past; as, preterlapsed ages. [R.] Glanvill.

preterlegal.c: Preterlegal Pre`ter*le"gal (?), a. [Pref. preter- + legal.] Exceeding the limits of law. [R.]

pretermission.c: Pretermission Pre`ter*mis"sion (?), n. [L. praetermissio. See Pretermit.] 1. The act of passing by or omitting; omission. Milton.

pretermit.c: Pretermit Pre`ter*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pretermitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Pretermitting.] [L. praetermittere, praetermissum; praeter beyond + mittere to send. See Mission.] To pass by; to omit; to disregard. Bacon.

preternatural.c: Preternatural Pre`ter*nat"u*ral (?; 135), a. [Pref. preter + natural.] Beyond of different from what is natural, or according to the regular course of things, but not clearly supernatural or miraculous; strange; inexplicable; extraordinary; uncommon; irregular; abnormal; as, a preternatural appearance; a preternatural stillness; a preternatural presentation (in childbirth) or labor.

preternaturalism.c: Preternaturalism Pre`ter*nat"u*ral*ism (?), n. The state of being preternatural; a preternatural condition.

preternaturality.c: Preternaturality Pre`ter*nat`u*ral"i*ty (?), n. Preternaturalness. [R.] Dr. John Smith.

preternaturally.c: Preternaturally Pre`ter*nat"u*ral*ly (?; 135), adv. In a preternatural manner or degree. Bacon.

preternaturalness.c: Preternaturalness Pre`ter*nat"u*ral*ness, n. The quality or state of being preternatural.

preterperfect.c: Preterperfect Pre`ter*per"fect (?), a. & n. [Pref. preter- + perfect.] (Gram.) Old name of the tense also called preterit.

preterpluperfect.c: Preterpluperfect Pre`ter*plu"per`fect (?), a. & n. [Pref. preter- + pluperfect.] (Gram.) Old name of the tense also called pluperfect.

pretervection.c: Pretervection Pre`ter*vec"tion (?), n. [L. praetervectio, fr. praetervehere to carry beyond. See Invection.] The act of carrying past or beyond. [R.] Abp. Potter.

pretex.c: Pretex Pre*tex" (?), v. t. [L. praetexere. See Pretext.] To frame; to devise; to disguise or excuse; hence, to pretend; to declare falsely. [Obs.]

pretext.c: Pretext Pre"text (?; 277), n. [F. prétexte, L. praetextum, fr. praetextus, p. p. of praetexere to weave before, allege as an excuse; prae before + texere to weave. See Text.] Ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color or cover for the real reason or motive; pretense; disguise.

pretibial.c: Pretibial Pre*tib"i*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated in front of the tibia.

pretor.c: Pretor Pre"tor (?), n. [L. praetor, for praeitor, fr. praeire to go before; prae before + ire to go. See Issue.] 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A civil officer or magistrate among the ancient Romans.

pretorian.c: Pretorian Pre*to"ri*an (?), a. [L. praetorians: cf. F. prétorien.] Of or pertaining to a pretor or magistrate; judicial; exercised by, or belonging to, a pretor; as, pretorian power or authority.
Pretorian Pre*to"ri*an, n. A soldier of the pretorian guard.

pretorium.c: Pretorium ‖Pre*to"ri*um (?), n. [L. praetorium, fr. praetor.] 1. The general's tent in a Roman camp; hence, a council of war, because held in the general's tent.

pretorship.c: Pretorship Pre"tor*ship (?), n. The office or dignity of a pretor. J. Warton

pretorture.c: Pretorture Pre*tor"ture (?; 135), v. t. To torture beforehand. Fuller.

prettily.c: Prettily Pret"ti*ly (?), adv. In a pretty manner.

prettiness.c: Prettiness Pret"ti*ness, n. The quality or state of being pretty; -- used sometimes in a disparaging sense.

pretty.c: Pretty Pret"ty (?), a. [Compar. Prettier (?); superl. Prettiest.] [OE. prati, AS. prættig, prætig, crafty, sly, akin to præt, prætt, deceit, trickery, Icel. prettugr tricky, prettr a trick; probably fr. Latin, perhaps through Celtic; cf. W. praith act, deed, practice, LL. practica execution, practice, plot. See Practice.] 1. Pleasing by delicacy or grace; attracting, but not striking or impressing; of a pleasing and attractive form a color; having slight or diminutive beauty; neat or elegant without elevation or grandeur; pleasingly, but not grandly, conceived or expressed; as, a pretty face; a pretty flower; a pretty poem.
Pretty Pret"ty (?), adv. In some degree; moderately; considerably; rather; almost; -- less emphatic than very; as, I am pretty sure of the fact; pretty cold weather.

prettyism.c: Prettyism Pret"ty*ism (?), n. Affectation of a pretty style, manner, etc. [R.] Ed. Rev.

prettyspoken.c: Pretty-spoken Pret"ty-spo`ken (?), a. Spoken or speaking prettily. [Colloq.]

pretypify.c: Pretypify Pre*typ"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pretypified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pretypifying.] To prefigure; to exhibit previously in a type. Bp. Pearson.

pretzel.c: Pretzel Pret"zel (?), n. [G. pretzel, bretzel. Cf. Bretzel.] A kind of German biscuit or cake in the form of a twisted ring, salted on the outside.

prevail.c: Prevail Pre*vail" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Prevailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prevailing.] [F. prévaloir, OF. prevaleir, L. praevalere; prae before + valere to be strong, able, or worth. See Valiant.] 1. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand, or the mastery; to succeed; -- sometimes with over or against.

prevailing.c: Prevailing Pre*vail"ing, a. 1. Having superior force or influence; efficacious; persuasive. Shak.

prevailingly.c: Prevailingly Pre*vail"ing*ly, adv. So as to prevail.

prevailment.c: Prevailment Pre*vail"ment (?), n. Prevalence; superior influence; efficacy. [Obs.] Shak.

prevalence.c: Prevalence Prev"a*lence (?), n. [L. praevalentia: cf. F. prévalence. See Prevail.] The quality or condition of being prevalent; superior strength, force, or influence; general existence, reception, or practice; wide extension; as, the prevalence of virtue, of a fashion, or of a disease; the prevalence of a rumor.

prevalent.c: Prevalent Prev"a*lent (?), a. [L. praevalens, -entis, p. pr. of praevalere. See Prevail.] 1. Gaining advantage or superiority; having superior force, influence, or efficacy; prevailing; predominant; successful; victorious.

prevalently.c: Prevalently Prev"a*lent"ly, adv. In a prevalent manner. Prior.

prevaricate.c: Prevaricate Pre*var"i*cate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Prevaricated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prevaricating.] [L. praevaricatus, p. p. of praevaricari to walk crookedly, to collude; prae before + varicare to straddle, fr. varicus straddling, varus bent. See Varicose.] 1. To shift or turn from one side to the other, from the direct course, or from truth; to speak with equivocation; to shuffle; to quibble; as, he prevaricates in his statement.
Prevaricate Pre*var"i*cate, v. t. To evade by a quibble; to transgress; to pervert. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

prevarication.c: Prevarication Pre*var`i*ca"tion (?), n. [L. praevaricatio: cf. F. prévarication.] 1. The act of prevaricating, shuffling, or quibbling, to evade the truth or the disclosure of truth; a deviation from the truth and fair dealing.

prevaricator.c: Prevaricator Pre*var"i*ca`tor (?), n. [L. praevaricator: cf. F. prévaricateur.] 1. One who prevaricates.

preve.c: Preve Preve (?), v. i. & i. To prove. [Obs.] Chaucer.

prevenance.c: Prevenance Prev"e*nance (?), n. [F. prévenance.] (Metaph.) A going before; anticipation in sequence or order. “The law of prevenance is simply the well-known law of phenomenal sequence.” Ward.

prevenancy.c: Prevenancy Prev"e*nan*cy (?), n. The act of anticipating another's wishes, desires, etc., in the way of favor or courtesy; hence, civility; obligingness. [Obs.] Sterne.

prevene.c: Prevene Pre*vene" (?), v. t. & i. [F. prévenir, L. praevenire. See Prevent.] To come before; to anticipate; hence, to hinder; to prevent. [Obs.] Philips.

prevenience.c: Prevenience Pre*ven"i*ence (?; 106), n. The act of going before; anticipation. [R.]

prevenient.c: Prevenient Pre*ven"i*ent (?), a. [L. praeveniens, p. pr.] Going before; preceding; hence, preventive. “Prevenient grace descending.” Milton.

prevent.c: Prevent Pre*vent" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prevented; p. pr. & vb. n. Preventing.] [L. praevenire, praeventum; prae before + venire to come. See Come.] 1. To go before; to precede; hence, to go before as a guide; to direct. [Obs.]
Prevent Pre*vent", v. i. To come before the usual time. [Obs.]

preventability.c: Preventability Pre*vent`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being preventable.

preventable.c: Preventable Pre*vent"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being prevented or hindered; as, preventable diseases.

preventative.c: Preventative Pre*vent"a*tive (?), n. That which prevents; -- incorrectly used instead of preventive.

preventer.c: Preventer Pre*vent"er (?), n. 1. One who goes before; one who forestalls or anticipates another. [Obs.] Bacon.

preventingly.c: Preventingly Pre*vent"ing*ly, adv. So as to prevent or hinder.

prevention.c: Prevention Pre*ven"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. prévention.] 1. The act of going, or state of being, before. [Obs.]

preventive.c: Preventive Pre*vent"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. préventif.] 1. Going before; preceding. [Obs.]
Preventive Pre*vent"ive, n. That which prevents, hinders, or obstructs; that which intercepts access; in medicine, something to prevent disease; a prophylactic.

preventively.c: Preventively Pre*vent"ive*ly, adv. In a preventive manner.

prevertebral.c: Prevertebral Pre*ver"te*bral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated immediately in front, or on the ventral side, of the vertebral column; prespinal.

previous.c: Previous Pre"vi*ous (?), a. [L. praevius going before, leading the way; prae before + via the way. See Voyage.] Going before in time; being or happening before something else; antecedent; prior; as, previous arrangements; a previous illness.

previously.c: Previously Pre"vi*ous*ly, adv. Beforehand; antecedently; as, a plan previously formed.

previousness.c: Previousness Pre"vi*ous*ness, n. The quality or state of being previous; priority or antecedence in time.

previse.c: Previse Pre*vise" (?), v. t. [L. praevisus, p. p. of praevidere to foresee; prae before + videre to see. See Vision.] 1. To foresee. [R.]

prevision.c: Prevision Pre*vi"sion (?), n. [Cf. F. prévision.] Foresight; foreknowledge; prescience. H. Spencer.

prevoyant.c: Prevoyant Pre*voy"ant (?), a. [F. prévoyant.] Foreseeing; prescient. [R.] Mrs. Oliphant.

prewarn.c: Prewarn Pre*warn" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Prewarned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prewarning.] To warn beforehand; to forewarn. [R.]

prey.c: Prey Prey (?), n. [OF. preie, F. proie, L. praeda, probably for praeheda. See Prehensile, and cf. Depredate, Predatory.] Anything, as goods, etc., taken or got by violence; anything taken by force from an enemy in war; spoil; booty; plunder.

Prey Prey (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Preyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Preying.] [OF. preier, preer, L. praedari, fr. praeda. See Prey, n.] To take booty; to gather spoil; to ravage; to take food by violence.

preyer.c: Preyer Prey"er (?), n. One who, or that which, preys; a plunderer; a waster; a devourer. Hooker.

preyful.c: Preyful Prey"ful (?), a. 1. Disposed to take prey. [Obs.]

prezygapophysis.c: Prezygapophysis ‖Pre*zyg`a*poph"y*sis (?), n.; pl. Prezygapophyses (#). [NL. See Pre-, and Zygapophysis.] (Anat.) An anterior zygapophysis.

prial.c: Prial Pri"al (?), n. A corruption of pair royal. See under Pair, n.
