prian.c: Prian Pri"an (?), n. [Cornish, clayey ground, from pri clay.] (Mining) A fine, white, somewhat friable clay; also, the ore contained in a mixture of clay and pebbles. [Written also pryan.]

priapean.c: Priapean Pri`a*pe"an (?), n. [Cf. L. Priapeius pertaining to Priapus.] (Lat. Pros.) A species of hexameter verse so constructed as to be divisible into two portions of three feet each, having generally a trochee in the first and the fourth foot, and an amphimacer in the third; -- applied also to a regular hexameter verse when so constructed as to be divisible into two portions of three feet each. Andrews.

priapism.c: Priapism Pri"a*pism, n. [L. priapismus, Gr.?, from Priapus the god of procreation, the penis, Gr.?: cf. F. priapisme.] (Med.) More or less permanent erection and rigidity of the penis, with or without sexual desire.

priapulacea.c: Priapulacea ‖Pri*ap`u*la"ce*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Priapism.] (Zool.) A suborder of Gephyræa, having a cylindrical body with a terminal anal opening, and usually with one or two caudal gills.

price.c: Price Price (?), n. [OE. pris, OF. pris, F. prix, L. pretium; cf. Gr.? I sell? to buy, Skr. pa? to buy, OI. renim I sell. Cf. Appreciate, Depreciate, Interpret, Praise, n. & v., Precious, Prize.] 1. The sum or amount of money at which a thing is valued, or the value which a seller sets on his goods in market; that for which something is bought or sold, or offered for sale; equivalent in money or other means of exchange; current value or rate paid or demanded in market or in barter; cost. “Buy wine and milk without money and without price.” Isa. lv. 1.
Price Price, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Priced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pricing.] 1. To pay the price of. [Obs.]

priced.c: Priced Priced (?), a. Rated in price; valued; as, high-priced goods; low-priced labor.

priceite.c: Priceite Price"ite (?), n. [From Thomas Price of San Francisco.] (Min.) A hydrous borate of lime, from Oregon.

priceless.c: Priceless Price"less, a. 1. Too valuable to admit of being appraised; of inestimable worth; invaluable.

prick.c: Prick Prick (?), n. [AS. prica, pricca, pricu; akin to LG. prick, pricke, D. prik, Dan. prik, prikke, Sw. prick. Cf. Prick, v.] 1. That which pricks, penetrates, or punctures; a sharp and slender thing; a pointed instrument; a goad; a spur, etc.; a point; a skewer.

Prick Prick (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Pricked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Pricking.] [AS. prician; akin to LG. pricken, D. prikken, Dan. prikke, Sw. pricka. See Prick, n., and cf. Prink, Prig.] 1. To pierce slightly with a sharp-pointed instrument or substance; to make a puncture in, or to make by puncturing; to drive a fine point into; as, to prick one with a pin, needle, etc.; to prick a card; to prick holes in paper.
Prick Prick, v. i. 1. To be punctured; to suffer or feel a sharp pain, as by puncture; as, a sore finger pricks.

prickeared.c: Prick-eared Prick"-eared` (?), a. (Zool.) Having erect, pointed ears; -- said of certain dogs.

pricker.c: Pricker Prick"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, pricks; a pointed instrument; a sharp point; a prickle.

pricket.c: Pricket Prick"et (?), n. [Perhaps so called from the state of his horns. See Prick, and cf. Brocket.] (Zool.) A buck in his second year. See Note under 3d Buck. Shak.

pricking.c: Pricking Prick"ing, n. 1. The act of piercing or puncturing with a sharp point. “There is that speaketh like the prickings of a sword.” Prov. xii. 18 [1583].

prickingup.c: Pricking-up Prick"ing-up (?), n. (Arch.) The first coating of plaster in work of three coats upon laths. Its surface is scratched once to form a better key for the next coat. In the United States called scratch coat. Brande & C.

prickle.c: Prickle Pric"kle (?), n. [AS. pricele, pricle; akin to LG. prickel, D. prikkel. See Prick, n.] 1. A little prick; a small, sharp point; a fine, sharp process or projection, as from the skin of an animal, the bark of a plant, etc.; a spine. Bacon.
Prickle Pric"kle, v. t. To prick slightly, as with prickles, or fine, sharp points.

pricklefish.c: Pricklefish Prickleback { Pric"kle*back` (?), Pric"kle*fish` (?), } n. (Zool.) The stickleback.

prickliness.c: Prickliness Prick"li*ness (?), n. [From Prickly.] The quality of being prickly, or of having many prickles.

pricklouse.c: Pricklouse Prick"louse` (?), n. A tailor; -- so called in contempt. [Old slang] L'Estrange.

prickly.c: Prickly Prick"ly, a. Full of sharp points or prickles; armed or covered with prickles; as, a prickly shrub.

Prickly ash Prickly ash (Bot.), 1. A prickly shrub (Xanthoxylum Americanum) with yellowish flowers appearing with the leaves; also called toothache tree. All parts of the plant are pungent and aromatic. The southern species is Xanthoxylum Carolinianum. Gray.

prickmadam.c: Prickmadam Prick"mad`am (?), n. [F. trique-madame. Cf. Tripmadam.] (Bot.) A name given to several species of stonecrop, used as ingredients of vermifuge medicines. See Stonecrop.

prickpunch.c: Prickpunch Prick"punch` (?), n. A pointed steel punch, to prick a mark on metal.

pricksong.c: Pricksong Prick"song` (?; 115), n. [See Prick, v. t., 4.] Music written, or noted, with dots or points; -- so called from the points or dots with which it is noted down. [Obs.]

prickwood.c: Prickwood Prick"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) A shrub (Euonymus Europæus); -- so named from the use of its wood for goads, skewers, and shoe pegs. Called also spindle tree.

pricky.c: Pricky Prick"y (?), a. Stiff and sharp; prickly. Holland.

pride.c: Pride Pride (?), n. [Cf. AS. lamprede, LL. lampreda, E. lamprey.] (Zool.) A small European lamprey (Petromyzon branchialis); -- called also prid, and sandpiper.

Pride Pride, n. [AS. prȳte; akin to Icel. prȳði honor, ornament, pr??a to adorn, Dan. pryde, Sw. pryda; cf. W. prydus comely. See Proud.] 1. The quality or state of being proud; inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority in talents, beauty, wealth, rank, etc., which manifests itself in lofty airs, distance, reserve, and often in contempt of others.
Pride Pride, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prided; p. pr. & vb. n. Priding.] To indulge in pride, or self-esteem; to rate highly; to plume; -- used reflexively. Bp. Hall.
Pride Pride, v. i. To be proud; to glory. [R.]

prideful.c: Prideful Pride"ful (?), a. Full of pride; haughty. Tennyson.

pridian.c: Pridian Prid"i*an (?), a. [L. pridianus.] Of or pertaining to the day before, or yesterday. [R.] Thackeray.

prie.c: Prie Prie (?), n. (Bot.) The plant privet. [Obs.] Tusser.
Prie Prie, v. i. To pry. [Obs.] Chaucer.

pried.c: Pried Pried (?), imp. & p. p. of Pry.

priedieu.c: Priedieu Prie`dieu" (?), n. [F., literally, pray God.] A kneeling desk for prayers.

prier.c: Prier Pri"er (?), n. [From Pry.] One who pries; one who inquires narrowly and searches, or is inquisitive.

priest.c: Priest Priest (?), n. [OE. prest, preost, AS. preóst, fr. L. presbyter, Gr.? elder, older, n., an elder, compar. of? an old man, the first syllable of which is probably akin to L. pristinus. Cf. Pristine, Presbyter.]
Priest Priest (?), v. t. To ordain as priest.

priestcap.c: Priestcap Priest"cap` (?), n. (Fort.) A form of redan, so named from its shape; -- called also swallowtail.

priestcraft.c: Priestcraft Priest"craft` (?), n. Priestly policy; the policy of a priesthood; esp., in an ill sense, fraud or imposition in religious concerns; management by priests to gain wealth and power by working upon the religious motives or credulity of others.

priestery.c: Priestery Priest"er*y (?), n. Priests, collectively; the priesthood; -- so called in contempt. [R.] Milton.

priestess.c: Priestess Priest"ess, n. A woman who officiated in sacred rites among pagans. Abp. Potter.

priesthood.c: Priesthood Priest"hood (?), n. 1. The office or character of a priest; the priestly function. Bk. of Com. Prayer.

priesting.c: Priesting Priest"ing, n. The office of a priest. [Obs.] Milton.

priestism.c: Priestism Priest"ism (?), n. The influence, doctrines, principles, etc., of priests or the priesthood. [R.]

priestless.c: Priestless Priest"less, a. Without a priest. Pope.

priestliness.c: Priestliness Priest"li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being priestly. R. Browning.

priestly.c: Priestly Priest"ly, a. Of or pertaining to a priest or the priesthood; sacerdotal; befitting or becoming a priest; as, the priestly office; a priestly farewell. Shak.

priestridden.c: Priest-ridden Priest"-rid`den (?), a. Controlled or oppressed by priests; as, a priest-ridden people. Swift.

prieve.c: Prieve Prieve (?), v. t. To prove. [Obs. or Scot.]

prig.c: Prig Prig (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Prigged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prigging (?).] [A modification of prick.] To haggle about the price of a commodity; to bargain hard. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Prig Prig, n. 1. A pert, conceited, pragmatical fellow.

priggish.c: Priggish Prig"gish (?), a. Like a prig; conceited; pragmatical. -- Prig"gish*ly, adv. -- Prig"gish-ness, n.

priggism.c: Priggism Prig"gism (?), n. 1. The quality or state of being priggish; the manners of a prig. Ed. Rev.

prighte.c: Prighte Prigh"te (?), obs. imp. of Prick. Chaucer.

prill.c: Prill Prill, v. i. To flow. [Obs.] Stow.
Prill Prill, n. [Etymol. uncertain.] 1. (Mining) (a) A nugget of virgin metal. (b) Ore selected for excellence.

prillion.c: Prillion Pril"lion (?), n. Tin extracted from the slag.

prim.c: Prim Prim, a. [OF. prim, prin, prime, first, principal. sharp, thin, piercing, fr. L. primus first. See Prime, a.] Formal; precise; affectedly neat or nice; as, prim regularity; a prim person. Swift.
Prim Prim, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Primmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Primming.] To deck with great nicety; to arrange with affected preciseness; to prink.
Prim Prim, v. i. To dress or act smartly. [R.]

primacy.c: Primacy Pri"ma*cy (?), n. [LL. primatia, fr. L. primas, -atis, one of the first or principal, chief, fr. primus first: cf. F. primatie. See Prime, a.] 1. The state or condition of being prime or first, as in time, place, rank, etc., hence, excellency; supremacy. [R.] De Quincey.

prima.c: Prima donna ‖Pri"ma don"na (?); pl. E. Prima donnas (#), It. Prime (#) Donne (#). [It., fr. primo, prima, the first + donna lady, mistress. See Prime, a., and Donna.] The first or chief female singer in an opera.
Prima facie ‖Pri"ma fa"ci*e (?). [L., from abl. of primus first + abl. of facies appearance.] At first view; on the first appearance.

primage.c: Primage Pri"mage (?; 48), n. [F.] (Com.) A charge in addition to the freight; originally, a gratuity to the captain for his particular care of the goods (sometimes called hat money), but now belonging to the owners or freighters of the vessel, unless by special agreement the whole or part is assigned to the captain. Homans.

primal.c: Primal Pri"mal (?), a. [LL. primalis, fr. L. primus the first. See Prime, a.] First; primary; original; chief.

primality.c: Primality Pri*mal"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being primal. [Obs.]

primarily.c: Primarily Pri"ma*ri*ly (?), adv. In a primary manner; in the first place; in the first place; in the first intention; originally.

primariness.c: Primariness Pri"ma*ri*ness, n. The quality or state of being primary, or first in time, in act, or in intention. Norris.

primary.c: Primary Pri"ma*ry (?), a. [L. primarius, fr. primus first: cf. F. primaire. See Prime, a., and cf. Premier, Primero.] 1. First in order of time or development or in intention; primitive; fundamental; original.
Primary Pri"ma*ry, n.; pl. Primaries (?). 1. That which stands first in order, rank, or importance; a chief matter.

primate.c: Primate Pri"mate (?), n. [OE. primat, F. primat, L. primas, -atis one of the first, chief, fr. primus the first. See Prime, a.] 1. The chief ecclesiastic in a national church; one who presides over other bishops in a province; an archbishop.

primates.c: Primates ‖Pri*ma"tes (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) The highest order of mammals. It includes man, together with the apes and monkeys. Cf. Pitheci.

primateship.c: Primateship Pri"mate*ship (?), n. The office, dignity, or position of a primate; primacy.

primatial.c: Primatial Pri*ma"tial (?), a. [Cf. F. primatial.] Primatical. [R.] D'Anville (Trans.).

primatical.c: Primatical Pri*mat"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a primate. Barrow.

prime.c: Prime Prime (?), a. [F., fr. L. primus first, a superl. corresponding to the compar. prior former. See Prior, a., Foremost, Former, and cf. Prim, a., Primary, Prince.] 1. First in order of time; original; primeval; primitive; primary. “Prime forests.” Tennyson.
Prime Prime (?), n. 1. The first part; the earliest stage; the beginning or opening, as of the day, the year, etc.; hence, the dawn; the spring. Chaucer.
Prime Prime, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Primed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Priming.] [From Prime, a.] 1. To apply priming to, as a musket or a cannon; to apply a primer to, as a metallic cartridge.
Prime Prime, v. i. 1. To be renewed, or as at first. [Obs.]

primely.c: Primely Prime"ly, adv. 1. At first; primarily. [Obs.] South.

primeness.c: Primeness Prime"ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being first.

primer.c: Primer Prim"er (?), n. One who, or that which, primes; specifically, an instrument or device for priming; esp., a cap, tube, or water containing percussion powder or other compound for igniting a charge of gunpowder.
Primer Prim"er, a. [OF. primer, primier, premier, F. premier. See Premier.] First; original; primary. [Obs.] “The primer English kings.” Drayton.

Primer Prim"er (?), n. [Originally, the book read at prime, the first canonical hour. LL. primae liber. See Prime, n., 4.] 1. Originally, a small prayer book for church service, containing the little office of the Virgin Mary; also, a work of elementary religious instruction.

primero.c: Primero Pri*me"ro (?), n. [Sp. primera, fr. primero first, from L. primarius. See Premier.] A game at cards, now unknown. Shak.

primerole.c: Primerole Prim"er*ole (?), n. (Bot.) See Primrose. [Obs.] “She was a primerole.” Chaucer.

primeval.c: Primeval Pri*me"val (?), a. [L. primaevus; primus first + aevum age. See Prime, a., and Age.] Belonging to the first ages; pristine; original; primitive; primary; as, the primeval innocence of man. “This is the forest primeval.” Longfellow.

primevally.c: Primevally Pri*me"val*ly, adv. In a primeval manner; in or from the earliest times; originally. Darwin.

primigenial.c: Primigenial Pri`mi*ge"ni*al (?), a. First born, or first of all; original; primary. See Primogenial.

primigenous.c: Primigenous Primigenious { Pri`mi*ge"ni*ous (?), Pri*mig"e*nous (?), } a. [L. primigenus, primigenius. See Primogeniture.] First formed or generated; original; primigenial. Bp. Hall.

primine.c: Primine Pri"mine (?), n. [L. primus first: cf. F. primine.] (Bot.) The outermost of the two integuments of an ovule.

priming.c: Priming Prim"ing (?), n. 1. The powder or other combustible used to communicate fire to a charge of gunpowder, as in a firearm.

primipara.c: Primipara ‖Pri*mip"a*ra (?), n. [L., fr. primus first + parere to bring forth.] (Med.) A woman who bears a child for the first time.

primiparous.c: Primiparous Pri*mip"a*rous (?), a. [See Primipara.] Belonging to a first birth; bearing young for the first time.

primipilar.c: Primipilar Pri*mip"i*lar (?), a. [L. primipilaris, fr. primipilus the centurion of the first cohort of a Roman legion, fr. primus pilus the division made up of the triarii in the Roman army.] Of or pertaining to the captain of the vanguard of a Roman army. Barrow.

primitia.c: Primitia ‖Pri*mi"ti*a (?), n.; pl. Primitiæ (#) (Primitias (#), obs.). [L. primitiae, pl., fr. primus first. Cf. Premices.] (Eng. Law) The first fruit; the first year's whole profit of an ecclesiastical preferment.

primitial.c: Primitial Pri*mi"tial (?), a. Being of the first production; primitive; original. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

primitive.c: Primitive Prim"i*tive (?), a. [L. primitivus, fr. primus the first: cf. F. primitif. See Prime, a.] 1. Of or pertaining to the beginning or origin, or to early times; original; primordial; primeval; first; as, primitive innocence; the primitive church. “Our primitive great sire.” Milton.
Primitive Prim"i*tive, n. An original or primary word; a word not derived from another; -- opposed to derivative.

primitiveness.c: Primitiveness Prim"i*tive*ness, n. The quality or state of being primitive; conformity to primitive style or practice.

primity.c: Primity Prim"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being first; primitiveness. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

primly.c: Primly Prim"ly, adv. In a prim or precise manner.

primness.c: Primness Prim"ness, n. The quality or state of being prim; affected formality or niceness; preciseness; stiffness.

primogenial.c: Primogenial Pri`mo*ge"ni*al (?), a. [See Primigenial.] First born, made, or generated; original; primary; elemental; as, primogenial light. Glanvill.

primogenitive.c: Primogenitive Pri`mo*gen"i*tive (?), a. [See Primogeniture.] Of or pertaining to primogeniture. [R.]

primogenitor.c: Primogenitor Pri`mo*gen"i*tor (?), n. [LL., fr. L. primus first + genitor a begetter.] The first ancestor; a forefather.

primogeniture.c: Primogeniture Pri`mo*gen"i*ture (?; 135), n. [LL., fr. L. primus first + genitura a begetting, birth, generation, fr. genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. primogéniture, L. primogenitus firstborn. See Prime, a., and Genus, Kin.] 1. The state of being the firstborn of the same parents; seniority by birth among children of the same family.

primogenitureship.c: Primogenitureship Pri`mo*gen"i*ture*ship (?), n. The state or privileges of the firstborn. Burke.

primordial.c: Primordial Pri*mor"di*al (?), a. [L. primordialis, from primordium the first beginning; primus first + ordiri to begin a web, to begin: cf. F. primordial.] 1. First in order; primary; original; of earliest origin; as, primordial condition. “The primordial facts of our intelligent nature.” Sir W. Hamilton.
Primordial Pri*mor"di*al, n. A first principle or element.

primordialism.c: Primordialism Pri*mor"di*al*ism (?), n. Devotion to, or persistence in, conditions of the primordial state. H. Spencer.

primordially.c: Primordially Pri*mor"di*al*ly, adv. At the beginning; under the first order of things; originally.

primordian.c: Primordian Pri*mor"di*an (?), n. [L. primordius first of all, fr. primordium.] (Bot.) A name given to several kinds of plums; as, red primordian, amber primordian, etc.

primp.c: Primp Primp (?), v. i. & t. [Cf. Prim, a.] To be formal or affected in dress or manners; -- often with up. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.

primrose.c: Primrose Prim"rose` (?), n. [OE. primerole, F. primerole, a derivative fr. LL. primula, from L. primus first. See Prime, a.] (Bot.) (a) An early flowering plant of the genus Primula (Primula vulgaris) closely allied to the cowslip. There are several varieties, as the white-, the red-, the yellow-flowered, etc. Formerly called also primerole, primerolles. (b) Any plant of the genus Primula.
Primrose Prim"rose`, a. Of or pertaining to the primrose; of the color of a primrose; -- hence, flowery; gay. “The primrose path of dalliance.” Shak.

Primrose League Prim"rose` League. (Eng. Politics) A league of both sexes among the Conservatives, founded in 1883. So called because primrose was (erroneously, it is said) taken to be the favorite flower of the Conservative statesman Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.

primula.c: Primula ‖Prim"u*la (?), n. [LL. See Primrose.] (Bot.) The genus of plants including the primrose (Primula vera).

primulaceous.c: Primulaceous Prim`u*la"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to an order of herbaceous plants (Primulaceæ), of which the primrose is the type, and the pimpernel, the cyclamen, and the water violet are other examples.

primum.c: Primum mobile ‖Pri"mum mob"i*le (?). [L., first cause of motion.] (Astron.) In the Ptolemaic system, the outermost of the revolving concentric spheres constituting the universe, the motion of which was supposed to carry with it all the inclosed spheres with their planets in a daily revolution from east to west. See Crystalline heavens, under Crystalline.

primus.c: Primus ‖Pri"mus (?), n. [L., the first.] One of the bishops of the Episcopal Church of Scotland, who presides at the meetings of the bishops, and has certain privileges but no metropolitan authority. Internat. Cyc.

primy.c: Primy Prim"y (?), a. [From Prime, a.] Being in its prime. [Obs.] “The youth of primy nature.” Shak.

prince.c: Prince Prince (?), n. [F., from L. princeps, -cipis, the first, chief; primus first + capere to take. See Prime, a., and Capacious.] 1. The one of highest rank; one holding the highest place and authority; a sovereign; a monarch; -- originally applied to either sex, but now rarely applied to a female. Wyclif (Rev. i. 5).
Prince Prince, v. i. To play the prince. [R.] Shak.

princedom.c: Princedom Prince"dom (?), n. The jurisdiction, sovereignty, rank, or estate of a prince.

princekin.c: Princekin Prince"kin (?), n. A petty prince; a princeling.

princeless.c: Princeless Prince"less, a. Without a prince. Fuller.

princeliness.c: Princeliness Prince"li*ness (?), n. The quality of being princely; the state, manner, or dignity of a prince.

princeling.c: Princeling Prince"ling (?), n. A petty prince; a young prince.

princely.c: Princely Prince"ly, a. 1. Of or relating to a prince; regal; royal; of highest rank or authority; as, princely birth, character, fortune, etc.
Princely Prince"ly (?), adv. In a princely manner.

princess.c: Princess Prin"cess (?), n. [F. princesse. See Prince, and cf. Princesse.] 1. A female prince; a woman having sovereign power, or the rank of a prince. Dryden.

princesse.c: Princesse Prin*cesse" (?), a. [F., a princess.] A term applied to a lady's long, close-fitting dress made with waist and skirt in one.

princewood.c: Princewood Prince"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) The wood of two small tropical American trees (Hamelia ventricosa, and Cordia gerascanthoides). It is brownish, veined with lighter color.

princified.c: Princified Prin"ci*fied (?), a. [Prince + L. -ficare (in comp.).] Imitative of a prince. [R. & Colloq.] Thackeray.

principal.c: Principal Prin"ci*pal (?), a. [F., from L. principalis. See Prince.] 1. Highest in rank, authority, character, importance, or degree; most considerable or important; chief; main; as, the principal officers of a Government; the principal men of a state; the principal productions of a country; the principal arguments in a case.

Principal Prin"ci*pal, n. 1. A leader, chief, or head; one who takes the lead; one who acts independently, or who has controlling authority or influence; as, the principal of a faction, a school, a firm, etc.; -- distinguished from a subordinate, abettor, auxiliary, or assistant.

principality.c: Principality Prin`ci*pal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Principalities (#). [L. principalitas preëminence, excellence: cf. F. principalité, principauté. See Principal.] 1. Sovereignty; supreme power; hence, superiority; predominance; high, or the highest, station. Sir P. Sidney.

principally.c: Principally Prin"ci*pal*ly (?), adv. In a principal manner; primarily; above all; chiefly; mainly.

principalness.c: Principalness Prin"ci*pal*ness, n. The quality of being principal.

principate.c: Principate Prin"ci*pate (?), n. [L. principatus: cf. F. principat.] Principality; supreme rule. [Obs.] Barrow.

principia.c: Principia ‖Prin*cip"i*a (?), n. pl. [L. principium. See Principle.] First principles; fundamental beginnings; elements; as. Newton's Principia.

principiant.c: Principiant Prin*cip"i*ant (?), a. [L. principians, p. pr. of principiare to begin, fr. principium. See Principle.] Relating to principles or beginnings. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

principiate.c: Principiate Prin*cip"i*ate (?), v. t. [See Principiant.] To begin; to initiate. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

principiation.c: Principiation Prin*cip`i*a"tion (?), n. Analysis into primary or elemental parts. [Archaic] Bacon.

principle.c: Principle Prin"ci*ple (?), n. [F. principe, L. principium beginning, foundation, fr. princeps, -cipis. See Prince.] 1. Beginning; commencement. [Obs.]

Principle Prin"ci*ple (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Principled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Principling (?).] To equip with principles; to establish, or fix, in certain principles; to impress with any tenet, or rule of conduct, good or ill.

princox.c: Princox Princock { Prin"cock (?), Prin"cox (?), } n. [Prim + cock.] A coxcomb; a pert boy. [Obs.]

prink.c: Prink Prink (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Prinked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prinking.] [Probably a nasalized form of prick. See Prick, v. t., and cf. Prig, Prank.] To dress or adjust one's self for show; to prank.
Prink Prink, v. t. To prank or dress up; to deck fantastically. “And prink their hair with daisies.” Cowper.

prinpriddle.c: Prinpriddle Prin"prid`dle (?), n. (Zool.) The long-tailed titmouse. [Prov. Eng.]

print.c: Print Print (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Printed; p. pr. & vb. n. Printing.] [Abbrev. fr. imprint. See Imprint, and Press to squeeze.] 1. To fix or impress, as a stamp, mark, character, idea, etc., into or upon something.
Print Print, v. i. 1. To use or practice the art of typography; to take impressions of letters, figures, or electrotypes, engraved plates, or the like.

Print Print, n. [See Print, v., Imprint, n.] 1. A mark made by impression; a line, character, figure, or indentation, made by the pressure of one thing on another; as, the print of teeth or nails in flesh; the print of the foot in sand or snow.

printable.c: Printa-ble Print"a-ble (?), a. Worthy to be published. [R.]

printer.c: Printer Print"er (?), n. One who prints; especially, one who prints books, newspapers, engravings, etc., a compositor; a typesetter; a pressman.

printery.c: Printery Print"er*y (?), n. A place where cloth is printed; print works; also, a printing office. [R.]

printing.c: Printing Print"ing, n. The act, art, or practice of impressing letters, characters, or figures on paper, cloth, or other material; the business of a printer, including typesetting and presswork, with their adjuncts; typography; also, the act of producing photographic prints.

Printing in Print"ing in. (Photog.) A process by which cloud effects or other features not in the original negative are introduced into a photograph. Portions, such as the sky, are covered while printing and the blank space thus reserved is filled in by printing from another negative.
Printing out Printing out. (Photog.) A method of printing, in which the image is fully brought out by the direct actinic action of light without subsequent development by means of chemicals.

printless.c: Printless Print"less, a. Making no imprint. Milton.
Printless Print"less, a. Making no imprint. Milton.

printshop.c: Printshop Print"shop`, n. A shop where prints are sold.

prior.c: Prior Pri"or (?), a. [L. prior former, previous, better, superior; compar. corresponding to primus first, and pro for. See Former, and cf. Prime, a., and Pre-, Pro-.] 1. Preceding in the order of time; former; antecedent; anterior; previous; as, a prior discovery; prior obligation; -- used elliptically in cases like the following: he lived alone [in the time] prior to his marriage.
Prior Pri"or, n. [OE. priour, OF. priour, prior, priur, F. prieur, from L. prior former, superior. See Prior, a.] 1. (Eccl.) The superior of a priory, and next below an abbot in dignity.

priorate.c: Priorate Pri"or*ate (?), n. [LL. prioratus: cf. F. priorat.] The dignity, office, or government, of a prior. T. Warton.

prioress.c: Prioress Pri"or*ess, n. [OF. prioresse.] A lady superior of a priory of nuns, and next in dignity to an abbess.

priority.c: Priority Pri*or"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. priorité. See Prior, a.] 1. The quality or state of being prior or antecedent in time, or of preceding something else; as, priority of application.

priorship.c: Priorship Pri"or*ship, n. The state or office of prior; priorate.

priory.c: Priory Pri"o*ry (?), n.; pl. Priories (#). [Cf. LL. prioria. See Prior, n.] A religious house presided over by a prior or prioress; -- sometimes an offshoot of, an subordinate to, an abbey, and called also cell, and obedience. See Cell, 2.

pris.c: Pris Pris (?), n. See Price, and 1st Prize. [Obs.]

prisage.c: Prisage Pris"age (?; 48), n. [OF. prisage a praising, valuing, taxing; cf. LL. prisagium prisage; or from F. prise a taking, capture, prize. See Prize.] (O. Eng. Law) (a) A right belonging to the crown of England, of taking two tuns of wine from every ship importing twenty tuns or more, -- one before and one behind the mast. By charter of Edward I. butlerage was substituted for this. Blackstone. (b) The share of merchandise taken as lawful prize at sea which belongs to the king or admiral.

priscillianist.c: Priscillianist Pris*cil"lian*ist (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of Priscillian, bishop of Avila in Spain, in the fourth century, who mixed various elements of Gnosticism and Manicheism with Christianity.

prise.c: Prise Prise, n. & v. See Prize, n., 5. Also Prize, v. t.

prism.c: Prism Prism (prĭz'm), n. [L. prisma, Gr. pri`sma, fr. pri`zein, pri`ein, to saw: cf. F. prisme.] 1. (Geom.) A solid whose bases or ends are any similar, equal, and parallel plane figures, and whose sides are parallelograms.

Prism glass Prism glass. Glass with one side smooth and the other side formed into sharp-edged ridges so as to reflect the light that passes through, used at windows to throw the light into the interior.

prismatical.c: Prismatical Prismatic { Pris*mat"ic (?), Pris*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. prismatique.] 1. Resembling, or pertaining to, a prism; as, a prismatic form or cleavage.

prismatically.c: Prismatically Pris*mat"ic*al*ly, adv. In the form or manner of a prism; by means of a prism.

prismatoidal.c: Prismatoidal Pris`ma*toid"al (?), a. [Gr.?,?, prism + -oid: F. prismatoïde.] Having a prismlike form. Ure.

prismoid.c: Prismoid Pris"moid (prĭz"moid), n. [Cf. F. prismtoïde.] A body that approaches to the form of a prism.

prismoidal.c: Prismoidal Pris*moid"al (?), a. Having the form of a prismoid; as, prismoidal solids.

prismy.c: Prismy Pris"my (?), a. Pertaining to a prism. [R.]

prison.c: Prison Pris"on (?; 277), n. [F., fr. L. prehensio, prensio, a seizing, arresting, fr. prehendre, prendere, to lay hold of, to seize. See Prehensile, and cf. Prize, n., Misprision.] 1. A place where persons are confined, or restrained of personal liberty; hence, a place or state o? confinement, restraint, or safe custody.
Prison Pris"on, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prisoned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prisoning.] 1. To imprison; to shut up in, or as in, a prison; to confine; to restrain from liberty.

prisoner.c: Prisoner Pris"on*er (?), n. [F. prisonnier.] 1. One who is confined in a prison. Piers Plowman.

pristinate.c: Pristinate Pris"tin*ate (?), a. Pristine; primitive. [Obs.] “Pristinate idolatry.” Holinshed.

pristine.c: Pristine Pris"tine (?), a. [L. pristinus, akin to prior: cf. F. pristin. See Prior, a.] Belonging to the earliest period or state; original; primitive; primeval; as, the pristine state of innocence; the pristine manners of a people; pristine vigor.

pritch.c: Pritch Pritch (?), n. [See Prick.] 1. A sharp-pointed instrument; also, an eelspear. [Prov. Eng.]

pritchel.c: Pritchel Pritch"el (?), n. A tool employed by blacksmiths for punching or enlarging the nail holes in a horseshoe.

prithee.c: Prithee Prith"ee (?), interj. A corruption of pray thee; as, I prithee; generally used without I. Shak.

prittleprattle.c: Prittle-prattle Prit"tle-prat`tle (?), n. [See Prattle.] Empty talk; trifling loquacity; prattle; -- used in contempt or ridicule. [Colloq.] Abp. Bramhall.

privacy.c: Privacy Pri"va*cy (?), n.; pl. Privacies (#). [See Private.] 1. The state of being in retirement from the company or observation of others; seclusion.

privado.c: Privado Pri*va"do (?), n. [Sp., fr. L. privatus. See Private.] A private friend; a confidential friend; a confidant. [Obs.] Fuller.

privatdocent.c: Privatdocent ‖Pri*vat"do*cent` (?), n.; G. pl. -docenten (#). [Also Privatdozent.] [G.; privat private + docent teacher. See Docent.] In the universities of Germany and some other European countries, a licensed teacher or lecturer having no share in the university government and dependent upon fees for remuneration.

private.c: Private Pri"vate (?; 48), a. [L. privatus apart from the state, peculiar to an individual, private, properly p. p. of privare to bereave, deprive, originally, to separate, fr. privus single, private, perhaps originally, put forward (hence, alone, single) and akin to prae before. See Prior, a., and cf. Deprive, Privy, a.] 1. Belonging to, or concerning, an individual person, company, or interest; peculiar to one's self; unconnected with others; personal; one's own; not public; not general; separate; as, a man's private opinion; private property; a private purse; private expenses or interests; a private secretary.
Private Pri"vate (prī"vat), n. 1. A secret message; a personal unofficial communication. [Obs.] Shak.

privateer.c: Privateer Pri`va*teer" (prī`vȧ*tēr"), n. [From Private.] 1. An armed private vessel which bears the commission of the sovereign power to cruise against the enemy. See Letters of marque, under Marque.
Privateer Pri`va*teer", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Privateered (prī`vȧ*tērd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Privateering.] To cruise in a privateer.

privateering.c: Privateering Pri`va*teer"ing, n. Cruising in a privateer.

privateersman.c: Privateersman Pri`va*teers"man (prī`vȧ*tērz"main), n.; pl. Privateersmen (prī`vȧ*tērz"mein). An officer or seaman of a privateer.

privation.c: Privation Pri*va"tion (pri*vā"shŭn), n. [L. privatio: cf. F. privation. See Private.] 1. The act of depriving, or taking away; hence, the depriving of rank or office; degradation in rank; deprivation. Bacon.

privative.c: Privative Priv"a*tive (?), a. [L. privativus: cf. F. privatif. See Private.] 1. Causing privation; depriving.

privatively.c: Privatively Priv"a*tive*ly, adv. In a privative manner; by the absence of something; negatively. [R.] Hammond.

privativeness.c: Privativeness Priv"a*tive*ness, n. The state of being privative.

privet.c: Privet Priv"et (?), n. [Cf. Scot. privie, Prov. E. prim-print, primwort. Prob. for primet, and perh. named from being cut and trimmed. See, Prim, a., and cf. Prime to prune, Prim, n., Prie, n.] (Bot.) An ornamental European shrub (Ligustrum vulgare), much used in hedges; -- called also prim.

privilege.c: Privilege Priv"i*lege (?), n. [F. privilège, L. privilegium an ordinance or law against or in favor of an individual; privus private + lex, legis, law. See Private, and Legal.]
Privilege Priv"i*lege (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Privileged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Privileging.] [Cf. F. privilégier.]

privileged.c: Privileged Priv"i*leged (?), a. Invested with a privilege; enjoying a peculiar right, advantage, or immunity.

privily.c: Privily Priv"i*ly, adv. In a privy manner; privately; secretly. Chaucer. 2 Pet. ii. 1.

privity.c: Privity Priv"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Privities (-tĭz). [From Privy, a.: cf. F. privauté extreme familiarity.]

privy.c: Privy Priv"y (?), a. [F. privé, fr. L. privatus. See Private.]

Privy Priv"y, n.; pl. Privies (?). 1. (Law) A partaker; a person having an interest in any action or thing; one who has an interest in an estate created by another; a person having an interest derived from a contract or conveyance to which he is not himself a party. The term, in its proper sense, is distinguished from party. Burrill. Wharton.

prize.c: Prize Prize (prīz), n. [F. prise a seizing, hold, grasp, fr. pris, p. p. of prendre to take, L. prendere, prehendere; in some senses, as 2 (b), either from, or influenced by, F. prix price. See Prison, Prehensile, and cf. Pry, and also Price.]
Prize Prize (?), v. t. To move with a lever; to force up or open; to pry. [Written also prise.]

Prize Prize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prizing.] [F. priser, OF. prisier, preisier, fr. L. pretiare, fr. pretium worth, value, price. See Price, and cf. Praise.] [Formerly written also prise. ]
Prize Prize, n. [F. prix price. See 3d Prize. ] Estimation; valuation. [Obs.] Shak.

prizeman.c: Prizeman Prize"man (?), n.; pl. Prizemen (?). The winner of a prize.

prizer.c: Prizer Priz"er (?), n. [See 3d Prize.] One who estimates or sets the value of a thing; an appraiser. Shak.
Prizer Priz"er, n. [See 1st Prize.] One who contends for a prize; a prize fighter; a challenger. [Obs.] Shak.

prizing.c: Prizing Priz"ing, n. [See 2d Prize.] The application of a lever to move any weighty body, as a cask, anchor, cannon, car, etc. See Prize, n., 5.

pro.c: Pro- Pro- (?). [L. pro, or Gr.?. See Pro.] A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.
Pro ‖Pro, prep. [L.; akin to prae before, Gr.?, and E. for. See For, prep., and cf. Prior, a.] A Latin preposition signifying for, before, forth.
Pro Pro, adv. For, on, or in behalf of, the affirmative side; -- in contrast with con.
Pro rata ‖Pro` ra"ta (?). [L.] In proportion; proportionately; according to the share, interest, or liability of each.

Pro thyalosoma ‖Pro* thy`a*lo*so"ma (?), n.; pl. Prothyalosomata (#). [NL., fr. Gr. prw^tos first + "y`alos glass +?,?, body.] (Biol.) The investing portion, or spherical envelope, surrounding the eccentric germinal spot of the germinal vesicle.

proa.c: Proa Pro"a (?), n. [Malay prā?, prāh?.] (Naut.) A sailing canoe of the Ladrone Islands and Malay Archipelago, having its lee side flat and its weather side like that of an ordinary boat. The ends are alike. The canoe is long and narrow, and is kept from overturning by a cigar-shaped log attached to a frame extending several feet to windward. It has been called the flying proa, and is the swiftest sailing craft known.

proatlas.c: Proatlas Pro*at"las (?), n. [Pref. pro- + atlas.] (Anat.) A vertebral rudiment in front of the atlas in some reptiles.

probabiliorism.c: Probabiliorism Prob`a*bil"i*o*rism (?), n. The doctrine of the probabiliorists.

probabiliorist.c: Probabiliorist Prob`a*bil"i*o*rist (?), n. [From L. probabilior, compar. of probabilis probable.] (Casuistry) One who holds, in opposition to the probabilists, that a man is bound to do that which is most probably right.

probabilism.c: Probabilism Prob"a*bil*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. probabilisme.] The doctrine of the probabilists.

probability.c: Probability Prob`a*bil"i*ty, n.; pl. Probabilities (#). [L. probabilitas: cf. F. probabilité.]

probable.c: Probable Prob"a*ble (?), a. [L. probabilis, fr. probare to try, approve, prove: cf. F. probable. See Prove, and cf. Provable.]

probably.c: Probably Prob"a*bly (?), adv. In a probable manner; in likelihood.

probacy.c: Probacy Pro"ba*cy (?), n. [See Probate.] Proof; trial. [Obs.] Chaucer.

probality.c: Probality Pro*bal"i*ty (?), n. Probability. [Obs.] “With as great probality.” Holland.

probang.c: Probang Pro"bang (?), n. [See Probe.] A slender elastic rod, as of whalebone, with a sponge on the end, for removing obstructions from the esophagus, etc.

probate.c: Probate Pro"bate (?), n. [From L. probatus, p. p. of probare to prove. See Prove.]
Probate Pro"bate, a. Of or belonging to a probate, or court of probate; as, a probate record.
Probate Pro"bate (?), v. t. To obtain the official approval of, as of an instrument purporting to be the last will and testament; as, the executor has probated the will.

probation.c: Probation Pro*ba"tion (?), n. [L. probatio, fr. probare to try, examine, prove: cf. F. probation. See Prove.]

probationary.c: Probationary Pro*ba"tion*a*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to probation; serving for trial.

probationership.c: Probationership Pro*ba"tion*er*ship, n. The state of being a probationer; novitiate. Locke.

probationship.c: Probationship Pro*ba"tion*ship, n. A state of probation.

probative.c: Probative Pro"ba*tive (?), a. [L. probativus: cf. F. probatif.] Serving for trial or proof; probationary; as, probative judgments; probative evidence. South.

probator.c: Probator Pro*ba"tor (?), n. [L.] 1. An examiner; an approver. Maydman.

probatory.c: Probatory Pro"ba*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. probatoire.] 1. Serving for trial; probationary. Abp. Bramhall.

probe.c: Probe Probe (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Probed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Probing.] [L. probare to try, examine. See Prove.]

Probe Probe, n. (Surg.) An instrument for examining the depth or other circumstances of a wound, ulcer, or cavity, or the direction of a sinus, of for exploring for bullets, for stones in the bladder, etc. Parr.

probepointed.c: Probe-pointed Probe"-point`ed (?), a. (Surg.) Having a blunt or button-shaped extremity; -- said of cutting instruments.

probity.c: Probity Prob"i*ty (?), n. [F. probité, fr. L. probitas, fr. probus good, proper, honest. Cf. Prove.] Tried virtue or integrity; approved moral excellence; honesty; rectitude; uprightness. “Probity of mind.” Pope.

problem.c: Problem Prob"lem (?), n. [F. problème, L. problema, fr. Gr.? anything thrown forward, a question proposed for solution, fr.? to throw or lay before;? before, forward +? to throw. Cf. Parable. ]

problematical.c: Problematical Problematic { Prob`lem*at"ic (?), Prob`lem*at"ic*al (?), } a. [L. problematicus, Gr.?: cf. F. problématique.] 1. Having the nature of a problem; not shown in fact; questionable; uncertain; unsettled; doubtful; as, his theory is problematic because it fails to explain several facts. -- Prob`lem*at"ic*al*ly, adv.

problematist.c: Problematist Prob"lem*a*tist (?), n. One who proposes problems. [R.] Evelyn.

problematize.c: Problematize Prob"lem*a*tize (?), v. t. To propose problems. [R.] “Hear him problematize.” B. Jonson.

proboscidate.c: Proboscidate Pro*bos"ci*date (?), a. [See Proboscis.] (Zool.) Having a proboscis; proboscidial.

proboscidea.c: Proboscidea ‖Pro`bos*cid"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Proboscis.] (Zool.) An order of large mammals including the elephants and mastodons.

proboscidian.c: Proboscidian Pro`bos*cid"i*an (?), a. (Zool.) Pertaining to the Proboscidea. -- n. One of the Proboscidea.

proboscidiform.c: Proboscidiform Pro`bos*cid"i*form (?), a. Having the form or uses of a proboscis; as, a proboscidiform mouth.

proboscis.c: Proboscis Pro*bos"cis (?), n.; pl. Proboscides (#). [L. fr. Gr.?;? before +? to feed, graze.] 1. (Zool.) A hollow organ or tube attached to the head, or connected with the mouth, of various animals, and generally used in taking food or drink; a snout; a trunk.

procacious.c: Procacious Pro*ca"cious (?), a. [L. procax, -acis, fr. procare to ask, demand.] Pert; petulant; forward; saucy. [R.] Barrow.

procacity.c: Procacity Pro*cac"i*ty (?), n. [L. procacitas.] Forwardness; pertness; petulance. [R.] Burton.

procambium.c: Procambium ‖Pro*cam"bi*um (?), n. [NL. See Pro-, and Cambium.] (Bot.) The young tissue of a fibrovascular bundle before its component cells have begun to be differentiated. Sachs.

procatarctic.c: Procatarctic Pro`cat*arc"tic (?), a. [Gr.? beginning beforehand. fr.? to begin first;? before +? to begin;? intens. +? to begin: cf. F. procatarctique. ] (Med.) Beginning; predisposing; exciting; initial. [Obs.]

procatarxis.c: Procatarxis ‖Pro`cat*arx"is (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? first beginning.] (Med.) The kindling of a disease into action; also, the procatarctic cause. Quincy.

procedendo.c: Procedendo ‖Pro`ce*den"do (?), n. [Abl. of the gerundive of L. procedere. see Proceed.] (Law) (a) A writ by which a cause which has been removed on insufficient grounds from an inferior to a superior court by certiorari, or otherwise, is sent down again to the same court, to be proceeded in there. (b) In English practice, a writ issuing out of chancery in cases where the judges of subordinate courts delay giving judgment, commanding them to proceed to judgment. (c) A writ by which the commission of the justice of the peace is revived, after having been suspended. Tomlins. Burrill.

procedure.c: Procedure Pro*ce"dure (?), n. [F. procédure. See Proceed.] 1. The act or manner of proceeding or moving forward; progress; process; operation; conduct. “The true procedure of conscience.” South.

proceed.c: Proceed Pro*ceed" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Proceeded; p. pr. & vb. n. Proceeding.] [F. procéder. fr. L. procedere, processum, to go before, to proceed; pro forward + cedere to move. See Cede.] 1. To move, pass, or go forward or onward; to advance; to continue or renew motion begun; as, to proceed on a journey.

proceeding.c: Proceeding Pro*ceed"ing, n. 1. The act of one who proceeds, or who prosecutes a design or transaction; progress or movement from one thing to another; a measure or step taken in a course of business; a transaction; as, an illegal proceeding; a cautious or a violent proceeding.

proceeds.c: Proceeds Pro"ceeds (?), n. pl. That which comes forth or results; effect; yield; issue; product; sum accruing from a sale, etc.

proceleusmatic.c: Proceleusmatic Proc`e*leus*mat"ic (?), a. [L. proceleusmaticus, Gr.?, fr.? to rouse to action beforehand;? +? to incite; cf. F. procéleusmatique.]
Proceleusmatic Proc`e*leus*mat"ic (?), n. (Pros.) A foot consisting of four short syllables.

procellarian.c: Procellarian Pro`cel*la"ri*an (?), n. [L. procella a storm.] (Zool.) One of a family of oceanic birds (Procellaridæ) including the petrels, fulmars, and shearwaters. They are often seen in great abundance in stormy weather.

procellous.c: Procellous Pro*cel"lous (?), a. [L. procellosus, fr. procella a storm.] Stormy. [Obs.] Bailey.

procephalic.c: Procephalic Pro`ce*phal"ic (?), a. [Pref. pro- + cephalic.] (Zool.) Pertaining to, or forming, the front of the head.

proception.c: Proception Pro*cep"tion (?), n. [Pref. pro- + L. capere to take.] Preoccupation. [Obs.] Eikon Basilik?.

procere.c: Procere Pro*cere" (?), a. [L. procerus tall.] Of high stature; tall. [Obs.] Evelyn.

procerebrum.c: Procerebrum Pro*cer"e*brum (?), n. [Pref. pro- + cerebrum.] (Anat.) The prosencephalon.

proceres.c: Proceres ‖Proc"e*res (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. procer? chief.] (Zool.) An order of large birds; the Ratitæ; -- called also Proceri.

procerite.c: Procerite Proc"er*ite (?), n. [Pref. pro- + Gr.?? horn.] (Zool.) The segment next to the flagellum of the antennæ of Crustacea.

procerity.c: Procerity Pro*cer"i*ty (?), n. [L. proceritas.] Height of stature; tallness. [R.] Johnson.

process.c: Process Proc"ess, n. [F. procès, L. processus. See Proceed.]

Process plate Proc"ess plate. (a) A plate prepared by a mechanical process, esp. a photomechanical process. (b) A very slow photographic plate, giving good contrasts between high lights and shadows, used esp. for making lantern slides.

procession.c: Procession Pro*ces"sion (?), n. [F., fr. L. processio. See Proceed.]

Procession Pro*ces"sion, v. t. (Law) To ascertain, mark, and establish the boundary lines of, as lands. [Local, U. S. (North Carolina and Tennessee).] “To procession the lands of such persons as desire it.” Burrill.
Procession Pro*ces"sion, v. i. To march in procession. [R.]
Procession Pro*ces"sion, v. i. To honor with a procession. [R.]

processional.c: Processional Pro*ces"sion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a procession; consisting in a procession.

processionalist.c: Processionalist Pro*ces"sion*al*ist, n. One who goes or marches in a procession. [R.]

processionary.c: Processionary Pro*ces"sion*a*ry (?), a. [Cf. LL. processionarius, F. processionnaire.] Pertaining to a procession; consisting in processions; as, processionary service.

processioning.c: Processioning Pro*ces"sion*ing, n. A proceeding prescribed by statute for ascertaining and fixing the boundaries of land. See 2d Procession. [ Local, U. S.] Bouvier.

proces.c: Proces verbal ‖Pro`cès" ver`bal" (?). [ F.] (French Law) An authentic minute of an official act, or statement of facts.

prochein.c: Prochein Pro"chein (?), a. [F. prochain, fr. L. (assumed) proximanus, fr. proximus.] Next; nearest.

prochordal.c: Prochordal Pro*chor"dal (?), a. [Pref. pro + chordal.] (Anat.) Situated in front of the notochord; -- applied especially to parts of the cartilaginous rudiments in the base of the skull.

prochronism.c: Prochronism Pro"chro*nism (?), n. [Gr.? preceding in time;? before +? time: cf. F. prochronisme.] The dating of an event before the time it happened; an antedating; -- opposed to metachronism.

prochronize.c: Prochronize Pro"chro*nize (?), v. t. To antedate. Fitzed. Hall.

procidentia.c: Procidentia Procidence { Proc"i*dence, ‖Proc*i*den"ti*a (?), }, n. [L. procidentia, fr. procidens, p. pr. of procidere to fall down forward.] (Med.) A falling down; a prolapsus. [R.] Parr.

prociduous.c: Prociduous Pro*cid"u*ous (?), a. [ L. prociduus.] Falling from its proper place.

procinct.c: Procinct Pro*cinct" (?), n. [L. procinctus, fr. procingere, procinctum, to gird up.] A state of complete readiness for action. [Obs.] “War in procinct.” Milton.

proclaim.c: Proclaim Pro*claim" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Proclaimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Proclaiming.] [OE. proclamen, L. proclamare; pro before, forward + clamare to call or cry out: cf. F. proclamer. See Claim.]

proclamation.c: Proclamation Proc`la*ma"tion (?), n. [F. proclamation, L. proclamatio. See Proclaim.]

proclitic.c: Proclitic Pro*clit"ic (?), a. [Gr.? to lean forward;? forward +? to lean or incline. Cf. Enclitic.] (Gr. Gram.) Leaning forward; -- said of certain monosyllabic words which are so closely attached to the following word as not to have a separate accent.

proclive.c: Proclive Pro*clive" (?), a. [L. proclivis sloping, inclined; pro forward + clivus hill: cf. F. proclive. See Declivity, and cf. Proclivous.] Having a tendency by nature; prone; proclivous. [R.] Mrs. Browning.

proclivity.c: Proclivity Pro*cliv"i*ty (?), n. [L. proclivitas: cf. F. proclivité.]

procoele.c: Procoele Pro*cœle" (?), n. [Pref. pro + Gr.? hollow.] (Anat.) A lateral cavity of the prosencephalon; a lateral ventricle of the brain. B. G. Wilder.

procoelia.c: Procoelia ‖Pro*cœ"li*a (?), n.; pl. Procœliæ (?). [ NL.] (Anat.) Same as Procœle.
Procoelia ‖Pro*cœ"li*a, n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A division of Crocodilia, including the true crocodiles and alligators, in which the dorsal vertebræ are concave in front.

procoelian.c: Procoelian Pro*cœ"li*an (?), a. [See Procœle.] (Anat & Zool.) Concave in front; as, procœlian vertebræ, which have the anterior end of the centra concave and the posterior convex.
Procoelian Pro*cœ"li*an, n. (Zool.) A reptile having procœlian vertebræ; one of the Procœlia.

proconsul.c: Proconsul Pro*con"sul (?), n. [L., fr. pro for + consul consul.] (Rom. Antiq.) An officer who discharged the duties of a consul without being himself consul; a governor of, or a military commander in, a province. He was usually one who had previously been consul.

proconsulary.c: Proconsulary Proconsular { Pro*con"su*lar (?), Pro*con"su*la*ry (?), } a. [L. proconsularis: cf. F. proconsulaire.]

proconsulate.c: Proconsulate Pro*con"su*late (?), n. [L. proconsulatus: cf. F. proconsulat.] The office jurisdiction of a proconsul, or the term of his office.

procrastinate.c: Procrastinate Pro*cras"ti*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Procrastinated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Procrastinating.] [L. procrastinatus, p. p. of procrastinare to procrastinate; pro forward + crastinus of to-morrow, fr. cras to-morrow.] To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day; to defer; to postpone; to delay; as, to procrastinate repentance. Dr. H. More.
Procrastinate Pro*cras"ti*nate, v. i. To delay; to be dilatory.

procrastination.c: Procrastination Pro*cras`ti*na"tion (?), n. [L. procrastinatio: cf. F. procrastination.] The act or habit of procrastinating, or putting off to a future time; delay; dilatoriness.

procrastinator.c: Procrastinator Pro*cras"ti*na`tor (?), n. One who procrastinates, or defers the performance of anything.

procrastinatory.c: Procrastinatory Pro*cras"ti*na*to*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to procrastination; dilatory.

procreant.c: Procreant Pro"cre*ant (?), a. [L. procreans, p. pr. of procreare. See Procreate.] Generating; producing; productive; fruitful; assisting in procreation. [R.] “His pendent bed and procreant cradle.” Shak.
Procreant Pro"cre*ant, n. One who, or that which, procreates.

procreate.c: Procreate Pro"cre*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Procreated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Procreating.] [L. procreatus, p. p. of procreare; pro forward, forth + create to create.] To generate and produce; to beget; to engender.

procreation.c: Procreation Pro`cre*a"tion (?), n. [F. procréation, L, procreatio.] The act of begetting; generation and production of young. South.

procreative.c: Procreative Pro"cre*a`tive (?), a. Having the power to beget; generative. Sir M. Hale.

procreativeness.c: Procreativeness Pro"cre*a`tive*ness, n. The power of generating.

procreator.c: Procreator Pro"cre*a`tor (?), n. [L.] One who begets; a father or sire; a generator.

procris.c: Procris ‖Pro"cris (?), n. [L., the wife of Cephalus, Gr.?.] (Zool.) Any species of small moths of the genus Procris. The larvæ of some species injure the grapevine by feeding in groups upon the leaves.

procrustean.c: Procrustean Pro*crus"te*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Procrustes, or the mode of torture practiced by him; producing conformity by violent means; as, the Procrustean treatment; a Procrustean limit. See Procrustes.

procrusteanize.c: Procrusteanize Pro*crus"te*an*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Procrusteanized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Procrusteanizing (?).] To stretch or contract according to some rule or standard.

procrustes.c: Procrustes Pro*crus"tes (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to beat out, to stretch;? forward +? to strike.] (Gr. Antiq.) A celebrated legendary highwayman of Attica, who tied his victims upon an iron bed, and, as the case required, either stretched or cut of their legs to adapt them to its length; -- whence the metaphorical phrase, the bed of Procrustes.

proctitis.c: Proctitis ‖Proc*ti"tis (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? anus + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the rectum.

proctocele.c: Proctocele Proc"to*cele (?), n. [Gr.? anus +? tumor.] (Med.) Inversion and prolapse of the mucous coat of the rectum, from relaxation of the sphincter, with more or less swelling; prolapsus ani. Dunglison.

proctodaeum.c: Proctodaeum ‖Proc`to*dæ"um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? the anus +? to divide.] (Anat.) See Mesenteron.

proctor.c: Proctor Proc"tor (?), n. [OE. proketour, contr. fr. procurator. See Procurator.] One who is employed to manage to affairs of another. Specifically: (a) A person appointed to collect alms for those who could not go out to beg for themselves, as lepers, the bedridden, etc.; hence a beggar. [Obs.] Nares. (b) (Eng. Law) An officer employed in admiralty and ecclesiastical causes. He answers to an attorney at common law, or to a solicitor in equity. Wharton. (c) (Ch. of Eng.) A representative of the clergy in convocation. (d) An officer in a university or college whose duty it is to enforce obedience to the laws of the institution.
Proctor Proc"tor, v. t. To act as a proctor toward; to manage as an attorney or agent. Bp. Warburton.

proctorage.c: Proctorage Proc"tor*age (?), n. Management by a proctor, or as by a proctor; hence, control; superintendence; -- in contempt. “The fogging proctorage of money.” Milton.

proctorial.c: Proctorial Proc*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a proctor, esp. an academic proctor; magisterial.

proctorship.c: Proctorship Proc"tor*ship (?), n. The office or dignity of a proctor; also, the term of his office. Clarendon.

proctotomy.c: Proctotomy Proc*tot"o*my (?), n. [Gr.? anus +? to cut.] (Surg.) An incision into the rectum, as for the division of a stricture.

proctucha.c: Proctucha ‖Proc"tu*cha (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? anus +? to have.] (Zool.) (a) A division of Turbellaria including those that have an intestine terminating posteriorly. (b) The Nemertina.

procumbent.c: Procumbent Pro*cum"bent (?), a. [L. procumbens, -entis, p. pr. of procumbere to fall, bend, or lean forward; pro forward + cumbere (in comp.), akin to cubare to lie down: cf. F. procombant. Cf. Incumbent.]

procurable.c: Procurable Pro*cur"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being procured; obtainable. Boyle.

procuracy.c: Procuracy Proc"u*ra*cy (?), n.; pl. Procuracies (#). [LL. procuratia: cf. F. procuratie. See Procuration, and cf,. Proxy.]

procuration.c: Procuration Proc`u*ra"tion (?), n. [L. procuratio: cf. F. procuration. See Procure.]

procurator.c: Procurator Proc"u*ra`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. procurateur. See Procure, and cf. Proctor. ]

procuratorial.c: Procuratorial Proc`u*ra*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a procurator, or proctor; made by a proctor. Ayliffe.

procuratorship.c: Procuratorship Proc"u*ra`tor*ship (?), n. The office or term of a procurator. Bp. Pearson.

procuratory.c: Procuratory Pro*cu"ra*to*ry (?), a. [L. procuratorius.] Tending to, or authorizing, procuration.

procure.c: Procure Pro*cure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Procured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Procuring.] [F. procurer, L. procurare, procuratum, to take care of; pro for + curare to take care, fr. cura care. See Cure, and cf. Proctor, Proxy.]

procuress.c: Procuress Pro*cur"ess, n. A female procurer, or pander.

procyon.c: Procyon Pro"cy*on (?), n. [L., a constellation which rises before the Dog Star, Gr.?;? before +? a dog. ]

prod.c: Prod Prod (?), n. [Cf. Gael. & Ir. brod goad, prickle, sting, and E. brad, also W. procio to poke, thrust.]

Prod Prod, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prodded (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prodding.] To thrust some pointed instrument into; to prick with something sharp; as, to prod a soldier with a bayonet; to prod oxen; hence, to goad, to incite, to worry; as, to prod a student. H. Taylor.

prodd.c: Prodd Prodd (?), n. A crossbow. See Prod, 3.

prodigal.c: Prodigal Prod"i*gal (?), a. [L. prodigus, from prodigere to drive forth, to squander away; pro forward, forth + agere to drive; cf. F. prodigue. See Agent. ] Given to extravagant expenditure; expending money or other things without necessity; recklessly or viciously profuse; lavish; wasteful; not frugal or economical; as, a prodigal man; the prodigal son; prodigal giving; prodigal expenses.

Prodigal Prod"i*gal, n. One who expends money extravagantly, viciously, or without necessity; one that is profuse or lavish in any expenditure; a waster; a spendthrift. “Noble prodigals of life.” Trench.

prodigality.c: Prodigality Prod`i*gal"i*ty (?), n. [F. prodigalité, L. prodigalitas. See Prodigal.] Extravagance in expenditure, particularly of money; excessive liberality; profusion; waste; -- opposed to frugality, economy, and parsimony.“The prodigality of his wit.” Dryden.

prodigalize.c: Prodigalize Prod"i*gal*ize (?), v. i. To act as a prodigal; to spend liberally. Sherwood.
Prodigalize Prod"i*gal*ize, v. t. To expend lavishly. Ld. Lytton.

prodigally.c: Prodigally Prod"i*gal*ly, adv. In a prodigal manner; with profusion of expense; extravagantly; wasteful; profusely; lavishly; as, an estate prodigally dissipated.

prodigate.c: Prodigate Prod"i*gate (?), v. t. To squander. Thackeray.

prodigence.c: Prodigence Prod"i*gence (?), n. [L. prodigentia, fr. prodigens, p. pr. of prodigere. See Prodigal. ] Waste; profusion; prodigality. [R.] Bp. Hall.

prodigious.c: Prodigious Pro*di"gious (?), a. [L. prodigiosus, fr. prodigium a prodigy; cf. F. prodigieux. See Prodigy.]

prodigiousness.c: Prodigiousness Pro*di"gious*ness, n. The quality or state of being prodigious; the state of having qualities that excite wonder or astonishment; enormousness; vastness.

prodigy.c: Prodigy Prod"i*gy (?), n.; pl. Prodigies (#). [ L. prodigium; pro before + (perh.) a word appearing in adagium adage: cf. F. prodige. Cf. Adage. ]

prodition.c: Prodition Pro*di"tion (?), n. [L. proditio, from prodere to give forth, betray: cf. OF. prodition.] Disclosure; treachery; treason. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

prodromal.c: Prodromal Prod"ro*mal (?), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to prodromes; as, the prodromal stage of a disease.

prodrome.c: Prodrome Pro"drome (?), n. [Gr.? running before;? before +? to run: cf. F. prodrome.] 1. A forerunner; a precursor.

produce.c: Produce Pro*duce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Produced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Producing (?).] [L. producere, productum, to bring forward, beget, produce; pro forward, forth + ducere to lead. See Duke.]
Produce Pro*duce", v. i. To yield or furnish appropriate offspring, crops, effects, consequences, or results.

Produce Prod"uce (?; 277), n. That which is produced, brought forth, or yielded; product; yield; proceeds; result of labor, especially of agricultural labors; hence, specifically, agricultural products.
Produce race Prod"uce race. (Horse Racing) A race to be run by the produce of horses named or described at the time of entry.

producent.c: Producent Pro*du"cent (?), n. [L. producens, p. pr.] One who produces, or offers to notice. [Obs.] Ayliffe.

producers.c: Producer's goods Pro*duc"er's goods (?). (Polit. Econ.) Goods that satisfy wants only indirectly as factors in the production of other goods, such as tools and raw material; -- called also instrumental goods, auxiliary goods, intermediate goods, or goods of the second and higher orders, and disting. from consumers' goods.

Producer's rent Producer's surplus Producer's surplus. (Polit. Econ.) Any profit above the normal rate of interest and wages accruing to a producer on account of some monopoly (temporary or permanent) of the means or materials of production; -- called also Producer's rent.

producibility.c: Producibility Pro*du`ci*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being producible. Barrow.

producible.c: Producible Pro*du"ci*ble (?), a. Capable of being produced, brought forward, brought forth, generated, made, or extended. -- Pro*du"ci*ble*ness, n.

product.c: Product Prod"uct (?), n. [L. productus, p. pr. of producere. See Produce.]

productibility.c: Productibility Pro*duct`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state of being productible; producibility. Ruskin.

productible.c: Productible Pro*duct"i*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. productible.] Capable of being produced; producible.

productile.c: Productile Pro*duc"tile (?), a. [L. productilis, fr. producere to stretch out.] Capable of being extended or prolonged; extensible; ductile.

production.c: Production Pro*duc"tion (?), n. [L. productio a lengthening, prolonging: cf. F. production. See Produce. ]

productive.c: Productive Pro*duc"tive (?), a. [F. productif, L. productivus fit for prolongation.]

productivity.c: Productivity Pro`duc*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being productive; productiveness. Emerson.

productus.c: Productus ‖Pro*duc"tus (?), n. [NL. See Product.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of brachiopods, very characteristic of the Carboniferous rocks.

proeguminal.c: Proeguminal Pro`e*gu"mi*nal (?), a. [Gr.?, p. pr. of? to lead the way: cf. F. proégumène.] (Med.) Serving to predispose; predisposing; as, a proeguminal cause of disease.

proem.c: Proem Pro"em (?), n. [L. prooemium, Gr.?;? before +? way, course or strain of a song: cf. F. proème.] Preface; introduction; preliminary observations; prelude.
Proem Pro"em, v. t. To preface. [Obs.] South.

proembryo.c: Proembryo Pro*em"bry*o (?), n. [Pref. pro- + embryo. ] (Bot.) (a) The series of cells formed in the ovule of a flowering plant after fertilization, but before the formation of the embryo. (b) The primary growth from the spore in certain cryptogamous plants; as, the proembryo, or protonema, of mosses.

proemial.c: Proemial Pro*e"mi*al (?), a. Introductory; prefatory; preliminary. [R.] Hammond.

proemptosis.c: Proemptosis Pro`emp*to"sis (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? to fall in before;? before +? in +? to fall.] (Chron.) The addition of a day to the lunar calendar. [R.] See Metemptosis.

proface.c: Proface Pro"face (?), interj. [OF. prou face, prou fasse; prou profit + faire to make, do.] Much good may it do you! -- a familiar salutation or welcome. [Obs.]

profanation.c: Profanation Prof`a*na"tion (?), n. [L. profanatio: cf. F. profanation. See Profane, v. t.] 1. The act of violating sacred things, or of treating them with contempt or irreverence; irreverent or too familiar treatment or use of what is sacred; desecration; as, the profanation of the Sabbath; the profanation of a sanctuary; the profanation of the name of God.

profane.c: Profane Pro*fane" (?), a. [F., fr. L. profanus, properly, before the temple, i. e., without the temple, unholy; pro before + fanum temple. See 1st Fane.]
Profane Pro*fane", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Profaned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Profaning.] [L. profanare: cf. F. profaner. See Profane, a.]

profanely.c: Profanely Pro*fane"ly, adv. In a profane manner.

profaneness.c: Profaneness Pro*fane"ness, n. The quality or state of being profane; especially, the use of profane language.

profaner.c: Profaner Pro*fan"er (?), n. One who treats sacred things with irreverence, or defiles what is holy; one who uses profane language. Hooker.

profection.c: Profection Pro*fec"tion (?), n. [See Proficient.] A setting out; a going forward; advance; progression. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

profectitious.c: Profectitious Pro`fec*ti"tious (?), a. [L. profectitius, fr. proficisci to set out, proceed.] Proceeding from, as from a parent; derived, as from an ancestor. [R.]

profert.c: Profert Pro"fert (?), n. [L., he brings forward, 3d pers. pr. of proferre. See Proffer. ] (Law) The exhibition or production of a record or paper in open court, or an allegation that it is in court.

profess.c: Profess Pro*fess" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Professed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Professing.] [F. profès, masc., professe, fem., professed (monk or nun), L. professus, p. p. of profiteri to profess; pro before, forward + fateri to confess, own. See Confess.]
Profess Pro*fess" (pro*fĕs"), v. i. 1. To take a profession upon one's self by a public declaration; to confess. Drayton.

professed.c: Professed Pro*fessed" (?), a. Openly declared, avowed, acknowledged, or claimed; as, a professed foe; a professed tyrant; a professed Christian.

profession.c: Profession Pro*fes"sion (?), n. [F., fr. L. professio. See Profess, v.] 1. The act of professing or claiming; open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment; as, professions of friendship; a profession of faith.

professional.c: Professional Pro*fes"sion*al (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a profession, or calling; conforming to the rules or standards of a profession; following a profession; as, professional knowledge; professional conduct. “Pride, not personal, but professional.” Macaulay. “A professional sneerer.” De Quincey.
Professional Pro*fes"sion*al, n. A person who prosecutes anything professionally, or for a livelihood, and not in the character of an amateur; a professional worker.

professionalism.c: Professionalism Pro*fes"sion*al*ism (?), n. The following of a profession, sport, etc., as an occupation; -- opposed to amateurism.

professionally.c: Professionally Pro*fes"sion*al*ly, adv. In a professional manner or capacity; by profession or calling; in the exercise of one's profession; one employed professionally.

professor.c: Professor Pro*fess"or (?), n. [L., a teacher, a public teacher: cf. F. professeur. See Profess.] 1. One who professed, or makes open declaration of, his sentiments or opinions; especially, one who makes a public avowal of his belief in the Scriptures and his faith in Christ, and thus unites himself to the visible church. “Professors of religion.” Bacon.

professorial.c: Professorial Pro`fes*so"ri*al (?), a. [L. professorius: cf. F. professorial.] Of or pertaining to a professor; as, the professional chair; professional interest.

professorialism.c: Professorialism Pro`fes*so"ri*al*ism (?), n. The character, manners, or habits of a professor. [R.]

professoriate.c: Professoriate Pro`fes*so"ri*ate (?), n. 1. The body of professors, or the professorial staff, in a university or college.

professorship.c: Professorship Pro*fess"or*ship (?), n. The office or position of a professor, or public teacher. Walton.

professory.c: Professory Pro*fes"so*ry (?), a. [L. professorius.] Of or pertaining to a professor; professorial. [R.] Bacon.

proffer.c: Proffer Prof"fer (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Proffered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Proffering.] [OE. profren, proferen, F. proférer, fr. L. proferre to bring forth or forward, to offer; pro forward + ferre to bring. See Bear to produce.] 1. To offer for acceptance; to propose to give; to make a tender of; as, to proffer a gift; to proffer services; to proffer friendship. Shak.
Proffer Prof"fer, n. 1. An offer made; something proposed for acceptance by another; a tender; as, proffers of peace or friendship.

profferer.c: Profferer Prof"fer*er (?), n. One who proffers something.

proficiency.c: Proficiency Proficience { Pro*fi"cience (?), Pro*fi"cien*cy (?) }, n. The quality of state of being proficient; advance in the acquisition of any art, science, or knowledge; progression in knowledge; improvement; adeptness; as, to acquire proficiency in music.

proficient.c: Proficient Pro*fi"cient (?), n. [L. proficiens, -entis, p. pr. of proficere to go forward, make progress; pro forward + facere to make. See Fact, and cf. Profit, (?)] One who has made considerable advances in any business, art, science, or branch of learning; an expert; an adept; as, proficient in a trade; a proficient in mathematics, music, etc.
Proficient Pro*fi"cient (?), a. Well advanced in any branch of knowledge or skill; possessed of considerable acquirements; well-skilled; versed; adept,

proficiently.c: Proficiently Pro*fi"cient*ly, adv. In a proficient manner.

proficuous.c: Proficuous Pro*fic"u*ous (?), a. [L. proficuus.] Profitable; advantageous; useful. [Obs.] Harvey.

profile.c: Profile Pro"file (?), n. [It. profilo, fr. L. pro before + filum a thread, an outline, shape: cf. F. profil. See File arow, and cf. Purfle, Purl, a fringe.] 1. An outline, or contour; as, the profile of an apple.

Profile Pro"file, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Profiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Profiling] [Cf. F. profiler, It. profilare. See Profile, n.] 1. to draw the outline of; to draw in profile, as an architectural member.

profiling.c: Profiling Pro"fil*ing, n. (Fort.) In the construction of fieldworks, the erection at proper intervals of wooden profiles, to show to the workmen the sectional form of the parapets at those points.

profilist.c: Profilist Pro"fil*ist, n. One who takes profiles.

profit.c: Profit Pro"fit (?), n. [F., fr. L. profectus advance, progress, profit, fr. profectum. See Proficient.] 1. Acquisition beyond expenditure; excess of value received for producing, keeping, or selling, over cost; hence, pecuniary gain in any transaction or occupation; emolument; as, a profit on the sale of goods.

Profit Prof"it, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Profited; p. pr. & vb. n. Profiting.] [F. profiter. See Profit, n.] To be of service to; to be good to; to help on; to benefit; to advantage; to avail; to aid; as, truth profits all men.
Profit Prof"it, v. i. 1. To gain advantage; to make improvement; to improve; to gain; to advance.

profitable.c: Profitable Prof"it*a*ble (?), a. [F. profitable.] Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; helpful; advantageous; beneficial; as, a profitable trade; profitable business; a profitable study or profession.

profitless.c: Profitless Prof"it*less, a. Without profit; unprofitable. Shak.

profligacy.c: Profligacy Prof"li*ga*cy (?), n. [See Profligate, a.] The quality of state of being profligate; a profligate or very vicious course of life; a state of being abandoned in moral principle and in vice; dissoluteness.

profligate.c: Profligate Prof"li*gate (?), a. [L. profligatus, p. p. of profligare to strike or dash to the ground, to destroy; pro before + a word akin to fligere to strike. See Afflict.]
Profligate Prof"li*gate, n. An abandoned person; one openly and shamelessly vicious; a dissolute person. “Such a profligate as Antony.” Swift.
Profligate Prof"li*gate (?), v. t. To drive away; to overcome. [Obs.] Harvey.

profligately.c: Profligately Prof"li*gate*ly (?), adv. In a profligate manner.

profligateness.c: Profligateness Prof"li*gate*ness, n. The quality of being profligate; an abandoned course of life; profligacy.

profligation.c: Profligation Prof`li*ga"tion (?), n. [L. profligatio.] Defeat; rout; overthrow. [Obs.] Bacon.

profluence.c: Profluence Prof"lu*ence (?), n. [L. profluentia.] Quality of being profluent; course. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.

profluent.c: Profluent Prof"lu*ent (?), a. [L. profluens, p. pr. of profluere; pro forward + fluere to flow.] Flowing forward, [R.] “In the profluent stream.” Milton.

profound.c: Profound Pro*found", a. [F. profond, L. profundus; pro before, forward + fundus the bottom. See Found to establish, Bottom lowest part.] 1. Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to a great depth; deep. “A gulf profound.” Milton.
Profound Pro*found" (?), n. 1. The deep; the sea; the ocean.
Profound Pro*found", v. t. To cause to sink deeply; to cause to dive or penetrate far down. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Profound Pro*found", v. i. To dive deeply; to penetrate. [Obs.]

profoundly.c: Profoundly Pro*found"ly, adv. In a profound manner.

profoundness.c: Profoundness Pro*found"ness, n. The quality or state of being profound; profundity; depth. Hooker.

profulgent.c: Profulgent Pro*ful"gent (?), a. [Pref. pro- + L. fulgere to shine.] Shining forth; brilliant; effulgent. [Obs.] “Profulgent in preciousness.” Chaucer.

profundity.c: Profundity Pro*fun"di*ty (?), n.; pl. -ties (#). [L. profunditas: cf. F. profondite. See Profound.] The quality or state of being profound; depth of place, knowledge, feeling, etc. “The vast profundity obscure.” Milton.

profuse.c: Profuse Pro*fuse" (?), a. [L. profusus, p. p. of profundere to pour forth or out; pro forward, forth + fundere to pour: cf. F. profus. See Fuse to melt.] 1. Pouring forth with fullness or exuberance; bountiful; exceedingly liberal; giving without stint; as, a profuse government; profuse hospitality.
Profuse Pro*fuse" (?), v. t. To pour out; to give or spend liberally; to lavish; to squander. [Obs.] Chapman.

profusely.c: Profusely Pro*fuse"ly (?), adv. In a profuse manner.

profusion.c: Profusion Pro*fu"sion (?), n. [L. profusio: cf. F. profusion.]

prog.c: Prog Prog (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Progged (?). p. pr. & vb. n. Progging.] [Cf. D. prachen, G. prachern, Dan. prakke, Sw. pracka, to beg, L. procare, procari, to ask, demand, and E. prowl.] 1. To wander about and beg; to seek food or other supplies by low arts; to seek for advantage by mean shift or tricks. [Low]
Prog Prog, n. 1. Victuals got by begging, or vagrancy; victuals of any kind; food; supplies. [Slang] Swift.

progenerate.c: Progenerate Pro*gen"er*ate (?), v. t. [L. progeneratus, p. p. of progenerare to beget; pro forth, forward + generare to generate.] To beget; to generate; to produce; to procreate; as, to progenerate a race. [R.] Landor.

progeneration.c: Progeneration Pro*gen`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. progeneratio.] The act of begetting; propagation. [R.]

progenitor.c: Progenitor Pro*gen"i*tor (?), n. [OF. progeniteur, L. progenitor, fr. progignere, progenitum, to bring forth, to beget; pro forth + gignere to beget. See Gender kind.] An ancestor in the direct line; a forefather.

progenitorship.c: Progenitorship Pro*gen"i*tor*ship, n. The state of being a progenitor.

progeniture.c: Progeniture Pro*gen"i*ture (?), n. [F. progéniture.] A begetting, or birth. [R.]

progeny.c: Progeny Prog"e*ny (prŏj"e*ny̆), n. [OE. progenie, F. progénie, fr. L. progenies, fr. progignere. See Progenitor.] Descendants of the human kind, or offspring of other animals; children; offspring; race, lineage. “ Issued from the progeny of kings.” Shak.

proglottis.c: Proglottis ‖Pro*glot"tis (?), n.; pl. Proglottides (#). [NL. fr. Gr. proglwtti`s the tip of the tongue; pro` forward + glw^tta the tongue.] (Zool) One of the free, or nearly free, segments of a tapeworm. It contains both male and female reproductive organs, and is capable of a brief independent existence.

prognathi.c: Prognathi ‖Prog"na*thi (prŏg"nȧ*thī), n. pl. [NL. See Prognathous.] (Zool) A comprehensive group of mankind, including those that have prognathous jaws.

prognathism.c: Prognathism Prog"na*thism (prŏg"nȧ*thĭz'm or prŏg*nā"thĭz'm), n. (Anat.) Projection of the jaws. -- Prog"na*thy (#), n.

prognathous.c: Prognathous Prog"na*thous (prŏg"nȧ*thŭs), a. [Gr. pro` before + gna`qos the jaw] (Anat.) Having the jaws projecting beyond the upper part of the face; -- opposed to orthognathous. See Gnathic index, under Gnathic.

progne.c: Progne Prog"ne (prŏg"ne), n. [L., a swallow, traditionally said to be fr. Progne (The sister of Philomela), who was changed into a swallow, Gr. Pro`knh.] (Zool.) (a) A swallow. (b) A genus of swallows including the purple martin. See Martin. (c) An American butterfly (Polygonia Progne syn. Vanessa Progne). It is orange and black above, grayish beneath, with an L-shaped silver mark on the hind wings. Called also gray comma.

prognosis.c: Prognosis Prog*no"sis (prŏg*nō"sĭs), n. [L., fr. Gr. pro`gnosis, fr. progignw`skein to know beforehand; pro` before + gignw`skein to know. See Know.] (Med.) The act or art of foretelling the course and termination of a disease; also, the outlook afforded by this act of judgment; as, the prognosis of hydrophobia is bad.

prognostic.c: Prognostic Prog*nos"tic (?), a. [Gr. prognwstiko`n. See Prognosis.] Indicating something future by signs or symptoms; foreshowing; aiding in prognosis; as, the prognostic symptoms of a disease; prognostic signs.
Prognostic Prog*nos"tic, n. [L. prognosticum, Gr.?: cf. F. pronostic, prognostic. See Prognostic, a.]

prognosticable.c: Prognosticable Prog*nos"tic*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being prognosticated or foretold. Sir T. Browne.

prognosticate.c: Prognosticate Prog*nos"ti*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Prognosticated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Prognosticating.] [See Prognostic.] To indicate as future; to foretell from signs or symptoms; to prophesy; to foreshow; to predict; as, to prognosticate evil. Burke.

prognosticator.c: Prognosticator Prog*nos"ti*ca`tor (?), n. One who prognosticates; a foreknower or foreteller of a future course or event by present signs. Isa. xlvii. 13.

programma.c: Programma ‖Pro*gram"ma (?), n.; pl. Programmata (#). [ L. See Programme.]

programme.c: Programme Pro"gramme (?), n. [L. programma a public proclamation, manifesto, Gr. pro`gramma, fr. progra`fein to write before or in public; pro` before, forth + gra`fein to write; cf. F. programme. See Graphic.] That which is written or printed as a public notice or advertisement; a scheme; a prospectus; especially, a brief outline or explanation of the order to be pursued, or the subjects embraced, in any public exercise, performance, or entertainment; a preliminary sketch.

progress.c: Progress Prog"ress (?; 277), n. [L. progressus, from progredi, p. p. progressus, to go forth or forward; pro forward + gradi to step, go: cf. F. progrès. See Grade.]
Progress Pro*gress" (?; formerly pronounced like Progress, n.), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Progressed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Progressing.]
Progress Prog"ress (?; see Progress, v. i.), v. t. To make progress in; to pass through. [Obs.] Milton.

progression.c: Progression Pro*gres"sion (?), n. [L. progressio: cf. F. progression.]

progressional.c: Progressional Pro*gres"sion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to progression; tending to, or capable of, progress.

progressist.c: Progressist Prog"ress*ist (?), n. One who makes, or holds to, progress; a progressionist.

progressive.c: Progressive party Progressive party. (U. S.
